US Orchestra Drops Kremlin-Linked Russian Violinist Vadim Repin After Ukraine Steps In
The Annapolis Symphony Orchestra (ASO) in Maryland has canceled planned performances with Russian violinist Vadim Repin, who has participated in Kremlin-backed cultural events and received Russian state support.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to the Annapolis Symphony Orchestra on September 4, Repin had been scheduled to perform Dmitri Shostakovich’s Violin Concerto No. 1 at Maryland Hall on November 6 and 7. The orchestra described the decision to cancel the collaboration as mutual.
“ASO and Mr. Repin have concluded that the current circumstances are not conducive to a successful collaboration, nor are they in the best interests of ASO patrons, for whom the uninterrupted enjoyment of live music remains the highest priority,” the orchestra said.
The decision followed an appeal from the Ukrainian Embassy in the United States, which had urged the orchestra in late August to remove Repin from the concerts, citing his participation in Russian state-backed cultural initiatives.
Ukraine’s Embassy welcomed the cancellation, arguing that Moscow uses cultural diplomacy as an element of its international influence campaign.
“Russia uses cultural diplomacy as part of its soft power to whitewash the image of a country that continues to kill innocent Ukrainians every day with missile and drone attacks,” Ukraine’s chargé d’affaires in the US, Denys Senik, said.
“We are grateful to everyone who helped draw attention to this issue and to the importance of supporting Ukraine as it works to bring a just and lasting peace closer,” he added.
Repin received the title of People’s Artist of Russia from Russian leader Vladimir Putin in April 2022. In subsequent years, the violinist participated in official Russian cultural events, including performances connected to the Russian military.
In February 2024, Repin performed with the State Kremlin Orchestra at an event organized with support from a Kremlin-linked foundation for Russia’s Defender of the Fatherland Day. His arts foundation has also received financial support from Russia’s Presidential Fund for Cultural Initiatives.
The Annapolis concerts are not the first Repin performances to be canceled following objections over his links to Russian state institutions. Orchestras in Mannheim, Germany; Budapest, Hungary; and Palm Beach, Florida, have previously dropped planned appearances by the violinist.
The move marks a reversal from September 3, when the ASO said it planned to proceed with Repin’s performances after reviewing his public record.

JP Aerospace teases airship-launched hypersonic concept
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
09:50:05 UTC
18:50:05 KST

- JP Aerospace released concept images of a vehicle called Hazel being launched from a high-altitude airship called SuperTandem, describing them as stills from an upcoming video.
- The volunteer-run group's most confirmed achievement remains a 2011 airship flight to 95,085 feet, and no Hazel test vehicle has been reported as built or flown.
JP Aerospace, a volunteer-run organization that has spent decades pursuing an unconventional path to orbit using airships instead of rockets, has released still images from an upcoming concept video showing a vehicle it calls Hazel being launched from a high-altitude airship called SuperTandem.
The images, shared by JP Aerospace president John Powell, show an animated rendering of a dark, wing-shaped aircraft dropping away from twin balloons connected by a long truss structure. Powell described the images as “stills from the upcoming Hazel video,” making clear the material is a computer-generated concept rather than footage of an actual flight or test.
JP Aerospace calls itself “America’s Other Space Program” and has operated as an all-volunteer nonprofit for more than four decades under Powell’s leadership. The group’s long-term goal, known as the Airship to Orbit program, envisions reaching space through a series of lighter-than-air vehicles rather than conventional rockets: a stratospheric airship would carry people and cargo to a high-altitude platform the group calls a Dark Sky Station, which would then serve as a staging point for a much larger airship designed to slowly accelerate to orbital velocity over several days using electric propulsion.
The organization’s most notable confirmed achievement to date came in October 2011, when its Tandem airship, an earlier twin-balloon design connected by a 30-foot carbon fiber truss, reached an altitude of 95,085 feet over Nevada’s Black Rock Desert, a record for airships at the time. Powell said at the time that the program had spent roughly $30,000 developing that vehicle over five years, a fraction of what major aerospace companies typically spend pursuing new launch concepts.
JP Aerospace has also flown roughly two hundred smaller research and student-payload missions using balloons and small rockets, including its long-running PongSat program, which has carried student science experiments to high altitude.
Beyond the 2011 Tandem flight, JP Aerospace has not publicly confirmed building or flight-testing any of the larger orbital-class airships central to its long-term plan, and no hypersonic test vehicle matching the description of Hazel has previously been reported as flown. The concept images released this week do not establish a timeline for when, or whether, a physical Hazel vehicle will be built or tested, and JP Aerospace has not disclosed technical specifications, funding sources, or a launch date for the concept shown in the video.

Netanyahu accused of 'slow response' on 7 October amid elections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06

Breadcrumb
Netanyahu accused of 'slow response' to 7 October attack ahead of Israeli election
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu was slow to respond to alerts from Israel's security apparatus of Hamas' 7 October attack, a report from Israel's Channel 12 said on Friday, as Israel's opposition continues to criticise his conduct during the day.
Netanyahu was reportedly alerted to the attack at 6.29 am, according to the Channel 12 report.
However, he failed to contact Israeli army chief of staff Herzi Halevi or Shin Bet head Ronen Bar between then and arriving at the Kirya, Israel's central military hub, at 9 am.
A source said that though the Prime Minister's Office unpublished diaries marked his arrival at 9, his actual arrival time was at 9.30. This is in contradiction to Netanyahu's own account, which he made on Thursday, saying that he arrived at the hub at 8 am.
Netanyahu also laid blame on Israel's security chiefs for not waking him up to share news of a Hamas attack, saying he would have immediately mobilised Israel's military, despite the C12 report saying he was woken up at 6.29.
This is in contrast to former defence minister Yoav Gallant, who arrived at Kirya at 7.30 after being alerted. Gallant lives farther from Kirya than Netanyahu.
Ahead of Israel's October election there have been accusations and recriminations between the government and the opposition over responsibility to prevent the October 7 2023 Hamas attack.
Netanyahu has continuously denied calls for a state commission of inquiry into the events of the day that would determine how the attack played out and offer recommendations on personal culpability.
As part of that election sparring, on Wednesday Netanyahu's biggest challenger, former general and leader of the Yashar party Gadi Eisenkot bought up another incident in which the current premier was reportedly slow to respond.
He claimed that he was unable to reach Netanyahu for two hours following the shootdown of an Israeli jet by Syrian anti-aircraft fire in 2018.
In comments made at a Yedioth Ahronoth conference, Eisenkot said that the downing was a "very serious incident."
"I sought to update and consult with the prime minister, but I could not reach him for an hour or two," he said, adding that he decided to destroy Syrian air defence batteries without consulting Netanyahu.
He also accused Netanyahu of culpability over 7 October, claiming that the Prime Minister's office receives regular intelligence, including that which is given to heads of the Israeli army and Shin Bet.
"He should ask himself how he built an environment that does not update him on important information, and he can blame himself for why he wasn't updated."
Netanyahu's long-time right-wing opponent Naftali Bennett also joined the pile in on the Israeli premier, accusing him of spreading a "blood libel" as part of his electioneering over his claims against Israel's security agencies.
"In Netanyahu's blood libel, spreading lies and making the security bodies into the enemy in an effort to cleanse him from direct responsibility for October 7 is a kosher and legitimate action," he said, according to the Times of Israel.
Israel's election is gearing up to be a close race, with recent polling from Channel 13 showing both the far-right coalition led by Netanyahu and Eisenkot's opposition bloc at 53 seats each in the Knesset. Palestinian parties, which make up the joint Hadash-Ta'al-Balad list and Ra'am, make up the remaining 14 seats.

The Best Gaming Chairs (2026): Are They Worth It?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
09:45:00 UTC
18:45:00 KST

The best gaming chairs will be different from person to person. It boils down to the one that you prefer based on your own priorities and sitting styles, but gaming chairs can sometimes fall into the trap of focusing on gamer aesthetics and gimmicks over comfort. There are, however, a few that avoid this pitfall. As I continue the hunt for gaming chairs that don't suck, here are a few picks I've tested that are a good place to start.
Whether you get in some gaming sessions between work and the gym, or you play from 5 on Friday to 11 on Sunday, we've got a recommendation for you here.
The Branch Ergonomic Chair Pro is our favorite office chair, and it's also my favorite gaming chair. As it turns, out a comfortable and reliable design is ideal regardless of the use case. The real “gaming” piece boils down to aesthetics. And now, this chair is available in three different Sega-branded styles, all of which are super comfortable and adjustable. Assembly wasn't too difficult, and the chair isn't too fiddly to get dialed in, though there definitely is a learning curve when it comes to all the different knobs.
Each of the designs is both fun and attractive, and that the chair offers incredible value for the price. The Sonic version has a mesh back, while the Sega Genesis and Sega Dreamcast versions have leather backs. I didn't find the leather-backed version that I tested to be too sweaty. All the little details of the designs pop, and it's hard to find a better gaming chair for the money. I like that I can always lean back and “have a think” when I'm staring at a blank text field or waiting for my Discord friends to get back to the mic. As a 5'1" woman, I do wish this chair got just a little bit lower to the ground, which is a bit ironic considering that Branch sells an optional Tall Cylinder for people above 6 feet tall. I also found the headrest pretty much useless. But again, for the price, and for your health, good luck getting more value. If you're locking in for hours and hours, this chair can help you do it more safely.
The Razer Iskur V2 Newgen is comfortable and stylish. It definitely feels like a “gaming” chair more than an office chair, with thick foam padding and an aesthetic that serves more “Twitch streamer” than “white-collar employee.” It isn't as breathable as I want it to be, and while the phase-change material keeps me relatively cool, it does get a little warm during long gaming sessions, especially if my house is already hot. This sentiment was echoed by my fellow chair tester Julian Chokkattu. It's not a dealbreaker for me, but if you run hot, it may not be ideal.
What I really love about this chair is its adaptive lumbar support, which can be dialed in using a know on the side, and its back tilt and wide seat. I can sit cross-legged or put up one foot with no issues. I wish the seat were a little deeper, though, and the pillow-like headrest is admittedly silly. I'll also flag that my cat is seemingly obsessed with trying to scratch the backrest. But the full reclining action is so good that I wanted to keep this chair around for long-term testing, so now I just pop a blanket over the back.
The Embody is taking me a long time to get used to. After my week of testing, it feels a bit slippery and stiff. It even creaks here and there. I try not to read other testimonials about products before I form my own opinions, but for a chair this expensive, I thought I must have been missing something. Many people across the Internet say that this chair requires a break-in period, so I'm trusting the process.
WIRED's own Julian Chokkattu tells me that it'll be worth my patience. And I can objectively see how it could be a great chair, with eye-catching aesthetics, memory foam cushions with copper infusion to keep you cool, and active support points to accommodate however you like to sit. So I'm sticking it out, making this my primary chair of choice for the next few weeks, and will update this accordingly once the chair has been fully assessed. But my very smart colleagues like the non-gaming version of this chair which is very similar, so I can't imagine I'll feel too differently. And so far I do like it—just not quite as much as the other two in this guide, at least not yet. Fortunately, it comes fully assembled and the back conforms to my spine for excellent counter-pressure. I hope once it's more broken in that this chair will meet my expectations.
The best way to get comfortable and to sit ergonomically is to have the option for a lot of adjustments. You want to be able to tweak and dial in the armrests, seat height and depth, level of lumbar support, and seat tilt and recline. A good chair should feel seamless and supportive. Adequate ventilation and cooling are also important, especially if you game for hours at a time.

Russia keeps building Su-34 fighter-bombers despite Ukraine war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
09:39:56 UTC
18:39:56 KST

- A newly built Su-34 fighter-bomber in factory primer was photographed at an air show in Novosibirsk, where the jet is manufactured.
- Russia had received 212 Su-34s by early 2026, including 18 delivered in 2025, continuing steady production despite the ongoing war in Ukraine.
Photos taken at an air show in Novosibirsk captured a newly built Su-34 fighter-bomber still in factory gray primer, adding to a steady stream of the twin-seat jets Russia has produced for its air force even as it continues fighting in Ukraine.
The aircraft was spotted at Mochishche Aerodrome in Novosibirsk during the 15th annual Viva Avia air festival, held August 1 and 2 to mark the 110th anniversary of Russian naval aviation and the 95th anniversary of Russia’s military transport aviation branch. The jet was built at the Novosibirsk Aviation Plant, known as NAZ or NAPO, the sole manufacturer of the Su-34 and part of Russia’s United Aircraft Corporation.
By the start of 2026, Russia’s air force had received a total of 212 Su-34s built at the Novosibirsk plant, including seven prototype and pre-production aircraft, according to available production figures. The plant delivered 16 production aircraft in 2024 and 18 more in 2025, a pace that has held roughly steady over the past several years despite Western sanctions targeting Russia’s defense industry.
Oryx, an open-source group that tracks visually confirmed military equipment losses in the war, has documented 43 Su-34s destroyed since Russia’s full-scale invasion began in February 2022, a figure that covers only losses supported by photographic or video evidence and likely understates the true total. At roughly 18 to 20 new aircraft a year, Russia’s current production pace has been running behind the confirmed combat loss rate for extended stretches of the war, according to open-source trackers.
The Su-34, known to NATO by the reporting name Fullback, is a twin-engine, two-seat fighter-bomber that replaced the older Su-24 in Russian service. It was formally accepted into the Russian military’s inventory in March 2014, following a program that traces back to a Soviet-era design contract signed in 1989. The aircraft carries a Sh141 phased-array radar, an L-150 Pastel radar warning receiver, and 12 hardpoints for weapons, and it can refuel in flight and operate from airfields without ground support equipment thanks to an onboard auxiliary power unit.
Production has continued through a series of contracts rather than one long-running deal. Russia’s defense ministry ordered 32 Su-34s in 2008, all delivered by 2013, followed by a second contract for 92 more aircraft due by 2020. A further order for 20 aircraft with upgraded electronic warfare equipment followed in 2020, and Russian media reported in prior years that at least 76 more Su-34s, upgraded under the Su-34M designation with new electronics and precision weapons carried in underwing pods, were expected to be delivered by 2027.
Russia has used the Su-34 extensively during its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, employing it to drop glide bombs on Ukrainian positions and cities from standoff ranges that keep the aircraft largely outside the reach of Ukrainian air defenses. The aircraft’s continued production, even in wartime, has made it one of the more closely tracked programs in open-source assessments of Russia’s defense industrial output.

Indonesia volcano eruptions cancels hundreds of flights in major airport hub
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Indonesia volcano eruption cancels hundreds of flights in major airport hub
A volcano eruption in Indonesia on Sunday has forced the cancellation of all flights at the capital city's airport as volcanic ash drifted across the western parts of the country.
No casualties were reported and no evacuation orders were issued as the nearest settlement is more than 10 miles away, but authorities warned people to stay at least 2 miles clear of the crater.
Footage filmed from a fishing boat at sea showed lava shooting up from the volcano into the air.
Indonesia's Geological Agency said the volcanic island located in Indonesia's Sunda Strait between the main Java and Sumatra islands had showed signs of activity since Friday before erupting for 30 seconds in the early hours of Sunday.
Volcanic ash spread across parts of Jakarta and Lampung province on Sumatra's southern tip, Indonesia's Center for Volcanology and Geological Hazard Mitigation said.
AirNav Indonesia closed airspace around Soekarno-Hatta and Halim Perdanakusuma airports in Jakarta, as well as four other airports, including Radin Inten II Airport in Lampung, because of volcanic ash.
By mid-afternoon local time in Jakarta, the closure had affected 516 flight movements, with 202 in Jakarta's Soekarno-Hatta airport alone that affected about 22,800 passengers, on Sunday.
"Safety remains our top priority in every operational decision," Lukman F. Laisa, Ministry of Transportation director general of civil aviation, said in a statement.
He warned flight schedules could face cascading disruptions affecting aircraft rotations, fleet availability and terminal capacity as airlines work to restore operations.
The name of the volcano Anak Krakatau, means "child of Krakatau," which is the offspring of the famous Krakatau, whose monumental 1883 eruption triggered a period of global cooling.
The eruption caused a tsunami in 2018 that killed at least 430 people in Sumatra and Java. Researchers believe volcanic activity triggered an underwater landslide and caused a large chunk of Anak Krakatau's southwest slope to collapse and displace a large volume of water. Scientists said Anak Krakatau island was only about a quarter of its original size after that eruption.

Taiwan seeks repeat U18 Asian baseball title at Taipei Dome
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
09:35:12 UTC
18:35:12 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan will open its title defense against South Korea on Monday as the 14th U18 Asian Baseball Championship gets underway in Taipei.
The tournament will run from Sept. 7 to 13 at Tianmu Baseball Stadium in Taipei and Xinzhuang Baseball Stadium in New Taipei. The Super Round and medal games will move to the Taipei Dome, where the championship game will become the first international U18 baseball final played at the venue, per a press release.
Taiwan enters the tournament with what local baseball analysts have described as one of its strongest U18 squads in recent years, featuring several players considered professional or overseas prospects.
The 18-player roster consists of seven pitchers, two catchers, five infielders, and four outfielders. Leading players include infielder Chen Po-kai (陳柏凱), selected first overall by the Fubon Guardians in this year’s Chinese Professional Baseball League draft, and left-handed pitcher Liu Jen-yu (劉任右), per TTV.
Chen signed with the Guardians last month for a record NT$6.5 million (US$203,000) signing bonus. Liu is among several Taiwanese pitchers attracting attention from overseas scouts.
Taiwan manager Yang Hsiao-cheng (楊孝承) has prepared the team for nearly two months. The squad played a series of internal games before the final roster was selected and attended a training camp in Okinawa before returning to Taiwan on Wednesday.
Taiwan will face South Korea at 6:30 p.m. Monday at Tianmu Baseball Stadium.
South Korea has also brought a highly regarded group of prospects. Left-handed pitcher Ha Hyun-seung is among its leading players, while 18-year-old two-way player Eom Jun-sang reportedly received a US$1.5 million signing bonus after opting out of the Korean professional baseball draft.
Eight teams are divided into two groups. Taiwan, South Korea, Singapore, and Thailand are in Group B, while Japan, Hong Kong, the Philippines, and Sri Lanka make up Group A. The top two teams from each group will advance to the Super Round, per RTI.
Taiwan is seeking its second consecutive title after defeating Japan 6-1 in the 2024 championship game. That victory ended a 17-year title drought and gave Taiwan its third championship, following victories in 2001 and 2007.
The top three teams in Taipei will qualify for the 2027 U18 Baseball World Cup, per the press release.

US labor leaders visit Taiwan to deepen cooperation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
09:34:58 UTC
18:34:58 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Leaders of US labor unions and organizations visited Taiwan last week to deepen cooperation with their Taiwanese counterparts.
Deputy Labor Minister Huang Ling-na (黃玲娜) said the US is an important global partner for Taiwan during a meeting with the delegation last Monday, according to the labor ministry.
Taiwan and the US share values such as democracy, freedom, and human rights and have maintained close exchanges and cooperation on labor issues, Huang said.
The ministry has invited US union leaders to visit Taiwan every two years since 2013. Huang expressed hope that the latest exchange would further expand Taiwan-US labor cooperation.
The ministry and delegation discussed legislation regulating delivery platforms and the impact of artificial intelligence on workers.
The visitors also attended a Taiwan-US labor union forum, where they exchanged views with Taiwanese union representatives on labor relations and union practices. Topics included labor-management negotiations, monitoring labor rights and regulatory compliance in global supply chains, and current US labor relations practices.
The delegation visited Taiwanese labor organizations including the Chunghwa Telecom Workers’ Union, the ROC International Airport Union Federation, and the Taiwan Nurses Union.
The visits allowed delegates to gain a deeper understanding of Taiwan’s labor movement and working environment while fostering continued cooperation on shared labor issues, the ministry said.

Ukrainian drones took Ryazan’s blending unit after knocking out two of its four crude units
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
09:32:01 UTC
18:32:01 KST

Ukrainian drones struck the Ryazan oil refinery in Russia on the morning of 6 September and set one of its core units on fire, Ukrainian defense outlet Militarnyi reported. The unit produces the high-octane component the Rosneft plant needs for its higher grades of gasoline. Russian regional authorities acknowledged a fire without naming the site. Ryazan is situated southeast of Moscow, about 470 km from Ukraine.
What burned at Ryazan
Drones hit the low-temperature isomerization unit for pentane-hexane fractions, designated Izomalk-2-LIN-800, according to Militarnyi's analysis. The unit sits on the refinery's grounds and is one of the critically important links in the plant's production cycle.
It converts low-octane straight-run oil fractions into a cleaner high-octane blending component. That component is what allows the refinery to produce gasolines of the higher environmental classes, Euro-5 among them, without adding harmful additives.
Ukrainian monitoring channel Exilenova+ published videos of the strike.
The same unit was hit in December
Drones already attacked this unit in December 2025 and damaged it. Earlier waves targeted the plant's ELOU-AVT-3, ELOU-AVT-6, and AVT-1 units.
By May 2026 the refinery had lost 90–100% of its refining capacity. Satellite imagery from 3 August 2026 showed Ukraine's Defense Forces had disabled two of the four crude distillation units on site.
Ukrainian drones struck the refinery in May, and FP-1 drones set it and a nearby warehouse burning in July.
Russian officials report a fire, not a target
Ryazan Oblast governor Pavel Malkov confirmed the region came under drone attack. Drone debris damaged residential buildings in Ryazan and Sapozhkovsky district, he stated, and a fire broke out at an enterprise he did not name. He said there were no casualties and that emergency services were working.
Russian news Telegram channel Astra said its analysis of photographs taken by residents established that the fire was on the grounds of the Ryazan refinery. Ukrainian channel Exilenova+, which tracks such attacks, also reported a hit on the plant.
Russia's fuel squeeze
Ukraine's General Staff said strikes on 26 August and 1 September fully stopped two large refining enterprises: Lukoil-Nizhegorodnefteorgsintez in Kstovo, Nizhny Novgorod Oblast, and the Novatek-Ust-Luga complex in Leningrad Oblast. Both supply the Russian army.
Short of gasoline, Russia has been buying more fuel abroad. Moscow discussed importing gasoline from Kazakhstan in June, and a Kazakh refinery deal would cover 0.3% of Russian demand. Belarus increased its gasoline supplies to Russia nearly 20-fold in the first half of the year.

High-speed rail links two major revolutionary sites of China's Long March
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
17:31:39 CST
18:31:39 KST

Crew members of the train G3998 pose for a group photo at Ruijin Station in Ruijin, east China's Jiangxi Province, Sept. 6, 2026. With the departure of high-speed train G3998 from Ruijin Station heading for Yan'an on Sunday morning, the two sacred revolutionary sites were directly linked by high-speed rail service for the first time. This year marks the 90th anniversary of the victory of the Central Red Army's Long March. Ruijin and Yan'an, serving as the starting point of the Long March and the revolutionary heartland of the Communist Party of China after the Long March, are located in east and northwest China, respectively. (Xinhua/Shao Rui)
NANCHANG, Sept. 6 (Xinhua) -- With the departure of high-speed train G3998 from Ruijin Station heading for Yan'an on Sunday morning, the two sacred revolutionary sites were directly linked by high-speed rail service for the first time.
This year marks the 90th anniversary of the victory of the Central Red Army's Long March. Ruijin and Yan'an, serving as the starting point of the Long March and the revolutionary heartland of the Communist Party of China after the Long March, are located in east and northwest China, respectively.
The new train service is the first direct high-speed rail link between the two cities, covering 1,857 kilometers at a maximum operating speed of 300 km per hour, with the full journey taking about 11 hours. It serves as a vital artery connecting eastern China with the city clusters in the northwest, with a host of red landmarks and key cities on the route, including Ruijin, Yudu, Nanchang, Wuhan, Xi'an and Yan'an.
For a long time, no direct train or flight connected the two relatively remote cities, requiring passengers to transfer at least twice in Nanchang, Wuhan, Xi'an or other cities, with the entire journey taking 16 to 22 hours.
In recent years, several high-speed railways, including the Nanchang-Ganzhou, Xi'an-Yan'an, and Xi'an-Shiyan lines, have been put into operation, significantly shortening the distance between northwest and east China. With increasingly close exchanges between the old revolutionary bases in southern Jiangxi and northern Shaanxi, such as red-themed study tours, Party-related exchanges, family visits and business travel, the demand for point-to-point direct services has been rising steadily, according to China Railway Nanchang Group Co., Ltd.
In response, the railway authority optimized transport capacity deployment and opened the direct service between Ruijin and Yan'an.
Wang Tao, a researcher at the China Executive Leadership Academy, Yan'an, said, "From Ruijin to Yan'an, the Central Red Army once trekked 25,000 li (12,500 kilometers) on the Long March, braving countless hardships and perils. Today, a high-speed link in the high-tech era connects the two points."
Song Xuelin, deputy director of the development and reform commission of Ruijin City, said that the direct high-speed rail link has not only shortened the distance between the two cities, but also built an important passage for economic connectivity.
It will boost the development of cultural tourism and agriculture along the route, fueling the high-quality development and common prosperity of the old revolutionary base areas, Song said. ■

Ukraine receives first RCH 155 howitzers after years of delay
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
09:30:10 UTC
18:30:10 KST

- German Aid to Ukraine confirmed the first delivery of RCH 155 wheeled howitzers to Ukraine, four years after Germany pledged 54 of the systems in 2022.
- The €890 million ($1.03 billion) program combines a 155mm gun system with the GTK Boxer chassis and can fire out to roughly 70 kilometers.
Ukraine has received its first RCH 155 wheeled howitzers, according to German Aid to Ukraine (GAU), an independent tracker of military assistance to Ukraine, which said September 5 it had confirmed the delivery through a source outside political and industry circles.
The system arrives roughly four years after Germany first pledged it, in September 2022.
GAU said it had held off confirming the delivery for months despite public hints, since neither Ukrainian nor Russian sources had published photos or video of the system inside Ukraine, and the program’s history of missed deadlines made earlier claims difficult to verify. Nicholas Drummond, an advisor to manufacturer KNDS Deutschland, suggested on X in early July that the first RCH 155 had reached Ukrainian forces and could now be called “combat proven.” Weeks later, German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius said during a visit to KNDS Deutschland that the howitzer had been “very well received” in Ukraine, without directly confirming a delivery.
The RCH 155 combines a highly automated 155mm/L52 gun system, known as the Artillery Gun Module, with the wheeled GTK Boxer armored vehicle chassis. The system can carry 30 shells and 144 modular propellant charges, and depending on the ammunition used, can fire out to roughly 70 kilometers (43 miles). It is also built to fire while the vehicle is moving, a capability GAU described as new for this class of weapon, though industry publication hartpunkt reported as of late 2025 that this only works on certain terrain and at speeds up to 30 km/h (19 mph).
Germany ordered a total of 54 RCH 155 units for Ukraine, split into three batches of 18, at a cost to the German government of €890 million ($1.03 billion). More than 600 Ukrainian soldiers had completed RCH 155 training, including on the underlying GTK Boxer platform, as of March 2026, according to GAU.
The path to delivery involved repeated delays. Industry analysts predicted as early as 2022 that the first systems would not arrive before 2025. KNDS said in August 2023 that delivery was expected in the first quarter of 2024, then pushed that to the end of 2024 by that November, according to German magazine Der Spiegel. The first unit was formally handed over in January 2025 in a ceremony attended by Ukraine’s ambassador to Germany, Oleksii Makeiev, and Pistorius, but the howitzer remained in Germany afterward so Ukrainian crews could train on it at KNDS’s facility in Kassel and the Bundeswehr’s artillery school in Idar-Oberstein. That training was originally expected to wrap up by around April 2025, a timeline KNDS’s then-CEO Ralf Ketzel also cited that November. When the deadline slipped again, KNDS’s chief executive told Deutsche Welle’s Ukrainian service in August 2025 that changes identified during training, along with integration work tied to Ukraine’s battle management system, had caused further delays. It was not until July 2026 that public signs of an actual handover or deployment resurfaced.
Drummond has said Ukrainian crews have consistently hit targets at a range of 40 kilometers (25 miles) with the first round fired from the system, a claim GAU noted has not yet been backed by detailed performance reporting. GAU said it has not yet obtained independent confirmation of how the RCH 155 has performed in combat conditions, or how many of the 54 ordered units have reached Ukraine so far.

Tiit Hennoste: This lying, lying, lying world
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
09:26:00 UTC
18:26:00 KST

Tiit Hennoste: This lying, lying, lying world
People are still driven by Vanity, Envy, Fame, Convenience, Money and Power. Unfortunately, it is impossible to make any of them disappear, writes Tiit Hennoste, originally in Sirp magazine.
Lie big, lie colossally. I earned a million. I ran six marathons in as many days. If you get caught, just say you're a victim of racism, sexism, autism etc. Or that you just have the latest universal disease ADHD. Unfortunately, there is nothing new under the sun.
Criminals and lawyers have always lied. I lied to you, star attorney Monika Mägi told a journalist. I've also lied numerous times in court, she added with effortless audacity. It used to be believed that the Prosecutor's Office doesn't lie. Today, we've read plenty about its lies, too.
Politicians lie without batting an eye. Let us recall Kaja Kallas and her "read my lips" ... Trump has taken the practice to astronomical heights, which no one can match. Yet.
The church has always lied; for example, so that a saint's thumb bone is housed in ten different churches simultaneously. Some of these saints never even existed. This led people to doubt whether the clergy was simply lying about God, too, some time ago.
Journalism is a factory of half-lies. Misleading headlines, facts and opinions mixed together, not to mention content marketing. Advertising is a factory of full lies, even though the people involved in it make efforts to shake off the burden.
The world of sports, of measurable results, at least should be free of lies. But no. Doping is a banal lie, but I had to pick my chin off the floor after reading about the tricks being pulled to fight drag in women's cycling.
It is claimed that science is looking for the truth and does not lie. It has rules to avoid lies. Transparency in research procedures, reproducibility of studies, blind peer review and so on. In truth, a lot of half-lies and outright lies have been found there, too, including in very highly respected journals. Writing dissertations has been a relatively public small business for some time. Some have even boasted in the media of how their works have always gotten maximum marks.
We might ask how has this pyramid of lies continued to stand? One reason, of course, is that not everybody lies. Secondly, big lies are a privilege of the privileged and getting caught often does not leave the room. And then there were those who unmasked lies. Some did it to expose their competition, others were simply ethical people.
Then came social media, which helped lying go global and birthed an army of online fraudsters. But it also brought the lies of ordinary people to millions. This wretched place is full of people lying to make themselves seem prettier, wealthier, happier and more famous. Faking a more complimentary countenance on passport photos seems to be the latest trend. When necessary, people lie about having a disease to justify their lying.
Finally, we made AI, which lies with complete abandon. We affectionately refer to it as hallucinating. Watching this device invade every corner of human society at the speed of light is scary. Its use is promoted shamelessly.
I still cannot believe the proponents of AI are foolish enough to believe their own pitch, according to which people who attend their seminars will use AI responsibly. There used to be a saying that if you beat a rabbit long enough, it will eventually learn how to strike a match. But beating is not allowed these days, we can only gently stroke. The results are beginning to became evident in universities. People writing their theses tell newspapers how AI helped them do a much faster and better job. AI will soon simply replace those who write for money.
What lies behind the lies? Some still believe it to be Soviet rule, and creating a world permeated by lies was indeed one of its more disgusting achievements. But that's a lie. In truth, people are driven by Vanity, Envy, Fame, Convenience, Money and Power. Unfortunately, we cannot make any of them disappear. Besides, Soviet authorities were small fry compared to social media and the AI lies factory the output of which keeps growing in perfect keeping with capitalism. We can only hope that the growth of lying will be linear and not exponential in the age of AI.
PS. I wanted to write about something nice, but nothing came of it. Well, maybe next time.
--
Editor: Marcus Turovski

Chainsaw maker STIHL chief calls for longer hours without extra pay
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
09:23:01 UTC
18:23:01 KST

In an opinion piece for Euronews, Dr Nikolas Stihl, chairman of world-leading chainsaw maker STIHL, calls for reforms including a 40-hour working week without extra pay to safeguard Germany's prosperity and welfare state.
The family entrepreneur from Waiblingen in southern Germany does not mince his words: "The German economy has been stuck in crisis mode for years. The prerequisite for overcoming the persistent weakness in growth is better framework conditions," Stihl said.
STIHL: €5.48bn in revenue and more than 20,000 employees
In 2025, STIHL generated €5.48 billion in revenue and employed 20,246 people worldwide. Founded by Andreas Stihl in 1926, the company is celebrating its 100th anniversary. Nikolas Stihl is the founder's grandson.
Family businessman Stihl takes a long-term view, and for him one thing is clear: "The situation of the German economy is serious, very serious. In the past eight years we have lost around 15 percent of our industrial output. Month after month Germany is losing around 15,000 industrial jobs."
The industrial base, he warns, is at risk of eroding – and with it prosperity and the welfare state. According to the company, STIHL has been the world's best-selling chainsaw brand since 1971. Nikolas Stihl acknowledges that "the US tariffs, China's aggressive industrial policy and geopolitical tensions" are also weighing on companies like his. But he argues that it is mainly home-grown problems holding firms back: "an overregulated economy, high energy costs, high labour costs, high taxes and a declining level of education and qualifications."
The Government's planned reforms fall short
The federal government’s planned reforms – covering statutory health insurance, pensions, taxes and the labour market – are good compromises, but they do not go far enough to pull Germany out of its structural crisis. If these compromises were now to be "unpicked", it would have devastating consequences for business confidence in politics, the entrepreneur warns.
Stihl says: "Now we need to muster all our strength for further reforms that will then generate tangible investment and growth impulses. For that, the governing coalition and the social partners must overcome their own reservations in order to live up to their responsibility towards Germany."
The next steps, he argues, should include cutting red tape, increasing the overall volume of work in the economy, reducing labour costs and creating additional incentives for research and development.
Germans need to work more to preserve prosperity
Stihl is calling for "high-quality public administration" with clear rules, streamlined and swift procedures, reasonable reporting requirements, and processes that are digital and supported by AI. "Accordingly, statutory reporting requirements should generally be abolished and retained only where their necessity is explicitly justified. If public authorities act much more as service providers for citizens and companies, that increases trust in Germany as a business location and in politics."
For Stihl, the key issue is increasing the volume of work – in other words, Germans need to work more again: "If we want to maintain our prosperity and keep social benefits at a high level, the total volume of work in the economy has to increase. A higher volume of work boosts economic output. In that sense, the debate about more work is a debate about preserving our prosperity, and by no means a debate about employees being lazy."
40-hour week without pay rises
Germany must use every available option to increase the volume of work: by incentivising overtime, extending working lives with fair exceptions for physically demanding jobs, making better use of the existing labour pool – including unemployed and part-time workers – and attracting skilled workers from abroad.
Stihl also calls for sick pay to be paid only from the second day of sickness and for phone-in sick notes to be abolished. Productivity gains from digitalisation and the growing use of AI will not offset the negative effects of demographic change.
From October 2026, collective bargaining talks in the metalworking and electrical industries are due to begin between trade unions and employers. Stihl warns: "We no longer have the productivity advantage over key competitors that used to justify our high labour costs. That is why I advocate increasing weekly working hours to 40, without any pay compensation.
Promoting AI, robotics, biotech, space and quantum technology
He acknowledges that he is asking a great deal of employees, but says he does not want to take anything away from anyone.
The aim, he insists, is to remain competitive, keep production in Germany and safeguard jobs. STIHL has production companies in eight countries, as well as 40 of its own sales and marketing subsidiaries and more than 50,000 specialist dealers worldwide.
When it comes to non-wage labour costs – including contributions to pension, health, long-term care and unemployment insurance – he says a ceiling of 40% of gross wages is the maximum that can be accepted.
Stihl is also calling for more attractive conditions for innovative companies, including regulatory breathing space, greater tax incentives and wider access to venture capital. "Overall, innovation and the granting of approvals must be given an even higher priority than at present and must not be held back by bureaucracy."
Future-focused fields such as the industrial use of artificial intelligence, robotics, biotechnology, medical technology, space travel and quantum technologies should receive more targeted support.
'Germany has proved many times that it can reinvent itself'
The conclusion reached by the head of the world's leading chainsaw brand and a global technology company is clear: "We must not waste any more time, because only a high-performance and competitive business location can secure prosperity and a strong welfare state. Germany has proved many times that it can reinvent itself."
For the public to embrace the challenges ahead, "a ruthless stocktake of the current situation" is needed, followed by an overall plan setting out the changes people can expect. "The time has come to act with determination," says Nikolas Stihl.

Soviet-era rifle still beats Russia’s newest AK-12, analysis shows
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
09:21:01 UTC
18:21:01 KST

- A Ukrainian gunsmith examined five captured Russian rifles and found barrel defects in all three AK-12 generations, including one nearly unfired 2026-made model.
- He said two Soviet-era AK-74 rifles, despite decades of heavy use and poor maintenance, held up better internally than the newer AK-12 samples.
A Ukrainian gunsmith who services captured Russian assault rifles for Ukrainian troops says the newest generation of Kalashnikov rifle, the AK-12, consistently shows worse barrel quality than the decades-old AK-74 it was meant to replace, based on a detailed inspection of five trophy weapons spanning more than 40 years of production.
Dmytro, who runs a weapons service channel called OrkovNetMedia, opened the video by noting that Ukrainian law allows soldiers to legally declare captured firearms, including rifles still configured for automatic fire, a policy he called “maximally civilized.” He said five declared trophy rifles arrived at his shop on a single day. Under Ukrainian law, owners of declared trophy weapons cannot convert them to civilian semi-automatic configuration or otherwise modify them until martial law ends. Each rifle must be kept, registered and inspected in the same condition it was captured.
For the inspection, Dmytro laid out three AK-12 rifles representing three separate production generations, alongside two AK-74 rifles serving as comparison points. He used a borescope, a thin camera on a flexible or rigid cable, to examine the inside of each barrel without disassembly, and said the tool costs only a few thousand hryvnia. He argued every soldier picking up a battlefield rifle should carry one, since a weapon’s exterior condition tells a buyer almost nothing about the state of its bore, and he has had soldiers arrive at his shop disappointed after hauling a 15 to 20 kilogram rifle out of the field only to learn its barrel was ruined.
The first rifle he examined was a first-generation AK-12 from 2019, already seven years old. He said its bore had clearly suffered from prolonged exposure to poor conditions, describing a foul-smelling residue inside consistent with organic decay near where the rifle had lain in the field. Despite that, once cleaned, the barrel’s overall condition along its length was reasonable, with chrome damage concentrated mainly at the muzzle crown, the precisely machined edge at the barrel’s opening that governs accuracy, rather than throughout the bore. Dmytro said damage limited to the crown, while still a defect, would only modestly affect the rifle’s grouping at typical combat ranges and would not be considered disqualifying.
The second rifle, a second-generation AK-12, arrived in comparatively better external condition, having spent limited time in the field rather than in long-term storage. Under the borescope, however, Dmytro found the bore’s chrome plating had already begun flaking away, and he described the muzzle crown as looking “like beavers had gnawed it,” calling the damage worse than what he found in either the older first-generation model or, notably, in a much older AK-74. He concluded the rifle offered no real advantage over an unusable weapon and recommended discarding it outright, joking that its only remaining use was as a cleaning-rod holder.
The most striking rifle in the video was a third-generation AK-12 manufactured in 2026 and captured in what Dmytro said was nearly unfired condition. He said the weapon had belonged to a Russian soldier identified only as Yemelyanov, who was killed while still holding the rifle in a firm grip, having reportedly used it for roughly one week before his death. The rifle’s cleaning rod remained in place, unused, a detail Dmytro cited as further evidence the weapon had seen almost no service. Externally and even partway into the bore, the rifle looked close to new. Deeper inspection near the gas port, however, revealed what he described as pitted cavities in the metal, comparing the damage to the progression of a perforating ulcer, which he warned could eventually develop into holes straight through the barrel wall. The muzzle crown was also poorly formed despite the rifle’s minimal use. Dmytro’s verdict was that the rifle, brand new and nearly unfired, was still not worth carrying into combat and was suitable only as a keepsake.
By contrast, an AK-74 manufactured in 1983, shown as a comparison baseline, displayed an extremely high round count and had reportedly spent roughly 90% of its service life without proper maintenance. Despite that history, Dmytro said the bore remained in what he called a “living” condition along its full length, with a clean muzzle crown and no chrome damage of the kind he found in the newer rifles. A second AK-74 from 1990, shown briefly afterward, had heavier external rust and a dirtier muzzle assembly, and Dmytro admitted he had expected it to be in better shape than it was, but its bore still showed less wear than the AK-12 samples and its chamber remained undamaged.
Beyond barrel condition, Dmytro flagged a specific mechanical failure he said he has traced to at least one Russian soldier’s death. He described a small part on early AK-12 rifles known as the two-round-burst limiter, made, in his assessment, from substandard metal that can jam and lock the bolt in the rearward position. He said he had been told secondhand that a Russian soldier whose rifle jammed in this way during combat was unable to clear it and was killed shortly afterward, with the disabled rifle later brought to him for inspection.
Dmytro closed the review with a broader assessment based on his repeated experience servicing trophy weapons, cautioning it reflected his personal opinion rather than a formal engineering study. He said that, counterintuitively, older AK-12 production batches have tended to have better barrels than newer ones, citing several AK-12K carbines he had separately inspected, most of which he judged to be poor quality. He argued the AK-74 remains easier to maintain and modify in the field, since components like muzzle devices and barrel liners can be swapped in minutes, while equivalent parts on the AK-12, including its safety selector, are often pinned or swaged in place and effectively impossible to remove despite factory documentation suggesting otherwise. His overall conclusion was that the original AK-74 was built for military durability, while today’s Kalashnikov-brand rifles, in his view, are built primarily to win state procurement contracts rather than to withstand sustained combat use.
Reports of manufacturing defects have followed the AK-12 since its earliest development. Russian arms testing officials publicly acknowledged unspecified “technical faults” during the rifle’s 2012 preliminary trials without disclosing details, and Kalashnikov Concern scrapped that original design entirely in 2016, rebuilding the rifle around the AK-400 prototype to address the Russian military’s concerns over cost and reliability in automatic fire before adopting the redesigned version as today’s AK-12.

Propaganda and military training are being intensified in Russian schools

Propaganda and military training are being intensified in Russian schools
Kyiv • UNN
In particular, social studies and foreign languages have been reduced, while the teaching of history based on Medinsky’s textbooks, military training, and propaganda of "traditional values" have been intensified.
In the new academic year, propaganda has been intensified in Russian schools. Children have had their study of social studies reduced to free up classroom hours for history and military training, and schools have also introduced subjects about "traditional values." This is reported by the Foreign Intelligence Service of Ukraine, according to UNN.
Details
The new academic year in Russian schools has brought seven new or updated propaganda initiatives—nearly three times more than last year. One of the main changes is the further reduction of social studies. It will be removed from the eighth grade, and the freed-up hours will be given to history. This means less time for law, economics, politics, and the work of state institutions—knowledge that helps schoolchildren understand society and critically assess the authorities’ decisions
Instead, according to available data, eighth- and ninth-grade students will study from unified history textbooks prepared with the participation of Putin’s propagandist Medinsky. They will devote even more attention to the confrontation with the West, "traditional values," and the war, while in ninth grade the school year in history will begin with lessons on "Russia—our sacred state."
In grades 5–7, foreign-language instruction will be reduced from three lessons per week to two. At the same time, fifth-graders will be given "Spiritual and Moral Culture of Russia" in the second semester. The subject is intended to shape "traditional values" through the study of state officials and military personnel, primarily participants in the war against Ukraine. The military component is also being strengthened. "Fundamentals of Life Safety and Defense of the Fatherland" will be divided into two compulsory courses—life safety and basic military training—with 34 hours each. Schools are also introducing grades for behavior and a new concept of historical education, which is intended to raise "patriotically minded "youth"
These changes continue the Kremlin’s policy toward school education, which intensified after the start of the full-scale invasion in 2022. At that time, schools introduced "Conversations About Important Things," flag-raising ceremonies, the "Movement of the First," new history textbooks, military training, and advisers to school principals for educational work.
Last year, social studies was already removed from grades 6–7. Now it is being reduced by another year, freeing up time for "history," military training, and state ideology

russia is introducing military training, propaganda, and drone-operation instruction in the occupied territories of Ukraine. Cadet classes are planned from 2026.

The incidents are the latest flashpoints in renewed confrontation between the two nations.
On Saturday, US Central Command (CENTCOM) announced that its forces had struck three Iranian oil tankers in response to what it said were ballistic missile strikes launched by the IRGC against two navy warships.
"Following Iran’s failed attacks, CENTCOM permanently disabled the IRGC crude oil carriers M/T Downy off the coast of Kharg Island and M/T Stark 1 near Jask," it said in a statement. "American forces also completely destroyed the unladen crude oil carrier M/T Kylo (also known as the “Noxen”) in the Gulf of Oman, striking the vessel in multiple critical locations to render it inoperable after the crew was directed to abandon ship".
"A U.S. aircraft carrier and guided-missile destroyer successfully evaded multiple unprovoked Iranian attacks. No American personnel were harmed," it added.
CENTCOM has also shared video footage on social media appearing to show the strikes.
The conflict reignited last Sunday after US forces targeted Iranian rocket launchers in the Strait of Hormuz.
The IRGC later confirmed strikes had hit Larak Island, before launching retaliatory attacks on US bases across the Middle East.
On Saturday, Admiral Brad Cooper, the commander of CENTCOM, issued a warning to Tehran and its oil fleet in the wake of the strikes.
"Let the message to the IRGC be clear: If you shoot at two of our ships, we will impose an even higher economic cost —taking out three of yours. We will not hesitate to defend American forces, and if necessary, destroy Iran’s limited and exposed oil fleet," he said.

Two women were killed and six people wounded in an air attack on Arab Salim after Israeli forces issued a forced displacement order for a building in the town, NNA reported.
Lebanon’s Health Ministry reported that at least two people were killed in an Israeli air strike on Nabatieh al-Fawqa.
An air strike on Nabatieh city also destroyed a historical building owned by the brother of a Lebanese member of parliament, damaging several buildings nearby.
In Kfar Reman, an air attack destroyed the home of the town’s late former mayor. Five people were treated in Nabatieh hospitals and discharged.

Israel says it carried out the strikes in response to Hezbollah launching two drones towards its forces in southern Lebanon, describing the attack as a “blatant violation” by the Lebanese armed group.
Since March, when Hezbollah attacked Israel during the US-Israel war on Iran, Israel has carried out air strikes across Lebanon and launched a ground invasion. Lebanon says the attacks have killed more than 4,300 people.
Israeli forces are still operating inside a self-declared “security zone” about 10km (six miles) deep inside Lebanon.
The number of attacks has decreased since a US-Iran Memorandum of Understanding on the broader conflict in June, while Israel and Lebanon signed a framework agreement later that month.

Earlier this week, Israel said it had taken “operational control” of the strategic Ali al-Taher ridge near Nabatieh. Hezbollah has not commented on the announcement.
Israel weighs pullback
Israel is also considering pulling its troops occupying Lebanese territory closer to the Israeli border. Israeli public broadcaster Kan, citing security sources, said the military was preparing to scale back its presence and reposition three to four kilometres closer to the Israeli border, along a new “Grey Line” where outposts would be built.
That would pull troops back from parts of the “Yellow Line”, which extends north of the Litani River. The plan has not been approved by Israel’s political leadership, and the handover of territory to the Lebanese army remains unresolved, Kan said.
Hezbollah condemned Israel’s campaign, which it said was taking place amid “complete international silence and blatant American complicity”. The group reiterated its rejection of Beirut’s “fruitless direct negotiations” with Israel.
Qatar’s Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman bin Jassim Al Thani spoke by phone with Lebanese Prime Minister Nawaf Salam on Saturday, Qatar’s Foreign Ministry said, as Doha pressed for de-escalation.

Egypt sentences TV presenter, 11 others to death in drugs case

Breadcrumb
Egypt sentences TV presenter, 11 others to death in drugs case
An Egyptian court sentenced a well-known television presenter and 11 others to death for manufacturing and trafficking narcotics in a sprawling drugs case, official media reported on Saturday.
The presenter, Sarah Khalifa, 39, is best known for her program "Mission Impossible", which dealt with issues concerning security and crime.
The state-linked Al-Ahram newspaper said a Cairo court sentenced "Khalifa and 11 other defendants to death by hanging on charges of forming an organised criminal gang specialising in procuring materials used in manufacturing narcotics, with the intent to traffic them, and possessing and carrying unlicensed firearms and ammunition".
The verdict came after the court consulted the Grand Mufti of Egypt for his religious opinion, a procedure required by Egyptian law in capital cases.
The verdict is subject to appeal.
Khalifa also owns a plastic surgery clinic and a production company that specialises in organising parties and events.
According to the state-run Akhbar Al-Youm newspaper, the defendants were charged with "manufacturing synthetic drugs with the intent to traffic them, by importing the materials used in manufacturing from abroad".
Al-Ahram reported that authorities seized more than 750 kilograms of narcotics and raw materials, and found two apartments used as laboratories as well as unlicensed firearms and ammunition.d
The court also sentenced Khalifa and others to five years in prison over a separate case involving the kidnapping and assault of a young man.
Egypt applies the death penalty for premeditated murder, terrorism, some rape offences and drug trafficking.
According to the Egyptian Commission for Rights and Freedoms, 541 death sentences were issued in Egypt in 2025.

====================================================================================================

US aircraft carriers within Iran's reach
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
09:09:15 UTC
18:09:15 KST

Amid the intensifying military confrontation between Iran and the United States, the news of Iran firing ballistic missiles at a US aircraft carrier and a destroyer is not merely a development on the battlefield; it could be a sign of a shift in the operational environment for American forces and an increase in the cost of Washington's military presence in the region's waters.
The US Central Command (CENTCOM) has announced that the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) fired ballistic missiles at a US aircraft carrier and a guided-missile destroyer, and that these vessels managed to survive several attacks. According to the American account, none of the US forces were harmed in these attacks.
At first glance, the most important question might be whether the missiles actually struck the American ships. But from a strategic perspective, the significance of this development goes beyond the extent of direct damage. The more important issue is the change that such attacks can create in the calculations of American commanders regarding the level of security and freedom of action of US naval vessels in the region.
An aircraft carrier is one of the most important instruments of US military power projection beyond its borders. By deploying an aircraft carrier and its accompanying strike group, Washington in effect moves a portion of its air and naval power to the closest possible point to a crisis. This presence is intended to create deterrence, strike capability, and the ability to react quickly for the United States.
But this same feature also brings a vulnerability; the closer a carrier is to a conflict zone, the more important its protection becomes, and more resources must be allocated to defend it.
A carrier strike group is not limited to the carrier itself. A collection of destroyers, air defense systems, fighter jets, early warning and reconnaissance aircraft, and other military equipment are responsible for its protection. Therefore, a missile threat against an aircraft carrier effectively means challenging a vast defensive network.
From this angle, even if the launched missiles are intercepted and no damage is inflicted on the carrier, the attack itself can have operational consequences. Because American commanders must assume that their vessels are within range and that any presence in the region faces the possibility of attack. This is what can be called the "cost of presence."
To change the other side's calculations, Iran does not necessarily need to destroy a US carrier in every attack. Increasing the cost of protecting carriers, limiting their freedom of movement, changing the operational distance, increasing the need for reconnaissance, and creating psychological pressure on forces deployed in the region can also be part of the deterrence objective.
In modern warfare, a weapon is sometimes effective when it forces the opposing side to engage a large set of resources and equipment to counter it. From this perspective, a ballistic missile is not just a tool for inflicting damage; it can also be a tool for changing the operational behavior of the opposing side.
Of course, one should not conclude from this incident that the military balance between Iran and the United States has changed. The United States still possesses significant superiority in various military, intelligence, air, and naval domains, and its aircraft carriers have multiple layers of defense. Therefore, a distinction must be made between the "ability to target" and the "ability to destroy" a military target.
What matters now is the repeatability of this threat. If American forces conclude that the presence of aircraft carriers in certain areas continually exposes them to missile attacks, they will be forced to review their deployment and operational patterns.
In such circumstances, the distance of carriers from coastal areas, their movement patterns, the level of escort, the number of protective fighter jets, and the volume of reconnaissance operations could change. Each of these changes would mean an increase in operational costs for the United States.
On the other hand, the US response is also noteworthy. Washington will attempt to show, by responding to Iranian military and economic targets, that attacking US forces will not remain without cost. This approach could lead to the formation of a dangerous cycle of attack and response; a cycle in which each military action pushes the other side toward a more severe reaction.
Meanwhile, the region's waters are gradually becoming one of the main arenas of competition. The importance of this issue is not limited to military operations. The security of shipping, energy transit, oil tankers, and trade routes are also directly affected by this confrontation.
In such an environment, Iran enjoys an important geographical advantage. The proximity of the operational theater to Iran's coasts means that Washington cannot separate the issue of protecting its naval forces from the geographical conditions of the region.
In contrast, the United States will try to neutralize this advantage by relying on its air and naval superiority and defense systems. For this reason, the battle between the two sides is not only a battle of missiles against ships; it is also a battle over the calculation of the costs and benefits of continued military presence.
If Iran can increase the cost and risk of the US military presence without needing to inflict direct and widespread damage, it will have achieved part of its deterrence objective. On the other hand, if the United States can continue to keep its carriers deployed in the region and simultaneously use them in military operations, Iran's effort to limit Washington's freedom of action will face greater difficulty.
Ultimately, the importance of the recent news should not be summarized merely as "whether the missiles hit the American ship or not." The real significance is that a US aircraft carrier, which is a symbol of Washington's power and military presence in distant regions, must now operate in an environment where the missile threat against it has become a serious variable in operational calculations.
This development could be one of the most important signs of a changing deterrence equation in the region; an equation in which military power is not measured only by the amount of weaponry, but also by each side's ability to impose costs, increase risk, and limit the other side's freedom of action.
In such circumstances, the future of the US carrier presence in the region will become more than ever a strategic issue; because as the cost of protecting these carriers increases, the question of the benefits of their continued presence will also become more serious for American decision-makers.

Crans-Montana victims’ foundation seeking more funds
The Beloved Foundation, which provides support to victims of the New Year’s Day fire in the Swiss town of Crans-Montana, has so far received around 70 applications. Some have been approved, whilst others are still being processed, said its director, Christian Cardon.
“There have been no refusals so far,” Cardon said in an interview published by Le Matin Dimanche. According to him, several tens of thousands of francs have already been handed out.
The Beloved FoundationExternal link was set up in March at the initiative of the Canton of Valais for victims of the fire at the Le Constellation bar in Crans-Montana, which left 41 people dead and 115 injured. It has received donations or pledges totalling CHF24 million ($29.7 million) from the cantons of Valais and Vaud, the municipality of Crans-Montana, and private donors.
+ Rehabilitation underway for Crans-Montana fire victims
“We are funding rehabilitation programmes that will help patients recover or reintegrate into society,” said former federal government minister Doris Leuthard, president of the foundation, also speaking to the newspaper.
Seeking additional funds
“In particular, young people have approached us regarding professional development […] We also support projects initiated by the parents of victims or by people who have been facing financial difficulties since the tragedy,” said Cardon.
The foundation’s scope of action is broad, but centres on “education, psychological support and financial assistance for families in need”, he said. Furthermore, “we do not act in isolation”, explains the director, emphasising that the foundation will not “duplicate” the benefits provided under the Federal Act on Victim Support (LAVI), “but will step in where there is a shortfall”.
+ Crans-Montana: all Swiss patients have returned home
Despite a budget of CHF24 million, the Beloved Foundation is seeking additional funding, as “needs will evolve and persist in the long term”, said Leuthard. “Even though the budget is substantial, given the psychological and physical consequences of the tragedy, we will need additional resources to carry out our work over several years,” said Cardon.

Gaza holds funeral for 100 Palestinians recovered from rubble of destroyed homes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
09:06:08 UTC
18:06:08 KST

Ramzi Mahmud and Sahin Demir
06 September 2026•Update: 06 September 2026
Palestinians held a funeral procession on Sunday for 100 people recovered from under the rubble of destroyed homes in Gaza City’s Zeitoun neighborhood following Israel’s genocidal war on the enclave.
Thousands of Palestinians, including relatives of the victims as well as community and political figures, attended the procession, with the bodies and remains laid out in an area near the ruins of the destroyed homes and draped in Palestinian flags.
The funeral includes memorial addresses by Gaza’s Civil Defense, whose teams carried out the recovery operations, as well as representatives of the victims’ families and community figures.
The bodies and remains are expected to be buried at Al-Ahli cemetery in the Zeitoun neighborhood after funeral prayers.
Civil Defense teams recovered them in recent days as part of the second phase of a project launched on July 19 to retrieve Palestinians still buried beneath the rubble of buildings destroyed during the Israeli war.
The victims belonged to the Rahim, Balawi, Malaka, Qanbour and Salmi families and were killed when Israeli forces struck several residential homes around two and a half years ago, according to local authorities.
Recovery operations are being carried out with limited resources, including only a small number of excavators and deteriorating equipment, amid Israeli restrictions on the entry of heavy machinery and equipment needed to search the rubble.
Sunday’s ceremony is among the largest funerals in Palestinian history in terms of the number of bodies and remains being buried, according to an Anadolu tally. A similar funeral was held in early August for 112 Palestinians recovered from the rubble of homes in Gaza City’s Sabra neighborhood.
The second phase of the recovery project involves 800 hours of work at 147 destroyed homes across Gaza City and the northern and central parts of the enclave, where 1,072 bodies are believed to remain buried.
The first phase began in late November 2025 and involved 500 hours of work. Civil Defense teams recovered around 333 bodies and remains out of an estimated 559 missing beneath the rubble of 54 homes and buildings.
Under the first phase of the Gaza ceasefire agreement, in effect since Oct. 10, 2025, Israel was expected to allow the entry of heavy machinery and equipment needed for recovery operations, according to Palestinian authorities in the enclave.
The ceasefire followed nearly two years of Israeli attacks on Gaza, which killed more than 73,000 Palestinians and injured over 174,000, while destroying or damaging much of the enclave’s civilian infrastructure.

Iran launches 'economic war headquarters' to tackle wartime disruptions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
09:04:47 UTC
18:04:47 KST

Iran’s Economy Ministry has established an “economic war headquarters” to coordinate and accelerate responses to economic problems arising from wartime conditions, Deputy Economy Minister Morteza Zamanian said on Sunday.
Zamanian told the Tasnim news agency that the body would initially focus on issues falling within the ministry’s responsibilities and authorities.
He said it would seek to quickly address war-related problems affecting businesses, trade, financing and other areas of the economy.
For issues extending beyond the ministry’s authority, Zamanian said the ministry would use its role in broader economic policymaking, including through the government’s economic commission and economic headquarters, to coordinate among institutions and pursue solutions at higher levels.
The main function of the new body is to centrally identify disruptions caused by wartime conditions and develop practical solutions, he said.
Zamanian added that the mechanism is intended to prevent issues requiring cooperation among several government agencies from becoming stalled by bureaucracy.
Measures being pursued include tax and customs support, banking facilities and financial instruments for businesses affected by the conflict, he said.
Tightened US sanctions
The move comes amid an ongoing conflict that began when the US and Israel launched strikes on Iran in February, followed by Iranian retaliatory attacks against US targets across the region.
Iran and the US signed a memorandum of understanding in June, mediated by Pakistan and Qatar, outlining steps toward ending hostilities, reopening the Strait of Hormuz and addressing economic restrictions.
Tehran has accused Washington of failing to fulfil its commitments under the memorandum, including sanctions relief and the release of frozen Iranian assets.
Washington, for its part, has accused Tehran of failing to meet its obligations and has maintained economic pressure on Iran, arguing that sanctions are aimed at restricting revenue and financial networks that it says support Tehran’s military and regional activities.

The move comes amid an ongoing conflict that began when the US and Israel launched strikes on Iran in February, followed by Iranian retaliatory attacks against US targets across the region.
Iran and the US signed a memorandum of understanding in June, mediated by Pakistan and Qatar, outlining steps toward ending hostilities, reopening the Strait of Hormuz and addressing economic restrictions.
Tehran has accused Washington of failing to fulfill its commitments under the memorandum, including sanctions relief and the release of frozen Iranian assets.
Washington, for its part, has accused Tehran of failing to meet its obligations and has maintained economic pressure on Iran, arguing that sanctions are aimed at restricting revenue and financial networks that it says support Tehran’s military and regional activities.

Far-right AfD predicted to win big in crucial German state election
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
09:00:02 UTC
18:00:02 KST

German voterswent to the polls on Sunday for a crucial regional election where the far-right, anti-immigration and Moscow-friendly Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) is expected to win.
AfD, polling at more than 40% for months in Saxony-Anhalt, even has its sights on winning its first-ever state government, although this is far from assured.
Polls opened at 8am and 1.7 million voters have until 6pm to cast their ballots, with first projections expected shortly after.
The eastern German state is governed by the centre-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU) – the party of Friedrich Merz, the chancellor – in coalition with two smaller parties, and its state premier, Sven Schulze, hopes to rebuild a multiparty coalition to cling to power.
All other major parties have so far maintained a “firewall” of non-cooperation with the AfD, whose Saxony-Anhalt branch is categorised as “right-wing extremist” by Germany’s domestic intelligence agency.
The AfD’s top candidate Ulrich Siegmund – a 35-year-old who is feted like a rock star at campaign events and has a large social media following – has confidently predicted gaining an absolute majority.
“It was the others who erected the firewalls,” he told Bild. “If no one wants to work with us, then we’ll just have to do it alone.”
Such a scenario would shake Germany, which has so far kept extremist parties in check.
A strong AfD win would also heap pressure on Merz, who has vowed to reboot a stagnant economy and restrict irregular immigration, but has seen his party beaten by the AfD in national surveys too.
“If the AfD wins in Saxony-Anhalt, Merz’s critics will become even more vocal, and calls for better leadership will become impossible to ignore,” said the political scientist Wolfgang Schroeder of the University of Kassel.
Siegmund has promised to lead a political revolution from the state of 2.1 million people and propel the AfD to national victory in 2029.
The AfD’s key campaign promises include a “remigration and deportation offensive”, a ban on LGBTQ rainbow flags at public schools, and an end to new windfarms.
The party has also tapped into a sense of nostalgia for communist East Germany and lingering resentment about an enduring wealth gap with the west, decades after the 1989 fall of the Berlin Wall.
The prospect of an AfD state government has sparked alarm among mainstream parties and minority groups.
Thousands of the AfD’s opponents joined a “festival of democracy” rally in Magdeburg on the eve of the vote.
The German Economic Institute said the AfD’s immigration policy would be “ruinous” for the state, where the population is already ageing, shrinking and highly reliant on foreign-born workers.
Others have voiced fears an AfD-run state security apparatus could leak sensitive information to Russia.
The Kremlin “makes no secret of the fact that the AfD is the most important instrument for destabilising Germany for Putin”, the Thuringia state interior minister, Georg Maier, told the Handelsblatt.
The latest poll, released on Thursday by the public broadcaster ZDF, gave the AfD 41% of the vote.
The CDU was predicted a 23% share, the centre-left Social Democratic party (SPD) 8.5%, and the Greens 6%, while two smaller parties failed to cross the 5% hurdle to reenter parliament.
A similar result may allow a scenario where the CDU and others form a minority government with ad hoc support from the far-left Die Linke, which polled at 11.5%.
