Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
08:21:00 UTC
17:21:00 KST

With voters in the eastern German state of Saxony-Anhalt heading to the polls on Sunday, tensions are mounting within the governing Christian Democrats over their possible coalition options.
Three days before the election, Friedrich Merz’s CDU was trailing well behind the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) at just over 20%. Polls put the AfD as high as 43%.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
That would make the AfD by far the strongest force in the state parliament. Yet the party currently appears unlikely to win an absolute majority, leaving open the question of whether it can translate an electoral breakthrough into executive power.
Its lead candidate, Ullrich Siegmund, has ruled out entering a coalition and says he wants the AfD to govern alone.
The CDU, led by incumbent Minister-President Sven Schulze, is facing a dilemma of its own. One of his current coalition partners, the liberal FDP, is unlikely to clear the threshold for returning to the state parliament.
The projected numbers also appear to rule out a majority coalition with the SPD and Greens.
Schulze could, nevertheless, seek to form a minority government with the support of the Left Party, which is expected to emerge as the third-strongest political force.
Speaking to journalists last week, Schulze said neither AfD nor Left Party ministers would have a seat at his cabinet table. The wording was notable for what it did not exclude: a CDU-led minority government tolerated by the Left from outside the coalition.
Lithuania to Launch Integrated AI Drone Defense System
A similar arrangement is already in place in neighbouring Thuringia, another east German region, where CDU Minister-President Mario Voigt has been governing for almost two years with a government dependent on votes from the Left Party in the state parliament.
But replicating such an arrangement in Saxony-Anhalt would collide with a long-standing CDU red line.
A party “incompatibility” resolution adopted at the CDU’s 2018 conference rules out cooperation with both the AfD and the Left, which has roots in the Party of Democratic Socialism, itself the successor to East Germany’s ruling Socialist Unity Party (SED).
While Schulze has left a narrow path towards toleration by the Left, the CDU district executive committee in the Harz region has issued a position paper explicitly rejecting exploratory talks, coalition agreements or tolerance arrangements that would depend on Left Party support.
“We are aware of the paper in question, and it was circulated as a handout at the most recent meeting of the CDU district executive committee in Harz. The district executive committee will not consider its substance until its next meeting,” CDU Secretary-General Mario Karschunke told Euractiv.
Until that discussion takes place, it is explicitly a contribution to the debate, which is, of course, something every party member is entitled to make“, he added, while insisting that no position of the CDU Harz district branch or of the CDU in Saxony-Anhalt can be inferred from it. “If we started publicly commenting on every single opinion expressed within our party, we would probably have little time for anything else.”
Shortly afterwards, the chairs of the Christian Democratic Employees’ Association (CDA) in Saxony-Anhalt, Berlin, and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania issued an election appeal explicitly ruling out both the AfD and the Left Party.
Within the AfD, they argued, “far-right positions are socially acceptable”, and the party is “hostile to Europe and friendly towards Putin”.
“Equally clearly, the Left Party, which is the successor to the SED, whose rule was responsible for a lack of freedom and suffering in the GDR and which today openly promotes antisemitism, cannot be a partner for Christian Democratic politics,” the paper stated.
The appeal was also co-signed by Sepp Müller, deputy chairman of the CDU parliamentary group in the Bundestag. Müller, who hails from Dessau in Saxony-Anhalt, has repeatedly spoken out against any form of cooperation with either the AfD or the Left Party.

AA Photo
Under the new framework, the bridges, highways and ring roads will not be privatized as a single package but may be offered either together or separately.
A presidential decree published in the Official Gazette on Sept. 5 expanded the privatization program covering the Bosphorus (15 July Martyrs) Bridge and the Fatih Sultan Mehmet Bridge, as well as four highways, to include the Nigde-Pozanti Motorway, the Gaziantep Ring Motorway and the Caglayan Junction-Yenisehir Junction section of the Bursa Ring Road.
Under a 2010 decision, the bridges and highways were planned to be privatized as a single package through the transfer of operating rights for a period of 25 years from the date of physical handover.
The latest presidential decision introduced three key changes. The bridges and highways may now be privatized either as a whole or in separate groups, while the operating period has been extended to 30 years.
In a written statement on the decision, the Privatization Administration (OİB) emphasized that efforts concerning the highways and bridges operated by the General Directorate of Highways and included in the privatization portfolio do not involve the sale of public assets.
The administration said the model is based on transferring operating rights for a specified period while ownership remains with the state.

In China, 531 people are still considered missing after the massive flood
Kyiv • UNN
The flood destroyed China's border port with Nepal. Thirty-one people were killed and 531 are missing, including more than 250 foreigners.
In China's border zone, which was devastated by a catastrophic flood, rescuers continue searching for 531 people reported missing. CNN reports, according to UNN.
Details
All that remains of the former Gyirong port is a rocky fissure. The high-altitude hub was completely washed off the face of the earth, leaving behind a lunar landscape of rocks, gravel and mud, which rescuers are still searching
Before the deadly disaster, this port was a bustling border crossing between China and Nepal. Hundreds of tourists and traders passed through it every day. On August 26, the port was hit by a powerful surge of water, which triggered a landslide and a massive flood.
Not a single survivor has been found at the port, which became an information-gathering center for families both in China and around the world. The answers are not immediately apparent here. The public five-story border control facility, which towered over the surrounding area in the imposing style of Chinese government institutions, was destroyed. All that can now be seen of the building is the remains of its foundation
According to Chinese authorities, 31 people have died, while another 531 are considered missing. More than 250 of those being sought are foreigners.
According to the publication, Chinese authorities have still not released a list of the people who were at the port during the disaster or are considered missing. This has raised questions about transparency, particularly among families desperately seeking news about missing loved ones.
In addition, search-and-rescue efforts are being hampered by the mountainous terrain, heavy rains and the risk of further landslides. Barrier lakes have also formed as debris and mud blocked parts of the river, creating an additional risk.
According to the authorities of China and Nepal, the deaths of more than 1,000 people have been confirmed in total following the disaster on August 26, while thousands still remain missing.

The first option is to continue alongside Yoaz Hendel in an independent run through the election. Some within the party are pressing for precisely that course, arguing against rushing to withdraw from the race or join an existing party.

Joining up with Eisenkot, Bennett, or Liberman

Unlike his party colleague, Hendel did not categorically rule out serving in a government led by Netanyahu.
"If a broad unity government is formed with Eisenkot, Bennett, Liberman, Netanyahu and others, we will be part of it," Hendel said.

After fighting ISIS, Kurdish women fighters search for a place in Syria's new order - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
08:13:54 UTC
17:13:54 KST

More than 1,500 fighters from the Kurdish Women’s Protection Units (YPJ) are seeking a place in Syria’s new security institutions after the force was excluded from the army integration arrangements that followed the dissolution of the Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF) as an independent military organization.
For more stories from The Media Line go to themedialine.org
YPJ commander Nowruz Ahmed said Syrian officials rejected the group’s proposal to enter the army as an independent women’s brigade or battalion. Speaking to Reuters from a military base in Qamishli in an interview published September 2, Ahmed said the proposal grew from the force’s years of combat experience against the Islamic State group (ISIS).
“We were aiming to join the army, because our forces have experience and expertise that would enable them to protect themselves in an organized way in the form of an independent brigade or battalion,” Ahmed told Reuters.
The YPJ is now discussing a possible role within the Interior Ministry’s special operations forces. Ahmed told Reuters that the YPJ has more than 1,500 fighters and has asked whether they could be incorporated as a single force. She said a response was expected in the coming days.
The dispute concerns more than employment within the new state. YPJ leaders want their members to remain together as an organized women’s formation rather than be split among different units or assigned individually across the country.
“When we hear that the men will be integrated into the army while we are told there is no place for us, it is natural for us to feel excluded,” a Kurdish fighter who asked to be identified as Hevrin Jwan to protect her identity told The Media Line. “We did not carry weapons for a short period. We spent years fighting and training, and we have military experience that we do not believe can simply be ignored,” she said.
YPJ fought ISIS alongside US-backed SDF
The YPJ was formed during Syria’s civil war and fought alongside the US-backed SDF in campaigns that drove ISIS from large parts of northern and eastern Syria. Its all-women ranks became internationally recognized during the fight against the terrorist group.
That wartime role now collides with Damascus’ effort to bring armed formations under unified state command. On August 25, SDF commander Mazloum Abdi announced that the SDF had ended its mission as an independent military force after integration into Syrian army brigades.
The January integration agreement called for SDF military and security personnel to enter the Defense and Interior ministries individually following security vetting.
Another Kurdish fighter, who asked not to be named, told The Media Line that the reported rejection raised concerns about the role envisioned for women in Syria’s armed institutions.
“If the disagreement is about the structure of the unit or who it reports to, that is something that can be negotiated,” she said. “But when the message is that there is no place for us in the army at all, the problem becomes much bigger. We want to be part of state institutions, but without being asked to give up everything we have built over the past years,” she said.
The Syrian Defense and Interior ministries did not immediately respond to Reuters’ requests for comment about the discussions. Interior Ministry spokesman Noureddine al-Baba told Kurdish broadcaster Rudaw that YPJ fighters would be welcome in the ministry, without specifying their duties or whether they could serve as a unified formation. He said Interior Ministry personnel could be deployed across Syria.
Sources familiar with the discussions have also spoken of an earlier proposal for the fighters to join the tourist police. A YPJ spokeswoman denied that such an offer had been made.
For many YPJ members, the negotiations concern their collective identity as much as their future assignments.
“They always look at women as weak,” YPJ fighter Goksu Afrin told The Media Line. “We do not derive our strength from men or from the current state, and we insist on maintaining our own distinct identity. This is our choice, and this is our cause. We are open to everyone.”
Kurdish commander says women fighters have constitutional right to role
Another Kurdish commander said Syria’s constitution should guarantee a defined role for women fighters.
“We did not wait until today for someone to defend us,” she told The Media Line. “We women defended ourselves.”
Service in the Interior Ministry’s special operations forces could offer a compromise: formal entry into the state while preserving some collective structure and leveraging the fighters’ training. Whether Damascus will accept that arrangement remains unclear.
“We do not want a confrontation with the state, and we do not want to remain outside its institutions,” one fighter told The Media Line. “But we also do not want the price of integration to be the end of our existence as an organized women’s force.”

Israel prevented many terror threats against Jews abroad over past year, NSC official tells 'Post'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
08:13:45 UTC
17:13:45 KST

Israeli security agencies have thwarted dozens of plots over the past year, while maintaining heightened vigilance ahead of the Jewish holiday season, a senior National Security Council official told The Jerusalem Post ahead of the High Holy Days.
Iran and Hezbollah are expanding efforts to carry out terrorist attacks against Israelis and Jews worldwide, with Israeli security officials identifying a growing number of plots and preparations,
Iran has devoted increasing resources to promoting terrorism globally, the official said, including through individuals and newly established mechanisms focused specifically on attacks against Israelis and Jews.
“There are many people who wake up in the morning and their entire mission is to promote attacks against Israelis and Jews around the world,” the official said.
The effort involves multiple parts of Iran’s security apparatus, including the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps’ Quds Force and intelligence bodies, the official said. He stressed that the buildup of these capabilities was a long-term process that had intensified over time.
“Even if the rounds of fighting have ended, and we know their limitations, in the end the Iranian feeling is not good in the kinetic balance,” he said. “So they move to their ultimate arena” – efforts to carry out terrorist attacks and target Israelis at various levels.
No country wants terrorism
The official said Israeli strikes inside Iran during the recent fighting had also targeted elements involved in terrorism, including senior figures in Iran’s security establishment.
This, he said, had changed Israel’s operational environment.
“Unlike in the past, given the circumstances, it is possible to act inside Iran itself, particularly in Tehran,” he said, adding that Israel continued to counter Iranian terrorism worldwide, both independently and with foreign partners.
Israeli security agencies have thwarted dozens of terrorist plots over the past year, the official said. Cooperation with foreign governments had also proved critical, including with countries that do not necessarily maintain close political relations with Israel.
“No country wants terrorism on its territory,” he said.
“There is information, warning intelligence, preparations and alerts,” he said. “All these activities together are directed against all the mechanisms, all the organizations and all the countries.”
Israeli authorities had thwarted concrete, “hot” plots during the past year, including cases in which attacks were stopped at the highest levels of warning, the official said.
Some operations were disrupted within hours, while others took days or weeks to halt. Preventing an attack, he added, does not necessarily require striking the terrorist cell itself.
“There are many ways” to disrupt and stop an attack, he said.
The official declined to provide details on specific plots, targets, or prevention methods.
Hezbollah also remained a major concern, particularly because of its close strategic relationship with Iran.
“There is no status quo with Hezbollah,” the official said.
Hezbollah, Iran suffered significant damage
Hezbollah, like Iran, has suffered significant kinetic damage while failing to inflict anything close to the damage it had sought to cause Israel, he said.
“There is a huge gap between what it has absorbed and what it caused us – a gap that is only growing,” the official said.
Hezbollah and Iran should therefore be viewed as partners in the same broader campaign, he added. The Lebanese terrorist organization is now receiving greater attention in Israel’s counterterrorism efforts than in previous years.
The official also identified Africa as an increasingly important arena in efforts to prevent attacks against Israelis and Jews. Several African countries have weaker security mechanisms, while parts of the continent host established Islamist infrastructure, including local extremist networks and foreign elements.
Global jihadist organizations have long maintained infrastructure in parts of Africa, he said, while the Houthis’ position near the Horn of Africa has created an additional potential threat.
The Houthis possess both kinetic and other capabilities that could potentially be used in the region, the official said. Israel is particularly concerned by the group’s attention to Israeli activity in countries in the Horn of Africa, including Somaliland.
The Houthis view Israeli activity there as both a potential threat to their interests and a potential source of future terrorist targets, he said.
Israeli security agencies have increased vigilance ahead of the Jewish holiday season, a period that terrorist organizations have historically sought to exploit because of large gatherings and increased Israeli and Jewish community activity abroad.
The official pointed to previous incidents and attempted attacks around Jewish holidays. With the anniversary of the October 7 massacre also falling during the holiday period, Israeli authorities are maintaining a particularly high level of alert, he said.

When a DNA test reveals unexpected Swiss ancestry
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
08:10:00 UTC
17:10:00 KST

When a DNA test reveals unexpected Swiss ancestry
At the age of 53, Robert Thayer discovered his genes didn’t match his presumed family tree. Finding himself suddenly connected to the Liechti family, he travelled to Switzerland to visit the hamlets his ancestors had lived in before emigrating to the United States.
On a cloudy day in May, a small white car takes a right into Erlenbach im Simmental, a little village in the valley behind Spiez, canton Bern. Finding its way on the narrow streets through the houses, the car turns onto the single-lane country road that heads up the hill, closely followed by a second car. The scenery is picturesque: idyllic steep green meadows on both sides of the road, a stunning view over the valley, and little traffic that would otherwise require precise manoeuvring.
In the white car, Albert Liechti checks with his wife whether this is the way they’d taken the previous time. She confirms it is. Liechti, 82, is a passionate genealogist, and today, for the second time, he’s bringing some of his distant American relatives on an ancestry tour in canton Bern. In the second car, Robert Thayer, his wife, his sister Gloria and her son are slightly overwhelmed by all the twists and turns up the hill. This is a road only used by locals who know where they’re going.
The mystery of history
A twist of fate is what brought the American tourists here in the first place. In 2018, Robert found out he wasn’t a Thayer. When his sister gifted two of her brothers a DNA test, their results surprisingly linked them to the Leichty family (an Americanised spelling of the Swiss surname Liechti).
“It would seem that there had been an encounter between my grandmother and the farmer across the street. We grew up not knowing our father was the illegitimate child of this relationship. We don’t even think he knew,” Robert explains.
“The Leichty and the Thayers lived in adjacent farms. They lived very close to each other,” he adds – so close that Robert and his siblings didn’t know they were going to school with their cousins. “Good thing we didn’t date them,” Robert and Gloria laugh.
The unexpected revelation and the matches provided by his DNA test got Robert into genealogy research. “Both Elizabeth and Jacob Leichty Sr. were the common ancestors to myself and my closest DNA matches, and also my paternal great-grandparents,” says Robert. “What isn’t certain and may never be is which one of their sons living at the time of dad’s conception in 1926 was our biological grandfather: Jacob Robert Jr. or his brother Frederick Ernest”.
Today Robert is a member of the Collin County Genealogical Society, of which he leads the special interest group “All things technology”, where he discusses how AI is helping to decode handwritten documents and the ethical concerns around this technology being used for genealogical research.
The research into his biological grandfather’s lineage in Switzerland is how Robert got to know Albert Liechti, his guide for the day. “About five years ago, I came across an article by AlbertExternal link published in the December 2018 newsletter of the Genealogical-Heraldic Society of Bern,” Robert says. “In that piece, he documented several generations of my ancestors, including my previously unknown fourth great-grandparents, Christen Liechti and Katharina (née Augsburger)”.
Through the article, he found Albert’s email address and got in touch with him, starting a fervent exchange of genealogical information. A couple of years later, the two decided to take a Y-DNA test, and discovered they have a common ancestor who lived in Landiswil, canton Bern, around 1530.
A Y-DNA test analyses the Y chromosome, which is passed down almost unchanged from father to son through the direct paternal line. Because only biological males carry a Y chromosome, females can’t take this test.
To trace the maternal line, both men and women can take a mtDNA test, which analyses mitochondrial DNA passed down virtually unchanged by the egg cell.
Nearly all mainstream commercial at-home kits use Autosomal DNA tests. This analyses genetical material inherited from both parents, grandparents etc, making it the best and most affordable way for finding relatives, from immediate family to 5th or 6th cousins.
A trip down history lane
For his 40th wedding anniversary, Robert and his wife decided to travel to Switzerland for the first time, to see the country where Jakob and Elizabeth Liechti lived before boarding a ship headed for New York in 1883. Albert naturally offered to take them on a small tour of the Bernese Ober- and Mittelland, to show them the houses where their ancestors lived, and the churches where they were christened and married.
Albert had already taken Robert’s cousin Siena on the same tour the year before. He meticulously researched the places of residence of some of their ancestors, chatted with the current owners about the possibility to stop by for a quick visit, and prepared a precise itinerary that would take the group up and down the Bernese hills, starting in Spiez – where Robert’s second great-grandparents got married in 1849 – and ending in Ätzlischwand, where four Liechti families lived between 1612 and 1715.
The group diligently follows Albert’s lead, who keeps a close eye on his watch to get back to the car in time to drive to the next location. Robert’s sister Gloria is fascinated by the old buildings, while her son documents their trip with his camera and they all marvel at the postcard scenery surrounding the small quiet hamlets.
“I feel like this is such a blessing,” says Robert emotionally. “I owe [Albert] so much for what he’s done, and I don’t know how to repay him. He’s like, ‘I don’t want repayment’ but I just feel like I owe him thousands of US dollars for this. Most people pay good money to have somebody take you on a tour of their homeland. I guess that’s the beauty of this passion for genealogy”.
It’s just the beginning
At their last stop in Ätzlischwand, Elisabeth and Alfred Jegerlehner, the current owners of the house and farm Albert has brought the group to see, treat everyone to a small Zvieri, a traditional Swiss-German afternoon snack. Cured meat, Swiss cheese, and biscuits are passed around, while guests and hosts exchange a few anecdotes thanks to Albert’s translation from English to Swiss German and vice-versa.
Upon departure, they all embrace each other tightly, as if they’d known each other for years, and extend mutual invites for future visits. Robert is looking forward to translating all the voice memos he’s recorded throughout the day of Albert speaking Swiss German with people they met along the way. The two distant relatives say their goodbyes, knowing they’ll be keeping in touch to advance in their genealogical research.

Iran’s top negotiator threatens ‘faster, more intense’ response to US attacks

TEHRAN – Iran’s top negotiator Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf threatened on Sept 6 to launch a “faster, more intense and more painful response” to US attacks on Iranian targets.
“The Americans must have understood that the era of proportionate responses has come to an end,” said Ghalibaf in a speech carried by state media, adding that “any aggression against Iran’s interests and security will receive a faster, more intense and more painful response”.
Iran said on Sept 6 that its forces attacked a US naval drone trying to enter the Strait of Hormuz, hours after targeting ships in retaliation for American strikes on three oil tankers.
Iran has maintained its stranglehold on the strategic Strait of Hormuz while Washington continues a counter-blockade of Iranian ports.
Washington is also seeking to choke Iran’s economy, rolling out sanctions on entities with financial links to the Islamic republic in a bid to force it into submission.
The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), the ideological arm of Iran’s military, said on Sept 6 it “attacked an American military unmanned surface vessel” attempting to enter the strait, according to a statement carried by state television.
Hours earlier, the IRGC said its naval forces “targeted three oil tankers on the unauthorised route of the Strait of Hormuz and three vessels affiliated with the child-killing America in other areas”.
It warned ships not to attempt to transit by unapproved routes.
On Sept 5, US Central Command (CENTCOM), which oversees American military operations in the region, said it struck tankers linked to the Iranian Guards, accusing the most powerful arm of the Iranian military of unsuccessfully firing at American warships.
“Following Iran’s failed attacks, CENTCOM permanently disabled the IRGC crude oil carriers M/T Downy off the coast of Kharg Island and M/T Stark 1 near Jask,” it said.
It added that it also “completely destroyed the unladen crude oil carrier M/T Kylo in the Gulf of Oman, striking the vessel in multiple critical locations to render it inoperable after the crew was directed to abandon ship”.
Video posted by CENTCOM showed large fireballs and billowing flames after projectiles slammed into the ships.
The three vessels were “part of a multibillion-dollar shadow network that funds the IRGC and its regional proxies”, it said.
‘Higher economic cost’
The Guards, meanwhile, claimed the two American warships they targeted had been “forced to retreat” after “suffering damage”, but CENTCOM said those ships successfully evaded Iranian attacks.
CENTCOM commander Admiral Brad Cooper said after the operation: “If you shoot at two of our ships, we will impose an even higher economic cost, taking out three of yours.”
The Iranian foreign ministry hit out at Washington over the strikes on oil tankers, calling them “illegal and aggressive actions”.
A correspondent for Iranian state TV in Jask in the southern province of Hormozgan said one of the tankers was empty and the second was carrying oil. The crews were transported to shore on lifeboats, they said.
Another state TV correspondent on Kharg Island said the attack there caused no casualties.
Iran’s Khatam-al Anbiya central military command warned that if the US continues its attacks, then Tehran’s retaliation against US warships will be “more severe than before, and there is a possibility of their expansion”.
The administration of US President Donald Trump has tried to downplay the significance of the six-month conflict, which has proven increasingly unpopular at home as midterm elections near.
US Vice-President J.D. Vance went so far as to say that he “wouldn’t call it a war”.
Trump reiterated that view on Sept 4, calling the war “small potatoes” for Washington.
Iran’s security chief Mohsen Rezaei warned this week that the Islamic republic had adopted a “new strategy” against Washington that “will shatter your foundations”.
The US has been trying to step up pressure on Tehran in a bid to wrestle control of the Hormuz strait, through which a fifth of world oil supplies previously flowed.
A fragile ceasefire between the two sides collapsed in July after attacks on commercial ships in the strategic waterway.
Trump has in recent weeks repeatedly threatened to claim sovereignty over the strait, even posting a map showing it as “new US territory”.
Vance has insisted the US will not reopen talks with Iran until it ends attacks on commercial shipping in Hormuz. REUTERS

Russia destroys three WHO warehouses in Ukraine over three months: organisation "deeply concerned"

Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06

Russia destroys three WHO warehouses in Ukraine over three months: organisation "deeply concerned"
Russian forces have destroyed three humanitarian warehouses belonging to the World Health Organization (WHO) in Ukraine over the past three months, including one of its main warehouses. Medical supplies intended for frontline and hard-to-reach areas were damaged as a result.
Source: WHO Regional Office for Europe (WHO/Europe)
Details: The WHO/Europe attributed the destruction of the warehouses to airstrikes, but did not mention that Russia was responsible.
Meanwhile, the organisation said one of the incidents occurred on 3 September, when Russian forces struck one of the country's largest pharmaceutical warehouses – the Biocon logistics complex in the Boryspil district of Kyiv Oblast.
The WHO also mentioned the destruction of a humanitarian warehouse in Dnipro in early August. Half of the medical supplies and equipment stored there, which were intended to assist approximately 225,000 people in frontline and hard-to-reach areas, were lost in the attack.
Another warehouse in Kyiv Oblast used by the WHO was damaged during a large-scale wave of Russian attacks on the capital and the oblast in July.
"When humanitarian warehouses storing critical supplies are attacked, the impact goes far beyond the loss of buildings or equipment. It can delay or disrupt the delivery of essential health support to people who need it most. Right now, our teams are spending valuable time and resources moving supplies from site to site to keep them safe; time and resources that should go into delivering health care, not protecting it from attack. We are deeply concerned by the growing pattern of attacks on health in Ukraine, including on humanitarian storage facilities," said Silviu Domente, WHO Representative to Ukraine, without naming the aggressor.
According to the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs, at least 20 warehouses storing humanitarian supplies have come under attack in 2026. In addition, the WHO has confirmed 15 attacks on warehouses storing medical supplies.
The organisation said it continues to work with Ukraine's Ministry of Health and other partners across the country despite the attacks. In particular, alternative ways of storing medical supplies have already been found following the latest strikes.
Quote from Domente: "We will continue to do everything we can to keep humanitarian health support moving across Ukraine. I also want to express my deepest gratitude to Ukraine's health-care workers, who continue to provide care to their communities with extraordinary courage and resilience, despite the enormous challenges they face every day."
Details: According to the WHO, this year the organisation has provided equipment and medical supplies to more than 300 facilities across the country, reaching approximately 3 million people.
Background:
- In a single attack on the night of 1-2 June, Russian forces damaged five medical facilities in Kyiv.
- As of May, Russian forces had carried out more than 3,000 attacks on Ukraine's healthcare system.

How are NATO DIANA innovators improving wound care on the front lines?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
08:07:44 UTC
17:07:44 KST

Combat wound care and management have come a long way over the last few decades. And while advances in trauma care have helped save countless lives on the battlefield, preventing infection and supporting recovery after the initial injury can be just as important.
In operational environments where evacuation may not be possible and antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is an increasing concern, there is a growing need for technologies that improve the way we treat wounds in the battlefield.
Innovators in NATO DIANA’s 2026 cohort are helping to meet that need by developing new approaches to wound care. From light-activated antimicrobial therapies to phage-based precision therapeutics and treatments, innovative solutions could revolutionise wound care for both civilian trauma patients and military personnel.
GutSee – Decoding the microbiome to treat infections
GutSee Health is a UK biotechnology company pioneering precision therapies for bacterial diseases. Its proprietary AI platform uses microbiome data to create precision treatments based on bacteriophage therapy. Phages are naturally occurring viruses that seek out and destroy specific bacteria without harming beneficial ones. This makes them useful for treating a variety of problems, from infected battlefield injuries to ongoing gut conditions like irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) and inflammatory bowel disease (IBD).
Although the science behind phage therapy is well established, developing these treatments remains fragmented, manual and focused on individual patients.
GutSee’s platform brings four key stages into one integrated process. First, it matches bacterial strains with the phages most likely to destroy them. Second, it predicts how bacteria may evolve and mutate, helping treatments stay ahead of emerging resistance. Third, it designs mixtures of several phages combined with beneficial bacteria to improve the overall bacterial balance rather than simply remove a harmful pathogen. Finally, it connects treatment design with manufacturing and clinical use. Together, these stages form a continuous learning cycle that improves treatment recommendations, accelerating therapy development by up to 98% compared with traditional laboratory-heavy processes.
GutSee is initially focusing on combat and civilian wound infections, working with NATO, governments and foundations, with support from the Ukrainian government. Longer term, GutSee plans to license its platform for further areas, including gut disorders and oncology.
LightOx – Using light to help control wound infections
LightOx is developing light-activated treatments that help kill harmful bacteria that colonise wounds. They produce a simple gel that can be applied directly to a wound. The gel is activated by a light, and the treatment helps kill harmful bacteria in a targeted way, right where the infection is developing.
In battlefield injuries, bacteria can quickly enter damaged tissue and cause infections that slow healing and increase the risk of complications, including sepsis, amputation, or even death. This is especially challenging when common antibiotics stop working against drug-resistant bacteria. LightOx’s approach offers a tool to help control infection in wounds while injured personnel await further treatment, while also fighting AMR.
Earlier this year, LightOx was recognised for its light-activated treatment for infected wounds, with an Outstanding Achievement Award at the Medilink Healthcare Business Awards 2026.
Deep Breathe – Helping medics detect hidden chest injuries faster
In battlefield trauma, injuries to the lungs or chest can be difficult to spot without hospital equipment, but failing to detect them can delay critical care. Deep Breathe, based in Canada, have developed a solution involving a portable ultrasound that frontline medical teams can use to detect serious chest and torso injuries faster, as well internal abdominal bleeding.
Deep Breathe combine ultrasound with AI that recognise signs of injuries such as a collapsed lung, bleeding in the chest, or bruising of lung tissue. Designed to work on phones or tablets and in places with limited or no connectivity, the technology could help medics make faster, more informed decisions closer to the point of injury, improving triage in remote areas and difficult environments.
By bringing this kind of support closer to the battlefield – at the point-of-injury – Deep Breathe’s solution could help improve diagnosis and treatment, avoiding unnecessary invasive procedures, and speeding up life-saving decisions when every second matters.
Biocellis – Instant detection of biological and chemical agents
After a Chemical, Biological, Radiological, and Nuclear (CBRN) attack, effective treatment requires a quick response and knowledge of the intoxicating agent. Biocellis is a company from France that has developed an ultra-sensitive diagnostic testing system that can rapidly detect and identify biological and chemical agents.
Traditionally, rapid testing methods sacrifice sensitivity and most sensitive tests do not provide results fast enough. Biocellis has patented a bioluminescence immunoassays platform that delivers laboratory grade sensitivity in less than 60 seconds. The technology uses a compact, portable format that is ideal for point-of-care and high-throughput screening.
Rapid and reliable detection helps clinicians treat patients with the most effective remedies available. Biocellis helps medical professionals understand what they are up against so that they can quickly provide the treatment and care that patients need.
These technologies are already filling some of the most urgent gaps in battlefield medicine. By giving frontline medical teams better tools to save lives and improve care when conditions are at their most challenging.
Through NATO DIANA, these innovators gain access to the tools and resources they need to take their promising, cutting-edge technologies from concept to real-world use. Through expertise from technical and defence mentors, opportunities to test their technologies, and access to operational exercises like Vigorous Warrior, innovators are supported by DIANA to ensure their solutions are not only technically strong, but deployable and relevant in the demanding environments where they are needed most.
Source: diana.nato.int

Russia Strikes Kyiv Airports Ahead of Scheduled US Delegation Arrival
Russia deliberately targeted airports in Kyiv and Boryspil overnight on September 5, in what Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said may have been a response to preparations for a possible US delegation to arrive in Ukraine by air.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Zelenskyy said the strikes marked the first deliberate Russian attacks on the two airports in a long time and linked them to discussions about allowing US representatives to fly directly into Ukraine.
“Obviously, such Russian strikes on airports are a reaction to discussions and preparations for the possibility of the American side using an aircraft to arrive in Ukraine and land at either Kyiv Airport or Boryspil Airport,” Zelenskyy said.
The Ukrainian president said Russia used Shahed-type attack drones in the strikes, describing the attack as a response to US diplomatic efforts.
Zelenskyy also said Ukraine would adjust its operation concerning Russian airspace next week, citing the risks created by drones and missiles operating over Russia. He did not provide further details on what the changes would involve.
According to Zelenskyy, the US representatives are expected to travel to Moscow and subsequently to Kyiv. Ukraine has said it is prepared to provide the necessary conditions for diplomatic travel and expects Russia to refrain from air attacks during the same period.
“Of course, there are no threats to diplomacy from our side and there will not be any. Ukraine is interested in bringing peace closer. Russia will be held accountable for what it does,” Zelenskyy said.
The overnight Russian attack also struck other locations across Ukraine. Zelenskyy said four people were killed and five wounded after a civilian enterprise was hit in Kamianske, Dnipropetrovsk region. Residential buildings were damaged in Kherson, Boryspil, and the Kharkiv region, while Russian drones targeted shopping centers in Sumy and Mykolaiv.
The airport strikes came as preparations continue for potential visits by representatives of US President Donald Trump. Zelenskyy said on September 4 that Ukraine would suspend aerial strikes against Russia for the period necessary to ensure the safe travel of Trump’s special envoy Steve Witkoff and his son-in-law Jared Kushner.

France can’t finance Ukraine forever – Le Pen party’s head
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
08:06:37 UTC
17:06:37 KST

France can’t finance Ukraine forever – Le Pen party’s head
France lacks money for itself and simply cannot keep funding Ukraine indefinitely, Jordan Bardella, the president of Marine Le Pen’s right-wing National Rally (NR) party, has said.
The main French opposition party faced harsh criticism from its rivals earlier this week after its vice president, Louis Aliot, said that NR “would turn off the tap” for Kiev if it comes to power after the 2027 presidential vote. Le Pen is seen as having strong chances to succeed in the election next year, no matter who her rival will be in the second round.
Bardella weighed in on the issue during his speech at the Ambrosetti Forum in Italy on Saturday, saying that Ukraine needs support from France and other Western nations during the conflict with Russia, but “our objective should not be to finance the war ad vitam æternam,” which means ‘forever’ in Latin.
France has a national debt of €3.5 trillion ($4.6 billion) and cannot be “giving money that we no longer have” to Vladimir Zelensky’s government, he argued.
“The extremely serious and worrying state of French public finances means we can’t give money without any guarantees or assurances that this money will be repaid one day,” the National Rally president said.
Paris has been one of the strongest backers of Kiev in the EU after the escalation of the Ukraine conflict in February 2022, providing it with billions in military aid and supplying various sophisticated weapons, including CAESAR self-propelled howitzers and Mirage fighter jets.
According to Bardella, the Americans were “much smarter” than the Europeans when it came to assistance for Kiev “because the money they gave to Ukraine is secured against rare earth mining.” He was referring to the deal agreed upon between Washington and Kiev last year, which grants the US preferential access to Ukrainian mineral resources.
During US President Donald Trump’s second term, Washington also significantly reduced aid to Ukraine, making European NATO members pay for American-made arms supplied to the country.
Earlier this week, Trump warned that he intends to present Europe with a belated bill for billions of dollars that Washington spent arming Ukraine under his predecessor, Joe Biden. He previously estimated that Biden gave Zelensky more than $300 billion worth of weapons for “free.”
Le Pen said on Thursday that the National Rally is skeptical about further assistance to Ukraine because it believes that the conflict with Russia needs a diplomatic solution.
A poll by Harris Interactive in late August suggested that Le Pen has the support of 34% of the French public, which should guarantee her a place in the second round of the presidential election, where she would likely win comfortably against either her left-wing rival Jean-Luc Mélenchon or the centrist candidate, former Prime Minister Edouard Philippe.
Russian officials said repeatedly that foreign weapons being sent to Kiev will not prevent Moscow from achieving its military goals, but will merely prolong the fighting, while increasing the risk of a direct confrontation between Russia and NATO.

2 years after Israeli forces killed Aysenur Ezgi Eygi, family still waits for justice
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
08:05:00 UTC
17:05:00 KST

Two years after Israeli forces killed Aysenur Ezgi Eygi in the occupied West Bank, her family says there has been virtually no progress toward accountability for her death.
"It's exactly where it was on day one," Hamid Ali, Eygi's husband, told Anadolu from his home in Seattle. "We're still asking for the same thing, which is an investigation as a first step into getting justice for her."
Eygi, 26, a dual Turkish-US citizen, was killed Sept. 6, 2024, while participating in a protest against Israeli settlement expansion in the West Bank town of Beita, near Nablus.
The Israeli military said she was hit "indirectly and unintentionally" by Israeli military fire that "was not aimed at her" as its forces fired at protesters allegedly throwing rocks.
Witnesses and her family disputed the Israeli account, saying she was targeted deliberately during a peaceful protest.
A Washington Post investigation found she was shot around 20 minutes after clashes had ended, when protesters had already retreated more than 200 yards (182 meters) from Israeli forces.
Then-Secretary of State Antony Blinken called Eygi's killing "unprovoked and unjustified" days after the shooting.
But two years later, the US has not opened an independent investigation into her death despite repeated calls from her family and members of Congress.
Washington instead deferred to an Israeli inquiry that has never produced a public finding.
For Eygi's father, Mehmet Suat Eygi, the absence of an investigation has left little hope that the US will deliver the accountability his family has sought.
"I don't have much hope for justice because America is the financier of Aysenur's killing. America therefore cannot investigate itself," he told Anadolu.
The lack of movement in Eygi's case comes as the number of Americans killed by Israeli forces or settlers has continued to grow.
Eygi is among 14 US citizens killed by Israeli forces or settlers since 2003, according to the rights group DAWN, which tracks the cases. None has resulted in a criminal prosecution.
The list includes Sayfollah Musallet, a 20-year-old beaten to death by settlers in the West Bank in July 2025, and Nasrallah Abu Siyam, a 19-year-old shot near Jerusalem in February.
Brad Parker, associate director of policy at the Center for Constitutional Rights and part of the legal team supporting Eygi's family, said two years have brought no US criminal investigation or other accountability measures.
“There's no new developments on the investigation front, criminal investigation from the US, or really anything focused on accountability for Aysenur's killing,” he said. "There's absolutely no follow-up, no update.”
He added that the family has little confidence that an Israeli-led investigation would produce meaningful accountability, pointing to previous cases, including that of Shireen Abu Akleh, a Palestinian-American journalist for Al Jazeera who was fatally shot on May 11, 2022.
"There's no indication that the Trump administration is interested in holding perpetrators accountable for killing American citizens in the West Bank, in Gaza, sort of anywhere," he said.
"The impunity that exists is perpetuated over the years by lack of action by the US government," Parker added.
With no independent federal investigation, the family's push for accountability has increasingly extended to Washington state, where Eygi grew up.
A joint memorial calling for a US investigation into her death advanced through the state Legislature this year but failed to win final passage before the end of the legislative session.
"The support we got from the members of the Washington State Legislature in that memorial was so heartening," Ali said.
He attributed its failure primarily to timing and legislative maneuvering, saying Republicans in the Washington State House used the limited time remaining in the session as leverage over other issues.
“I don't think it was because of lack of support. I think it was just more of a strategical kind of failure,” Ali said.
While pursuing accountability, Eygi's family and friends have also sought to preserve her memory in the community where she grew up.
Around her birthday on July 27, friends and supporters gathered in Seattle to paint a community mural of her portrait, designed by artist James Hesketh.
"It's not all negative. We've been building community," Ali said.
He said the family hopes Eygi's legacy will encourage ordinary people to believe their actions can matter.
“She’s become a symbol, and we can't really help that,” he said. “But it doesn't mean that what she did was exceptional.
“I don't think she thought by going to the West Bank and being a part of the protests, she was going to change the tide of the war or free Palestine,” he added. “But she understood that you can do something, and it does make a difference. It does have an effect.”
For Eygi's father, the two-year anniversary is also a measure of a loss that time has done little to diminish.
“It is impossible to get used to a life without Aysenur. She is always on our minds, every second,” he said.
Despite the lack of accountability, he said Eygi's emergence as a symbol of solidarity with Palestinians and protests against Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza was a source of pride.
"Ultimately, justice has not been served. What remains for us is a life without Aysenur."
Anadolu asked the US State Department whether it supports an independent investigation into Eygi’s killing, given the lack of accountability from Israel's inquiry.
“The Department of State has no higher priority than the safety and security of Americans. Embassy Jerusalem remained in touch with the family of Aysenur Eygi and the Government of Israel as it investigated this case,” it said.
The Justice Department did not respond to a request for comment. The Israeli military also did not respond.
The Turkish Foreign Ministry called Eygi's killing a "murder committed by the Netanyahu government," and Turkish prosecutors opened their own investigation into her death.
As Eygi's family enters a third year without the independent US investigation it first demanded after her killing, Ali said it is preparing for a longer fight.
"We've been developing a long-term strategy and what we want to do for Aysenur, for her legacy, but also to help others, unfortunately, who might be in a similar situation," he said.

4 killed, 20 injured in Israeli airstrikes in southern Lebanon despite US deal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
08:03:53 UTC
17:03:53 KST

Stephanie Rady and Sahin Demir
06 September 2026•Update: 06 September 2026
At least four people were killed and 20 others injured in Israeli airstrikes on several areas of southern Lebanon on Sunday morning, the Lebanese Health Ministry said, as Israel continued daily violations of a US-brokered framework agreement.
 
The ministry’s Emergency Operations Center said two people were killed and two injured in Nabatieh al-Fawqa, while eight people, including a woman and a girl, were injured in Nabatieh’s Al-Rahibat neighborhood.
 
In Arab Salim, two women were killed and six people, including two girls, were injured, while four women were wounded in Kfar Remman, the ministry said.
 
Lebanon’s National News Agency (NNA) earlier said Israeli warplanes struck a house in Arab Salim, killing two women and injuring six people, who were taken by emergency teams to hospitals in Nabatieh.
 
Israeli warplanes also struck another house in Arab Salim, completely destroying it, the agency said.
 
NNA said Israeli warplanes had carried out a series of strikes on several areas of southern Lebanon since early morning.
 
Among the targets was the home of Ali Moallem, the former mayor of Kfar Remman, near the town’s industrial area in Nabatieh district, leaving several people injured, according to the agency.
 
Israeli attacks on southern Lebanon have intensified in recent days after the Israeli army claimed it intercepted a drone that it was allegedly launched by Hezbollah toward its forces operating in what Tel Aviv calls a “security zone” in southern Lebanon.
 
The strikes come despite a US-sponsored framework agreement signed on June 26, which provides for a gradual Israeli withdrawal from Lebanese territory in exchange for the deployment of the Lebanese army.
 
Israel has carried out attacks on Lebanon since March 2, killing 4,358 people and injuring 12,359 others, while displacing more than 1 million people, according to Lebanese authorities.
 
Israel continues to occupy areas of southern Lebanon, including territory it has held for decades and other areas occupied during the 2023-2024 conflict, while its forces have advanced more than 10 kilometers into Lebanese territory during the current conflict.

The Hague’s historic jenever distillery is fighting for its life
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
08:02:35 UTC
17:02:35 KST

The Hague’s historic jenever distillery is fighting for its life
Brandon Hartley
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
The iconic Van Kleef Distillery dates back to 1776. It’s faced countless challenges since then, but the latest round could force it to close or substantially change.
For over two centuries, the Van Kleef Distillery in The Hague has been mixing up unique liqueurs and genever made with time-tested recipes. Vincent van Gogh is one of the customers known to have sampled its spirits.
Despite its rich history and status as the last remaining distillery in the city, owner Fleur Kruyt says Van Kleef is currently facing a series of setbacks that could shut down its long-time location on the Lange Beestenmarkt.
“Right now I have the same colour hair as my grandmother at the age of 96,” she told DutchNews during an interview in the distillery’ tasting room.
Kruyt has spent the past several years trying to come up with solutions to appease her landlord and city officials as she strives to expand Van Kleef’s operations, modernise its museum, and, more than anything else, prevent its doors from closing altogether.
It’s all enough to turn the hair of even the most steadfast and indomitable of small business owners completely white.
But these challenges are only the latest in Van Kleef’s tumultuous history. Over the years, it’s contended with the sudden death of an owner, a crime wave, overzealous safety inspectors, and the Covid pandemic.
The first few centuries
 The distillery dates all the way back to the late 18th century. It originally opened in 1776 as Distilleerderij “Anker” before being taken over by the Van Kleef family in 1842.
Kruyt is convinced Van Gogh stopped by at least once. The famous artist may have even been a regular given his proclivities. He lived down the street from 1869 to 1873 and spent those years working at Goupil & Cie, an art business in The Hague owned by his uncle.
Along with the rest of the Netherlands, the distillery managed to endure the impacts of the Spanish flu pandemic and two World Wars, but it was a safety inspection in 1986 that came much closer to shutting it down.
Explosive concerns
 The officials declared the 40,000 litres of alcohol sitting in the distillery’s vats were a huge safety risk that made it an almost literal ticking time bomb. They decided it was no longer safe to distill alcohol on the property.
At the time, Van Kleef was teetering on the edge of bankruptcy. The surrounding neighbourhood was considered a “no-go zone” for many of the city’s residents and the distillery wasn’t getting much foot traffic.
“If you walked these streets as a woman at night back then, you were either a prostitute or tired of your life,” Kruyt said. “There was lots of criminality. No one came here anymore.”
After much discussion and planning, production was moved off site. The building itself was purchased by a local development company called Stadsherstel Den Haag and Van Kleef officially became a tenant in its long-time home.
The books were eventually balanced after it attained historical status and Van Kleef finally reopened as a multipurpose operation in 1995. Along with the museum and a tasting room, Van Kleef’s liqueurs are bottled and labelled there to this day.
Even more setbacks
 The construction of a tram tunnel and the redesign of the street out front dragged on for over a decade and further drove customers away.
The distillery’s revenue dropped by 80% when the city began installing barriers around the neighbourhood to discourage auto traffic in 2009. Its suppliers and customers had to navigate a maze every time they tried to go there.
Kruyt, who was operating Van Kleef with her husband Louis Centazzo at the time, was forced to use their house as collateral on a loan to keep it open. Then he suddenly died in 2015, leaving her to manage the distillery on her own.
Foreclosure followed and Kruyt moved into an apartment on the property. The hits kept coming as gentrification quickly transformed the neighbourhood and raised the distillery’s monthly rent along with it.
Then the Covid crisis began, which forced Van Kleef to shut down its tasting room. Undaunted, Kruyt and her crew came up with clever ways to ensure revenue would keep coming in.
She joked that “booze was declared a necessity” during the pandemic. Kruyt developed a “vaccine” after inspiration struck while she was giving her dog injections for arthritis. “The Van Kleef Vaccine” is a mix of Limoncello, Vitamin C, and ginger-infused liqueur.
At first, Kruyt fretted that it wouldn’t go over well with customers who had spent weeks social distancing and worrying they’d be the next ones to catch Covid. Those fears proved unfounded.
“And the first people who bought it? Doctors and pharmacists,” she recalled. “They found it really cool. I thought, ‘If these people find it funny, I don’t care about the rest!’”
A “ginitiser” sold in spray bottles soon followed. It, too, was a hit.
The current dilemmas
 “We’ve always managed and, whenever I feel bad, I turn on the television and see how it could be a lot worse,” Kruyt said before discussing the latest round of threats to the distillery.
The city’s decision to impose a flat €50-a-day parking fee has taken another bite out of Van Kleef’s revenue. The policy was so controversial it was even covered by The Guardian in 2023. If all this wasn’t enough, Kruyt broke her ankle while on a summer holiday and the recovery process required several surgeries.
Determined to keep the distillery where it’s been for over 200 years, Kruyt has been combating another wave of financial woes coupled with bureaucratic headaches, soaring energy bills, and other increased costs. Even the price of the glass that goes into Van Kleef’s bottles has gone up recently.
A crowdfunding campaign has been underway since 2025. Plans were also made to expand operations to attract more visitors, but negotiations with Stadsherstel Den Haag have proven challenging.
After over two years of discussions about everything from the future of the museum to renovations for the apartments on the property, Kruyt said the situation has been handed over to a new director named Jan-Willem de Bruijn.
“Stadsherstel Den Haag is currently taking a comprehensive look at the complex,” De Bruijn told DutchNews. “This means that, in addition to the shop and the tasting room, we are also focusing on the redevelopment of the museum and garden as well as upgrades in the apartments. In doing so, we aim to invest sustainably in the preservation of this unique and characteristic part of The Hague.”
Delays with permitting haven’t helped. DutchNews contacted the office of Alderwoman Saskia Bruines for comment about this and other matters concerning the distillery, but had not received a response as of press time.
Fighting onward
 Regardless of what happens next, Kruyt says Van Kleef will continue in one form or another, even if that means turning it into a distillery-and-wholesaler-only operation at a facility closed to the public and likely located on the outskirts of The Hague.
“But all of this history would go away,” she said as she gestured towards the centuries-old equipment in Van Kleef’s museum.
Takeaway liqueurs and tastings have covered the costs of maintaining the distillery’s historical inventory, but the current circumstances have made that impossible to continue. As Kruyt faces another round of discussions with Stadsherstel Den Haag, she’s determined to stay optimistic.
“We met with Jan-Willem a few weeks ago,” she said. “We’re really happy that he is taking everything seriously and trying to preserve the heritage that we have here.”
Still open for business
 Visitors to Van Kleef can currently visit the small museum, enjoy drinks and snacks in its tasting room, host gatherings in a former storage cellar turned conference room, and purchase bottles of liqueurs made with recipes that date back to the 17th century.
Among them is Bridal Tears, which contains flakes of 24-carat gold. It was once a popular wedding gift. The bawdy tales and traditions surrounding it and two accompanying liqueurs could fill an entire book.
In an age of alcoholic beverages with preservatives and other ingredients that are difficult to describe, let alone pronounce the names of, Van Kleef is still doing things the old-fashioned way.
“All of our recipes have been preserved,” Kruyt said. “We have an archive full of them that began in the 1840s. Everything you’re tasting is real in the sense that there’s no artificial flavouring or colourings.”
The distillery continues to attract international visitors and aficionados of liqueurs. Kruyt said a few of them are household names, but she demurred when asked for the details.
“What happens at Van Kleef, stays at Van Kleef,” she said. “So any celebrities out there, you can come here and we won’t talk about you.”

Which overseas property markets will be the winners and losers if Fed raises US rates?
Fed chairman’s focus on inflation at meeting last month has heightened expectations of monetary tightening
Comments by US Federal Reserve chairman Kevin Warsh at its annual economic policy symposium in Jackson Hole last month have reinforced expectations of an impending interest rate rise in the world’s largest economy, which would have significant impacts on assets and investors around the world.
In the wake of Warsh’s comments, analysts said several property markets were more sensitive to higher interest rates in the United States and some stood to benefit.
Hong Kong
With the local currency pegged to the US dollar in a trading band of HK$7.75 to HK$7.85, property agents said any Fed movement would be mirrored by the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA), the city’s de facto central bank.
“The HKMA’s base rate tracks the Fed’s moves and borrowing costs linked to Hibor [the Hong Kong interbank offered rate] follow suit,” said Pamela Ambler, head of Asia-Pacific investor intelligence at consultancy JLL. “With Hong Kong’s debt costs rising in contrast to China’s … that makes Hong Kong less attractive to southbound capital from mainland China.”
Based on the frequency of pinyin surnames in purchase records, US-based investment bank JPMorgan Chase has estimated that mainland buyers have, in recent times, accounted for 29 per cent of home sales volumes in Hong Kong and 37 per cent of their value.
And in the second quarter of this year, mainland-based investors were the second-largest non-local buyers of commercial property assets in the city, with purchases worth HK$1.23 billion (US$157 million), behind Singapore-based investors’ HK$3.37 billion, according to Colliers.

London mayoral contenders limber up for a race that is Sadiq Khan’s to lose
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
08:00:00 UTC

The bicycles have been brought out and eager fists are getting ready to knock on hundreds of doors as the race for one of the most sought-after jobs in British politics springs into action.
Sadiq Khan has had a vice-like grip on London, but a range of candidates hoping to unseat him in 2028 have announced themselves. The three-time mayor has been coy about whether he will stand again, and said he would make a decision next year.
At the weekend, the former home secretary James Cleverly was seen riding a wobbly Lime bike through London, declaring that “London Bridge has got its mojo back” and that he has a “soft spot for Ealing”, where he met his wife, Susie. Cleverly, the MP for Braintree in Essex, has declared he will seek to be the Conservative mayoral candidate.
“I’m going to run as an aspirational, entrepreneurial, forward-thinking Conservative candidate that is in tune with the city,” he said, adding that he thought he could beat Khan even though London is a left-leaning city: “London is a much more pragmatic city when it comes to voting.”
Also standing in the contest to become the Tory mayoral candidate is Festus Akinbusoye, a Westminster councillor and Britain’s first ever black police commissioner. He says he is the right candidate because he is a “fresh face”, adding: “I’ve not been part of a government in the past, but I come with solid private sector experience.”
But the contest appears to be Khan’s to lose, at the moment. A recent poll by Savanta UK for the Mile End Institute, Queen Mary University of London, put Labour’s candidate in the mayoral race on 33%, the Tories 18%, Reform UK 18%, Green party 17% and Liberal Democrats 9%,.
The Conservatives’ bid to unseat Khan is complicated by the presence of Reform. Laila Cunningham, a former Crown Prosecution Service prosecutor, is Reform’s candidate. She has been pounding the streets of London since the beginning of this year trying to drum up support.
“I’m not stepping aside for the Tories,” she told the Guardian. “How many times have they tried to unseat Khan? They have failed.”
Cleverly, she says, is “literally the establishment and he’s gone from one ministerial job from another”. She thinks he will be picked as the Tory mayoral candidate and said: “It will be two Sirs versus a woman. Sir Khan and Sir Cleverly.”
Though the rightwing vote looks evenly divided between Tories and Reform, she is confident she can charm some of Khan’s voters: “It is not a left or right divide either, we won nine seats in Barking and Dagenham in the local elections, where the Tories wouldn’t dream of winning one.”
Cunningham, the daughter of Egyptian immigrants, said she was “not your typical Reform person. People often see me and say they are surprised I am in Reform.”
Akinbusoye is on the licensing committee of Westminster council, which is consulting to restrict “vertical drinking” in pubs – standing and drinking. Cunningham said: “That says it all. The fact they even call it vertical drinking is a joke.”
The Labour MP Dawn Butler hinted at her intention to run this week: a video of herself walking past a sign reading “a new Dawn for London”, captioned: “When London puts up signs saying ‘A New Dawn’ … what else was I supposed to do?”
She first floated her mayoral ambitions in 2023, and has since confirmed to the Guardian that she would run as soon as Khan confirmed he would not seek a third term. Khan did not respond to a request for comment.
There are no obvious contenders in sight for the Greens, with the party’s attention focused on its leader Zack Polanksi’s plan to fight the Holborn and St Pancras byelection. A Green party source said: “We do have a number of people who’d be incredible candidates but no firm name. We feel confident after our latest local election results that Londoners will be excited by our vision for London.”
Would Cunningham rather fight Butler or Khan? “[Khan’s] got incumbency. He may do better. It doesn’t make a difference because it’s what the party represents, she seems to think he was a great mayor so she seemingly wants more of the same.”

The automotive industry maintained its strong export performance during the eight-month period despite challenges in global trade, fluctuations in demand conditions and supply chain disruptions caused by geopolitical tensions in the Middle East.

Indonesia’s most dangerous fires are burning underground
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
07:57:45 UTC
16:57:45 KST

Indonesia’s most dangerous fires are burning underground
- Date:
- September 6, 2026
- Source:
- NASA Earth Observatory
- Summary:
- Indonesia’s dangerous peat fires are surging early in the 2026 fire season as a strengthening El Niño and severe drought dry out wetlands that can burn underground for months. These slow smoldering fires are especially destructive because they release far more fine particles and several pollutants than typical tropical forest fires, while thick smoke can make them difficult for satellites to detect.
- Share:
Tropical peatland fires rank among the most dangerous and stubborn fires on Earth. Instead of racing through trees and vegetation, these fires smolder through dried wetland soils and large deposits of peat, often continuing underground at relatively low temperatures. That makes them extremely difficult to extinguish and exceptionally polluting.
By one estimate, peat fires produce three times more fine particulate matter than other tropical forest fires, along with five times more sulfur dioxide, three times more organic carbon, and twice as much methane and carbon monoxide.
Satellite Images Reveal Indonesia's Fire Season
Indonesia's 2026 fire season was already underway when the MODIS (Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer) instrument aboard NASA's Aqua satellite captured an image of the region on September 1, 2026.
On the annotated map, each red dot represents a "fire detection." This means the satellite sensor and an algorithm identified a pixel containing thermal anomalies associated with fire. A single fire can produce multiple detections.
Peat fires are a persistent problem in Indonesia, which contains about 36 percent of the world's tropical peatlands. During severe droughts, these normally wet landscapes can dry enough to ignite. Over the past three decades, such conditions have repeatedly produced long-lasting fires that blanket large areas in smoke for weeks and disrupt the lives of millions of people.
El Niño Is Intensifying the Dry Season
Wildfires occur in Indonesia every year, but some of the most destructive seasons in recent decades came during El Niño, particularly in 1997 and 2015.
NOAA assessed El Niño as present and strengthening in August 2026. The climate pattern commonly reduces rainfall across Indonesia. The drying can become even more pronounced when El Niño occurs alongside a positive phase of the Indian Ocean Dipole, which was also underway.
"Indonesia is only about three weeks into its fire season, but we're seeing fire activity track sharply upward, similar to 2015," said Robert Field, a Columbia University researcher who developed a tool called the Global Fire Weather Database that produces experimental, real-time fire weather forecasts.
"The strong El Niño is making the dry season drier over the fire-prone parts of the country and exacerbating burning -- just as we anticipated it would," he said.
The comparison with 2015 is significant. After more than three months of burning that year, Indonesia's fires had emitted 1.75 billion tons of greenhouse gas equivalents -- more than Japan emits in an entire year. By September 2, the 2026 fires had been burning for about a month and had already released roughly 10 percent of the amount produced during the 2015 crisis.
Underground Peat Fires Can Burn for Months
Indonesia was also experiencing severe, widespread drought during the summer of 2026, much as it did in 2015. Data from the Indonesian meteorological agency showed that about 90 percent of the country received little or no rainfall in early August.
Under normal conditions, peat deposits in Kalimantan, Sumatra, and Papua are too wet for fire to move underground. Drought changes that dramatically, allowing flames to enter the peat itself and continue smoldering below the surface.
"Surface fires are less of a concern, but when fires get underground, they just won't stop," Field said. "They'll keep burning until the rains come in October or November."
Indonesia relies on observations from NASA and NOAA satellites to follow active fires in near-real-time. MODIS and VIIRS are among the main instruments used. Indonesia's Ministry of Forestry operates the SiPongi fire-monitoring platform using MODIS and VIIRS data, and the system counted 946 hotspots on August 31, 2026.
The Worst Fires Can Be Hardest to See From Space
Satellite monitoring has important limitations, however. MODIS and VIIRS can struggle to detect fires hidden by thick smoke or clouds, burning beneath the forest canopy, or smoldering underground inside peat deposits.
In fact, when Indonesian fires become especially intense, the number of fires detected by MODIS or VIIRS can sometimes decline because the smoke itself blocks the satellites' view.
"The worst smoke events, paradoxically, can be the hardest to observe from space with MODIS and VIIRS," said Mark Cochrane, an ecologist at the University of Maryland Center for Environmental Science who has conducted field research on peat fires in Indonesia for nearly a decade.
Some of Indonesia's modern fire vulnerability can be traced back decades. According to Cochrane, extensive construction of irrigation canals and drainage of peat swamps during the 1990s, undertaken in part to create massive rice farms, lowered water tables across wetland areas and made the landscape more combustible. Oil palm plantations and other plantation forestry are also widespread in the region.
Following the unusually grim fire season of 2015, governments and other organizations attempted to reverse some of that damage. Projects have included blocking irrigation canals to help restore wetlands, strengthening firefighting capabilities, and stepping up efforts to prevent accidental human ignitions.
2026 Could Be a Major Test of Fire Protections
"This year will be a real stress test of the measures that were put in place after 2015," said Shi Jun Wee, a University of Maryland graduate student.
Wee is part of a team working with NASA and MapBiomas to develop improved methods for spotting understory fires that MODIS and VIIRS may miss. Their approach uses shortwave infrared observations from Landsat and Sentinel-2 satellites.
As the 2026 fire season continues, Wee plans to follow conditions using NASA's Worldview data browser, FIRMS (Fire Information for Resource Management System), HLS (Harmonized Landsat and Sentinel-2) observations, and GFED (Global Fire Emissions Database).
Hazardous Smoke Is Already Disrupting Daily Life
For people living in Indonesia and neighboring countries, the effects are already being felt. Indonesian officials have warned that large portions of the population have been exposed to hazardous smoke.
According to news reports, some schools have begun switching to remote learning, nine national parks have closed, and several flights have been delayed because of heavy smoke.
Cochrane cautioned that attention to the problem often rises during major El Niño fire seasons and fades once conditions improve.
"People tend to focus on these fires during an El Niño and then forget about them," Cochrane said. "We need sustained focus, even during the years when they aren't as bad, to solve this," he said. "These fires create a tremendous amount of emissions."
Story Source:
Materials provided by NASA Earth Observatory. Original written by Adam Voiland. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

Lithuania’s fiercest storms: A history of extreme weather and growing risks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
07:56:40 UTC
16:56:40 KST

By Karolina Aleknavičė, LRT.lt.
The severe storm that swept across Lithuania last month is likely to go down in the country’s weather history, according to Donatas Valiukas, head of the Climate and Research Division at Lithuania’s Hydrometeorological Service.
While powerful storms are relatively uncommon in Lithuania, the country has experienced several destructive events over the past decades – some causing deaths, widespread power outages and major damage to infrastructure.
One of the most severe struck October 17-18, 1967, when hurricane-force winds battered western Lithuania. In Klaipėda, winds reached 40 metres per second, while individual gusts may have reached 55 metres per second, according to the Hydrometeorological Service.
The storm, known as Lena in Sweden, destroyed the Palanga pier, damaged dunes and flooded parts of Klaipėda. Some 3 million to 4 million cubic meters of timber were blown down across the Samogitia region.
Another major storm, Anatol, hit Lithuania in December 1999. Wind gusts reached 40 meters per second in some areas and produced waves up to 6 metres high. A Norwegian vessel, the Seines, was washed ashore near Palanga and was not pulled back into the sea until April 2000.

Indonesia’s Anak Krakatoa volcano erupts, disrupting flights at 6 airports
The suspension of operations at the airports affected 209 flights and more than 22,000 passengers
Indonesia halted operations at its main international airport outside Jakarta on Sunday after ash spewed from the Anak Krakatoa volcano more than 150km (93 miles) away, impacting thousands of passengers.
Mount Anak Krakatoa erupted on Saturday, producing a fountain of lava and booming sounds that could be heard up to a few hundred kilometres away, the geology agency said in a statement.
Two new eruptions were recorded on Sunday, the volcanology agency warned.
Ash from the volcano was detected in the airspace surrounding Soekarno-Hatta International Airport, prompting authorities to initially suspend operations from 1.30am on Sunday to 5.30am.

Operations have been suspended at six airports including the Hussein Sastranegara airport in Bandung and Radin Inten II airport near Bandar Lampung on Sumatra, the country’s Transportation Minister Dudy Purwagandhi said.
