====================================================================================================

Far-right surge challenges Germany’s postwar taboo as AfD closes in on historic state victory
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
05:18:48 UTC
14:18:48 KST

Germany’s political attention is fixed Sunday on the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt, where an election in a region of just 2.1 million people could become one of the most consequential moments in German politics since World War II. For the first time since 1945, a far-right party could win enough power to govern a German state.
Alternative for Germany, or AfD, enters the vote with a commanding lead. The latest ZDF poll put the party at 41%, compared with 23% for the Christian Democratic Union, or CDU, of incumbent state premier Sven Schulze. Another poll placed the AfD as high as 43%. That would represent close to a doubling of its 20.8% result in the previous Saxony-Anhalt election in 2021. The party has also surged nationally: in Germany’s 2025 federal election it doubled its support from 10.4% to 20.8%, becoming the largest opposition party in the Bundestag.
But winning the most votes does not necessarily mean taking power. Germany’s major parties have so far refused to enter coalitions with the AfD, maintaining the political “firewall” designed to isolate it. The party’s 35-year-old candidate for state premier, Ulrich Siegmund, has said he is not interested in coalition partners either and would seek the premiership only if the AfD wins an absolute majority and can govern alone.
That makes Germany’s 5% electoral threshold one of the biggest variables in Sunday’s vote. Parties that fail to cross it are excluded from the distribution of parliamentary seats, meaning the AfD would not necessarily need 50% of the popular vote to control more than half the legislature. The more votes cast for parties that fail to enter parliament, the greater the AfD’s relative share of seats could become.
The Social Democrats, or SPD, and the Greens are projected by some polls to clear the threshold, though the Greens remain close to the danger zone at around 5% to 6%. The Free Democratic Party, or FDP, and the Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance, BSW, are expected to fall short.
The prospect of an AfD majority has even triggered a campaign for tactical voting, urging opponents of the party to back the SPD or Greens even if they would not normally support them, simply to ensure those parties cross the threshold and reduce the AfD’s share of seats. As a result, one of the central questions Sunday is not only who finishes first, but how many parties make it into parliament at all.
“No matter what tomorrow’s result is, we have already made history,” Siegmund told an AfD closing rally in Magdeburg on Saturday night. “What we started here in Saxony-Anhalt, and what is now sweeping across all of Germany, can no longer be stopped.”
Immigration, schools and Pride flags
An AfD government in Saxony-Anhalt would have consequences far beyond symbolism. Germany’s states wield broad powers over education, culture and internal security, while also holding seats in the Bundesrat, the upper house of the federal parliament. Saxony-Anhalt controls four of its 69 votes.
In its “Vision 2026” platform, the AfD lays out how it would use that authority. The party pledges to launch a deportation drive and establish a task force to accelerate removals, reduce reliance on foreign workers it describes as coming from “culturally foreign backgrounds,” and challenge the status of Ukrainian refugees.
In schools, the AfD proposes placing refugee children in separate classes, returning students with disabilities to special education frameworks, banning Pride flags and requiring the German flag to be flown daily. It also wants to reshape school curricula in what it describes as a more patriotic direction, restrict Islamic practices including the Muslim call to prayer, dismantle the state’s current public broadcasting structure and withdraw funding from certain cultural institutions.
Ahead of the election, ynet spoke with two Jewish figures who have extensive experience with both antisemitism and Germany’s far right: Max Privorozki, chairman of the Jewish community in Halle, where a neo-Nazi gunman tried to storm a synagogue on Yom Kippur in 2019 before murdering two people outside; and Stephan Kramer, a German Jew who has headed the domestic intelligence agency in neighboring Thuringia since December 2015.
“Alternative must be under surveillance,” Kramer said. “There are strong indications that influential parts of the party are acting against human dignity and the German Constitution and are working against the democratic order.” He noted that the AfD has been classified as a confirmed far-right extremist organization by local domestic intelligence authorities in Thuringia and, since 2023, in Saxony-Anhalt.
At the federal level, the legal picture is more complicated. Germany’s domestic intelligence agency, the BfV, announced in May 2025 that it was classifying the AfD as a confirmed far-right extremist organization, but later temporarily suspended use of that designation pending a legal challenge by the party. The Saxony-Anhalt branch itself remains classified by the state intelligence service as confirmed far-right extremist.
“The party’s appeal comes from a mixture of protest, distrust of the traditional parties, concern about immigration and social change, and the sense that it is talking about problems the other parties ignore,” Kramer said. “In that sense, some of the attraction is also a symptom of the failure of the other parties to reach these voters. There are even Jews who support it because of its positions on Israel, Islam, security and immigration, despite the fact that it is an extremist party.”
Kramer cautioned against confusing control of one German state with control of the country as a whole. “You have to put things in proportion. In the upper house, it would have only four votes out of 69,” he said. “But if it forms a government, it will have power, access to sensitive information and the ability to appoint people in the police, intelligence services, security forces and the Interior Ministry. Using the machinery of government could also give the party momentum at the federal level.”
‘Jews don’t have the luxury of choosing whom to fear’
For Germany’s Jewish community, Kramer said, the contradiction surrounding the AfD is particularly stark. “Alternative presents itself as supporting Jewish life and Israel,” he said. “But it opposes kosher slaughter, it has leaders who use conspiracy theories and antisemitic language, and senior figures who want to challenge the way Germany deals with its historical responsibility and focus less on the darkest years of German history.”
“The problem is not that every Alternative voter is an antisemite,” he added. “The problem is that parts of the party promote ethno-nationalist ideas of belonging and want to weaken institutions that were built specifically after 1945 to protect democracy and minorities. At that point, the question is no longer whether Alternative is good for Jews, but whether liberal democracy is capable of protecting Jewish life and other minorities, whose rights can exist only if everyone is equal before the law.”
German law bans the public use of Nazi symbols and slogans, as well as Holocaust denial and the trivialization of Nazi crimes. Kramer said several senior AfD figures have repeatedly tested those limits. “There are leaders in the party who have clearly crossed the forbidden lines,” he said. “Björn Höcke, the party leader in Thuringia, was convicted of using the Nazi slogan ‘Everything for Germany.’ There are other examples of him using similar language. He is a trained history teacher. He knows what he is talking about. But in general, their language is much more sophisticated: coded language with several meanings that pushes and tests the boundaries of the law.”
Kramer said even banning the party would not solve the deeper social forces behind its rise. “Democracy cannot and should not ban frustration, anger or radical political opinions,” he said. “You have to act against an organization that works against the Constitution and the democratic order, but that will not address the social problem it represents. We have to ask why 40% do support it. That question should have been asked 10 years ago. If there is a ban in order to protect our democracy, the real challenge will begin the day after.”
Kramer has previously said he would consider leaving if the AfD came to power. He is now more cautious, but says the concern remains. “I still work in Thuringia, but of course my family and I are taking precautions for the possibility that a far-right party forms a government in a German state.”
Asked what it would mean if roughly 40% of voters backed the AfD but people nevertheless celebrated because it failed to win an outright majority, Kramer said the result would be deeply ambiguous. “First of all, it means that the majority, 60%, did not vote for the party,” he said. “But I hope people will be shocked and understand the danger our democracy is in and what needs to be done. It would be a very ambivalent moment. It would show how far the political center of gravity has shifted and how much our standard for political stability has been lowered.”
Kramer also rejected attempts to rank the threats facing German Jews today, whether from the far right or from the convergence of parts of the far left and Islamist movements since October 7. “I would take that argument seriously,” he said. “Last year there were 8,725 antisemitic incidents, more than three times the number in 2022, and 68% were classified as Israel-related antisemitism. That is a physical, immediate and visible problem that threatens Jewish life every day.”
The figures correspond with the 2025 annual report by Germany’s RIAS antisemitism monitoring organization.
“But far-right rule is dangerous in a different way, through appointments, budget priorities, education and memory culture,” Kramer said. “This is a party where many far-right extremists and antisemites have found a home. Jews today do not have the luxury of choosing whom to fear. The authorities have not helped them on this point. They have left that field open to Alternative as well.”
For Kramer, Saxony-Anhalt could serve as a preview of what lies ahead for Germany. “It is certainly a warning of what could happen,” he said. “This is a party that was once on the fringes of German politics, and today, without substantially changing its platform, it can govern.”
He said he sees three possible consequences. “The first is that people get used to it and understand that if it gets numbers like these, it has to be taken into account, and then the psychological barrier breaks. The second is that the eastern states become a laboratory where we can see how Alternative functions in government. And the third is what we are seeing now: parties band together simply to keep it out. That was possible when it was at 10%. When it reaches 25%, 35% or more, you cannot freeze it out forever.”
‘If I leave Germany, it will be for the same reason I left the Soviet Union’
In Halle, where a neo-Nazi gunman tried to storm the synagogue on Yom Kippur in October 2019 and murdered two people after failing to enter, the election is being watched particularly closely. Max Privorozki, chairman of the city’s Jewish community, said the past seven years have left little room for optimism.
“What happened on October 7 overshadowed even the attack on the synagogue on Yom Kippur,” he said. “Everything that has happened to us since leaves us little room for optimism, especially antisemitism and the connection between the far left and radical Islam.”
He said the rise of populist and extremist parties is not accidental. “There is disappointment here with the policies of the authorities in Germany and the European Union,” he said. “Disappointment with current politics causes people to look for alternatives, sometimes simply for the sake of an alternative. People do not always ask whether these parties are actually capable of solving the problems. I hope we manage to hit the brakes before it is too late.”
Despite the concerns, Privorozki insisted that Halle’s Jewish community has no intention of disappearing. “Whatever happens, Jewish life in Halle and Saxony-Anhalt will continue,” he said. “We have had problems in the past and dealt with them. There is no discussion of leaving.”
Then he added: “I left the Soviet Union because I did not want to continue living in a totalitarian state. If one day I leave Halle and Germany, it will be for the same reason I left the Soviet Union 37 years ago.”
Polls close at 6 p.m. local time, with initial results expected immediately afterward. Germany will then learn whether Saxony-Anhalt has simply become another powerful AfD stronghold, or whether it has broken the final postwar barrier preventing a far-right party from governing a German state.

Kintsu, Colchester, Essex: ‘Style as well as substance’ – restaurant review
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
05:00:58 UTC
14:00:58 KST

Amid all the bunting and hoopla of the platinum jubilee back in 2022, you may well have missed that Colchester, Britain’s oldest recorded settlement, got an upgrade from town to city status. And, as we all know, no true city is complete without at least one fancy restaurant that serves the likes of duck liver mousse on lattice tuiles. Well, in Colchester, Kintsu takes that slot.
Or at least it did until May 2025, when chef Paul Wendholt abruptly shut up shop, citing financial pressures. The name Kintsu plays on the term kintsugi, the Japanese art of repairing pottery with gold, silver or platinum or, more commonly, of embracing imperfection and making something pleasing out of bad luck. So it’s rather fitting that Wendholt, a two-time winner of the Essex Chef of the Year gong, managed to reopen Kintsu just four months later, and a year on is now offering eight courses, plus a few extras, for £90 a head in a Grade II-listed building, albeit one that’s down a back lane beside a multi-storey NCP car park. The setting will win no beauty contests, but when a man is so determined to cook dinner, it feels churlish to ignore him. Come for the secure parking, stay for the treacle-cured Dingley Dell pork from nearby Suffolk and the Colchester cherries with amaretto.
Even the very idea of a tasting menu will deter some customers: too faffy, too fiddly. But here, from the first warm-up snack – whipped Montgomery cheddar in a fluted tartlet casing under a blanket of crunchy yeast and yet more cheese – even the hardest of the “I just want me dinner” brigade might find their hearts softening. This is followed by that duck liver mousse-topped tuile with glossy, amber beads of onion gel piped on top and a fat, postage stamp-sized chunk of bread pudding piled with ricotta, lemon, and raw peas and shoots. Style as well as substance.
Hunks of warm sourdough arrive, clearly fresh from the oven and reminding you how sweet and fragrant sourdough can be, especially when it’s spread with glorious Fen Farm butter. A plague upon all that hard, spongy nonsense served up and down the land as a plinth for scrambled eggs. While we work our way through these opening snacks, Lionel Richie’s Dancing on the Ceiling plays in the background, and the bread turns up to Shattered Dreams by Johnny Hates Jazz. By the time the Braxted tomatoes arrive, we are deep into Living in a Box territory, which feels about right for a Saturday lunchtime in a listed barn. Why can’t all restaurants play mid-1980s chart music?
Those first course tomatoes are a rhapsody of very good fruit arranged strategically on silky whipped pecorino with a wicked green basil oil. It is 1pm on a Saturday and we are on one of only two tables occupied. The minimal staff – two in the kitchen and one on the floor – couldn’t be lovelier, ferrying thick, chunky and squat Cornish crab tarts that look almost like mince pies. There’s lots of brown meat layered under the white, and very good, crunchy pastry. This is good, thoughtful, clever cooking that errs on the side of tasty rather than flippant. I wish more people were here to taste it, but they are probably all at a bottomless brunch somewhere, eating ethylene-ripened avocado mush on fumaric acid-injected bread that tastes of old flip-flops. More fool them.
  We, meanwhile, are having wild Suffolk bass, its skin all crisp and blistered, cooked precisely and served on a foamed sauce flecked with chives and beads of orange oil. Next up, that treacle-cured pork, which is hot, juicy, pitch-black around the edges, and comes layered with sweet raw and cooked apple. At this point, a third booking arrives, which is great for Kintsu but curtails my enthusiastic crooning along to The Closest Thing to Heaven by the Kane Gang. The strongest course comes next in the form of Herdwick lamb, and features a moist, well-seasoned medallion with a dark, rich jus, tiny nests of shredded turnip, and yet more lamb, roasted, pulled and compacted on to a metal skewer, and topped with cream and shredded mint.
A pre-pudding of yoghurt, raspberry and lemon resets the mouth. Then an inventive dessert of Colchester cherries, both cooked and preserved, and served on something biscuity, something creamy and something with a whiff of amaretto. It doesn’t look like much on the plate – a collapsed Jenga of dessert ideas – but it is utterly fabulous. We pay the bill over slices of homemade fig-leaf fudge that I would happily hand out in boxes at Christmas. Or eat alone on the sofa.
Kintsu is a huge example of a small regional indie doing its very best in rather weird times. Use these places or lose them. Right now, Kintsu is open: beautifully restored, with shimmers of gold.
- 
  Kintsu 11a North Hill, Colchester, Essex, 01206 574361. Open lunch Fri & Sat, noon-1.30pm (last orders); dinner Weds-Sat, 6.30-8pm (8.30pm Fri & Sat; last orders). Tasting menus only, five courses for £65 or eight for £90, both plus drinks and service

Memory of water: the women reshaping Venice – in pictures
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
05:00:58 UTC
14:00:58 KST

Venice is a city of tradition and projection, a place feeding the imagination of millions of people arriving from elsewhere. The “impossible city”, suspended on water, often appears unchanged, fixed in time. Yet, like the water that carries it, the city is in constant, subtle transformation.
We often speak of Venice as if it were immobile. We call it timeless, suspended outside history, untouched by change. But Venice is changing. It is fragile, exposed, under pressure. On one side, rising sea levels and increasingly unpredictable tides are reshaping the lagoon and threatening a delicate equilibrium. On the other, mass tourism continues to transform the city from within. Homes become short-term rentals, local businesses give way to visitor-oriented commerce, and residents leave the historic centre in steadily increasing numbers. The spaces left empty by those who move away are often filled by tourism itself, both a cause and a consequence of this transformation.
Yet beyond the dominant narratives of overtourism and climate breakdown, another, quieter transformation is taking place. Venice lies on contradictions – appearance and structure, illusion and rootedness. One of these tensions emerges in the role of women in shaping the city’s identity. While many Venetian traditions are historically grounded in women’s labour, from lace-making to textile work and other forms of craftsmanship, women have long been excluded from what in Venice constitutes public space: water.
In Venice, water functions as the street. The city is crossed by about 150 navigable canals, which remain its main routes for movement, work and social exchange. For centuries, these waterways have been spaces governed by explicit rules and implicit codes that largely excluded women. As in many other cities where women have historically been marginalised from the street, in Venice they have been marginalised from the water. From navigating boats, from professions such as gondoliera and sandolista, from boatbuilding and competitive rowing. Today, these boundaries are beginning to shift.
The journalist Anna Toniolo has lived with Venice her entire life, having been born and raised only a few kilometres from the city. This project grew from years of observing Venice and from a shared awareness, with photographer Daniela Sala, that some of the city’s most vital spaces remain inaccessible to women – not through formal prohibition, but through traditions deeply embedded in everyday life. Between November 2025 and March 2026, they spent weeks documenting the experiences of women whose work and lives are closely connected to the lagoon, through field reporting, interviews and observation, seeking stories that challenge the dominant image of Venice.
The stories gathered in this project reveal how women are reclaiming space precisely through tradition, carrying forward skills and professions that have long defined Venetian identity while simultaneously reshaping them.
In 2010, Giorgia Boscolo became the first woman to obtain a gondolier licence, breaking a centuries-old barrier and opening the way for others. Today, women practising the profession are still few. According to fellow gondoliers, those actively working can be counted on the fingers of two hands, although more women have passed the qualification exam in recent years. There are about 440 licensed gondoliers in Venice, alongside approximately 200 substitutes – qualified gondoliers who have passed the exam but do not yet hold their own licence.
A similar profession is that of the sandolista, who rows a sandolo, a traditional flat-bottomed Venetian boat once widely used for everyday transport across the lagoon. Today, there are only about 20 sandolisti left, and just one of them is a woman: Chiara Curto.
In the city’s remaining squeri – the traditional boatyards where wooden boats are built and repaired – Silvia Scaramuzza is the only female maestra d’ascia, or master boatbuilder. Other women are creating new paths into these spaces.
In 2020, Marta Canino founded “Fie a Manetta”, a name that roughly translates as “Girls at Full Speed”, while also evoking the image of women taking the helm. It is the first, and still the only, motorboat navigation school in Venice run by women and open to everyone.
The idea grew from the awareness that navigation remains a predominantly male environment. “Girls, we need to start recognising each other and giving social value and political weight to our role in this city,” Canino said.
Slowly, and often without proclamation, women are entering and inhabiting Venice’s public spaces through practice. Their presence does not simply occupy the water, but begins to redefine it.

====================================================================================================

‘Britain’s Yellowstone’: restoration project aims to take the greed out of land acquisition
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
05:00:57 UTC
14:00:57 KST

It is difficult to find the most remote place in England. There is no public transport, no roads and no sign of any human habitation. Online route finders mistakenly direct cars up a grassy track. But miles along gravel forest roads in the far north of Northumberland is the largest contiguous rewilding site under single ownership in the country.
The vast glacial bowl of 7,500-acre Emblehope Moor has been bought for £8.5m by Restore, a nature restoration company that works with landowners across Britain.
The aim is to bring golden eagles, curlews, black grouse and beavers back to the moor which in former guises was a traditional grouse shooting and sheep farming estate and a dog-training ground.
But the restoration project, which is still seeking to raise £4m to fund its 20-year scheme, also has a unique proposition: after delivering new biodiversity and abundance alongside financial returns for investors and repaying the crucial £4.5m Triodos Bank loan that enabled the purchase, it will hand over the site to local community or charitable ownership.
“We want to prove that the bank is paid back, investors get their two-times return but we don’t need to become the next for ever laird,” said Benedict Macdonald, an environmental writer and the founder and director of Restore. “We’re keen to leave a well-funded community project for the future. It’s not an aggressive land-holding model; it’s both a capitalist and community model and I want it to become the national model for the uplands – we’ve got to take the greed out of it for it to work.”
The environmentalist Ben Goldsmith hails the burgeoning mosaic of increasingly wild estates in Northumberland as Britain’s Yellowstone.
Close to Emblehope in the north of Northumberland is Rothbury, the largest estate to come on the market for 30 years, which the Wildlife Trusts are seeking to buy with an unprecedented £30m fundraising appeal that is nearing its target.
Other private estates in the area, including 12,000-acre College Valley and 4,000-acre Hepple Wilds, are accelerating nature restoration while the vast 148,000-acre Kielder Forest is increasingly managed by Forestry England for biodiversity.
“We’re not the size of Yellowstone but we’re in England’s largest wild landscape by a long factor,” said Macdonald.
Emblehope, a site of special scientific interest (SSSI) which was managed for biodiversity by former owners the Royal Kennel Club for a number of years, already has exciting numbers of raptors, including merlin and prospecting golden eagles. The site’s streams still have trout and salmon, and there are red squirrels and pine martens in the area.
But Restore’s first tasks will be to return water to desiccated peat moorland and remove swaths of non-native sitka spruce.
A hidden network of land drains have left what should be water-soaked peatland completely parched. Patches of sphagnum moss that are usually water-filled sponges even in summer are dry. Modelling suggests Emblehope’s rewetted peat could store an additional 100,000 cubic metres of water, equivalent to about 40 Olympic swimming pools.
“It’s going to be a massive exercise to identify the exits of water from the land,” said Macdonald.
In the future, they will call on beavers to help hold back more water. There are promising patches of birch and willow growing beside one stream – beaver food – but Macdonald has witnessed beavers making dams out of heather on even more treeless moors in Norway and is confident they will thrive.
Before that, there is a more urgent task for the ponies that are to be introduced on to the site.
The cattle- and sheep-grazing on the estate’s moorland was reduced by the previous owners on the advice of conservationists but Macdonald is alarmed by dry “thatch” beneath the thick tussocks of moorland grass. “It’s quite dangerous from a fire point of view,” he said. His priority is to get Exmoor ponies on to the site, because they will eat down the grassy thatch and reduce the fire risk.
Opening up the site to more diverse grazing animals will reduce aggressive grass species and increase the diversity of the sward. The grass is also currently too thick and long for curlew chicks to survive and find food, and so other species will benefit from the grazing animals.
Destined for the chop are dense sitka plantations, which harbour little life and raise predation to unnaturally high levels because goshawks lurk in them.
On Emblehope, the removal of the trees will hit a few species, such as long-eared owls and crossbills. But these will remain in the wider landscape because there are huge tracts of plantation forestry across neighbouring Kielder.
Restore plans to leave patches of a few older trees but admits the problem with retaining any sitka – and the problem with its Forestry England neighbours – are what Macdonald calls the “little shitkas”, the baby trees that pop up all over the wilding moors from wind-blown seed.
The solution is to plant broadleaved screens around the edge of the site to stop wind-blown sitka seed.
While Restore’s promotional videos have tantalised people with glimpses of lynx, Macdonald is wary of being seen to endorse moves to bring back the lost predator, which many rewilders view as an ideal solution to Britain’s overpopulation of wild deer. While a survey suggests 72% of local people are in favour of reintroducing lynx, many sheep farmers in the area are vehemently opposed to an animal that could make their working lives harder.
“We have no funded plans for lynx, and we have no wish to be in the reintroduction party,” said Macdonald, although he conceded “the economic argument [in favour] is compelling”. Research to be published next year will quantify the potential tourism bonanza to Northumberland.
Although there are proposals to release lynx into surrounding Kielder, one was blocked by Natural England and a second, the Wildlife Trusts-backed Missing Lynx project, is still consulting. Emblehope is unlikely to be a key habitat for the forest-dwelling animal.
Despite Restore’s wilding manifesto, it is retaining the estate’s farmer and gamekeeper.
“What surprises me is how surprised people are that we’ve retained staff who know so much about the land,” said Macdonald. “The farmer is a real student of the history of grazing here and he’s very open-minded. The gamekeeper has been looking after some of Britain’s highest densities of birds of prey. These guys work 18-hour days, they live and breathe the area.”
Restore will fund the transformation of Emblehope via conventional income from forestry (removing the sitkas) and cattle, sheep and, in the future, education and carefully limited eco-tourism – as well as government environmental land management payments. But it expects most of its income to come from natural capital payments.
These include carbon credits for the sequestration in restored blanket bog and “30x30 Restore units” whereby corporations pay for the restoration of 30-metre by 30-metre patches of habitat. Restore’s vision is that corporations pay not for biodiversity outcomes but for conservation action on the land which provides more wildlife. Macdonald said: “It’s perfectly natural for large corporates to sponsor big sporting events across the world. In nature, in England, this is a big event.”

Travellers to the EU could face renewed border queues as flexibility measures for the bloc’s entry-exit system officially come to an end – although numerous sources have indicated that some member states will not enforce biometric checks.
Airlines last week called on the European Commission to extend discretionary powers to pause EES controls when necessary until the end of 2026, with the deadline for “flexibility” passing on 6 September.
Peak holiday season has not resulted in a repeat of the long queues seen at some European airports in early summer, which at worst led to numerous passengers missing flights. But the aviation and travel industry believes further chaos was averted only through relaxation of the rules demanding biometric information, including fingerprinting of non-EU-citizens.

A senior airline source said that while they would be monitoring closely, they did not expect to see full enforcement at the busiest European airports. The source said they expected the practice to continue.

The airlines trade body Iata has called for an official extension, saying last week that EES-related delays had resulted in people missing flights and connections.
Thomas Reynaert, the head of external affairs at Iata, said: “These are real impacts being felt by passengers. It gives Europe a bad reputation. When systems fail, passengers lose the trust in the system and when people are late, airlines pay a high cost.”
The European Commission declined to provide further comment. A spokesperson said early last week: “We are in close and constructive contact with those few member states where some adjustments are needed at certain border crossing points.
“And during an additional period of operational adjustment that is needed at these few operational border crossing points, the commission stands ready to provide additional support to these member states.”

Shein’s stock market debut was a major flop. Does it signal the death of ultra-fast fashion?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
05:00:50 UTC
14:00:50 KST

“A model that floods the market with thousands of new daily styles at single-digit price points can only exist by passing its true costs onto labour and the environment.”
Shein’s ultra-fast fashion empire has taken a dramatic fall following its post-IPO valuation collapse.
The e-commerce platform, which is headquartered in Singapore but outsources much of its manufacturing to China, failed to go public in London and New York following concerns around its supply chain and heavy criticism of its environmental impact.
Shein therefore pivoted to the Hong Kong Stock Exchange, where it was valued at around $27 billion (approximately €23.24 billion) on 1 September. It may seem like a huge financial win, but it’s 70 per cent lower than its private market peak of almost $100 billion (€86 billion) back in 2022.
Why was Shein’s IPO such a flop?
“Capital markets aren’t acting out of pure altruism: they’re reacting to material financial risk,” sustainability expert and founder of tech company E&S Solutions Ildiko Almasi Simsic tells Euronews Earth.
“Shein’s delayed public listings and severely discounted valuation prove that investors now recognise ESG issues as direct threats to terminal value.”
Simsic argues that a business model that has been exposed to multiple controversies, such as forced labour and hazardous chemicals in clothing, carries an “enormous risk profile”.
She says environmental and human rights issues have now crossed over from “ethics to equity”, signalling a watershed moment for the fast-fashion industry.
But what makes Shein so controversial in the first place, and can its super cheap garments and on-trend styles ever become sustainable?
Shein’s controversial supply chains
“For years, ultra-fast fashion grew by leveraging hyper-fragmented, outsourced supply chains that kept prices absurdly low while keeping liabilities at arm’s length,” Simsic tells Euronews Earth.
“But that model created a massive structural vulnerability. When your business relies on thousands of sub-contractors operating in grey regulatory zones, supply chain oversight isn’t just an operational headache – it becomes a central business risk.”
Shein’s supply chain has been shrouded in controversy since its conception. In 2022, an investigation by environmental NGO Greenpeace Germany found hazardous chemicals above the EU regulatory limits in seven of 47 Shein products tested.
At the time, Shein acknowledged the chemical contamination and pledged “substantial improvements” to its chemical management.
However, a 2025 investigation found that little had changed. Greenpeace purchased 56 garments from Shein across eight countries and analysed them for hazardous chemicals. They found that 18 of 56 (32 per cent) of the garments exceeded the EU limits, including children’s clothing.
Among other chemicals, the plasticizers phthalates and water- and dirt-repellent “forever chemicals” (PFAS) were detected. These are hazardous chemicals that have been linked to various health concerns, including cancer, reproductive disorders, growth disorders in children, and immunodeficiency disorders.
“Consumers are also at risk as they can be exposed to these chemicals through several ways – directly through the skin, by inhaling textile fibres in the air and, in the case of small children, through mouthing contaminated clothes.”
In 2023, Shein admitted to finding two cases of child labour in its supply chain during the first nine months of the year.
The firm introduced new rules so that any child labour or forced labour violations have become grounds for immediate termination of contracts.
“Both cases were resolved swiftly, with remediation steps including terminating contracts with underage employees, ensuring the payment of any outstanding wages, arranging medical checkups and facilitating repatriation to parents/ legal guardians as needed,” Shein said at the time.
“Following appropriate remediation, the contract manufacturers were permitted to resume business.”
Despite Shein’s clampdown on labour violations, concerns of poor working conditions remain rife. A 2025 investigation by the BBC found that workers were sitting behind sewing machines for around 75 hours a week in contravention of Chinese labour laws.
Many employers told the publication that they only have one day off each month and have to endure 12-hour shifts, which didn’t include breaks for lunch and dinner, often working until past 10pm.
A 2024 report by Swiss advocacy group Public Eye also found that excessive overtime was still common for many workers – despite Shein promising to improve conditions following previous probes.
Can Shein ever be sustainable?
As Shein geared up for going public, scrutiny on its fast-fashion model grew stronger.
The company’s draft prospectus included the slogan “We believe in doing well by doing good”. However, according to Public Eye, this was removed from the final document.
Shein insists that “commitment to sustainable and responsible growth is woven into the fabric” of its business model. However, the expected IPO proceeds allocate just 10 per cent to sustainability and corporate responsibility.
An investigation by global nonprofit Rest of World found that between July and December of 2021, Shein added anywhere between 2,000 and 10,000 SKUs (stock keeping units, or individual styles) to its app each day.
This is because Shein orders small batches of each garment, sometimes as low as a few dozen pieces, then waits to see how consumers respond. If a particular item seems to be selling well, Shein orders more.
“A model that floods the market with thousands of new daily styles at single-digit price points can only exist by passing its true costs onto labour and the environment,” Simsic says.
“Cheap prices are an illusion created by systemic outsourcing. When garments are produced at a fraction of a cent per stitch, it almost guarantees non-compliance with fair wages, excessive overtime, and cheap, fossil-fuel-derived synthetic fabrics.”
The expert acknowledges that while efficiency and tech-driven demand forecasting can reduce excess inventory, it cannot bypass the “physical limits of planetary resources or basic human rights”.
“Ultra-low cost and sustainability are fundamentally incompatible concepts,” she adds. “One inherently undermines the other.”
Can fast fashion survive the scrutiny?
Shein’s scrutiny has gone far beyond complaints from environmentalists and individuals. Earlier this week, France passed a law targeting companies known for selling large volumes of low-quality clothing at rock-bottom prices.
“The harmful effects of ultra-fast fashion on our environment and our economy are well known and documented,” says Mathieu Lefevre, the minister for ecological transition.
Under the bill, firms like Shein are assessed under two criteria: the volume of clothing placed on the market and the cost of repairing garments relative to their purchase price.
The per-item fee will vary on a set scale according to how each product scores on both of these standards.This year, companies will pay fines such as a 50-cent levy on underwear falling into the ultra-fast fashion category, rising to €2 for T-shirts, €9 for jeans and €12 for a jacket.
The levy could reach up to €19.50 per item by 2030, though the cap remains at 50 per cent of the product’s pre-tax price.
Beijing has bitten back, urging France to abandon the law and describing it as “clearly discriminatory” due to Shein – and sites like Temu – being located in Asia.
“Should France persist in this course of action, China will take necessary measures to safeguard the legitimate rights and interests of Chinese enterprises,” says commerce ministry spokeswoman Huang Ling. “France will bear full responsibility for all consequences arising from this.”
Simsic argues that while fast-fashion giants will still be able to survive new laws like this, it’s likely they won’t reach their historical growth model.
“Historically, labour issues or toxic chemical findings were managed by public relations or board-level sustainability committees. Today, with legislation like the EU’s Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive and Extended Producer Responsibility, these are strict legal compliance matters carrying fines of up to five per cent of global turnover.”
Simsic adds that if non-compliance directly threatens a company’s bottom line through hefty regulatory penalties and import bans, growth will inevitably slow. It means sites like Shein will have no choice but to internalise these costs, by investing heavily in supply chain traceability and safer materials.
Euronews Earth has contacted Shein for comment.

The Euronews Travel autumn bucket list: Our top picks for holidays in Europe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
05:00:35 UTC
14:00:35 KST

Planning a European autumn getaway? Why not take inspiration from the Euronews Travel team...
Forget mourning the end of summer. Autumn might just be one of the best times of year to travel in Europe – bringing fewer crowds, lower prices and destinations at their most atmospheric.
From crisp countryside walks and fiery autumn colours to cosy cafés and seasonal celebrations, these are the trips on the Euronews Travel team’s bucket list for the “-ber” months.
Saskia O’Donoghue: Why I choose Bavaria (and Malta)
If I’m honest, autumn is my absolute least favourite time of the year, with trees slowly dying and the nights drawing in. I think my hatred of the season is down to how miserable it is in England, where I call home. More recently, I’ve been trying to embrace autumn in other places which do it properly.
Last year, I visited Czechia and Nova Scotia in Canada, both of which manage to make the fall very enjoyable. This year, I’m planning to head to Bavaria when the summer crowds have thinned, and the landscape turns shades of gold, orange and deep red.
Despite my reservations about autumn, I’d happily spend my days wandering around Munich, hopping between cosy beer halls and markets, before heading south towards the mountains and, of course, the castles.
Neuschwanstein might be a little obvious as a must-see, but I’m not sure I’d ever get bored of seeing something that looks quite so spectacular surrounded by autumn colours.
Long walks followed by hearty Bavarian food, a local beverage and somewhere suitably cosy to warm up by an open fire? That sounds pretty close to the ideal autumn holiday – and it might just convert me into an autumn lover.
If I still despise it, I’ll head back to Malta, where I have happy memories of sunbathing in November and the sun setting at a non-depressing hour!
Dianne Apen-Sadler: Why I choose Latvia
As a travel journalist, I’m constantly being asked to share recommendations for my top spots in Europe, and nine times out of 10, I’m going to talk about either somewhere in the Balkans (think more Belgrade and Skopje than Budva and Split), or the Baltics.
With its picturesque – and UNESCO-listed – city centre, brilliant museums, and superb craft breweries, Latvia’s capital Riga has all the hallmarks of a great weekend break, and one that can be enjoyed equally in the peaks of summer or the depths of winter (or, for the purposes of this article, in autumn).
But the place I’m most excited about visiting during leaf-peeping season is Sigulda, Latvia’s "autumn capital", which lies around 45 minutes outside of Riga by train.
Come October, the banks of the Gauja River are transformed into shades of orange – which also just happens to be my favourite colour! – and the Sigulda Cable Car and Turaida Castle offer the best vantage points.
Who needs New England when we have spots like this right here in Europe?
Mike Starling: Why I choose Scotland
I don’t want to come across like I’m a stay-at-home Brit, but as someone who’s been based outside of the UK for many a year now, it’s always nice to go back to the motherland. However, even though I am English, I would say forget London, the Cotswolds and the Lake District and head “north of the border”.
Scotland is lovely at any time of the year, but in autumn it’s perfect – especially if you’re heading outdoors. Of course there may be the odd rain shower (or five), but the autumnal colours of the trees, glens and lochs make any hike, walk or outdoor adventure truly worth it. Then there’s the golf… truly spectacular.
Also, once you’ve finished 18 holes or “bagged a Munro” – reaching the summit of a Scottish mountain that is at least 3,000 feet (914.4 metres) high – you can then enjoy the country’s warm hospitality. Literally. Think log-burning fires in pubs, hearty food and a dram of whisky. What’s not to like?
Fakhriya M. Suleiman: Why I choose Monaco
Monaco’s luxury appeal has always been attractive to me. But as a principality on the French Riviera that only spans two square kilometres, the summer crowds? Less so. However, shoulder season travel to an autumnal Monaco? Now, that I wouldn’t turn down.
I’ve heard so much about exploring the city-state leisurely on foot. I picture myself taking in the futuristic architecture of Mareterra or the vibrant colours in Fontvieille's Princess Grace Rose Garden.
While I’m always game for new experiences (such as visiting Monaco for the first time…) admittedly, and paradoxically, I’m also a creature of comfort. I know I’d feel right at home travelling from Doha’s shopping paradise to Monte Carlo’s. My walking adventure will continue to the shopping promenade, where I’d work up an appetite before sampling Monte Carlo’s gastronomy scene.
The two-Michelin-starred Blue Bay by Chef Marcel Ravin offers guests an experience between Caribbean and Mediterranean cuisine, alongside a sea view. All that’s missing is a plane ticket.
Maya Abu Hajleh: Why I choose Italy
Italy is somewhere I’ve wanted to visit. I love the idea of walking around the streets, trying different food, sitting in little cafés and not really having to rush anywhere.
I’ve always liked the thought of living somewhere small and cosy, where you know the people around you and everything feels a bit slower. Maybe I’d find it boring after a while, but I actually want to experience it myself before deciding that.
As someone who’s lived most of their life in the Gulf, I’m used to hot weather and seeing a lot of desert and dry surroundings. That’s why I’d love to experience something completely different, like Italy in the autumn, with all the trees changing colour, the mountains, the lakes, and little towns.
I think one of my favourite things would honestly be walking through Italy’s beautiful streets and stepping on all those dry, coloured leaves after they’ve fallen. I think I’d really enjoy that slower kind of life, even if it’s just for a little while.
Rebecca Ann Hughes: Why I choose England
It’s been an intense summer in northern Italy, where I live. We’ve been more in heatwaves than out of them; long stretches of +35C degrees and 95% humidity. So I’ve found myself unexpectedly longing for what I’d normally consider a very mundane holiday idea – walking in the British countryside.
Europe has no shortage of spectacular hikes and natural parks, but I want that unmistakable environment of Britain’s forests: mizzling rain, the peaty, damp smell of fallen leaves underfoot, glimpses of scrabbling squirrels, and the warm country pub.
I’m lucky to have family living in two great spots of the English countryside (given I’m from Scotland, I’m heading in the opposite direction to editor Mike for a change of scenery!). My aunt lives in the Lake District, the ideal terrain for lung-busting hikes up mountain peaks or meanders around lakeside paths.
My uncle lives down south in the New Forest, where I’m envisaging delving into dark woods or striding across open heathlands – and making friends with the wild ponies that roam freely.

Calls for Hong Kong anti-stalking law after man acquitted of following teen girl
Magistrate said charge of loitering did not address defendant’s actions, and lawmakers urge government to revisit proposal for dedicated legislation shelved in 2014
Lawmakers and a government adviser have called for anti-stalking legislation to close a loophole that makes prosecuting repeated harassment difficult in Hong Kong, following the acquittal of a man who followed a teenage girl to her secondary school classroom.
Some experts said the government should revisit a proposal for such legislation raised 26 years ago, after the magistrate who acquitted the defendant of a loitering charge also noted the absence of laws to criminalise stalking under certain circumstances.
Unlike many jurisdictions with dedicated legislation to protect victims, Hong Kong can only prosecute suspects under a patchwork of different laws, with even the statutes on doxxing viewed as insufficient to punish cyberstalking.
The 57-year-old government statistician was found not guilty on August 25 of following the 16-year-old girl to her school and loitering outside the classroom in July last year.
The man also allegedly followed her during her commute to school for two to three years. He told police the girl resembled an old friend and he wanted to know her.
Eastern Court Magistrate Kestrel Lam Tsz-hong said that loitering causing concern was inappropriate for addressing the defendant’s actions, which could not be handled under existing criminal laws.

Young Malaysians brew goal for traditional tuak drink to become national success

Young Malaysians brew goal for traditional tuak drink to become national success
Given the drink’s origins in Sarawak, industry players have to balance between adhering to traditional processes and commercial limitations
At Raffly Langi’s family longhouse in Sarawak, on Malaysian Borneo, the tuak rice wine did not come in a branded bottle or a tasting flight.
His aunt has brewed the drink for Gawai, the harvest festival celebrated by Dayak communities, an umbrella term for indigenous groups in Sarawak whose longhouses have long been centres of family, rituals and communal life.
She made it from steamed glutinous rice and a cake called ragi, prepared with rice flour, yeast and spices to kick-start fermentation. Once ready, the tuak was drawn from a jar and served without flavouring.
Years later, 33-year-old Raffly has carried that family recipe to the Klang Valley, the urban region around Kuala Lumpur, where he produces tuak under the brand Tuak Alus and develops modern flavours for drinkers who are unfamiliar with the traditional brew.
Tuak traditionally comes in sweeter indu, or female, and drier laki, or male, versions, but artisan brands now also offer flavours derived from pandan, pineapple and roselle.
The drink can still be bought in Sarawak for US$5 to US$7.50 in an unlabelled plastic or glass bottle, while at Klang Valley pop-ups, producers sell premium bottles and promote brand collaborations and tasting flights, with prices around US$25 or more each.
But as it moves from longhouses into mainstream markets, brewers are confronting a persistent question: how much can tuak be changed before the culture that gives it meaning fades?

Lithuania’s fiercest storms: A history of extreme weather and growing risks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
05:00:00 UTC
14:00:00 KST

The severe storm that swept across Lithuania last month is likely to go down in the country’s weather history, according to Donatas Valiukas, head of the Climate and Research Division at Lithuania’s Hydrometeorological Service.
While powerful storms are relatively uncommon in Lithuania, the country has experienced several destructive events over the past decades – some causing deaths, widespread power outages and major damage to infrastructure.
One of the most severe struck October 17-18, 1967, when hurricane-force winds battered western Lithuania. In Klaipėda, winds reached 40 metres per second, while individual gusts may have reached 55 metres per second, according to the Hydrometeorological Service.
The storm, known as Lena in Sweden, destroyed the Palanga pier, damaged dunes and flooded parts of Klaipėda. Some 3 million to 4 million cubic meters of timber were blown down across the Samogitia region.
Another major storm, Anatol, hit Lithuania in December 1999. Wind gusts reached 40 meters per second in some areas and produced waves up to 6 metres high. A Norwegian vessel, the Seines, was washed ashore near Palanga and was not pulled back into the sea until April 2000.
In January 2005, Storm Erwin brought winds of up to 35 metres per second to the coast. Dunes and forests were damaged, the Danė River flooded parts of Klaipėda, and about 150,000 to 180,000 people lost electricity. Repairs took six days.
Summer storms have also proved deadly. A powerful squall in August 2010 killed four people after unusually strong winds swept across several municipalities. Another major squall struck central and eastern Lithuania in June 2016.
More recently, Lithuania has experienced severe summer storms associated with cyclones moving north from southern Europe. A storm in July 2024 left about 160,000 people without electricity. Last month’s storm affected about 268,000 customers at its peak and also caused fatalities.
Valiukas said climate change could increase the likelihood and intensity of such events.
“As the climate changes, the air warms, holds more moisture and potentially has more destructive power,” he said.
He added that Lithuania’s relative lack of frequent severe storms can leave residents less prepared than people in hurricane-prone regions.
“We need to be prepared,” Valiukas said.

====================================================================================================

Israel needs tikkun olam, not silence about its problems - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
04:59:26 UTC
13:59:26 KST

Before the digital age, washing of Israel’s dirty linen in the media was widely regarded as treason. However, there were exceptions, such as the failed Lavon affair of 1954 in which a group of Egyptian Jews was recruited to plant bombs in civilian targets owned by Western entities. The idea was that after the bombs detonated, the blame would be attributed to the Muslim Brotherhood and other extreme elements in Egypt. Once the plot was discovered and published in the international media, it could also be published in Israel – but not before.
A similar policy with a different slant existed during the Yom Kippur War. Israel obtained photographs of IDF soldiers who had been captured and tortured in Syria. These photos were distributed to members of the foreign press; and only after they had been published abroad could they be published in Israel.
One particular publication, the long defunct Haolam Hazeh, dared to publish political and social scandals, and was frequently in and out of court contesting charges of libel. In July, 1982, Its editor Uri Avnery, was the first Israeli journalist to interview PLO chairman Yasser Arafat.
Nowadays, it is very difficult to keep anything under wraps. The profusion of digital publications, social media outlets, webinars, and podcasts, along with the addition of AI increases the difficulty of keeping operations secret, and distinguishing between fact and fiction. In some cases, fake news evolves into real news.
Yet for all that, some people continue to believe that it’s treason to publish anything negative about Israel in the Israeli media. This, despite the fact that all the mainstream media publishes warts and all reports and features.
At the same time, both secular and religious leaders of organizations and institutions are talking about tikkun olam (repairing the world).
The expression has its origins in the Talmud and refers to being fair in legal and social rulings.
The essential question is: How can anyone practice tikkun olam if they refuse to acknowledge what needs repairing?
The most blatant example is the firm denial in certain quarters that there is such a thing as Jewish terrorism. In the minds of such people, Jews cannot be terrorists, but all Arabs are potential terrorists. Such an attitude borders on racism.
Yet when outside forces accuse Israel of racism or apartheid, political leaders are quick to point out that Jews and Arabs sit alongside each other on public transport, shop in the same markets, and work together in hospitals.
But let’s be honest. There are many places in Israel where Arabs suffer discrimination. For instance, they have a very hard time getting building permits, so they build illegally, and sooner or later their homes are demolished by the local authorities or the IDF.
Doesn’t such a situation come within the orbit of tikkun olam? Is it treason to make it public and thereby put ammunition in the hands of those who seek to delegitimize Israel?
Meetings and negotiations with the enemy are defined as treason by ultra right wing patriots. Yet as Yitzhak Rabin emphasized: Peace is made with enemies. There is no need to make peace with friends.
Members of peace movements often incur the wrath of the extreme Right because they reveal some of the worst characteristics of certain sectors of Israeli society. Peace movement activists, especially those who belong to Breaking the Silence, are regarded as traitors because they publicize human rights violations by certain military units or individuals in their dealings with Palestinians.
Holocaust survivor and acclaimed author Elie Wiesel often spoke of the perils of indifference because indifference allows the oppressor to continue to cause suffering to others.
We can see this in attitudes to anarchy in the West Bank where gangs of Israeli thugs make life miserable for the Palestinians. Yes, there have been condemnations from high quarters, but words are not enough. Words must be accompanied by deeds.
Israel has proved time and again that the most difficult obstacles can be overcome. So why is it so difficult to stop these masked, lawless individuals?
This is where tikkun olam is a vital necessity.
Discrediting opposing political parties
Another area where tikkun olam is essential is in putting an end to discrediting legitimate political parties and their members.
Leftist has become a dirty word under the present administration. Leftists are no less patriotic than the ultra right, but their patriotism takes a different route. Political leaders who identify with right wing policies but disagree with the present administration are labeled leftists. It is absolutely ridiculous to call Avigdor Liberman a leftist or to discredit Gadi Eisenkot by charging him with being a leftist. Yair Golan is a declared leftist, but that is no reason to launch conspiracy theories to undermine the heroism which he displayed on October 7, 2023.
Perhaps he’s just a thorn in the side of the political Right.
Some people on the Right spit out the word leftist as if it was synonymous with treason.
They conveniently forget that a left-wing politician declared the establishment of the State of Israel, and an army officer who became a left-wing politician declared in June, 1967: “the Temple Mount is in our hands.” The Left likewise tends to overlook the fact that the first peace agreement with an Arab country was signed by a right-wing prime minister.
There are possibly more numerous issues on which the Right and the Left agree than either side realizes.
They are just so busy trying to discredit each other that they tend to forget that when all is said and done, we are all Israelis – some by birth, some by choice, but nonetheless Israelis.
Perhaps the next government will see fit to create a ministry of tikkun olam or advisory council made up of Left and Right, religious and secular, Jews, Arabs, Druze, and Circassians who can discuss social injustices in a rational and mutually respectful manner. Such discussions could be live streamed to make the public aware, and to promote solutions in communities affected by the topics under discussion.

Saxony-Anhalt: Far-right AfD eyes power in German state vote

Saxony-Anhalt: Far-right AfD eyes power in German state vote
Published September 6, 2026last updated September 6, 2026
What you need to know
- Saxony-Anhalt voters are set to elect a new state parliament in a vote being closely watched across Germany
- The far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) is polling well ahead of the center-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU), which has led the state government since 2002
- The result could test Germany's political 'firewall' against the far right and put pressure on CDU Chancellor Friedrich Merz if his party performs badly
It is election day in Germany's Saxony-Anhalt state. Follow all the developments here.
CDU candidate Schulze casts vote in Saxony-Anhalt
Saxony-Anhalt State Premier Sven Schulze, the lead candidate for the center-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU), has cast his vote in the state capital Magdeburg.
Schulze arrived at the polling station with his wife Kati and said the election campaign had been a strenuous one.
"Now we'll wait and see," he said after casting his ballot.
Schulze said he hoped for a high turnout. He and his wife said they planned to spend some time with their family after voting before attending the CDU's election-night event later on Sunday.
AfD candidate Siegmund casts vote in Saxony-Anhalt
Ulrich Siegmund, the lead candidate for the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD), cast his vote on Sunday morning in Saxony-Anhalt's state election.
The 35-year-old arrived with his wife Julia on a motorcycle at a polling station in his home town of Tangermünde.
The AfD, which Saxony-Anhalt's domestic intelligence agency classifies as a confirmed right-wing extremist organization, is polling well ahead of the governing center-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU) of State Premier Sven Schulze.
Siegmund has said his target is "45% plus X."
WATCH: AfD's Ulrich Siegmund tells DW he wants to make history
The Alternative for Germany (AfD) lead candidate Ulrich Siegmund aims to turn his small state into a blueprint for right-wing politics across Germany.
The AfD's "100-day immediate action plan" contains a key promise to "deport from minute one" foreign nationals who have no legal right to stay but whose presence is tolerated for humanitarian reasons. Many have found work and established their lives in Germany.
The action plan also calls for cutting funding for pro-democracy NGOs, requiring refugees to work and prioritizing a love for the German homeland over social diversity.
DW's Matthew Moore spoke to him a couple of weeks ago:
Migration debate looms large in Saxony-Anhalt despite low foreign population
Migration was one of the major campaign issues in Saxony-Anhalt.
This is despite the fact that, compared with other German states, relatively few non-Germans live there.
At the end of 2025, foreign nationals accounted for around 9% of Saxony-Anhalt's population, roughly half the share of North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany's most populous state.
The claim that "foreigners are living off taxpayers" is also misleading. Compared with other German states, Saxony-Anhalt has a relatively low proportion of foreign nationals among potential recipients of welfare benefits such as basic income support.
Although Saxony-Anhalt is one of Germany's economically weaker states, its population has grown in recent years, according to migration figures.
Since 2016, more non-Germans have moved to Saxony-Anhalt than have moved away. The net migration balance for German citizens has also been positive for the past six years.
Polls open in Saxony-Anhalt state election
Polling stations have opened in the eastern German state of Saxony-Anhalt, where voters are choosing a new state parliament.
Around 1.7 million people aged 18 and over are eligible to vote. Polling stations opened at 8 a.m. local time (0600 GMT/UTC) and will close at 6 p.m., when counting begins.
Voters are electing the members of the new state parliament in Magdeburg.
They can cast two votes: one for a direct constituency candidate and one for a political party.
The new parliament will subsequently elect the state premier.
The state returning officer expects a preliminary final result in the early hours of Monday morning.
ANALYSIS: Why is this election so closely watched?
I have not experienced a more polarizing election since Brexit or Trump vs. Hillary Clinton in 2016. That is because the stakes are so high.
For a number of reasons, the decision voters in Saxony-Anhalt reach today is being watched closely in Berlin and beyond:
- Watershed moment: Should the AfD secure an absolute majority, it would be the first time a right-wing populist party has won power in a state in Germany in the postwar era.
- Firewall: Should the AfD not secure an absolute majority, the focus will turn to the conservative CDU. Pressure will mount on the party to rethink its longstanding policy of not governing with or passing laws with the far-right AfD or far-left Left Party. Such a debate risks splitting the CDU.
- Chancellor: A dire result for the conservatives may lead to calls for the deeply unpopular Chancellor Friedrich Merz to be replaced. In CDU circles in Berlin, the talk is of an election that could 'change the republic.'
Saxony-Anhalt heads to the polls as coalition math takes center stage
Saxony-Anhalt, one of Germany's 16 federal states, boasts a rich cultural and historical heritage.
 
Home to around 2.1 million people, it is one of Germany's most sparsely populated states. Only two cities, the state capital Magdeburg, and the city of Halle, have more than 200,000 inhabitants.
 
Today, voters will elect a new state parliament.
The center-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU) has led the state government since 2002 as the leading party in governing coalitions. But the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) has dominated polls in the run-up to the vote, typically drawing support in the 40% range, well beyond the CDU's low-to-mid-20% range.
If polling holds, the AfD would become Saxony-Anhalt's largest party for the first time. Every other major party has ruled out allying with it, meaning it would likely need to secure an outright majority in order to govern. A broader coalition made up of other parties is the other potential outcome.
 
A key thing to watch when exit polls and preliminary results are released tonight is whether smaller parties fall below the 5% threshold and lose representation.
 
Under election law, parties must obtain at least 5% of party-list votes (known as second votes) to secure representation.
 
This would mean more seats in the state parliament for the remaining parties, including the AfD, on a proportional basis. That could allow the AfD to secure an outright majority if enough smaller parties fail to clear the threshold.
Welcome to our coverage
Normally, there is not much new to report on polling day. But as voters in Germany's Saxony-Anhalt cast their ballots in a key state election, we'll explain why this vote is being watched so closely.
We'll remind you what the main candidates said in the run-up to today's election and bring you insights from our correspondents, who have spent months covering the parties and speaking to voters across the state. Once the exit polls and results start coming in, we'll provide analysis of what they mean.
Throughout the day, we'll also bring you live coverage from our television broadcasts and social media channels, along with background articles and videos to help make sense of it all.
Whether you're following the election closely or just catching up, we'll help you stay on top of the key moments and what they could mean for Germany.

Anonymous sources can become powerful tools of political manipulation - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
04:58:42 UTC
13:58:42 KST

“A senior diplomatic official said,” “a security official says,” “a source familiar with the details claims,” and “those close to the minister believe.” We hear and read phrases like these almost every day. They are sometimes followed by dramatic revelations, but one detail is missing: Who exactly is speaking to us?
The public is asked to accept information from an unknown person without knowing that person’s position or interests, whether they were present at the event they are describing or, most importantly, why they decided to share the information at that particular moment.
It is important to be clear: Confidential sources are essential to a free press. Journalists cannot do their jobs if everyone who provides them with information must be publicly identified.
Whistleblowers, public employees, and people working within large organizations sometimes need protection to bring important information to the public’s attention.
But there is a difference between protecting a source and turning anonymity into a standard practice.
Behind some of these unnamed “officials” is a well-oiled system for delivering carefully crafted messages. Politicians, advisers, security officials, associates, and other interested parties know they do not need to hold a news conference to influence the public agenda. Sometimes, a single phone call to a reporter is enough.
That is where a complicated relationship begins. The source needs the journalist to publish the information. The journalist needs the source to obtain information that competitors do not have. Both have an interest in the relationship, but their interests are not necessarily the same. The journalist wants a story. The source wants to achieve a goal.
That goal might be to damage a political opponent, prepare the ground for an impending decision, pressure decision makers, test the public’s response to an idea, or avoid responsibility for a failure.
In other words, a leak sometimes does not tell us what happened. It is intended to make something happen.
That is precisely the question a journalist must ask before publishing. The question should not only be, “Is the information true?” It should also be, “Why does this person want me to publish it?”
Even true information can be manipulative when it is incomplete. A source may provide one entirely accurate detail from a closed meeting while omitting five others that would change its meaning. Was a lie published? No. Did the public receive the full picture? No.
A leak can be accurate in its details yet misleading in the picture it creates.
The problem becomes more serious when anonymous information begins to circulate. A reporter publishes something attributed to “a senior official.” Another news outlet cites the report. From there, it spreads to social media and television studios. Before long, commentators are explaining the significance of a report when no one outside a small circle knows who is behind it.
The rumor has put on a suit and tie and become news.
The competition to be first only adds to the problem.
Competition among journalists has always existed and always will. Journalists want to break stories, and rightly so. But the public usually does not care whether it receives a report at 8:01 p.m. or 8:07 p.m. It does care enormously if those six minutes could have been used to verify that the information was true, complete, and accurate.
The public is not sitting with a stopwatch. Editors also bear considerable responsibility. Is one anonymous source enough? Was the information confirmed by another source? Was the person who could be harmed by the report given an opportunity to respond? Most importantly, does the public have a genuine interest in knowing the information, or is the media helping someone conduct a campaign through its platforms?
A news organization does not have to reveal a source’s identity to tell readers something about the source’s credibility. There is a meaningful difference between the vague phrase “a source said” and an explanation that the source has firsthand knowledge of the discussions, is not authorized to speak publicly, and provided information that was independently verified.
The more anonymous the source, the greater the journalist’s responsibility.
Politicians and public officials also find this system convenient. They can deliver a forceful message without publicly taking responsibility for it. If the message is well received, they can adopt it. If it causes an uproar, they can deny it, distance themselves from it, or claim it was not delivered on behalf of the authorized official.
This creates a politics of trial balloons.
The media must be careful not to become the factory that inflates them.
Confidential Sources as a means of reaching the truth
Journalism cannot and should not abandon confidential sources. Without them, it would lose a central part of its ability to expose what powerful people would prefer to conceal. But it must return to a simple principle: A source is a means of reaching the truth, not a substitute for it.
A good journalist is not a source’s messenger. On the contrary, precisely because journalists know their sources, speak with them, and trust them, they must repeatedly ask themselves the following: What is this person’s interest? What are they not telling me? Why are they telling me this now?
In an era when the public is overwhelmed with information, the great advantage of professional journalism is not that it is always the first to know everything.
Its advantage is that when it publishes something, the public can trust that someone first asked the difficult questions.
The next time we hear that “a senior official said” something, the important question is not only what was said. We should also ask who wanted us to know and what they want to happen once we do.
David Ben Basat is the CEO of Radios 100fm, an honorary consul and deputy dean of the Consular Diplomatic Corps, and president of the Israel Amateur Radio Club. He previously served as a monitor for Israel’s Army Radio and as a correspondent for NBC News.

Iraq targets 5 million bpd oil exports via Türkiye, Syria

AA Photo
Iraq boosted its crude oil export capacity to more than 3 million barrels per day and plans to reach 5 million by developing new routes to bypass the Strait of Hormuz.
 Oil Minister Basim Mohammed Khudair said Sept. 5 the government aims to expand alternative outlets to the Mediterranean Sea.
 Exports reached around 3 million bpd since the start of September, Khudair told the official Iraqi News Agency.
 The government wants to increase capacity to 5 million once strategic pipelines linking Iraqi fields to Fishkhabur in the north and Syria’s port of Banias are completed, the minister said.
 Prime Minister Ali Faleh al-Zeidi ordered work to proceed in August on two strategic pipeline routes to reduce dependence on the Strait of Hormuz.
 The northern route will connect southern oil fields with Fishkhabur near the Turkish border.
 The line opens access to the Kirkuk-Ceyhan pipeline and Türkiye’s Mediterranean port of Ceyhan.
 The western route will link Haditha with Syria’s Banias port.
 The connection gives Iraq another outlet to the Mediterranean and potentially revives a historic oil corridor between the two countries.
 Iraq holds around 145 billion barrels of proven oil reserves.
 Oil output fell to around 1.3 million bpd during the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran beginning in late February.
 Production dropped from 3.3 million before the conflict and began to recover in July and August.
 The push for alternative export routes follows continuing disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz linked to tensions between Washington and Tehran.
