Technology will not deepen India’s education divide
Technology will not deepen India’s education divide; used well, it could help close it.At the TOI Social Impact Summit, 2026, Pranav Kothari, CEO of Educational Initiatives, broke the myth that edtech is expensive or exclusionary. Technology, he stressed, is not a substitute for teachers, who remain better at inspiration, values, debates, experiments and project-based learning. But technology’s strength lies in continuity: Indian schools operate for about 180 days a year and children attend for roughly 140, while learning can continue through the year.Cyient founder chairman B V R Mohan Reddy said technology can also narrow the rich-poor gap by creating individual learning paths. Unlike a classroom model that often caters to the front benches, adaptive platforms can move each learner at his or her own pace.
Reddy also urged against fearing AI, warning that the real divide may be between those who understand AI and those who do not. His company adopted 37 govt schools, where the share of girls rose from 16-18% to 56% and his school students occupied a lion’s share of the merit rankers, and dropouts fell to about 2%.
The intervention also expanded into skilling, AI labs and employment-linked training. In one programme, what started as a summer project for his granddaughter Pratinya Bodanapu, rural girls are trained in skills identified through market surveys.
Similar experiences were shared by Abdul Salam KP, vice-chairman of Malabar Gold. The connection between poverty and education became stark during Covid while distributing food in urban slums, he said. “We found children on the streets even after schools reopened. That led to slum micro-learning centres, where teachers, uniforms, books and meals are provided and children without documents are helped into formal schools. The network has now grown to about 2,500 centres serving around 1.2 lakh children every day.”Gayatri Nair Lobo, CEO of Educate Girls, said school enrolment is only the first hurdle. Poverty, missing documents, domestic work, early marriage and the distance to secondary schools continue to push girls out. For every 100 primary schools, she said, there are only 20 senior secondary schools. Educate Girls is helping adolescent girls and young women return through open schooling. One, she said, returned after 10 years and went on to top Madhya Pradesh in Class 10.

EU member refuses to point finger at Russia over German drone incident
Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev has refused to assign blame for last month’s drone incident in Germany squarely to Russia, citing “reckless” Western weapons deliveries to Kiev.
Earlier this week, the German government said it had grounds to believe that Moscow was behind the incident, in which an explosive-laden UAV was found between Ukrainian Antonov cargo planes at Leipzig/Halle Airport on August 4.
Berlin subsequently announced the closure of the Russian Consulate General in Bonn and the Russian House in Berlin, as well as tighter border controls for Russian citizens. Moscow responded by shutting down the Goethe Institute centers in Moscow, St. Petersburg, and Ekaterinburg, which promote German language and culture.
Moscow has rejected the allegations, with President Vladimir Putin suggesting they were being used as a diversionary tactic to distract Germans from domestic economic woes.
While multiple fellow EU member states have issued statements backing Germany’s position, not all of them have jumped on the bandwagon of pointing the finger at Russia.
A case in point is Bulgaria, whose prime minister told the parliament on Friday that European shipments of long-range weapons to Ukraine have been just as “reckless” as the failed sabotage attempt in Germany last month. Radev pointed out that Kiev is using Western-made weaponry, backed by European intelligence and instructors, to conduct strikes deep inside Russian territory.
“And what can we expect when we attack deep inside another country with our long-range weapons? Will it stand by or will it respond?” the Bulgarian prime minister inquired rhetorically.
He went on to warn that the West’s insistence on achieving a “conventional military victory” over a major nuclear power is dramatically raising the risk of uncontrolled escalation with Moscow.
“Europe can exist without Russia, but Europe will hardly exist for long against Russia,” Radev concluded, calling on the EU to “sit down at the negotiating table [with Moscow] as soon as possible.”
Meanwhile, a number of prominent political figures in Germany have called into question the government’s response to the drone incident and, more broadly, Berlin’s current hostile policies toward Russia.
In a post on X on Wednesday, veteran left-wing politician Sahra Wagenknecht wrote that “even if Russia were behind it, a drone that caused no damage whatsoever is no reason to fuel a highly dangerous escalation that could end in a war with Russia, costing millions of lives.”
Similar assessments have been voiced by those at the opposite end of the political spectrum. Fielding questions from The Pioneer media outlet on Tuesday, Ulrich Siegmund – the lead candidate for the right-wing Alternative for Germany (AfD) party in Sunday’s regional elections in Saxony-Anhalt – said that a “continuous sequence of events” had led up to the drone incident at Leipzig/Halle Airport. He cited his country’s ever-deeper involvement in the Ukraine conflict, arguing that “it’s only logical that there will be some kind of reaction at some point.”
Siegmund criticized the anti-Russian policies pursued by successive German governments since the escalation of the Ukraine conflict in 2022, saying that weapons deliveries to Kiev and economic sanctions against Moscow have done little to resolve the conflict and save people’s lives.
The AfD politician insisted that it was high time Germany engaged earnestly in diplomacy with Russia instead.

The occupation authorities do not repair water pipelines, but instead task volunteers with delivering water to individual residents. The deliveries are accompanied by propaganda photos.
In the temporarily occupied territories of Zaporizhzhia region, access to drinking water is increasingly becoming a privilege. This is reported by the National Resistance Center of the Special Operations Forces of the Armed Forces of Ukraine (NRC), according to UNN.
Details
It is noted that the occupation administration is unable to properly provide the population with water and is failing to repair the water supply systems, forcing residents of entire settlements to wait for water deliveries.
Instead of restoring pumping stations, water pipelines and other critical infrastructure, Gauleiter Balytskyi instructs controlled volunteer organisations to resolve the problem. They deliver water to certain categories of the population, effectively doing work that should be provided by the occupation authorities
It is reported that people have to receive several five-litre bottles of water and wait for the next delivery. At the same time, each such trip is actively turned into a propaganda event: officials and volunteers take photographs with residents, creating an image of "care" and prosperity.
But several bottles of water delivered for the camera cannot replace a normal water supply
They add that while the occupation administration reports on "assistance to the population," residents of the temporarily occupied territories of Zaporizhzhia region are literally forced to survive without access to basic utilities. At the same time, water, which should be available from the tap, becomes a pretext for yet another propaganda report.
Reminder
Due to power outages, dozens of settlements in Kherson region remain without water. The occupation authorities suggest delivering water by tanker trucks instead of repairing the networks.

The amount of paperwork businesses are required to regularly carry out could be slashed, the business secretary has announced.
Jonathan Reynolds said he plans to simplify corporate reporting rules and exempt some small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) from the need to carry out certain form-filling exercises altogether.
The Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade said the corporate reporting changes could save businesses across the UK £450m.

“No one goes into business to fill out forms,” said Reynolds.
“For years, hardworking firms in this country have been weighed down by pen-pushing paperwork and frustrating costs, ticking boxes that do nothing to help them grow their business.
“We’re stripping back outdated bureaucracy and building a commonsense system fit for a 21st-century economy.
“This will cut the cost of doing business, giving breathing room to bosses across the country and free them up to focus on what they do best, creating jobs and growth.”
A consultation into the plans begins on 7 September.

This “new” frog was hiding in plain sight for 100 years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
22:35:48 UTC
07:35:48 KST

This “new” frog was hiding in plain sight for 100 years
- Date:
- September 5, 2026
- Source:
- Pensoft Publishers
- Summary:
- A common frog found across Ecuador and Colombia has finally been recognized as its own species after more than a century of mistaken identity. Museum specimens from the 1800s helped scientists reveal that Pristimantis milpe had been hiding in plain sight all along.
- Share:
Scientists at the Pontificia Universidad Católica del Ecuador have formally described Pristimantis milpe, a common and widespread frog that spent more than a century being mistaken for another species. The mystery was resolved by studying specimens collected in Ecuador during the 19th century and preserved at the Natural History Museum in London.
The finding stands out because many newly described species are rare or confined to small areas. Pristimantis milpe, by contrast, is widespread, relatively easy to find, and readily detected by its nighttime call. Its known range covers more than 67,000 square kilometers across the Chocó forests of western Ecuador and southern Colombia, from sea level to elevations of 1,200 meters.
The formal description appears in the international journal ZooKeys, which focuses on biodiversity and taxonomy.
A Century-Old Case of Mistaken Identity
Researchers were able to identify Pristimantis milpe by revisiting historical amphibian specimens housed at the Natural History Museum in London (NHM).
Santiago Ron, a researcher at PUCE and lead author of the study, traveled to England to investigate a classification problem that had persisted for more than 100 years. He examined the original specimens - known as "types" - that had been collected in Ecuador during the 19th century and preserved in the museum ever since.
By comparing those historical frogs with living populations from the Ecuadorian Chocó, the team found that the old specimens had been incorrectly linked to a different species. As a result, a frog that had been regularly seen and documented for decades never received a scientific name of its own.
"That such a common species has gone unnoticed under the wrong name for decades highlights the importance of correctly connecting scientific names with living populations in nature," notes Jhael Ortega, a PhD student at Virginia Tech and one of the study authors.
The Clicking Frog of the Chocó Forest
The Milpe Robber Frog (Cutín de Milpe) is active at night. Males typically call from leaves on shrubs and bromeliads several meters above the forest floor. Their calls are loud and distinctive, producing a sound similar to a "click."
Females and males also differ noticeably in appearance. Females have striking coloration around the groin and thighs, where orange or light blue tones can appear alongside black spots. Males generally have more uniform coloring.
The frog lives in the forests of the Ecuadorian Chocó and southern Colombia, a region considered especially important for biodiversity conservation.
Why Historic Museum Collections Still Matter
The discovery highlights the continuing scientific importance of natural history collections. Specimens preserved for decades or even centuries can give researchers a way to revisit old classifications, compare physical traits, and resolve questions that earlier scientists could not answer.
In this case, combining 19th-century museum specimens with observations of living frog populations allowed researchers to determine that Pristimantis milpe deserved recognition as a distinct species.
The findings also underscore how much remains to be learned about biodiversity. Even common, widespread animals can conceal surprises, and solving those mysteries often depends on bringing historical collections together with modern research and observations.
Story Source:
Materials provided by Pensoft Publishers. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Santiago R. Ron, Poulette Paredes-Aguirre, Diego A. Paucar, Yaara López, Katherine Apunte, Jhael A. Ortega. Long overdue: a new, widespread, species of Pristimantis (Anura, Strabomantidae) from the Chocó region and the synonymy of Pristimantis subsigillatus. ZooKeys, 2026; 1286: 121 DOI: 10.3897/zookeys.1286.194383

Feature: Chinese opera "Xiju" captivates audience at 33rd Cairo int'l theatre festival
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
06:31:15 CST
07:31:15 KST

The Chinese opera "Liaozhai: Purple Tail" is staged at the 33rd Cairo International Festival for Experimental Theatre (CIFET) in Cairo, Egypt, Sept. 4, 2026. (Xinhua/Ahmed Gomaa)
by Mahmoud Fouly
CAIRO, Sept. 5 (Xinhua) -- With a spotlight on him, a Chinese actor slowly descended from the stage and made his way through the aisles of a packed Cairo theatre, delivering an anguished soliloquy amid warm applause.
It was one of several moments when performers of "Liaozhai: Purple Tail," an experimental Chinese Xiju production, moved beyond the stage and into the audience during their performance at the 33rd Cairo International Festival for Experimental Theatre (CIFET).
The Chinese production, presented by Wuxi Xiju Theatre, brought to life a story weaving together the human and supernatural worlds.
"For moments, we felt we had been transported from Cairo to China," Hamada Shousha, an Egyptian actor, director and theatre professor at Heliopolis University, told Xinhua.
"We did not just see and hear the story; we lived its atmosphere," he said, noting "the costumes, music and presentation all carried a distinctly Chinese character."
The play follows Qiao Sheng, a kind and honest scholar who unexpectedly saves a fox maiden. In gratitude, she gives him a magical fox tail capable of granting any wish. Armed with this power, Qiao Sheng gradually succumbs to his desires, exposing the darker side of human nature.
The play is adapted from Liaozhai, or Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio, a classic collection of Chinese ghost stories and supernatural folk tales written over a period of 40 years from the late 1600s to the early 1700s.
Though performed in Chinese, English, Arabic and Chinese surtitles were displayed on a monitor to the left of the stage, allowing Egyptian and international spectators to follow the story without diverting their attention from the action.
Hui Haifeng, who plays Qiao Sheng, said the response of the Egyptian audience had left a deep impression on him.
"Although we speak different languages, I could tell from their eyes, expressions and reactions that they were following the story attentively and were deeply immersed in it," Hui said.
"Art knows no borders, and neither does emotional communication," he said. "Language may present a barrier, but emotions are shared, and body language and stage expression can also communicate across cultures."
Founded in 1951, Wuxi Xiju Theatre has spent over seven decades preserving and developing xiju, a form of traditional Chinese opera, while taking its productions to audiences abroad.
Li Mengheng, a lead performer, said audiences could feel the story and its emotions through the stylized movements and body language of traditional Chinese opera even without prior familiarity with the form.
"I feel that Egyptian audiences understand the rhythm of our performance particularly well. They know when to applaud and when to give the performers some encouragement," Li said.
The Chinese play is one of 15 productions from 13 countries in the festival's official competition, including entries from Egypt, Saudi Arabia, Britain, Spain, Germany, and Russia, spanning dramatic and physical theatre, contemporary dance, puppetry, visual theatre and multimedia performances.
Sabine Liebherr from Germany described the production as "absolutely magical," saying it carried "something of a general truth about human existence."
"You have to be careful what you wish for," she said, referring to a theme of the play. "If your wish does not come from a good heart, the result can be disastrous."
She was also struck by the performers' movements. "The way they moved was so graceful -- they were almost floating."
Running from Sept. 1 to 8, this year's CIFET brings together Egyptian, Arab and international theatre practitioners for performances, workshops and discussions centered on experimentation and new approaches to theatrical expression.
For Malak Mahmoud, a fourth-year Chinese-language student at Cairo University, the performance offered a chance to experience Chinese culture firsthand rather than through a screen.
"The show was breathtaking. I could see how engaged the Egyptian spectators were, and I could hear people behind me reacting with surprise as they followed the performance," Mahmoud said.
"Through such performances, we can learn more about Chinese culture, the way people think and their beliefs," she added. ■
The Chinese opera "Liaozhai: Purple Tail" is staged at the 33rd Cairo International Festival for Experimental Theatre (CIFET) in Cairo, Egypt, Sept. 4, 2026. (Xinhua/Ahmed Gomaa)

====================================================================================================

Roundup: Gun violence tests Brussels security as drug trafficking fuels cycle of violence
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
06:30:55 CST
07:30:55 KST

BRUSSELS, Sept. 5 (Xinhua) -- Gun violence has surged again in Brussels, with six shootings reported over just four days in the Midi police zone in late August and poses a challenge to the security in the Belgian capital.
Brussels Chief Prosecutor Julien Moinil said at a press conference on Aug. 28 that the capital recorded 102 shootings in 2025 and another 69 in 2026 so far. Several recent incidents have been linked to conflicts between drug trafficking networks, while Interior Minister Bernard Quintin has described the situation as a "national emergency."
Moinil warned that the violence was no longer confined to criminal circles and that ordinary residents were increasingly at risk. "Any citizen can get shot," he said, citing the case of a father with no known links to criminal activity who was left paralyzed after being shot.
The latest wave included an attack on a police facility in the Midi police zone. Prosecutors have linked some of the recent violence to retaliation between two drug trafficking networks.
However, they said no link has yet been established between that conflict and the attack on the police facility. Moinil called the incident "a direct attack on the state."
Belgium's National Drugs Commissioner Ine Van Wymersch recently told Belgian media, citing an estimate by a Brussels police official, that a single street-level drug-dealing point can generate between 50,000 euros and 80,000 euros (about 58,000 to 93,000 U.S. dollars) a day for criminal groups.
She said rival groups once maintained relatively stable territories when cannabis dominated parts of the street drug market. As the more lucrative cocaine trade became more prominent, dealing points grew more profitable, increasing the incentive to fight for territory.
Prosecutors said criminal networks are increasingly recruiting young people as street-level operatives. Belgian media investigations have also found that some networks use social media and messaging platforms to recruit people for violent assignments.
Some gang leaders operate from abroad, while others remain capable of directing criminal activity from prison. Moinil cited a shooting case this summer in which a suspected organizer was in prison and used a smuggled mobile phone to communicate with people outside. He has called for tighter controls on prison communications, including mobile-phone signal jammers in areas housing organized crime figures.
The drug economy extends well beyond street dealers. Federal police investigations have uncovered networks involved in drug supply, storage, packaging and distribution.
Brussels prosecutors said about 203 million euros (235 million dollars) in criminal assets have been seized since the beginning of 2025, while hundreds of businesses linked to drug trafficking have been closed.
The gun violence has also renewed debate over the fragmented structure of policing in Brussels. The capital's 19 municipalities are currently divided among six local police zones. Following the latest shootings, Brussels mayors agreed to place anti-drug violence operations across the six zones under a single "Gold Commander."
Separately, legislation approved earlier this year provides for the six zones to be merged into a single Brussels police zone on Jan. 1, 2028. Local media reported that the Brussels region is also expected to appoint a regional commissioner for security and drugs within about 40 days.
The Brussels prosecutor's office currently has 49 prosecutors, compared with an authorized staffing level of 63. Moinil has called for around 10 million euros (11.6 million dollars) in additional resources, while stressing that judicial action alone cannot solve the problem and that prevention, public health and youth policy must also form part of the response.
Quintin and Justice Minister Annelies Verlinden outlined additional measures in parliament on Sept. 2. Quintin said authorities had "too often looked away" from drug-related violence in the past and that investigative tools must evolve as organized crime changes. He also acknowledged that there was "no miracle solution."
Earlier measures included deploying 40 additional federal police officers, installing 20 mobile cameras in drug-trafficking hotspots and strengthening coordination among police, prosecutors and municipal authorities.
On Aug. 28, more than 600 personnel, including over 450 police officers and at least 60 military personnel, took part in a large-scale operation. It marked the first time the military had joined this type of integrated security operation. Police detained dozens of people and seized weapons, drugs and cash.
Quintin said the operation was intended to send the message that Brussels' streets and metro stations belong to residents. He stressed that no single measure would be enough to dismantle organized crime linked to drug trafficking.
The latest shootings point to a criminal economy that goes beyond isolated incidents, linking local dealing points to wider networks, prison-based coordination and substantial illicit profits.
"Shootings may come and go in waves, but the drug trade behind them remains," Moinil said. Despite months of raids, seizures and reinforced patrols, the trade continues to sustain the conditions in which such violence can recur. ■

Feature: Syrian families count cost of back-to-school season amid economic strain
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
06:30:32 CST
07:30:32 KST

by Hummam Sheikh Ali
DAMASCUS, Sept. 5 (Xinhua) -- In the narrow lanes of Damascus' old markets, parents moved from shop to shop on Saturday, comparing prices for pens, notebooks, and school bags and making the final preparations for the 2026/2027 school year.
At al-Asrounieh market, a traditional stationery hub in Old Damascus, Abu Masa was shopping for his two daughters ahead of Syria's school reopening on Sunday, Sept. 6.
"We are here to buy school supplies. I have two daughters," Masa told Xinhua. "Everything is expensive, and people don't have enough money to buy what they need. There are shoppers, but prices are very high."
To save money, his family is passing supplies down among the children.
"We give the older sister's school bag to her younger sister and buy only one new bag," he added.
At nearby al-Khaja market, Fadi, another Damascus resident, was shopping for a school bag but said his family could not afford to purchase everything the children need at once.
"Prices have no connection to people's actual incomes. They are very high, and most people are looking rather than buying," he told Xinhua.
Saturday's local market estimates put a basic stationery set for a primary-school student at 100,000-250,000 old Syrian pounds, or about 8-19 U.S. dollars, varying with item count and quality. A notebook costs around 3,000-10,000 old pounds, while a pen 700-3,000.
Adding clothing, shoes and a school bag pushes the bill higher. Primary-school clothing can cost roughly 4-10 dollars, while a school bag or pair of shoes can cost around 5-15 dollars each. Altogether, basic supplies and clothing for one child can easily reach several dozen dollars.
Those expenses take on added weight when measured against incomes. The country's minimum monthly wage now stands at 12,560 new Syrian pounds, or about 105 dollars. The Finance Ministry notes this isn't the average salary, though no current official nationwide figure exists.
Against that benchmark, even basic preparations for one child eat a large slice of monthly earnings. A stationery set, a school bag, shoes, clothing, and other essentials could together amount to roughly one-fifth to over half of the minimum monthly wage.
"We only buy what is immediately necessary. We don't purchase all the school supplies at once because we simply cannot afford to do that," Fadi added.
The pressure is also visible from behind shop counters.
Mohammad Khair Jaqmaqji, who owns a stationery shop in Old Damascus, said customers are buying much more selectively than they did a year ago.
"To be frank about the economic situation, business this year is slower than last year," Jaqmaqji told Xinhua. "Last year, customers would come and buy complete sets and large quantities. This year, people are forced to buy only what they actually need."
The restrained spending comes despite signs of broader economic stabilization. The World Bank said inflation in Syria dropped to an estimated 11.5 percent in 2025, down significantly from 72.1 percent in 2024. Still, high living costs, a weak labor market and reconstruction needs weigh on households in the country.
Meanwhile, Syria's education system is still recovering from years of conflict, displacement and destruction.
The Education Ministry said Saturday that 1,370 schools had been rehabilitated or restored during 2026, following 2,017 in 2025, while more than 6,000 schools still need rehabilitation and maintenance.
More than 500,000 Syrian children have returned from abroad, adding pressure on the education system to absorb students with varied backgrounds. About 2.45 million children remain out of school, according to figures from the UN Children's Fund cited by the ministry.
For families walking through Damascus' markets on the eve of the new academic year, however, the immediate concern is simpler: getting kids back to school without breaking already stretched budgets.
On Sunday morning, Syrian children will once again head to classrooms. For parents such as Abu Masa and Fadi, getting them there has meant carefully weighing what can be bought now, what can be reused and what will have to wait. ■

German company successfully launches rocket to space
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
22:26:00 UTC
07:26:00 KST

German company successfully launches rocket to space
September 6, 2026
A Spectrum space rocket built by German company Isar Aerospace was launched into space from the Norwegian spaceport at Andoya.
"We're in orbit! And just made European history: This is the first time a privately developed rocket reached orbit from continental Europe," the company wrote on X.
"Germany has spaceflight capabilities," said the country's Ministry for Research, Technology and Space on X, praising a "milestone that impressively demonstrates our country's innovative strength and technical expertise".
This was the German company's second attempt to launch the Spectrum rocket into space. The first attempt, which took place 18 months ago, was unsuccessful.
What is Spectrum rocket?
The Spectrum rocket is designed for small and medium-sized payloads. It carried five smal satellites and an in-flight technological experiment, the company said.
According to Isar Aerospace, the launch was for "both the vehicle's qualification mission and its first flight carrying payload."
The move is believed to bring Europe closer to being able to offer satellite flights from its own territory. Several countries voiced interest in the growing market of commercial space missions, including Britain and Sweden.
In March, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz visited the launch site of Isar, a Bavaria-based company, showing support for its efforts and for European autonomy at a time when the world order is changing under US President Donald Trump.
Isar is also working on the development of a second launch site, located in Canada.
The company said that while the US launched 198 rockets last year, Europe's tally was just eight. Isar's goal is to produce some 40 rockets a year.
Competition includes SpaceX
Although the rocket is not yet ready for mass production, Isar has already received orders through 2028.
The Spectrum rocket is intended to send both civilian and military satellites into low Earth orbit, meaning a few hundred kilometers above the Earth's surface.
The industry includes Elon Musk's SpaceX and ArianeGroup, a French joint venture between Airbus and Safran that operates a spaceport in French Guiana, located in South America.
For the sake of developing new rockets and extend its testing and launch infrastructure, Isar said last week it received €200 million ($232 million) from the European Space Agency (ESA).

Taylor crowns boxing career in stylish Croke Park triumph
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
23:22:47 BST
07:22:47 KST

Taylor crowns career in stylish Croke Park triumph
- Published
Katie Taylor ended her illustrious career as a three-time undisputed world champion as Croke Park gave one of Ireland's greatest sporting figures the grandest of farewells on a night of celebration, spectacle and music.
The 40-year-old outclassed unbeaten Flora Pili on points in front of 80,000 jubilant fans to add the vacant WBC belt to her WBA, WBO and IBF light-welterweight titles.
With the footwork, speed and sharp pressure fighting that defined her career, Taylor produced one final stylish performance against the overmatched Frenchwoman to win by scores of 100-90, 100-90 and 98-91.
Promoter Eddie Hearn paid tribute to Taylor, calling her "Ireland's greatest sportsperson", before she took one final lap of the ring, waving to the crowd before ceremonially placing her gloves and belts in the centre of the canvas.
After almost a quarter of a century in the sport, Taylor - an Olympic champion, two-weight world champion and one of the pioneers of women's professional boxing - finally got her fairytale ending at her dream venue.
She bows out with a record of 26 wins and just one defeat, but this was about more than one final result.
It was a night steeped in Irish pride, with a spine-tingling atmosphere and chart-topping pop group Westlife helping provide a fitting send-off.
Taylor in a world of her own in Dublin
On an unforgettable night for the city, around 80 per cent of those inside Croke Park had never previously attended a boxing event, but turned out to honour a fighter who dragged women's sport from the margins and took an entire nation on her journey.
The crowd was the sixth largest recorded post-war attendance for a boxing event anywhere in the world. By early evening, the stands were awash with green and white, tricolours draped over shoulders.
Westlife performed 'World of Our Own' and 'You Raise Me Up', with tens of thousands joining in as phone lights flickered around the towering tiers of Croke Park.
The atmosphere softened for an a cappella version of 'Grace', the well-known Irish ballad linked to the 1916 Easter Rising, before the national anthem rang out.
Chants of "Ole, Ole, Ole" drowned out Pili's ringwalk music before Taylor finally emerged to 'All Hail King Jesus', a nod to the faith she has spoken so openly about throughout her career.
She stretched her arms wide, sang along and tried to take in every second of her final walk to the ring. There was emotion on her face, but also the familiar focus as fireworks shot into the Dublin sky.
Taylor had spent fight week insisting there was still a job to do, but even for a fighter who had sold out Madison Square Garden and performed on some of boxing's grandest stages, it was hard to imagine her being untouched by a reception like this.
- 'One of the best' - boxing world reacts to Taylor's farewell win 
  - Published10 hours ago
- Taylor's 'dream ending to a dream career' 
  - Published3 hours ago
Taylor puts on a show in finale
After a quiet opener, Taylor - who turned professional in 2016 - burst into life in the second round, firing quick combinations before darting back out of range.
She repeatedly beat Pili to the punch, working in bursts and making the most of the two-minute rounds.
Pili, 29, arrived unbeaten in 12 contests and had previously held the European title. With little expectation on her shoulders, she had everything to gain.
But she had never faced anyone remotely close to Taylor's level and the gulf in class soon began to show.
The party atmosphere continued between rounds as it became increasingly clear there would be no gatecrashing from the Frenchwoman.
Former world champion Prince Naseem Hamed and UFC star Paddy Pimblett watched from ringside as Pili swung wildly in the fifth, only for Taylor to make her miss and fire back.
Pili enjoyed her best spell in the seventh, a quick flurry briefly snapping Taylor's head back, but it did little to alter the direction of the fight.
Croke Park rose for the final two minutes as Taylor continued to press forward, letting her hands go while the noise poured down from the stands.
She embraced her mother, trainer and manager in the ring as 'Celebration' rang around Croke Park before the inevitable result was read out.
"Let me just look around for a second", she said afterwards, soaking up every ounce of the reception.
'The greatest Irish sportsperson of all time'
Taylor has been unequivocal that Croke Park would be the end and she walks away having beaten every opponent she faced as a professional.
Her only defeat came against Chantelle Cameron in Dublin in 2023. Six months later, Taylor returned to the 3Arena and avenged it to become undisputed champion in a second weight division.
After the final bell, she paid tribute to her family and somehow held the tears back as she spoke to the crowd.
"There's nothing like an Irish mammy," she said, smiling as she thanked those closest to her.
For a fighter who has never hidden her dislike of media interviews, there was something striking about the confidence with which she walked around the ring, microphone in hand, soaking up the final moments.
"We did it. We brought boxing back to Croke Park. You were with me in London 2012, you were with me with the heartbreak of Rio. You stayed with me when I turned pro," Taylor said.
"I don't know any other country that would sell 80,000 tickets for a female athlete. I'm convinced Ireland is the only country."
Taylor will forever be defined by her trilogy wins against Amanda Serrano and leaves with a staggering list of accolades, but her true impact cannot be measured in statistics alone.
That legacy belongs to the young girl who once pretended to be a boy just to box when girls were not allowed.
She fought tirelessly to get the sport sanctioned in Ireland and included in the Olympics, before going on to conquer both the amateur and professional codes.
The belts will eventually gather dust, but the trail Taylor blazed across the sport will never fade.

German rocket reaches space as Europe enters satellite launch race

German start-up Isar Aerospace on Saturday launched its first rocket into space from a site in Arctic Norway, bringing Europe closer to offering satellite flights from its own soil.

“We’re in orbit! And just made European history,” Isar said in a post on social media.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz visited Isar’s launch site in March, underscoring Europe’s efforts to establish greater autonomy as the global order once championed by the United States is shifting under US President Donald Trump.
Blasting off from Norway’s Arctic Andoeya Spaceport, the uncrewed Spectrum, designed for small and medium-sized payloads, carried five small satellites as well as an in-flight technological experiment, according to Isar.

US Envoys Head To Kyiv After  Stop In Moscow, Late-Night Meeting With Putin
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
22:03:14 UTC
07:03:14 KST

KYIV -- After a day of crucial meetings in Moscow, including with President Vladimir Putin, US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner are switching wartime venues, heading to Kyiv for talks with Ukrainian leader Volodymyr Zelenskyy with aims of ending the conflict now in its fifth year.
Russian state news agency RIA Novosti reported that talks between the envoys and Putin lasted about three hours, with the US representatives leaving the Kremlin at about 11 p.m. on September 5. Shortly after midnight, TASS reported the Americans had departed Moscow.
A White House official told RFE/RL that "the two sides discussed substantive plans for next steps, which will be announced in the coming weeks" and that the envoys "look forward to equally productive meetings" in Ukraine on September 6.
As the session started near 8 p.m., RIA Novosti quoted Putin as saying the three men would have to address a "difficult situation" during their Kremlin discussions.
Kremlin aide Yury Ushakov, who participated in the session, called the talks "substantive, very frank, and constructive." He added that the envoys stated the US position and promised to present Putin's views to Ukrainian leaders during their talks in Kyiv.
"They not only expressed their traditional interest in bringing the hostilities to a quick end, they put forward a number of ideas on possible routes to a settlement," he said.
Ushakov insisted Russia would achieve its goals and that the "root causes" of the conflict must be resolved, Kremlin code for putting an end to Ukraine's hopes of NATO membership and steps to effectively disarm the Ukrainian military, among other historical grievances -- items Kyiv has long rejected.
Even as the diplomatic push continued, Russian forces launched another large-scale drone attack on Ukraine overnight into September 6.
Ukraine's Air Force said Russia launched 108 drones, including Shahed attack drones and jet-powered variants. It said air defenses had shot down or suppressed 88 drones by 9:30 a.m., while strikes were recorded at 11 locations and falling debris at seven.
The attack followed a day of Russian strikes across Ukraine that killed seven people and left 57 others injured or otherwise affected in five regions, according to regional military administrations. Four of those killed were in the Kharkiv region, including an 11-year-old boy.
As the United States pressed ahead with its latest effort to end the war, President Donald Trump had said his envoys would be presenting a peace deal to the Russians and then would relay the offer to Ukraine the next day.
Trump said Washington had "an idea for peace" and that his envoys were "bringing with them a proposal to end the war," now in its fifth year since Putin launched the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
"I sent them over to see whether or not we can get something done, and there may be a good chance that we'll do it," Trump told reporters on September 4.
'Diplomatic Activities'
Zelenskyy said he had spoken to the envoys on September 5, revealing few details about the call but saying that "the plan of diplomatic activities for tomorrow in Kyiv with the participation of the American team has been approved."
"We are waiting for Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner and are ready for a meaningful conversation," Zelenskyy said on Telegram.
The US envoys' visit to Kyiv would mark their first visit to Ukraine since taking leading roles in the administration's efforts to end the war and comes amid a renewed diplomatic push aimed at reaching a peace agreement.
Trump made ending the largest war in Europe since 1945 a priority when he took office in January 2025, but an agreement has been elusive, and diplomacy had been largely stalled since the start of the US-Israeli war with Iran in late February.
Reflecting the hard-line stance put forward by Ushakov, Putin has shown no sign of compromise in recent comments, among other things insisting that Russia must control all of eastern Ukraine's Donetsk region, including the parts its forces have failed to capture in years of heavy fighting.
Before the envoys departed the US, Zelenskyy said Ukrainian forces would "ensure the normal functioning of Russia airspace so that the negotiators can arrive there safely" and demanded that Moscow reciprocate.
Following his September 5 call with the envoys, Zelenskyy said that "from now through the end of Saturday, as well as on Sunday and Monday, Ukraine is ready to refrain from strikes on Moscow."
Putin subsequently ordered a halt to strikes on Kyiv from September 6-8, according to spokesman Dmitry Peskov, who made no mention of other parts of Ukraine amid reports that Russia had continued its attacks elsewhere.
Airport Attacks
Zelenskyy said Russian forces had targeted Kyiv's Zhulyany and Boryspil airports overnight on September 4-5, accusing Moscow of seeking to create uncertainty over the US envoys' planned journey to Ukraine.
The Kyiv visit will come just days after a Russian drone strike hit the headquarters of Ukraine's domestic security service -- known as the SBU and a key agency that would be responsible for the US envoys' safety during a visit.
"Clearly, these Russian strikes on the airports are a reaction to the discussions and preparations for the possibility of the US side using an aircraft to travel to Ukraine," Zelenskyy said on X, adding there would be "no threats to diplomacy" from the Ukrainian side.
Flying into Kyiv would be highly unusual. Ukrainian airspace has been closed to regular civilian flights since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in 2022, and visiting foreign leaders and officials have generally reached the capital by train.

Massive review confirms the connection between emotional intelligence and human flourishing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
22:00:05 UTC
07:00:05 KST

A review of psychological research indicates that emotional intelligence has a robust and reliable connection to human flourishing, predicting success across school, work, and personal health. The findings suggest that people with higher emotional intelligence tend to experience greater well-being, though the strength of this connection depends on how the traits are measured. The research was recently published in the journal PNAS.
For decades, psychologists have debated what makes some people thrive while others struggle. One popular idea is emotional intelligence, a concept that rapidly gained public attention in the 1990s. Broadly speaking, the term refers to how well a person navigates their own feelings and the feelings of others.
Since its introduction, the idea has spawned thousands of academic papers and grown into a multibillion-dollar training industry. Yet, because researchers define and measure this concept in various ways, its exact relationship with life success has remained difficult to synthesize.
Psychologists generally divide emotional intelligence into three categories. The first is an ability-based model. This model treats emotional skills like a cognitive test, assuming there are objectively right and wrong answers when identifying or managing emotions.
The ability model specifically looks at how well people recognize emotions, use them to guide decisions, and regulate them. The second category is a trait-based model, which relies on self-reported personality characteristics. Under this model, researchers ask participants to rate their own adaptability, assertiveness, and impulse control.
A third category, called a mixed model, combines both objective abilities and self-reported traits into a single assessment. Beyond the differing definitions of emotional intelligence, researchers also look at a wide variety of life outcomes. To find out how these different models connect to positive life experiences, researchers Tyler J. Robinson and Ethan Zell from the University of North Carolina at Greensboro analyzed decades of data.
The researchers wanted to see if emotional intelligence consistently relates to human flourishing. Flourishing is a broad psychological term encompassing mental health, physical health, psychological adjustment, and workplace success. To answer this question, Robinson and Zell conducted a second-order meta-analysis.
A standard meta-analysis is a statistical technique that pools the results of many individual studies to find an overall trend. A second-order meta-analysis goes a step further, combining the results of multiple previous meta-analyses. This approach acts as a quantitative summary of previous summaries, providing a broad view of an entire scientific field.
By pooling data from 62 previous meta-analyses, the researchers gathered information from more than 3,000 individual studies. This massive sample included over one million participants, allowing the researchers to look for overarching patterns across different ages and cultures. The data included populations from Western nations, non-Western nations, children, adolescents, and adults.
The researchers found a reliable, positive association between overall emotional intelligence and human flourishing. This positive link appeared across 77 unique life outcomes. The most prominent associations emerged in areas like workplace leadership, job performance, and psychological adjustment.
The data showed that emotional intelligence was linked to better outcomes regardless of the participants’ age group or geographic region. When looking at different categories of life outcomes, the researchers noticed slight variations in the strength of the connection. Emotional intelligence was most strongly related to success in the workplace.
The connection was slightly weaker, though still reliably present, for cognitive abilities and general academic performance. The researchers also found strong associations between emotional intelligence and specific outcomes like lower rates of job burnout, higher subjective well-being, and better romantic relationship satisfaction.
To put these findings into perspective, the researchers compared emotional intelligence to the Big Five personality traits. The Big Five is a well-established psychological framework that measures openness, conscientiousness, extraversion, agreeableness, and neuroticism. The analysis revealed that emotional intelligence is just as strongly, if not more strongly, associated with human flourishing than any of the Big Five personality traits.
Out of all the specific outcomes analyzed, only one showed a negative relationship with emotional intelligence. That outcome was a form of self-centeredness known as nonpathological narcissism. The researchers noted that individuals with this specific type of narcissism tend to artificially inflate their own scores on self-report questionnaires.
Because they overrate their own emotional abilities, the data showed an inverse relationship between their actual traits and their reported emotional intelligence. More conventional, pathological narcissism was linked to lower emotional intelligence. Measurement styles heavily altered the broader results as well.
The association with human flourishing was most pronounced when researchers used the mixed or trait-based models, which rely on participants rating their own emotional skills. When studies used objective performance tests to measure emotional abilities, the association with life outcomes was weaker. This pattern became especially apparent when looking at how both emotional intelligence and life outcomes were measured.
The researchers found the strongest connections when both variables were assessed using self-report questionnaires. When one variable was measured subjectively and the other was measured objectively, the relationship between the two shrunk considerably. This dependence on measurement methods highlights an important limitation in the data.
When participants fill out multiple surveys about themselves, they may naturally rate themselves positively across the board. This shared method of data collection can artificially inflate the statistical connection between self-reported emotional intelligence and self-reported life satisfaction. The researchers noted that the particularly strong link to workplace outcomes might be partly driven by this shared measurement style, as many workplace studies rely on self-reported surveys.
Because the data in this review is entirely correlational, it cannot prove that high emotional intelligence causes a person to flourish. It is entirely possible that flourishing in life makes a person more emotionally intelligent over time. Alternatively, a third unmeasured factor, such as a stable upbringing or access to resources, could independently contribute to both higher emotional intelligence and greater life success.
The researchers also excluded studies that evaluated training programs. Because of this exclusion, they could not determine if actively training emotional intelligence causes a subsequent increase in human flourishing. Objective tests of emotional intelligence also face modern challenges.
The authors pointed out that recent studies show artificial intelligence language models perform just as well as, or better than, humans on objective emotional intelligence tests. This raises questions about what these tests are actually measuring. It remains debated whether text-based tests capture practical emotional skills or if they simply measure a person’s reading comprehension and ability to understand written scenarios.
To improve the quality of future research, the authors suggest refining how emotional intelligence is categorized. They recommend moving away from the mixed model, which blends traits and abilities in a way that creates conceptual confusion. Instead, they suggest that future studies explicitly separate objective emotional abilities from self-reported personality traits. Separating these variables would help scientists determine exactly how distinct emotional skills contribute to a fulfilling life.
The study, “Robust associations of emotional intelligence with human flourishing: A second-order meta-analysis,” was authored by Tyler J. Robinson and Ethan Zell.

When we act from compassion, we do what is needed to make our own lives and the lives of the people…
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
21:46:43 UTC
06:46:43 KST

When we act from compassion, we do what is needed to make our own lives and the lives of the people around us better. By meeting the needs of ourselves and others, we eliminate suffering and we create joy. We meet needs directly and also indirectly, by helping others towards the awareness they need to overcome their suffering.
It might then seem like compassion is concerned only with improving individual lives. But it is by creating change in individuals that compassion also creates collective change. For a person who is aware does not restrict their compassion to specific others. Genuine compassion is never limited only to our own family, friends, or neighbours. It is always action to meet needs and eliminate suffering for all living beings.
It is precisely when we are most free of our self-produced suffering that we are also most able to see that systemic changes are needed and necessary. We can then see how the suffering of individuals and their automatic reactions to that suffering combine to produce social and economic forces that perpetuate suffering for all of us.

With bare hands, lone warrior cleans up dumpyard of a river
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
21:45:40 UTC
06:45:40 KST

21-year-old BSc student has been a solitary warrior against civic mess and pollution in his hometown
BHOPAL: His online followers know him as 'Bittu Tabahi'. In reality, Surendra Singh Choudhary is the exact opposite of what the moniker 'Tabahi', meaning destruction, implies.For the past seven months, this 21-year-old BSc student has been a solitary warrior against civic mess and pollution in his hometown, Biaora in MP's Rajgarh district, picking up plastic bottles, tangled weeds and other solid waste from Ajnar river, which had virtually become a dumpyard.With no heavy machinery or protective gear at his disposal, he removed the garbage with his bare hands, often at great risk to his health.
Bittu's dogged pursuit has helped restore a section of the river, earning him widespread praise across the country and an invite from CM Mohan Yadav Saturday. They had a warm exchange at the CM's residence in Bhopal, where Yadav assured Bittu of every possible support from govt.The chief minister also shared a video on X, calling Bittu a "son of Biaora" who not only restored Ajnala (the river stretch passing through Biaora) to its original form through sheer resolve and effort, but also sent out a larger message that one man's determination is all it takes to bring meaningful change.
There were also reports that the CEO of an organisation from the Netherlands had offered him a job, but Bittu said he had only heard this from media reports. "I am yet to receive any information about it first hand," he told TOI.Encouraged by his success, Bittu, whose parents work in the health department, has decided to expand his work. "My sole objective is to keep my hometown clean. I have decided to take my work to other public places," he said.Bittu started his mission on Republic Day this year. Upset that everyone complained about the mess, but none - including the municipal administration - addressed it, the college-goer decided to get his hands dirty. From removing garbage piles on streets to pulling out weeds from water bodies, his activism eventually drew national attention.
Unfortunately, his selfless service is being undone by the same people he is trying to help. In his interaction with the chief minister, Bittu shared the pain of watching people throw garbage into the river again, oblivious to the effort that went into cleaning it. "I don't know why people keep dumping waste into the river," he said, his voice betraying anger.The silver lining is that the local municipal corporation has now woken up to its civic mandate, and has deployed JCBs and Poclain machines to clear waste piles from the streets. However, the larger problem - habitual littering and a lack of collective ownership - remains unaddressed.

Putin praises Moscow’s role in supporting troops
Russian President Vladimir Putin has praised Moscow’s contribution to the country’s military and technological development, declaring that Russia will overcome the challenges it faces because they are “temporary and transient.”
The president made the remarks during an address marking Moscow’s 879th birthday; the city celebrates the anniversary of its founding every year in in early September. Putin lauded residents of the capital and the rest of the nation’s citizens, describing Moscow as a symbol of Russian statehood, unity and resilience.
“Together with all citizens of our country, we will overcome any difficulty and any challenge. They are temporary and transient, while Moscow and Russia are eternal,” Putin said.
He drew parallels between the challenges facing the country today and key episodes in its history, including the 1812 French invasion and the Battle of Moscow against Nazi Germany in 1941.
“Today, the capital, together with the entire country, has mobilized all its forces, like 85 years ago, for the sake of a common, rightful cause. Tens of thousands of Muscovites are fighting against the neo-Nazis on the line of engagement, advancing and displaying valor, courage and heroism.”
Putin highlighted Moscow’s contribution to Russia’s military-industrial sector, saying more than 450 defense plants, high-tech enterprises and companies in the capital are producing goods for the needs of the armed forces.
Moscow hospitals are also playing a major role in treating and rehabilitating wounded servicemen, Putin said, while specialists from the capital are involved in reconstruction efforts in Donbass.

More voters identifying as Democrats and not calling themselves Republican
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
21:44:19 UTC
06:44:19 KST

More voters are identifying as Democrats and shying away from calling themselves Republican, according to the latest quarterly data published by Gallup.
Some 49% of voters surveyed leaned Democrat, including independent voters asked to pick one party or the other. Only 39% of respondents leaned Republican.
That 10-point spread marks a sharp reversal from the four-point advantage that Republicans held over Democrats in the fourth quarter of 2024, when voters sent Donald Trump back to the White House and Republicans swept both houses of Congress. Democrats are seeing their most sizable advantage since 2008, when Barack Obama was elected president, according to the New York Times.
The data offers the latest evidence that Trump’s second term has proved unpopular with voters, driving a potential backlash.
Trump’s approval rating stood at 52% at the time of his second inauguration in January of 2025, according to an average of polls published by the New York Times.
But his popularity dwindled immediately, as he cleaved the federal workforce, imposed price-inflating tariffs, passed a profligate spending bill and launched a rudderless war with Iran. Some 58% of voters now disapprove of his performance, with only 38% approving, according to the Times.
Democrats are hoping to take advantage of Trump’s tanking popularity. Liberals are likely to retake the US House of Representatives in midterm elections this November. The party is much less certain to retake the US Senate, though polling is giving Democrats reasons to feel optimistic.
A growing share of American voters have not identified with either party in recent years. Back in 2002, roughly a third of voters surveyed by Gallup identified as either Republican, Democrat or independent. By last year, 45% of respondents called themselves independents, with only 27% identifying as either Democrat or Republican.

06:42:11 KST

Thousands of workers at Jaguar Land Rover (JLR) will be offered redundancies after Britain’s largest car manufacturer had its revenues slashed by falling sales, a cyber-attack and Donald Trump’s tariffs.
JLR informed workers and their union on Saturday that the company would be opening a voluntary redundancy programme for salaried and management team members, the BBC and Sunday Times reported.
As many as 4,000 jobs would be cut over two years, the Times reported. JLR told the BBC it was yet to confirm the number but the company, which is owned by the Indian conglomerate Tata Motors, needed to save about £1.7bn over the next two years.
Unite’s general secretary, Sharon Graham, told the BBC she and the business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, would meet JLR’s chief executive, PB Balaji, next week, after a weekend of intensive talks to mitigate job losses.
About 30,000 of the company’s 44,000 employees are based in the UK. Most of them work at 14 plants across the West Midlands, where the company is one of the region’s largest employers.
The job cuts will be unwelcome news for the prime minister, Andy Burnham, who has pledged to “safeguard sovereign manufacturing” and reindustrialise Britain.
Under his predecessor, Keir Starmer, Labour said it would underwrite a £1.5bn loan guarantee to JLR after it halted production for several weeks last year in response to a cyber-attack.
The attack led to a 27% drop in overall production and cost the company about £200m. It was one of several factors contributing to JLR posting a profit before tax of just £14m – down from £2.5bn the year before.
Tariffs on vehicles imported into the US – which Trump raised to 25% before agreeing a deal for 10% for the UK – also caused turmoil for the carmaker, which is attempting to push more luxury cars to the US market. This contributed to the company’s retail and wholesale volumes – sales via dealerships – falling by about 70,000 and 90,000 respectively.
“These challenges arrived with the global automotive industry already under continued pressure from cost inflation, slower-than-expected uptake of electric vehicles, and the deterioration of market conditions in China,” Balaji said in the company’s annual report published in May.
The carmaker this week launched its first electric Range Rover in an effort to appeal to climate-conscious fans of the luxury SUV – at a starting price of £154,070.

US envoys meet Putin in Moscow for Ukraine talks

US envoys meet Putin in Moscow for Ukraine talks
- Published
US President Donald Trump's top negotiators have met Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow, as efforts to end the war in Ukraine gather pace.
Footage released by the Kremlin showed Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner being greeted by Putin, who said the current situation "is not so easy".
Witkoff thanked Putin for agreeing with Ukraine to halt strikes on each other's capitals for three days. On Sunday the envoys will travel to Kyiv for more talks - their first such visit to Ukraine's capital.
On Friday, Trump said Witkoff and Kushner were "bringing with them a proposal to end the war". So far, efforts by the US and its allies to broker a peace deal have failed.
At Saturday's talks in the Kremlin, Putin also said that "whatever happens, such contacts are undoubtedly always useful". He also thanked Trump for his peacemaking efforts.
He told the envoys that he was "comfortable" working with them, adding: "Of course on our side there is quite a high level of trust during this work."
The talks – held behind closed doors in Putin's official residence in the heart of the Russian capital – lasted for three hours, according to Russian state media.
Details are still emerging, but Putin adviser Yuri Ushakov described the talks as "constructive, extremely frank".
"The talks were not limited to an exchange of views on resolving the Ukrainian crisis - economic issues and potential major, mutually beneficial Russian-American projects were discussed in considerable detail," he said.
Ushakov also said "note was made of the Russian army's tangible advances in the combat zone" and that there was acknowledgement that talks needed to address "the root causes of the conflict".
Despite an escalation of Russian missile and drone strikes on Ukrainian cities including Kyiv, Russian ground forces have made very slow advances for most of the conflict, incurring enormous casualties. Russia still controls about one-fifth of Ukrainian territory - areas that it seized back in 2022.
Zelensky said earlier on Saturday that he had spoken to the envoys, who have "already begun working with the Russian side today".
"The plan for tomorrow's diplomatic engagements in Kyiv, involving the US team, has been approved. We are waiting for Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner and are ready for a substantive conversation," he added.
"From now through the end of Saturday, as well as on Sunday and Monday, Ukraine is ready to refrain from strikes on Moscow, and we expect the Russians to do the same regarding Kyiv."
Russian state media reported that Putin had ordered a halt to strikes on Kyiv for three days due to the US visit.
In televised remarks, Putin said Russia had not agreed to a ceasefire for the rest of Ukraine outside of the capital.
The Russian president said he would "ensure the security of the negotiating process" and of the mediators.
Kushner and Witkoff have visited Russia several times but the talks on Sunday would be the first in Ukraine. It is not clear how the US envoys will be travelling from Moscow to Kyiv.
Ukraine's airspace has been closed since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022.
Delegations from Ukraine have attended talks in the US over the past 18 months.
Earlier on Saturday, Zelensky said Russia had fired "demonstrative" strikes on airports in Kyiv and Boryspil overnight ahead of his planned meeting with the US.
Ukraine's president added: "Clearly, these Russian strikes on the airports are a reaction to the discussions and preparations for the possibility of the US side using an aircraft to travel to Ukraine and land at Kyiv Airport or Boryspil Airport."
Zelensky said on Friday he would guarantee the safety of Russian airspace during the envoys' visit and called for Russia to do the same for Ukraine.
He also said an overnight Russian strike on a civilian building in the Dnipro region killed four people and injured five others.
Witkoff and Kushner's visit to Moscow comes just over a week after a rare visit to the Russian capital by the head of the CIA, John Ratcliffe.
There was no official comment from Washington or the Kremlin on what was discussed. Speaking last week, Trump described the meeting as "semi-routine".
Last year, the US, Ukraine and Russia separately suggested that a deal to end the war was edging closer following a flurry of talks brokered by the Americans.
European allies also held talks in Paris but discussions ultimately ended without a breakthrough. Key disagreements remain between the warring sides on issues such as territory and security guarantees for Ukraine.
In recent months, both Russia and Ukraine have intensified their aerial attacks as fighting continues.
Ukraine said it has struggled to repel ballistic missile attacks due to a lack of interceptor missiles, while Kyiv has focused its strikes on Russian economic infrastructure targets.

Gen Z is turning filial piety into a career path
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
21:30:06 UTC
06:30:06 KST

Advertisement
Opinion
Gen Z is turning filial piety into a career path
Tough job and housing markets have graduates questioning whether the old bargain of hard work bringing progress and stability still applies
3-MIN READ3-MIN
5
 Listen
Dr Ken Ip is an assistant professor specialising in business innovation and entrepreneurship at Saint Francis University, Hong Kong. 
Hong Kong has always had a simple answer to what young people should do with their lives: study hard, get a job, work harder, buy a flat and eventually complain about the next generation. That formula is becoming harder to sell.
A whole lexicon has grown up around Generation Z’s uneasy relationship with work. In mainland China, there are “full-time children”, young adults who stay home and receive an allowance from their parents in return for doing household chores and running errands. Elsewhere, there is the “kangaroo tribe”, an updated version of adults remaining financially dependent on their parents. There are Neets, or young people not in education, employment or training.
While the labels differ, the underlying phenomenon is harder to ignore. More young adults are struggling to make the traditional transition to independence.
Hong Kong offers an especially revealing case. Consider university graduates with a respectable degree and little work experience. They apply for dozens of jobs, perhaps hundreds, only to find that “entry level” increasingly means “entry level for someone who already has experience”.
Employers want experienced workers, but young people need jobs to gain that experience. A position for fresh graduates can demand several years of achievements before an applicant has even had a chance to begin.
Against this backdrop, becoming a full-time child looks less absurd than it sounds. If a young adult can stay at home, avoid Hong Kong’s punishing housing costs, receive an allowance and help around the house, why rush into a poorly paid job with little security and even less prospect of progression?

CBI has filed an FIR against Essel Group Chairman Subhash Chandra
NEW DELHI: CBI has filed an FIR against Essel Group Chairman Subhash Chandra and some other individuals for allegedly defrauding LICHFL (LIC Housing Finance Ltd) of Rs 1,322 crore between 2018 and 2026. LICHFL alleged that Chandra had submitted a 'net worth certificate' of Rs 59,113 crore in 2018 while availing credit facilities but in 2024 stated that his net worth was just Rs 31.7 crore. The FIR was registered on a complaint filed by LICHFL on Aug 31.According to the FIR, LICHFL had sanctioned two loan facilities totalling Rs 980 crore to four companies. A Rs 500-crore facility was sanctioned to Vasant Sagar Properties Pvt Ltd and Pan India Infraprojects Pvt Ltd, while another Rs 480 crore was given to Digital Subscriber Management and Consultancy Services Pvt Ltd and Spirit Infrapower and Multiventures Pvt Ltd.Chandra denied possessing net worth stated in certificatesBoth facilities were backed by personal guarantees furnished by Essel Group chairman Subhash Chandra. The complaint alleged that the loans were sanctioned on the basis of net-worth certificates submitted on behalf of Chandra. One certificate, issued in March 2018, allegedly showed his net worth at $6,197.6 million, equivalent to around Rs 59,113 crore, as of March 31, 2017.
Another certificate put his net worth at Rs 40,562 crore.However, the complaint stated, during the subsequent insolvency proceedings, Subhash Chandra had denied possessing the net worth reflected in the certificates. He allegedly stated that his net worth in 2024 was Rs 31.79 crore and that even in 2017-18 it had not exceeded Rs 40,000 crore.
The outstanding amount against the Vasant Sagar facility was stated to be Rs 570.50 crore, while Rs 507.25 crore was outstanding against the Digital Subscriber facility.LICHFL alleged that Chandra, in collusion with the borrower companies and their directors, induced the housing finance company to release the funds by submitting false and inflated documents. It further alleged that the funds were subsequently misappropriated and assets were stripped to frustrate recovery efforts.

Crime gangs use bots to lure young men in sextortion scams
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
21:23:26 UTC
06:23:26 KST

Crime gangs use bots in sexual extortion of young Australian men
In short:
Young Australian men are being targeted by criminal organisations, usually operating from overseas, in sexual extortion attempts.
South Australia Police said three in four sextortion victims were men, with a similar national trend.
Cybercrime and youth mental health advocates say destigmatisation and conversations in school and at home can help young people navigate the risk of sextortion and image-based abuse.
Criminal gangs continue to have Australian men and boys in their sights as targets for sexual extortion, with more than $200,000 defrauded from victims in one state.
Sextortion usually involve scammers 'catfishing' victims into sending intimate pictures of themselves, which are then used to solicit money or more explicit material.
South Australia Police received reports from 220 male victims of image-based abuse and sextortion in the last financial year, up from 170 in the previous period.
Financial losses in these crimes reached $217,000 in 2025-26, according to police who said the spike was "significantly influenced" by a small number of incidents, including one victim who was extorted $53,000.
"These offenders deliberately exploit fear, embarrassment and urgency, and we want victims to know they should not give in to those demands," said SA Police Cybercrime Investigation Section Sergeant David Mitchell.
Male victims, largely aged under 25, accounted for 75 per cent of sextortion reports to SA Police, and nationally it was a similar story.
While women were twice as likely to experience image-based abuse, men were over-represented — almost 90 per cent — as sextortion victims, according to Australia's eSafety Commissioner.
The eSafety Commissioner said scammers deliberately lured young men by using AI to generate fake but attractive online characters.
Blackmailers also used intimate photos and identity information from previous victims to build credibility with new targets.
"Financial sexual extortion often targets young men, with criminals tricking victims into sharing intimate images of themselves before demanding money and threatening to expose the images to family, friends or the general public," an eSafety Commissioner spokesperson said.
The targeting of young men has been around for a number of years, said Nicola Palfrey, Head of Clinical Practice at the youth mental health organisation Headspace Australia.
"We think of a lot of image-based abuse being targeted at younger women or female-identifying people, but unfortunately there's also quite a lot of targeting of young men in this space," she said.
An Australian Institute of Criminology (AIC) report found more than one in 10 adolescents aged 16-18 had experienced sexual extortion in their lifetime, and only a small fraction reported it to authorities.
Crime gangs behind bots
The report also showed while people known to victims can be responsible for non-consensual sharing of intimate images, sextortion attempts were often sophisticated acts by online perpetrators who the victims have never met in person.
"They're crime gangs … the research and evidence is really clear on that," Ms Palfrey said.
These gangs, like the Nigeria-based network known as the Yahoo Boys, often used fake accounts on platforms like Tinder, Instagram and Grindr to target victims.
Generative AI, face-swapping and voice-cloning technologies were also used to create increasingly realistic lures, the eSafety Commissioner said.
Large language models have also enabled scammers to industrialise their business model, said Rahat Masood, a cybersecurity researcher at UNSW.
"Most of these accounts are created by the social bots," Dr Masood said.
"At the back end, it's the human, but all these accounts have been created by the bots using some scripts.
"It's really easy to generate it now."
Once they engage a victim, scammers will move communications to encrypted messaging apps like WhatsApp or Telegram to continue the deception, eSafety found.
According to the AIC, around two in five adolescent victims have had non-intimate images of themselves run through generative AI to create sexualised fakes.
Avoiding tragedy requires community awareness
Ms Palfrey said the consequences of sextortion can be tragic, the most extreme included suicide and self harm.
"We've had documented cases where families have been generous enough and concerned enough about this phenomenon to share their stories where young people have taken their lives as a result of exploitation, being feeling cornered, and things escalating very quickly," she said.
Ms Palfrey said the threat of criminal activity in online spaces presented an opportunity for families to open conversations similar to discussions of puberty, romantic relationships and transitioning to adulthood.
"Online and offline worlds are not separate for young people,"
"How you navigate relationships, consent, trust, transparency, all of those sorts of things need to integrate the online and offline worlds … and there's a space where we have some wisdom, or some experience, or some reassurance to give young people about how they navigate that."
The eSafety Commissioner's most recent campaigns have been tailored to assist young male victims, while Dr Masood said some interventions could start in the classroom.
"We need to do more curriculum-based awareness," he said.
"In our education from the primary school to the high school, we need to include that. Early intervention in the case is extremely important."
A spokesperson for the eSafety Commissioner said they were "deeply concerned" about the impacts of sexual extortion, which has rapidly become "'a critical online safety issue" over the last few years.
They recommend victims report any offending to police or the eSafety Commissioner, block the perpetrator and get support when they fall victim to sextortion.

Border rail exchanges proceeding uninterruptedly
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
