‘Grief becomes a routine’: Farhana lost five babies. A ‘culture of silence’ exacerbated her pain
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
20:00:45 UTC
05:00:45 KST

On a quiet street in western Sydney, Farhana Laffernis races her curious English staffy and boisterous three-year-old daughter in the front door.
Inside, her three-year-old wears a pink tutu and excitedly babbles as she cuddles her toy doll. The family life Laffernis has built did not come easy.
The 34-year-old has experienced five miscarriages. For someone who “always wanted to be a mum”, the experience “completely shattered” her.
“Grief almost becomes practised or like a routine. You still feel the sting of it every time it happens,” she says. “It’s almost like your mind and your body know the drill.”
Laffernis isn’t alone. Three in 10 women who gave birth in 2022 had previously experienced miscarriage, meaning pregnancy loss before 20 weeks’ gestation, according to the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare. One in 10 had experienced two or more.
The data comes from a first-of-its-kind study in Australia, heralded for helping create better understanding of the prevalence of early pregnancy loss. The study came about after a years-long push by Isabelle Oderberg, founder of peak advocacy group the Early Pregnancy Loss Coalition (EPLC), who was concerned about substandard care for women who had miscarriages after experiencing seven losses herself.
Currently, there is no requirement for doctors to report miscarriage, meaning the data is not collected.
But while the new study has been welcomed, experts fear the data does not capture large groups of women, particularly those from multicultural backgrounds – like Laffernis. And they say the lack of data could mean diverse families are missing out on services they desperately need.
‘The worst thing that had ever happened to me’
Laffernis’s first miscarriage occurred eight weeks into her first pregnancy. It was during the height of the Covid-19 lockdowns, and she couldn’t have her partner with her at any of her appointments and scans.
“It was the first time in my life that I’d ever experienced anything like that, or felt real grief and loss before,” she says. “I was getting all of this terrible news pretty much on my own and having to kind of process that and figure it out.”
That was the first of two miscarriages Laffernis had before successfully conceiving her daughter through IVF. She remembers being “so terrified the whole way through”.
“It seems like everywhere you turn, someone is having this, like, blissful ignorant pregnancy where nothing can possibly go wrong … I could not have that, I just could not be that blissful, relaxed, unaware pregnant woman.”
Another three pregnancy losses after her daughter’s birth marked “the end of the road” in her attempts to have more children.
For Laffernis, who comes from a migrant Indian family, the pain of the miscarriages was exacerbated by a reluctance within her family to talk about what was happening.
“When I was talking to my own family about my losses, the first one was sort of ‘bad luck’, the second one was like ‘Oh, that’s a little bit of extra bad luck’… but then it happens like five times and you kind of just like stop telling people at that point.
“I think in a lot of migrant families, or at least in my experience … there is that sort of mentality in a lot of our communities where our parents have come over [to Australia] from less than ideal circumstances,” she says.
“Maybe miscarriage isn’t the worst thing that’s ever happened to anyone ever, but it was the worst thing that had ever happened to me.”
After years to trying to avoid conflict around the “deeply upsetting” interactions, she had to confront her family about the support she needed.
“I went for a long time just sort of trying not to have the argument before it all just honestly got to me. I did have to have some really hard conversations with members of my family about exactly what it was that I needed from them at this time in my life,” she says.
That reluctance to talk about miscarriage within migrant families is something Dr Fatima El-Assaad has seen many times before.
“It’s something that’s considered very icky to talk about,” says El-Assaad, who founded Sydney-based The Still Nest, a platform supporting diverse families affected by infertility, pregnancy loss, birth trauma and infant loss.
She says cultural and religious practices tied to a women’s fertility journey “may make them feel like it is not in the public arena” and “like it’s something that is meant to be kept behind closed doors”.
While she is encouraged to see data on miscarriage come to light, she questions how representative it is of culturally and linguistically diverse families – and worries that a culture of silence, compounded by the way the data is collected, could be contributing to “a number of holes in the picture”.
The data was collected using existing surveys and clinical registries compiled by midwives and other birth attendants. El-Assaad says flaws in the system could be leading to significant gaps and inaccuracies in the data.
“Are [surveys] primarily in English? Is there a translator that is trauma-informed? … How was the survey conducted? … Where was it captured? Was it in a clinic? Was it at home on a personal device? Was the place safe?” she says, listing factors that can affect the process.
“And we’re also asking culturally and racially marginalised people, and culturally and linguistically diverse people, to just voluntarily answer a survey on top of all the other issues that they’re currently dealing with.”
The problems with the gaps
Although miscarriage is “the most common pregnancy complication”, there’s a lack of healthcare and social support – and Australia is “so far behind”, Oderberg says.
“We had no idea how many people in Australia were experiencing miscarriage, whether it was going up, down, sideways,” she says. There was also a lack of information about high-priority groups, including Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander women, newly arrived migrants, people whose second language is English, people from lower socioeconomic demographics.
Oderberg says data directly helps governments understand what kind of support services the community needs and where.
Assoc Prof Jade Bilardi from Miscarriage Australia says efforts to be inclusive must “go beyond” simply translating resources into different languages.
“That’s a great first step, but it’s to work more with women, pregnant people, partners, family members, and support services that work directly with people from Cald backgrounds so that we can better understand what their needs are,” she says.
Laffernis says she hopes to see greater awareness filter through the medical system, normalising conversations about pregnancy loss.
“No one had really talked to me about the risk of miscarriage until it was already looking like that was what was happening. And then, once they had talked about the fact that it was likely to happen, it became about the fact that this happens to so many people and it’s so common,” she says.
She also holds hopes to see a dedicated focus on post-miscarriage support, including mental health services, for all women.
“I don’t think there’s really anything that can prepare you for what happens. I think it’s more what happens next that makes the difference.”

Comedy is funnier when it is easier to process, new psychology study finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
20:00:03 UTC
05:00:03 KST

Comedy is funnier when it is easier to process, largely because fluency helps incongruous material make sense, according to research published in the Journal of Experimental Social Psychology.
Humour often depends on incongruity: something happens that conflicts with what an audience expects. But surprise alone is not enough. For an incongruity to be funny, people must notice it while still being able to understand how its conflicting elements fit together. If a joke is too confusing, meaningless, or threatening, it is less likely to succeed.
Processing fluency, the subjective experience that something is easy to perceive or understand, may help comedy achieve this balance. Fluent processing can make information feel more coherent and familiar, but it can also produce positive feelings that might make a violation seem less threatening.
Because earlier evidence was largely limited to text-based riddles, Drew Gorenz and Norbert Schwarz examined whether fluency would enhance appreciation of more familiar comedic formats and whether it worked primarily by increasing perceived coherence or by making potentially offensive humour seem more benign.
Across four experiments, the researchers analyzed data from 999 participants recruited through a U.S. university psychology subject pool, including 248 in Experiment 1, 273 in Experiment 2, 206 in Experiment 3, and 272 in Experiment 4. In Experiment 1, participants viewed eight internet memes, four in their original form and four degraded by reducing their exposure and colour saturation. They rated each meme’s funniness from 0, “not funny at all,” to 6, “very funny,” and its ease of processing from 1, “difficult,” to 101, “easy.” They also reported how frequently they encountered memes and sought out comedy in everyday life on seven-point scales. The order of the funniness and fluency ratings was counterbalanced.
In Experiment 2, participants completed 25 fill-in-the-blank jokes and selected the funnier of two substantively similar punchlines. Ten pairs compared rhyming with non-rhyming punchlines, ten compared alliterating with non-alliterating punchlines, and five were fillers. Experiments 3 and 4 presented eight short scenarios describing people who had received nicknames. Experiment 3 used aggressive nicknames, whereas Experiment 4 included both aggressive and benign ones; the researchers varied whether each nickname alliterated with the person’s name.
Participants rated funniness from 0 to 6, ease of processing from 1 to 101, and coherence from 0 to 6 using three items assessing whether the nickname sounded right, seemed fitting, and was likely to be used by the person’s peers. They also answered yes-or-no questions about whether each nickname could be considered “wrong” and “not wrong,” allowing the researchers to identify nicknames perceived as both violations and benign. All experiments also collected demographic information.
In Experiment 1, degraded memes were rated as substantially harder to process and, on average, 0.65 points less funny than the original versions. Participants who reported encountering memes more frequently also found the study’s memes easier to process and funnier. The mediation findings were consistent with the proposed explanation, such that, the visual manipulation’s relationship with humour was fully accounted for by experienced fluency, while fluency accounted for approximately half of the relationship between prior meme exposure and humour ratings.
In Experiment 2, participants selected the fluent punchline as funnier 76.45% of the time, compared with 23.55% for the alternative. This preference appeared for both rhyming punchlines, selected 78.38% of the time, and alliterating punchlines, selected 74.53% of the time.
The nickname experiments produced a similar pattern. In Experiment 3, alliterating aggressive nicknames were rated as easier to process, more coherent, and funnier than non-alliterating versions. In Experiment 4, alliterating nicknames were again easier to process and were rated 2.22 out of 6 for funniness, compared with 1.90 for non-alliterating nicknames; this benefit did not reliably differ between benign and aggressive nicknames.
Across both experiments, the relationship between alliteration and funniness was fully accounted for by greater experienced fluency and coherence. Alliteration did not make the nicknames more likely to be judged benign or less likely to be considered violations, offering no evidence that fluency increased humour by softening their aggressive or inappropriate qualities.
Given participants were predominantly young U.S. university students and the stimuli were limited to memes, punchlines, and nicknames, the findings may not generalize to broader populations or every form of comedy.
Together, these findings identify processing fluency as a potentially broad principle of humour appreciation.
The research, “Is comedy funnier when it is easier to process? The interplay of fluency and coherence in humor appreciation,” was authored by Drew Gorenz and Norbert Schwarz.

‘Jerusalem of Gold’ exhibit brings five Israeli artists to the capital’s theater
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
19:58:44 UTC
04:58:44 KST

Art finds a way, to paraphrase the famous line from Jurassic Park, and a new group exhibition that just opened at the Jerusalem Theatre grew out of curator Chaya Gross’s determination to find a more accessible showcase for Israeli artists as light-rail construction takes its toll on Emek Refaim.
The light-rail project has transformed Jerusalem’s Emek Refaim into a maze of ditches and detours, and presents a serious challenge to businesses along the German Colony’s main shopping street.
But for Gross, the owner of Chaya’s Place gallery, which she opened after Oct. 7 to promote Israeli fine art and crafts, the disruption also provided the impetus for this new exhibition at the Jerusalem Theatre. As the construction along Emek Refaim grew, Gross began looking for another way to bring artists and audiences together.
The Jerusalem Theatre, she said, offers Israeli artists “an accessible venue with the opportunity to meet the artists and buy their work directly from them.”
Jerusalem of Gold, a group exhibition featuring five Israeli artists – Aaron Kraus, Maureen Fain, Miriam Jaskierowicz-Arman, Danielle Meyer Feder, and Orit Simchoni – is open now and will be on display at the Jerusalem Theatre’s Salon Gallery until the end of September.
While the Jerusalem Theatre is known for presenting concerts, dance, festivals, arthouse films, theater, and more, its eight galleries are less well known. Each has a distinct atmosphere, but all are exceptional exhibition spaces.
The in-house curator Dr. Batsheva Ida keeps the galleries full throughout the year, and most exhibits run for a month.
The five artists in Jerusalem of Gold have strikingly different backgrounds and approaches.
Jerusalem-based artist Kraus entered professional art circles unusually early, painting at the Tel Aviv Museum of Art as a child alongside students roughly a decade older. He later trained at the David Wakstein Studio and HIT Holon and worked for years as senior assistant to Jerusalem post-impressionist Huvy Elisha.
Following Elisha’s death, Kraus opened his own Jerusalem studio.
His most unusual technique, one that also defines much of his work, is painting in near-total darkness.
Having been rigorously trained in realistic painting, Kraus turned to darkness as a way to escape the constraints of that technique and to convey not simply what Jerusalem looks like, but how the city feels to him – its holiness, longing, and hope.
The unique look of the city, reflected in Jerusalem stone that catches the sun with particular vividness at dawn and dusk, is central to his work.
Fain creates images of the city that spotlight its unique beauty
FAIN, ANOTHER Jerusalem artist, has a particularly deep connection to the city’s art establishment, as she taught watercolor at the Israel Museum for 30 years. Working in both oils and watercolors, she creates images of the city that spotlight its unique, sometimes rugged beauty.
She has exhibited in numerous solo and group exhibitions in Israel and abroad. She is also sought after as a portrait painter and has exhibited her work widely, with 30 solo and over 50 group exhibitions in eight countries to her credit.
Her works are in the collection of the Israel Museum, in the Brauer Museum of Art, in the Friends of Art Poster Project (Brauer Museum of Art), and in private collections in England, the US, Canada, France, Holland, Norway, Germany, South Africa, Senegal, and Israel.
For Simchoni, her art followed an entirely different professional life. Before becoming a full-time artist, she was a scientist and earned a Ph.D. in archaeobotany. Although she left research behind, Simchoni said that her scientific training and experience remain central to her creative process.
She begins not with a predetermined image but with color, material, and movement, building and scraping away layers until a painting gradually emerges, using brilliant colors and lines to express her vision.
Textiles play an important role in her work. The daughter of a seamstress, Simchoni grew up learning embroidery, knitting, and sewing, surrounded by fabrics and patchwork. She sometimes stitches cloth directly onto her canvases.
A faceless female figure recurs throughout her work. Although not a self-portrait, Simchoni said the figure carries her experiences and emotions while remaining open enough for viewers to see themselves in her.
Evoking the essence of Jerusalem
Meyer Feder traces her attraction to art back to childhood and to the influence of the artist Benn. Later, visits to museums throughout France and Europe helped shape her visual sensibility and deepen her commitment to painting.
She uses texts, color, and varied imagery to evoke the essence of Jerusalem, painting scenes of daily life in the capital, as well as portraits and still-life canvases. Her work has been shown in Israel and abroad, including a solo exhibition, Ladies without Gentlemen, at the Jerusalem Theatre in 2017.
She represented Israel at the international FabrianoInAcquarello watercolor exhibition in 2025, and is also taking part this September in the group exhibition Cinq regards sur l’art at the Centre Européen du Judaïsme in Paris.
Jaskierowicz-Arman, an artist, writer, educator, and specialist in voice development, returned to Israel in 2025 after over eight years in Italy. The daughter of Holocaust survivors, Jaskierowicz-Arman was born in Germany and has lived and worked in countries around the world. She said antisemitism has forced her to change countries repeatedly throughout her life.
After Oct. 7, while living in Reggio Calabria in southern Italy, she became increasingly isolated and eventually decided to return to Israel. She has created hundreds of works, many of which incorporate glass and three-dimensional techniques.
Her long career has also encompassed teaching, writing, and voice development; she is the author of The Voice: A Spiritual Approach to Singing, Speaking and Communicating.
While the artists’ biographies could hardly be more different, their inclusion in Jerusalem of Gold reflects Gross’s broader goal for Chaya’s Place: keeping Israeli art visible at a time when artists and small cultural businesses face unusual pressures.
The Jerusalem Theatre gives Jerusalem audiences another venue to encounter contemporary Israeli art while one of the city’s traditional cultural and commercial streets undergoes a difficult transformation.■
‘Jerusalem of Gold’ will be on display at the Jerusalem Theatre’s Salon Gallery until September 30, while the theater is open.

====================================================================================================

Ma’ayan: New Jersey-born artist shares how art, faith, and loss shaped her journey to Israel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
19:58:21 UTC
04:58:21 KST

The New Jersey-born painter known only by her first name – Ma’ayan, Hebrew for “wellspring” – found the junction of her creative and spiritual journey in Jerusalem.
On the creative side, she started art lessons at eight. As a young adult, she honed her craft in New York at the Art Students League and the National Academy of Design.
Her spiritual side also got early nurturing, thanks to the subtle influence of her paternal grandmother, whose Orthodox rituals and Friday night dinners (“We never called them Shabbat dinners”) touched the young girl’s soul. She was 28 when her grandmother passed away, leaving Ma’ayan with an inner longing for something she couldn’t yet name.
Ma’ayan: From New York to Jerusalem, 2012
By that time, she had a degree in graphic design and advertising from the School of Visual Arts in New York, where she minored in fine arts. She moved to Manhattan, continued painting on Saturdays at the Art Students League, and began teaching at the Montclair Museum of Art while working her way up the ad agency ladder as a creative director.
“With the passage of time, I sought to fill my spiritual void by taking basic Judaism classes. I learned about the deep, soulful beauty of the heritage I never knew. I found my own place in the warmth of the Reb Shlomo Carlebach community on Manhattan’s Upper West Side, where my heart was opened up to Hashem and the Torah,” she says.
Experiential abstraction
Her creative and spiritual paths began converging. “It was not a conscious decision to bring these two worlds together,” she says. “It naturally evolved, as both speak from the heart.”
Eventually, Ma’ayan decided to leave her full-time advertising career and devote herself primarily to painting while proceeding step by step toward Orthodox observance.
“That decision was huge. But just when I had closed those doors, it felt like Hashem was opening new doors for me – I received two major, highly coveted art grants from the Art Students League. This was a confirmation that I had made the right decision.”
One of these grants enabled her to spend five life-changing months sketching and painting in the art capitals of Italy, France, Spain, and Germany. The second grant took her to the Marchutz School of Art in Aix-en-Provence, France.
“It was at the Marchutz School that my voice as an artist started to blossom,” recalls Ma’ayan. “Over the following years, my style moved from more representational and expressionist to what I call ‘experiential abstraction.’ All my paintings have an emotive, inner light and depth that allows the viewer to become immersed in the piece as they are drawn to become one with the painting.”
Each of her series originated with a shock, a transformative event in her life. Large in scale, ranging from 1.2 meters to 1.7 meters, her paintings straddle a middle ground between abstract secular art and traditional Jewish art. They are rooted on the one hand in her academic background; on the other in Jewish sources, including the weekly Torah portion; Psalms; and Perek Shira, Perek Shira, an ancient Jewish text in which elements of nature sing God’s praises.
“My paintings are not religious. What I gravitate to is not so much the message of the black-and-white text of the Torah. It is more the white space that lives in between the letters, which embodies the essence of the Scriptures. This space, for me, holds the spirit, the feeling, the soul of the text. It is this experience that I look to capture,” she says.
Finding home in Jerusalem
Ma’ayan’s new book, Hineni: An Artist’s Journey, presents her artistic story in words and paintings.
Twenty-eight of these paintings comprise her solo exhibition, What Lies Beneath, open free to the public from September 8 through October 21 on the third floor of the Hechal Shlomo Museum of Jewish Art next to the Great Synagogue – a few blocks from her studio at The Social Space on Achad Ha’am Street.
Jerusalem has been her home and inspiration for 14 years.
“I had wandered around the world, from Bali to Mexico, looking for something that I didn’t find. New York City was where I lived, but it wasn’t my home. When I came to Israel the first time almost 20 years ago, for a friend’s wedding, I stopped looking. I fell in love with the people and the land. I knew I was home and could stop wandering.”
She didn’t move right away because her father was gravely ill; after his passing in 2010, she created a painting series in her New York studio in his memory entitled Zalman’s Suite.
Finally, in 2012, she and her husband realized their dream of permanent relocation to Israel. A year later, the Israeli government awarded Ma’ayan a special artist grant as a “unique and exceptional talent.”
Rising from the ashes
Twenty-six of her works that were displayed at Marrache Fine Art Gallery in 2013 were the only ones spared from a devastating fire that reduced her first studio to ashes. In the fire, more than 50 of her oil paintings plus “countless” color and black-and-white oil sketches were destroyed.
“For months and months afterward, I couldn’t paint,” she says. “I asked my husband to go and video the remains of my burned studio and gather all the charred wood, broken glass, bits of canvas, to bring back to me.”
When she finally resumed working, she created a series of paintings and sculptures from those smoky fragments, entitled Out of the Dark.
A couple of years after the fire, a friend introduced Ma’ayan to curator Galit Zimbalist, who has since curated many of Ma’ayan’s group, solo, and Biennale exhibitions in Israel.
Zimbalist, who says she believes Ma’ayan’s art “can bridge gaps and open a window to new understandings of Jewish identity in both local and global contexts,” also curated her Hechal Shlomo show.
“This exhibition speaks about the parallel journey of an artist finding her voice as a Jewish woman and finding her voice as an artist,” says Ma’ayan, who has won 13 international awards, grants, and fellowships throughout her career.
Since the fire, she has created series including The Wanderers, Between Worlds, Where Do We Go from Here, and Continuum, which are on her website, ma-ayan.com. Selected works can also be viewed at Rosenbach Contemporary Gallery in Jerusalem.
She is now working on a new figurative series in which each painting tells the story of a woman and the significant life moment that shaped her. “These paintings say something about how an experience, positive or painful, made these women who they are.” ■
The gala opening of Ma’ayan’s show, combined with a book launch event, is scheduled for September 22 at 7 p.m. at the Hechal Shlomo Museum of Jewish Art.

‘Firewall’ breach? Germany is heading for potential upheaval in Saxony-Anhalt – here’s what you need to know
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
19:57:13 UTC
04:57:13 KST

‘Firewall’ breach? Germany is heading for potential upheaval in Saxony-Anhalt – here’s what you need to know
This weekend, Germans in the state of Saxony-Anhalt will elect their regional legislature and, by proxy, the new state government. A normally routine event in German political life that happens every five years, this year’s vote is drawing attention far beyond the state as its results could send shockwaves through German and, arguably, European politics.
The right-wing Alternative for Germany (AfD) – known for its anti-immigration stance – leads polls by a wide margin and could secure enough seats to form the regional government even if all other parties refuse a coalition with it.
Berlin is apparently so wary of this potential outcome that it is actively preparing mechanisms to cut a potential AfD government off from some federal resources, such as the intelligence-sharing network, according to Defense Minister Boris Pistorius.
What do polls say?
The AfD enjoys between 40% and 43% support in the state – about double that of Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s Christian Democratic Union (CDU) at 22-23%, according to the latest surveys conducted on behalf of the public broadcasters German ZDF and ARD.
Should those numbers hold, the AfD could emerge as the only political group in the parliament capable of forming a government, because all other parties would have to put together a broad coalition to challenge it. Such a coalition would require the right-of-center CDU to enter an agreement with The Left – the successors of the former East Germany’s Communist Party, which is projected to finish third. Such a scenario was already rejected out of hand by current Saxony-Anhalt government head Sven Schulze, the CDU’s leading candidate.
The election could also be a serious blow to the CDU, the party that has dominated the political landscape in Saxony-Anhalt since Germany’s reunification.
Saxony-Anhalt: Mirror of German woes
Saxony-Anhalt is a relatively sparsely populated, predominantly rural state but it also has a sizeable chemical industry. In many ways it has become a reflection of the troubles facing the entire German economy.
Unemployment in Saxony-Anhalt stood at 8.1% as of July 2026, far above the nationwide average of 6.4%.
Germany’s decision to abandon cheap Russian gas imports in 2022 has played a major role in slowing down the German economy. It contracted in both 2023 and 2024, the first back-to-back annual decline in more than two decades, and grew only by 0.2% in 2025. Corporate insolvencies also rose by more than 22% in each of those years, according to official data.
The residents of Saxony-Anhalt felt the crisis first-hand. Over 11,000 people lost their jobs in the state’s manufacturing sector since the escalation of the Ukraine conflict in 2022. Last year, the state’s real GDP contracted by 0.2% against the backdrop of a nationwide stabilization.
The state’s political agenda is thus dominated by economic issues, according to ZDF polling.
‘The most dangerous man in Germany’
The AfD’s election lead is Ulrich Siegmund, a charismatic 35-year-old wholesale and foreign trade specialist.
When the Der Spiegel weekly ran a cover story about him titled ‘Germany’s most dangerous man’ last month, the politician described by the Financial Times as “charming” with a “toothpaste-advert smile” turned it into a publicity stunt by autographing a pile of printed copies featuring his photo.
The party is not relying on Siegmund’s charisma alone, though. Its backing of a more restrictive immigration policy and reliance on German workers, as well as promises of extensive social benefits, lower taxes, and vows to avoid new government debts have resonated with the electorate.
Siegmund has criticized the German government for what he called “giving away money all over the world.” Tens of billions of euros are going to asylum and integration spending, he told the broadcaster MDR in an interview, adding that “every minute, 20,000 euros ($23,190) go to Ukraine. That’s all money we need, money the federal government could also pass on to the states.”
In a separate interview with Die Welt, he also vowed to fight “deindustrialization” and predicted “an economic boom” in Saxony-Anhalt.
A study by the Halle Institute for Economic Research (IWH), however, suggested that an AfD government could face an annual budget deficit of €2.2 billion if the party follows through on all of its election promises without external support.
Why is the AfD shunned by elites?
German officials and politicians have routinely referred to the AfD as “right-wing extremists” or a “far-right” party. They contend the party does not uphold modern “democratic” values and seeks to undermine the political system, though the AfD itself has never voiced such intentions publicly.
German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius tried in July to justify the federal government’s plans to deny any potential AfD government access to classified information by claiming that the party is “opposed to the very constitution of the Federal Republic of Germany” and willing to “destroy our democracy from within.”
The party itself has been battling the “far-right” label almost since its founding in 2013. At the height of the 2015 refugee crisis, it pivoted heavily towards harsh anti-immigration rhetoric, putting itself on a collision course with virtually every other major political party in Germany.
The party’s anti-immigrant stance appears to be at the heart of the standoff with the German political system. The Federal Office for the Protection of the Constitution (BfV), Germany’s domestic intelligence agency, sought to label it a “confirmed right-wing extremist organization” in 2025, claiming the party “disregards human dignity” and uses terms such as “knife-wielding migrants” to ascribe violent tendencies to non-European ethnic groups.
The AfD challenged the designation in the Administrative Court of Cologne, which issued a temporary injunction last year pending a final ruling.
Back in 2025, AfD co-chair Alice Weidel described her party as “libertarian conservative” and said it fights bureaucracy and seeks to “free the people from the state.” She also criticized the then-German government for fostering “immigration into the social system” and accused the EU of Hitler-like censorship in a lengthy interview with Elon Musk on X ahead of snap elections.
So is the AfD controversial?
The party still attract its fair share of controversy, mostly linked to Germany’s Nazi past or the Holocaust. In 2024, the AfD’s top candidate for the European Parliament elections, Maximilian Krah, had to step down after claiming that not all members of the Nazi SS were “automatically” criminals. In 2022, an AfD MP, Holger Winterstein, was accused by the Israeli ambassador of “dancing” on the Berlin Holocaust memorial, prompting the party to intervene and take “measures” against the lawmaker.
Most recently, German politicians have begun accusing the AfD of links with Russia, citing its opposition to EU sanctions and calls for normalizing bilateral trade, as well as criticism of Berlin’s unquestioning support for Kiev.
Why is the AfD so popular?
The AfD is the most popular party in Germany, according to polling agencies Forsa and INSA, maintaining a healthy 8% lead over its closest rival – the CDU.
Support for the party has surged outside its political heartland in the former East Germany, achieving electoral milestones in regional votes in two western German states.
AfD co-Chair Alice Weidel told ZDF in August that the party would bring “law and order to Germany,” adding that she was fed up of being “lied to.” Earlier, she also called for bringing back cheap Russian energy, claiming it was “the secret of the success of ‘Made in Germany’.”
The party’s rise in public standing comes as approval ratings for Merz’s government coalition comprising the Christian Democratic CDU/CSU bloc and the Social Democratic Party is at record lows. Merz was named Germany’s least popular chancellor in 30 years in July, with a disapproval rating of around 84%.
Merz, who came to power as a result of snap elections in February 2025, has spectacularly failed to deliver on his own campaign promises. The chancellor, who vowed to revive the struggling economy, ended up funneling money into the military while blaming the economic problems on Germans themselves.
He infamously told citizens to work more and claimed that the “welfare state as we have it today can no longer be financed.” In May, he announced plans for social cuts by telling people they would have to pay more for drugs previously covered by insurance even as their contributions continue to rise.
In July he admitted that the nation’s “ongoing energy crisis [was] due to the lack of Russian gas” but suggested no way out of it while ignoring suggestions from the AfD to “call Moscow.”
Merz has backed a massive military spending increase, vowing to make the German army the strongest conventional force in Europe, repeatedly pledging more support for Ukraine and resorting to megaphone posturing on any question of resolving the conflict.
In Saxony-Anhalt, a CDU member told Euractiv on Tuesday that the local party branch was paying the price for Berlin’s policies.
Is the Brussels-based consensus facing a shock?
An AfD victory would likely be met by a federal government attempt to limit the power of any new Saxony-Anhalt government. The Telegraph and Die Welt reported in July that Berlin was developing a “secret plan” to prevent any “obstructionism” on the part of the regional authorities in case it would need to facilitate a massive NATO troop movement through the German territory, potentially towards the Russian borders.
Under German laws, a regional government exerts control over the state’s police, education, environment, and health. It can also have limited influence on federal policies through the Bundesrat – a House of the German parliament consisting of the regional governments’ representatives.
The options reportedly considered by the federal government would revise nationwide emergency regulations to allow Berlin “overrule individual states or to take the necessary measures” without the states’ explicit consent.
A resounding AfD victory could weaken the already unpopular Merz and possibly hasten his resignation if it is followed by equally poor results in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania and Berlin, which will also go to the polls later this month.
A potential AfD government is also likely to be perceived as another sign of the continued right-wing resurgence across the EU, where support for such political parties has grown, by some accounts, as much as fivefold since 1995.
Ripples of this potential victory could possibly be felt even in Brussels. After all, the policies that made Merz so unpopular at home appear to be in lockstep with the EU leadership. European Commission head Ursula von der Leyen plans to spend €800 billion ($940 billion) on the massive ReArm Europe initiative while pitching Arctic militarization plans and vowing to turn the EU into a “military powerhouse.”
At the same time, the bureaucrats in Brussels are looking for ways to tap into citizens' savings and compel people to invest in the “EU’s strategic objectives” to address “new geopolitical dynamics.”
The Saxony-Anhalt election could represent a significant setback for Berlin and for the Brussels consensus, which it plays such a strong role in dictating.

France denies inciting failed Niger mutiny, calls accusation ‘pure fantasy’
Niger’s government has widened its blame to unnamed neighbours a week after the assault on a military base.
France has dismissed as “pure fantasy” Niger’s claim that Paris helped incite a mutiny in which soldiers stormed a military airbase and the presidential palace in the capital, Niamey.
French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot made the comment on Saturday, a week after the August 29 assault and a day after Niger’s ruling military council met for the first time since the unrest and repeated its accusations against France.
Recommended Stories
list of 2 items
- list 1 of 2Niger displays arsenal seized after failed military mutiny
- list 2 of 2Niger accuses France of orchestrating failed military mutiny
“This operation, with its international ramifications, was instigated and sustained by a vast network of collusion headed by the French regime of Mr [Emmanuel] Macron,” said Soumana Boubacar, Niger’s government spokesperson, in a statement read out on TV on Friday.
“Traitorous and renegade elements, to whom promises of great things were made, were tasked with carrying out unfulfilled ambitions of Macron and his cronies in our country,” he claimed, saying such “undermining manoeuvres will always fail”.
In response to the accusations, France’s Barrot dismissed the claims and told RFI radio on Saturday: “There never was any intention, nor means that France would have mobilised.”
The exchange marks the latest strain in a relationship that has soured sharply since General Abdourahamane Tchiani seized power in a 2023 coup and turned to Russia for military backing instead of France, Niger’s former colonial power.
The mutiny last week began at Base 101, a military facility inside Niamey’s international airport, when soldiers turned on their commanders and opened fire at several sites in the city.
Fighting spread to the presidential palace and knocked the state broadcaster off air for hours, before Niger’s army, helped by Russian paramilitary fighters known as Africa Corps, retook the base the next day.
State media said hundreds of soldiers took part, and dozens were killed or arrested.
Niger’s government has since widened its accusations beyond France, saying unnamed “African brothers” served as a bridge for the plot, after state television aired a video of an air force captain naming Benin, Chad, Ivory Coast and the regional bloc ECOWAS as backers of the attack.
Benin’s government has rejected the claim, with a spokesman saying “no one in their right mind” believes it.
In that same meeting, Niger’s government acknowledged for the first time that civilians had died in the violence.
That admission came amid a pattern in which Tchiani, who has not appeared in public since the mutiny, has blamed France and other West African states for unrest without producing evidence, which analysts say is aimed more at shaping opinion at home than any legal case.
The pivot to Russia has done little to stop attacks by fighters linked to al-Qaeda and ISIL (ISIS), leaving front-line soldiers who have suffered heavy losses increasingly frustrated, a grievance analysts regard as the true driver of the mutiny.
Relations with Paris have soured further still over Niger’s seizure of uranium assets from French nuclear firm Orano.

Israel opens first Chamber of Commerce office in Republika Srpska, Bosnia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
19:41:07 UTC
04:41:07 KST

BANJA LUKA, Republika Srpska – A new representative office of the Israel Chamber of Commerce was inaugurated in Banja Luka on Thursday night, marking a significant expansion of economic ties between Israel and Republika Srpska in Bosnia and Herzegovina.
Diaspora Affairs and Combating Antisemitism Minister Amichai Chikli attended the opening alongside outgoing non-resident Israeli Ambassador to Bosnia and Herzegovina Galit Peleg, Republika Srpska President Milorad Dodik, Zeljka Cvijanovic, who represents the Serb faction of the Bosnian presidency, and senior Republika Srpska officials. The move comes as Israel and the Serb-majority entity seek to turn increasingly close political relations into greater cooperation in trade, investment, and technology.
The new office will be headed by Israeli businessman Amir Gross Kabiri, who played a leading role in establishing the Chamber’s presence in Republika Srpska and developing the initiative ahead of Thursday’s inauguration.
Speaking exclusively to The Jerusalem Post shortly before the ceremony, Dodik said Republika Srpska wanted to raise its relationship with Israel “to the highest possible level,” with the new office intended to provide a permanent point of contact between Israeli and local businesses.
“We maintain a high degree of understanding and support for Israel and, of course, for the Jewish people as a whole,” Dodik said. “We wholeheartedly want to raise those relations to the highest possible level.”
The office, he said, would facilitate contacts not only in business, but also in culture, education, and other areas, creating “a new dynamic” between Israel and Republika Srpska.
Israeli technology expertise to be shared alongside Republika Srpska's opportunities close to EU market
Dodik said that Israeli technology and expertise could be particularly valuable to the region, while Republika Srpska could offer Israeli companies opportunities close to the European Union market.
“We intend to organize expert groups that will come here and, based on Israel’s experience, propose to us how we can organize various sectors,” he told the Post. “We want people in Israel to understand that they are welcome here and that they will be protected here – not only personally, but their businesses as well.”
He added that the chamber would seek to organize visits by business delegations in both directions.
Dodik also revealed that the proposal to establish the office had come from Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu during their meeting in Jerusalem earlier this year.
“This was primarily [Netanyahu’s] idea,” Dodik said. “For Israel, perhaps it is a small step, but for us, it is one of the most important things that has happened to us in the last decade.”
At Thursday night’s ceremony, Chikli said the office should serve as a practical mechanism for developing business rather than simply as another symbol of the close relationship.
“This chamber must not be merely ceremonial – it must work,” Chikli said. “It must become a permanent address for Israeli companies looking for opportunities in Republika Srpska and in the wider region, and it must be a permanent address for companies here that want to enter the Israeli market, find Israeli partners, and gain access to Israeli technology and expertise.”
“We are not opening another office; we are opening a door,” he added. “A door for investment, for innovation, for partnership – a door between our people.”
Chikli called for Israeli business delegations to visit Banja Luka and for local business leaders to travel to Israel, saying he wanted companies from both sides to move beyond discussions and begin identifying projects and signing agreements.
“Israel is determined to strengthen its relationship with its friends, with those who share our values and who are prepared to build the future together,” he said. “And we believe friendship should produce real results.”
He described the Republika Srpska leadership as “true friends of Israel and the Jewish people,” saying the opening provided an opportunity to “turn our friendship into action.”
Peleg, who is concluding her term as Israel’s non-resident ambassador to Bosnia and Herzegovina, described the inauguration as a fitting conclusion to her posting and recalled the support Israel received in Republika Srpska following the October 7 massacre.
Peleg said that, when the embassy sought to hold a commemoration for the victims in October 2024, it was unable to find a venue in Sarajevo willing to host the event. Republika Srpska officials instead offered a theater in East Sarajevo, where the commemoration was ultimately held.
“From that moment, we knew that we could commemorate our loved ones and get all the respect,” Peleg said.
She said the opening of the chamber was “not only a symbol of our relations,” but a practical step whose work was only beginning. She expressed hope that it would attract investors, entrepreneurs, and businesses from both sides.
Herzog sends message welcoming inauguration
Peleg also delivered a message from President Isaac Herzog, who welcomed the inauguration.
“The opening of this office gives practical expression to the friendship that has grown steadily over many years,” Herzog said in the message. “It will provide a permanent platform for expanding cooperation, bringing business leaders, entrepreneurs, and investors together, and translating goodwill into mutually beneficial partnership.”
Herzog highlighted advanced industry and manufacturing, agriculture, water management, and health as areas with potential for cooperation, adding that greater exchanges among entrepreneurs, researchers, students, and experts could further strengthen relations.
The president said that the Banja Luka office could ultimately serve as a bridge extending beyond Republika Srpska, acting as a catalyst for strengthening Israeli ties with Bosnia and Herzegovina, the Balkans, and the wider region.

JD Vance: Only US can protect Strait of Hormuz, prevent global energy crisis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
19:40:30 UTC
04:40:30 KST

US Vice President JD Vance blamed Iran on Thursday for rising fuel prices following attacks on commercial shipping and sharply criticized European countries for failing to do enough to ensure the continued flow of global energy supplies.
"The basic reality is that the reason gas prices are so high right now is that the Iranians are shooting at commercial shipping," Vance said. According to him, Iran resumed firing at vessels shortly after signing an agreement in which it committed to stop doing so.
Vance directed most of his criticism at Washington's European allies.
"I think it illustrates the ridiculous degeneration that we've seen from our European allies and their inability to actually do anything to help maintain a regular supply to the world's energy markets," he said.
According to Vance, Iranian fire has led some vessels to avoid the area, but traffic through the Strait of Hormuz has continued.
"Just yesterday, we got about 15 million barrels through the Strait of Hormuz, despite the Iranians continuing to shoot," he said. "And what has anybody else in the world done? Why should the United States be the only country in the world capable of ensuring that global energy markets continue to be supplied?"
The vice president presented what he described as two options facing Washington: withdraw and allow oil and gas supplies to be disrupted, or continue acting to prevent Iranian attacks from triggering a global energy crisis. According to Vance, Arab Gulf countries have also warned the US administration that withdrawing would be "the worst thing in the world."
Vance declined to say when fuel prices in the United States would return to $3, but argued that without American action they could be significantly higher. "We have to remember why we're doing this," he said. "First of all, so that Iran never has a nuclear weapon. And secondly, what we're doing right now is protecting commercial shipping to ensure that we don't have a global energy crisis."
Vance: US solely responsible for oil coming through the Hormuz
"We're the only country in the world that can guarantee, as you've heard the president say, control of the Strait of Hormuz," he said. Vance sought to demonstrate his point by saying that "the Iranians would like zero million barrels of oil to come out of the Strait of Hormuz. Last night, 15 million barrels came out of the strait."
"That's happening because of the United States," he said.
According to Vance, "If we don't do it, nobody else is going to do it."
"And if nobody else did it, we would face a catastrophic global energy crisis," he stressed. "Our message to the Iranians is simple," he said, adding that "it has been the same from the beginning: You have to stop shooting at commercial shipping."
"They have to stop," Vance reiterated. "It is that simple."
Vance also addressed negotiations. "The president has been very clear," he said. "We're not talking to them, and we're not going to talk to them, unless they stop shooting at commercial vessels."
When asked about the escalation in fire, he said: "I wouldn't call it a war. Right now there is no active shooting. I recognize that there have been places where it has flared up again, and there have been significant combat operations."
"The significant combat operations lasted about six weeks, and since then, of course, we destroyed their nuclear facilities as part of 'Midnight Hammer.' We destroyed their defense-industrial base for producing weapons, and also a large part of their conventional military," he added.
"And then we made it harder for them to rebuild their nuclear program," he said..
Looking ahead, Vance said that the US will "use the tools at our disposal to ensure, first, that the American people never have to face the threat of an Iranian nuclear program; and second, that global energy markets are properly supplied."
Vance: How it all ends depends on the Iranians
"So when does this end? That depends on the Iranians," he said.
"If the Iranians continue shooting at commercial vessels, I think we have a responsibility to act, and certainly we are the only ones who have the capability to ensure that the Iranians don't destroy global energy markets," he added.
"Our approach is that we're not going to set an artificial timetable," Vance said.
"Let's say, hypothetically, that I told you three months, or I told you three days, and then the Iranians start blowing up oil and gas ships, and the United States is the only country that has the capability to ensure that those oil and gas ships make it to market. I would say it would be irresponsible for us to lay out in advance our strategy and our timetable against an Iranian state that is simply incapable of keeping its commitments and incapable of stopping."
Vance also addressed concerns over potential Iranian cyberattacks in the US. "The American public should know that its government is obsessively focused both on identifying any possible cyber threat in advance, on providing an appropriate response to it, and on ensuring that it does not materialize," he stressed.
"If you look at the Iranian capability to disrupt the daily lives of Americans, I think it's pretty limited. It's not zero, but it's very limited," Vance said. "I would be much more concerned about cyberattacks from other actors."
However, he stressed that "we're doing everything we can to stay one step ahead of these things, and I think we're the best."
"We have the best government in the world when it comes to anticipating and preventing cyberattacks," he added.
"And so what I would say to the American public is that it is a risk that exists, but I don't think it's wise to worry too much about vague risks like that," Vance concluded.

NEW DELHI: State-run Coal India Limited (CIL) has offered power plants having fuel supply agreements with it and its subsidiaries to lift additional quantities of coal, over and above the quantities stipulated in their annual contracts, as stocks available at thermal power plants fell further.Central Electricity Authority (CEA) data showed that on Sept 4, the number of plants with critically low coal stocks had increased to 57. The total stock availability was estimated at 27.1 MT, or 47% of the recommended requirement of 57.7 MT. TOI Saturday reported that 50 of 190 coal-fired power plants had less than 25% of the recommended coal requirement.Coal ministry said the situation was likely to improve now as intense rains over coal command regions showed clear signs of easing, while production and supplies of the fuel at CIL's mines were gathering pace."Despite prolonged spells of rain through July and Aug, particularly across the East-Central parts, CIL maintained a steady supply run. During April-Aug of the current fiscal, CIL supplied 322.9 MT of coal, 6.7% higher than the 302.6 MT supplied during the corresponding period last year."
It said, "Supplies to the power sector in Aug 2026 also rose 4.5% to 48.46 MT, compared with Aug 2025." It added that CIL was holding a stock cushion of 76 MT at its pitheads, besides 46 MT of ready-to-mine coal.
The ministry said sticky and wet coal beds were now drying out, making freshly mined coal free-flowing and considerably easier to transfer, handle and dispatch. Coal seams at lower mine horizons that had been submerged were also being restored to production.The average daily coal production improved from 1.4 MT during the rain-affected first three days of Sept to nearly 1.7 MT on Sept 4, with just a single day's respite from rain, it said.

Competitors dig deep at Hungarian gravedigging contest
The event at a cemetery in Nyergesujfalu, northern Hungary, showcases the gravedigging trade and aims to shake off death-related taboos
A gravedigging contest in a Hungarian cemetery may sound like the opening line of a comedy sketch. It proved to be anything but as 38 competitors grabbed picks and shovels on Saturday.
The Hungarian Association of Cemetery Maintainers and Operators organises the contest to showcase the gravedigging trade and its skills, and shake off death-related taboos.
The dry summer-baked soil in the public cemetery in Nyergesujfalu, northern Hungary, proved a worthy adversary for the 19 two-man teams. They huffed and puffed and sweated as they raced for the title of quickest-dug and most stylish grave.
“Speed is the main thing here, not the beauty,” said Robert Nagy, the victor with his teammate Laszlo Kiss.
“When you have to dig a grave for a funeral, you have to be very careful about the exact dimensions and to make sure that it is beautifully carved.”
Their winning time was 1 hour 21 minutes, digging to contest specifications.

Police seize £200k Lamborghini under tightened antisocial driving laws
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
19:23:40 UTC
04:23:40 KST

Police have seized a Lamborghini potentially worth more than £200,000 under tightened laws introduced to crack down on dangerous driving.
Essex police confiscated the Lamborghini Huracan on Saturday afternoon after receiving reports of the supercar being driven dangerously in Southend. The car was travelling at speeds suspected to be more than twice the limit, police said.
“Antisocial driving can pose a danger to other people using the road and cause misery to residents,” a force spokesperson said.
“The safety of our communities will always be our priority and we’ll take action against those who risk the safety of others.”
The online marketplace Autotrader estimates the total retail value of the Lamborghini Huracan at £238,195, depending on the model.
The vehicle was seized under section 59 of the Police Reform Act, which was strengthened earlier this year to allow police to immediately confiscate a vehicle causing – or likely to cause – alarm, distress or annoyance to the public.
Previously, drivers received a warning under which their vehicle could only be seized if they were involved in another antisocial driving incident within 12 months.
Officers can still choose to give a warning at their discretion. The law allows officers to stop and seize vehicles, or enter premises where they believe the vehicle is being held – and “use reasonable force where necessary”.
Wheelspins and burnouts, drifting in public places, racing in residential areas and repeated revving “causing nuisance” were all reasons for which vehicles could be seized, the Essex police spokesperson said.
The Metropolitan police last year seized 72 luxury cars worth more than £6m in a crackdown on antisocial driving in London.
The vehicles – which included Ferraris, Lamborghinis and Bentleys – were either unroadworthy or being driven illegally, the Met said.
Last month, a police officer drove a Ferrari Monza SP2 worth £3.7m after the open-top limited-edition supercar was seized in a separate, record-breaking crackdown.

Cuban and Afghan immigrants deported from US under Trump arrive in Guyana
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
19:19:52 UTC
04:19:52 KST

Cuban and Afghan immigrants deported from US under Trump arrive in Guyana
The Trump administration has sought to expand third-country deportations, with more than 30 deals struck so far with foreign governments.
Guyana says that it has received six people deported from the United States, as the administration of President Donald Trump steps up so-called third-country deportations.
Guyana’s Foreign Secretary Robert Persaud announced that a group of Cuban and Afghan nationals had arrived in the South American nation on Saturday, after being deported due to immigration issues.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3‘Not a small issue’: People deported by US to Liberia face uncertain future
- list 2 of 3Relative of Afghans who aided US military deported to Africa
- list 3 of 3ICE agent charged with lying under oath about Minnesota shooting
“The US has not made any further requests” for non-citizen deportations to be sent to Guyana at this time, Persaud told The Associated Press news agency.
None had criminal backgrounds, according to Persaud. The removals are part of an ongoing campaign under Trump, who promised during his 2024 re-election bid to engineer the “largest deportation programme of criminals in the history of America”.
Persaud said that Guyana reached an agreement with the US to receive deportees after months of negotiations.
The human rights nonprofit Amnesty International estimates that more than 30 countries have entered into such agreements since Trump returned to office, including 15 in the Americas region.
The deal with Guyana will last for one year and does not constitute permanent resettlement, Persaud said.
Third-country deportations involve sending foreign nationals to places outside of their country of origin. Deportees often have no familiarity with the country they are sent to and sometimes do not even speak the language.
The Trump administration has sought to expand the use of third-country deportations.
It has struck agreements with a range of countries around the world, including several as far afield as Africa. Some of the deals have involved multimillion-dollar payments.
Trump officials have justified the effort by arguing that some countries, such as Cuba, refuse to accept deportees from the US.
Rights groups, however, have denounced the practice as an effort to punish migrants and pressure them into giving up their immigration claims in the US.
Many of the deportees have no criminal background, reflecting the expanding scope of Trump’s deportation efforts during his second term.
The Transactional Records Access Clearinghouse (TRAC), a research organisation at Syracuse University, estimates that 70.6 percent of foreign nationals currently in US immigration detention have no criminal conviction.
Third-country deportations have also raised concerns about conditions in the countries non-citizens are sent to. Some countries struggle with poverty, instability and conflict, as well as human rights abuses.
The deportees sent to Guyana on Saturday will receive resources through the Assisted Voluntary Return Programme, run by the United Nations International Organisation for Migration (IOM).
Under the arrangement, those deported will await the outcome of their immigration process in Guyana.
They could return to their countries of origin or seek relocation elsewhere.
Efforts to restrict immigration, deport foreign nationals and crack down on civil immigration infractions have become a hallmark of Trump’s second term.
As part of that campaign, the Trump administration has stripped tens of thousands of migrants in the country of their legal status, through the cancellation of programmes like Temporary Protected Status or humanitarian parole.
Reports have also emerged that the administration plans to strip visas from roughly 200,000 people seeking asylum.
The removal of their legal immigration status exposes foreign nationals to the risk of deportation, in some cases despite ongoing conflicts or unstable conditions in their destination countries.

Polymarket is restructuring its marketing operation under new leadership ahead of a busy fall sports calendar, CNBC previously reported.
The company recently hired Travis VanderZanden — formerly of Uber Technologies and Lyft, and the founder of E-Scooter startup Bird — as its chief growth officer. He is expected to oversee Polymarket's marketing, CNBC reported.

Trump turns up the heat on Warsh as Fed rate hike looms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
19:12:53 UTC
04:12:53 KST

Ten days ahead of a meeting in which the Federal Reserve will likely consider raising interest rates, the Trump administration looks to be in a full-court press to halt the hike in its tracks.
In the past week, the president, vice president, Treasury secretary and one of the president's senior economic counselors have all urged the Fed not to raise rates and, in some cases, to cut them — an unusually broad public pressure campaign even by the standards of Trump's long-running criticism of the central bank.
While President Donald Trump has avoided directly criticizing his new Fed chairman Kevin Warsh, as he did former chair Jay Powell, he escalated the pressure Friday by threatening to halt trade with countries that run trade surpluses with the U.S. unless the Fed cuts interest rates. Trump had never before directly threatened tariffs if the Fed didn't lower rates.
The president's post was followed by an interview that senior economic counselor Peter Navarro gave to former Trump advisor Steve Bannon on Friday in which he warned that a rate hike would be "careless" and "would hit precisely the sectors America needs to prosper most."
He called the members of the rate-setting Federal Open Market Committee "clowns" and said Warsh is trying to "do the right thing."
Earlier in the week, Vice President JD Vance said, "We believe that the Fed should be lowering interest rates." He added, "We're doing a lot of things to try to keep those interest rates down, but it would be nice to have some help from the Federal Reserve."
And Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, in a CNBC interview, noted that the Fed typically doesn't raise rates during a supply shock until there are second- or third-order inflationary effects.
The administration's pressure comes at a difficult time for Warsh.
Markets are barely pricing in a rate hike for the Sept. 15-16 meeting, at about 60% probability, bolstered somewhat by a strong jobs report Friday. The meeting comes just two months before the November midterm elections, in which polls show the administration faces widespread voter dissatisfaction with higher prices and interest rates.
But questions also remain about the effect the Trump administration's pressure campaign will have on Warsh. The Wall Street Journal reported last month that Trump talked to Warsh repeatedly, a report publicly backed by several of his aides. However, the president himself denied it, saying he had spoken only once to Warsh while in office.
Warsh himself has said the president has had no impact on his decisions and, in July congressional testimony, cited the Fed holding rates steady and not cutting as evidence of the central bank's independence. At the same time, Warsh has said that the president and other politicians have a right to comment on Fed policy.
In May 2019, during Trump's first term, Vice President Mike Pence, Treasury Secretary Steve Mnuchin and economic advisor Larry Kudlow all weighed in on the need for the Fed to consider cutting rates. The Fed did not immediately respond to that pressure but did end up cutting rates two months later.
The administration's argument was similar: Growth itself does not cause inflation, and additions to the supply side of the economy through tax cuts and strong capital investment expand the economy's capacity to grow without causing inflation.
On Friday, Trump said in a post on Truth Social that because the economy is growing so much, the U.S. should have the lowest interest rates in the world.
Administration officials have emphasized the recent three-month annualized rate of the cor Consumer Price Index (CPI) running at 1.6%. That compares with the three-month annualized rate of the core Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) price index, the Fed's preferred indicator, at just over 3%.
But several Fed officials have expressed concern that inflation has run substantially above the Fed's 2% target for five years, and that there are signs of inflation beyond Trump's tariffs and rising energy costs due to the U.S. war with Iran. Three dissented — Beth Hammack, Neel Kashkari and Lorie Logan — in favor of a quarter-point hike at the July meeting, where interest rates were left unchanged.
Warsh, in his speech in Jackson Hole, said the Fed's focus needs to be squarely on inflation, noting that 54% of the 199 components in the PCE price measure had risen more than 3% over the previous 12 months.
By rejecting the connection between growth and inflation, the administration is challenging a central concept in economics: that an economy growing beyond its productive capacity risks generating inflation. The most famous of these ideas, the Phillips Curve, sees tight labor markets and rising wages as the major conduit for inflation. That's likely why markets raised the probability of a Fed rate hike after Friday's strong jobs report. Yet wages were well contained in the report: Average hourly earnings rose 0.3% in August and 3.1% from a year earlier, while the unemployment rate remained at 4.1%.
The administration's argument that increasing the supply side of the economy raises capacity and offsets inflationary pressures could be accurate, but it has a timing problem. The flood of investment into artificial intelligence is projected to eventually increase productivity. But current data shows demand for the equipment needed to build out AI infrastructure is raising prices.
Markets will be focused on the Friday CPI report, which Fed officials have said will be a critical gauge of whether inflation is easing or still accelerating — and it could decide whether the Fed hikes or holds. No FOMC member has recently discussed rate cuts publicly.

Russian attacks kill 3, injure over 20 across Ukraine as Putin meets US envoys in Moscow
Russian attacks across Ukraine killed at least three people and injured more than 20 others on Sept. 5 as U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner met Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow for talks on ending the war.
Russian forces struck Chuhuiv in Kharkiv Oblast, killing three people, including a child, and injuring a woman. A jet-powered drone hit a house in the city center, destroying the building as well as a warehouse and a garage.
Kharkiv Oblast Governor Oleh Syniehubov said the strike killed nearly an entire family: a 19-year-old woman, an 11-year-old boy, and a 45-year-old man.
More than a dozen people were also injured in Zaporizhzhia, where Russian drones struck several buildings, including a high-rise residential building and an administrative building.
In Khmelnytskyi, debris from a Russian drone fell on a three-story building, injuring seven people, including a minor, according to National Police. Four of those injured were hospitalized, with one person in serious condition.
Russian forces also attacked a passenger train bound for Kherson with several Shahed-type drones around midday, according to Kherson Oblast Governor Oleksandr Prokudin.
Two diesel locomotives were damaged in the attack. Prokudin initially reported that a 55-year-old railway worker was hospitalized in moderate condition after sustaining a shrapnel wound to her arm, a concussion, blast injuries, and a closed head injury.
The attacks unfolded as Witkoff and Kushner were in Moscow for talks with Putin.
Earlier on Sept. 5, Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said Putin had ordered Russian forces to halt strikes on Kyiv for three days beginning at midnight.
Ukraine, however, had proposed a broader three-day ceasefire that would go beyond attacks on the two capitals and include fighting along the front line. Putin said during his meeting with the U.S. envoys that Russia had not agreed to the broader proposal.
The Ukrainian side has said it is prepared to refrain from strikes on Moscow during the U.S. envoys’ visit and has called on Russia to reciprocate.
Witkoff and Kushner are expected to travel to Kyiv following their talks in Moscow.

Drapatyi introduced the new Commander of the Ground Forces, Zaiets, and also acknowledged five key tasks

Mykhailo Drapatyi introduced Brigadier General Sviatoslav Zaiets to the personnel. The priorities include people, training, and leadership.
Commander-in-Chief of the Armed Forces of Ukraine Mykhailo Drapatyi introduced the new Commander of the Ground Forces, Brigadier General Sviatoslav Zaiets, to the personnel, and also outlined tasks for the commander and the team, UNN reports.
The basis for this choice was his experience in commanding troops, his ability to turn decisions into results, and his ability to implement new technologies where they provide a real combat advantage
The Commander-in-Chief outlined the following tasks for the Commander of the Ground Forces and the team:
-  People. A service member must be properly trained, equipped and protected from unjustified risk. They must understand what is expected of them today and what awaits them tomorrow. 
-  Training. A person must not enter combat unprepared. Training must correspond to what a service member will see at a position tomorrow, rather than to the programs of past years. 
-  Leadership. A professional must be able to see a path for their growth. Promotion should be based on competence, service results and leadership qualities. We must begin shaping the next generation of officers and sergeants. 
-  Technology. Unmanned, digital and other new capabilities must be implemented not for the sake of numbers in reports. The criterion is simple: the combat advantage felt by the enemy and the lives of our people that this advantage helped save. 
-  Combat experience. Conclusions about what is or is not working on the front line today must quickly reach those who train, plan and make decisions. 
All these changes have one practical criterion: what they change for a person in the military and for a unit in combat. The most valuable combat capability of the Armed Forces is our people. Therefore, the task of the new commander is not simply to change structures and processes. His task is to make the Ground Forces capable of carrying out combat missions and better for the people who serve in them
Drapatyi thanked Hennadiy Shapovalov for his work and wished the new Commander of the Ground Forces to accomplish more in this position.
We have a lot of diligent work ahead. Everything will work out
For reference
Sviatoslav Zaiets has been appointed the new Commander of the Ground Forces of the Armed Forces of Ukraine. The relevant Decree No. 853/2026 dated September 2, 2026, was signed by President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy.

AI chatbots like Buddy at Bunnings years from becoming norm

Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05

04:01:56 KST

AI chatbots like Buddy at Bunnings years from becoming norm for shoppers
In short:
Some of Australia's largest retailers are investing in autonomous AI agents shopping for customers.
But experts said it was expensive technology years away from being mainstream.
Retailers such as Wesfarmers, Woolworths and Coles made combined profits of more than $5 billion in the 2026 financial year.
AI chatbots are already in use by Australia's biggest retailers, from Buddy at Bunnings to Olive at Woolworths.
But experts say it will be years before these company-built artificial assistants can do more than just chat to shoppers.
During their full year financial results presentations, all major retailers earmarked "agentic commerce" — letting an AI program shop for you — as a key space to invest in.
"Olive, our much-loved digital shopping assistant, has transformed into a personal shopping companion," Woolworths CEO Amanda Bardwell said.
Coles, which has yet to develop its own AI chatbot, has flagged conversational shopping as an opportunity for further investment.
Australia's major retailers reported a combined profit in the last financial year of more than $5 billion.
"The earnings growth came out of cost, not out of customers spending more,"
Retailers also highlighted the growth in private label and online sales during their financial results presentations.
One in three purchases to be online, expert says
Some of the largest revenue growth for retailers came from online orders with Coles seeing a 26.4 per cent increase with sales reaching $5.6 billion, representing almost 14 per cent of all sales.
Woolworths saw its online orders grow by 18 per cent, which represented almost $11 billion.
As many as one in three products could be purchased online soon, according to Queensland University of Technology's Gary Mortimer.
But high transport and logistics costs will curb the profit margins for online sales, he said.
Since 2019, Coles has partnered with e-commerce company Ocado Group for its automated deliveries.
According to Ocado Group's 2024 annual report, the cost per item picked for its British clients was 52 British pence ($1.06).
Professor Mortimer said the growth could see store sizes and ranges shrink with repeat purchases such as toilet paper and cleaning goods delivered to homes.
"It is certainly cheaper to fill shelves and have shoppers physically select, scan and take their purchases with them,"
US supermarket chain Kroger announced last year it was closing three of its automated warehouses, which was in partnership with Ocado, due to sites not meeting financial expectations.
University of Sydney retail expert Lisa Asher said customers could soon bear the additional costs associated with online orders.
"Groceries will continue to go up if they're going to push forward with this as an option because the price point that you pay online versus in store is the same," she said.
AI privacy concerns as retailers move to 'agentic commerce'
Ms Asher said regulation was needed to curb "surveillance capitalism", and protect the privacy of shoppers as supermarkets deliberate how to roll out AI in stores and online
"They are essentially monetising our shopping habits and data points from a customer perspective to make more money from us," she said.
"We are not the product because we are trying to buy food to feed our families with rising cost of living."
Mr Rigby said it will take at least three years before agentic shopping becomes a standard practice in Australia.
"Woolworths is beta testing Smart Basket, which builds a basket from your previous purchases. [It] still puts a human at the check-out," he said.
"Nobody here is letting an agent complete a grocery shop unsupervised at any scale."
Mr Rigby has tested 'agentic shopping journeys' across a number of retail categories, and said grocery was the hardest to hand over.
"My read is grocery will be one of the last categories to go agentic, not the first,"
"People are particular about fresh. Substitutions are personal. Get one item wrong in a $200 basket and you've lost trust in the whole thing.
"When it lands it will be more routine replenishment, not fresh. Not to mention this tech is very expensive to rollout."
Home-brand growing as retailers become suppliers
Private label, or home branded products represent about 36 per cent of consumer sales across all supermarkets in Australia, and the category is growing according to Mr Rigby.
At the major supermarkets, Coles saw a 6.1 per cent lift in private label sales, while Woolworths saw that figure increase by 5.5 per cent in the year to June 30.
Mr Rigby said home-branded products have created savings for retailers but the growth was due to the quality gap closing between them and branded products.
"It's a rational trade rather than a sacrifice for a household under genuine financial pressure that's the difference between making the week and not," he said.
Mr Rigby highlighted Kmart's home-brand Anko which expanded to supply overseas retailers from Walmart in the United States, Hudson's Bay in Canada, Flipkart in India and Amazon.
"An Australian discount department store has turned its private label into a product design and sourcing business it sells to retailers overseas,"
"There's no other example like it here."
But the growth in home branded products especially at supermarkets could, over time, displace other competitors, and potentially impact costs for consumers.
"Where it goes wrong is conflict of interest," Mr Rigby said.
"The moment a retailer is also a supplier, every ranging and pricing decision it makes about a competing brand is open to question."
Home branded products were a short-term sales strategy to improve profitability but could limit customer choice long term, according to Ms Asher.
"So when they delete our competition, they delete the brand, we lose out from price competition … and they can do this because it's not unlawful," she said.
"And once they own a product in the category, they can just increase the prices because they'll have a monopoly over their shelves."
