Taiwanese creators develop ‘mecha’ content, characters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
16:39:29 UTC
01:39:29 KST

Taiwanese creators are bringing original mecha toy intellectual property (IP) featuring diverse designs to local and overseas market.
An original IP refers to a product or creative property developed from scratch by a person or a team, featuring unique characters and offering commercial potential across multiple fields. It can be further adapted into comics, games, films or TV productions, or developed into physical merchandise.
Veteran IP producer Luo Chi-ming (羅際明) said that he traced the history of robot toys, and that the trend took off in the 1970s when Japanese toy and snack companies invested in advertising and animation to promote their products.
Photo courtesy of ANRS
Well-known IPs included Gigantor, Mazinger Z and Transformers, which also helped fuel the chogokin toy craze, he said.
In the 1980s and 1990s, titles such as The Super Dimension Fortress Macross and the Gundam series expanded the genre beyond children’s toys, targeting teenagers and adults, Luo said.
In the past few years, as players have grown older and digital games have proliferated, mecha model kits have become a nostalgic passion for “kids at heart,” he said.
Photo: Wu Po-hsuan, Taipei Times
Taiwan was once home to numerous plastic injection-molding factories that served as major contract manufacturers for leading international toy companies, but that industry later moved overseas, he said.
However, Taiwan remains an important test market for Japanese companies, with products often piloted here before being launched overseas.
The mecha market is enormous, Luo said, adding that sales of the Gundam IP alone reached ￥254.3 billion (about US$1.63 billion) last year.
While it is difficult for Taiwanese original IPs to compete with established franchises, they can look to Southeast Asia for further market expansion, he said.
Among the Taiwanese creators is Chou Ta-mu (周大木), whose core business is automotive parts and customization, and who has loved mecha models since childhood.
Chou said the decision to enter the toy market was largely driven by the COVID-19 pandemic, when orders at his company ground to a halt.
Photo courtesy of Chiu Chi-kuan
Chou said that confident in his team’s creativity and design capabilities, and fueled by his own passion for mecha, he took what he called “a mysterious sense of confidence” and embarked on a journey to create an original Taiwanese mecha IP.
Chou founded the Giga Garage brand, blending elements such as anime-style heroines, mecha and space monsters with Taiwanese street food. The concept gave rise to the model toys Ignatius (英格納休斯) and Aurelian (奧雷利安), the first and second machines in the Shen Ji Mecha Wars (神姬機鬥傳) series. With Japanese-style packaging and a mid-range pricing strategy, the Shen Ji series has entered the Japanese market, where its sales outnumber those in Taiwan.
Separately, Chiu Chi-kuan (邱繼寬), founder of Model Oasis, has created an original humanoid mecha named Heron (蒼鷺), inspired by the migratory journeys of birds.
The design symbolizes the idea that Taiwanese can thrive wherever they go, but would ultimately return home to contribute to their country, he said, adding that it is the project’s first flying, military-style humanoid mecha.
While Heron’s realistic design occupies a relatively niche market, toys should possess a distinct identity, he said.
The product line adopts a customizable approach, offering a variety of interchangeable weapons and equipment that allow users considerable freedom in configuring their models, he said.
Chiu, who has operated Model Oasis in Chiayi for about five years, credited his venture to a deep love for Taiwan and a desire to pour his passion into developing an original Taiwanese mecha intellectual property.
He said that despite growing competition from low-cost Chinese products in the market, he remains optimistic.
He said while he believes copyright awareness in China still has room for improvement, he intends to continue focusing on original creations rather than following trends, providing discerning collectors with the unique products they seek.
Meanwhile, A.N.R.S-Heroes Assemble, a 2D pixel-art mecha action game developed by Taiwanese creative collective ANRS, is scheduled for release on PC next year, the group said.
ANRS was founded online 15 years ago by a group of mecha enthusiasts, with half of its members having experience in the gaming industry.
In addition to publishing fan magazines and producing podcast shows, the group regularly runs booths at the Fancy Frontier anime convention for over a decade.
The team’s marketing executive Liu Li-fan (劉立凡) said the game, targeting men in their 30s and 40s, features 2D side-scrolling action which allows players to execute combo attacks and ultimate moves using simple button inputs.
The game also pays homage to Japan’s Super Robot Wars series by incorporating a character progression system, featuring a close-combat fighter specializing in martial arts, he said, adding they plan to include 15 stages in the final game.
A demo version was showcased at the G-Eight Game Show in December last year and at the Taipei Game Show earlier this year, where it received positive feedback, he said, adding that they hope the title would recreate the exhilarating combat experience of classic arcade games when it is launched on PC next year.

Film about chips screened in The Hague
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
16:39:28 UTC
01:39:28 KST

A documentary tracing the development of Taiwan’s semiconductor industry over the past five decades was on Thursday screened at a special showing in The Hague.
In a news release on Friday, the Taipei Representative Office in the Netherlands said it held a screening of A Chip Odyssey (造山者-世紀的賭注) at the Bar Beton center in the city’s central train station for more than 100 attendees.
The screening included a special panel discussion on the film, which included Taiwanese expats and members of the Dutch media.
Photo courtesy of the Taipei Representative Office in the Netherlands via CNA
The film is Taiwan’s first documentary spotlighting its world-leading semiconductor industry and chronicling the nation’s rise from underdog to becoming the central hub of the global chip supply chain over the past five decades.
Its Chinese title, Mountain Builders, was derived from the film’s intention to “deliver the spirit of the mountain builders” — those who have helped propel the nation’s semiconductor ascent, the film’s director, Hsiao Chu-chen (蕭菊貞) said.
Another reason for the title is Taiwan’s nickname for semiconductor giant Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co (TSMC), “The Mountain that Guards the Nation,” she said.
As for the English title, Hsiao said she named it “Odyssey” after drawing inspiration from the ancient Greek epic about a hero’s long and arduous journey home — a path filled with challenges, much like Taiwan’s journey in developing its semiconductor industry.
At the screening, Taiwan’s representative to the Netherlands, Tien Chung-kwang (田中光), said that Taiwan’s semiconductor journey reflected the plight of the main character in Homer’s epic.
Tien said that, like Odysseus, it took several decades for Taiwan’s semiconductor industry to overcome obstacles and bring success home, through skills such as foresight and innovation.
Taiwan’s technological advancements were the result of a positive talent cultivation environment that was founded upon the respect for democracy and human rights, Tien said, adding that the nations would continue to work with like-minded governments to help further technological advancement around the world.
Besides Taiwanese and Dutch officials, several experts in tech and global politics were also among the guest list for the screening and the subsequent panel.
Panelists at the event included Chen Lin-lin (陳玲鈴), dean of the Industrial Design Department and a full professor of design innovation strategy at the Netherlands’ Eindhoven University of Technology, as well as the Hague Centre for Strategic Studies strategic analyst Benedetta Girardi and Bloomberg former Netherlands bureau chief Cagan Koc.
The panelists shared their insights on the challenges Taiwan’s industry faces as well as the tech industry’s relationship with global politics.

After the flood: human suffering on an unfathomable scale in Nepal’s worst-hit districts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
16:39:28 UTC
01:39:28 KST

Searching for the body of his wife in the mud, Dil Bahadur Shrestha lamented that he did not even have a shovel left. For now, he has been using his hands to try to find her as he picks through the ruins of his house.
On Wednesday morning last week, Jamuna Shrestha, his wife of 50 years, had been at home in Betrawati on the banks of Nepal’s Trishuli River, feeding her beloved chickens and goats.
As deadly flash floods coursed down the river valley, Jamuna was last seen going back into her house, trying to usher her chickens to safety, while others fled uphill. Now that house stands like a muddy carcass, everything inside it destroyed or washed away by the violent force of the water and debris that killed more than 1,200 people in Nepal and Tibet.
Photo: Reuters
Dil Bahadur Shrestha, 70, had been tending to his rice fields and feeding his cows on the opposite bank when he felt the ground tremble and saw a black wave, hundreds of meters high, coming down the valley. He ran to safety in the forest, but not before watching two bridges get swept away behind him.
“When it hit, everything was destroyed within two minutes,” he said.
He knows in his heart that his wife is gone, but like thousands caught up in the disaster, her body has yet to be found and she is counted among the missing. More than 5,000 people are reported missing in Nepal and a further 546 in the Tibet region of China.
Rescue workers have still not reached Dil Bahadur Shrestha’s home, so he returned to try to retrieve her body himself.
“Maybe she thought the flood wouldn’t reach inside the house,” he said, wiping away tears.
The couple had already rebuilt their home once after an earthquake in 2015 that killed about 9,000 people. As he spoke, his frail body collapsed to the barren, muddy ground where his neighbor’s house once stood.
Photo: AFP
“Even now, I cannot believe that she is gone,” he said. “I cannot forget her. That’s why I keep walking around looking for her. I still feel as if she might be walking around somewhere here. I keep getting this feeling that she might still be here, looking after the chickens and the goats.”
UNIMAGINABLE TRAGEDY
The scale of the tragedy in Betrawati is unfathomable. It was 8:37am when a melting glacier high up in the Himalayas on the border between Nepal and Tibet crashed into the valley below, setting off deadly flash floods down Nepal’s Bhotekoshi and Trishuli rivers. By 8:50am, with only a few minutes’ warning, the settlement of Betrawati was engulfed.
This once-thriving market town was submerged in mud so thick that only the top two floors of a six-storey building are visible. Most houses were washed away entirely or flipped on their sides by the sheer force of the floods. School buses lie overturned. A grocery shop was swept 200 meters from its original location and lies in ruins. The river itself has diverted to a new path that cuts through where the highway once was.
Fragments of the lives of the thousands who lived here lie scattered in the debris: kettles, teddy bears, a record-keeping book, saucepans, medicine packets, a pair of glasses. At least 250 people are missing, Dil Bahadur Shrestha’s brother and sister-in-law among them.
As Dil Bahadur Shrestha surveyed the ruins of his life, search and rescue teams stood on the opposite bank, looking for the dead. By the end of the day, they had pulled 24 bodies from a single house. A helicopter thundered overhead, white body bags swinging underneath.
“I feel there could still be hundreds of bodies here,” said Dil Bahadur Shrestha. “So many people were swept away all at once, carried off by the raging water.” His voice broke: “Now I’m alone. I am completely alone.”
A few meters away, Santamaya Lawat, 57, stood shaking a thick cake of dirt from the few clothes and blankets she had been able to retrieve from her brother’s home, now only partly standing, with a gaping hole in the side. Her own house, built just 10 months ago with her life’s savings, was still so filled with mud she had not yet been able to get inside. Five members of her family are gone.
“My heart broke when I came back,” she said. “This was supposed to be the house I lived in for the rest of my life, but everything is gone. It was like heaven here and now it has been turned into hell.”
VILLAGES SWEPT AWAY
Further up the river, in the district of Rasuwa, on the border with Tibet, the scale of destruction only gets worse. Many of the villages here were swept away entirely and are only accessibly by army helicopter. Some are still so cut-off and the ground conditions so precarious that the fate of hundreds of people remains unknown. On Tuesday, police search and rescue teams confirmed they had finally been able to begin ground operations in the border village of Timure, recovering 90 bodies so far.
A week after the disaster, survivors who fled up mountainsides were still being collected by army helicopters and evacuated to the army base in Dhunche, Rasuwa district’s administrative headquarters.
The mountain village of Syabru Besi was among those wiped clean away, with even the road to the village gone. According to local government officials, at least 500 people there are missing, a quarter of the population. The village resembles nothing more than a muddy riverbed, just one building left standing.
Chhiring Dorje, a 50-year-old farmer, was among those who managed to escape Syabru Besi, but five of his family are missing.
“There were 15 or 16 of us from the village who made it safely to the forest,” said Dorje. “We stayed there for two days before the army came in a helicopter. We had nothing to eat. We survived by drinking water from the forest.”
He stood tightly holding the hand of his nine-year-old granddaughter, Ritu Tamang, who wore a big pink rucksack as they waited at Dhunche army base for a ride down to Kathmandu. Rescue helicopters thundered in and out every few minutes. She said quietly that there was “nothing left where our house used to be. I used to go to school and was in Grade 1. Now the school is gone. There are no teachers either.”
With the highways washed away, the only road from Kathmandu to Rasuwa is a perilous unpaved track of mud and stones, weaving through tiny mountain villages. The journey often takes more than 12 hours. The treacherous conditions have made it difficult for aid to reach the worst-hit areas and hindered the rescue and relief operations. Many aid trucks are now stuck in Dhunche, unable to drive further north.
At a small relief camp on the road between Betrawati and Dhunche set up by Nepal’s Dhulikhel hospital, people collected medicine and food supplies. Doctors said dozens of the children here had lost their parents in the floods. More than 200 children from the local Nilakantha school, most aged between five and 11, are also missing, believed to have been washed away as they walked to morning classes.
Prakash Nepal, a teacher, said the school had received a warning just 10 minutes before the flood waters hit, when the school bus was already picking up students.
“Luckily, we immediately contacted the bus driver and the vehicle stopped midway so the students were able to survive,” he said. “The surge of water did reach the vehicle, but thankfully it did not cause much damage.”
However, many of the local families had been displaced by the 2015 earthquake and still lived in informal settlements along the riverbank. Most of those children had been walking to school when the flood struck. Prakash Nepal’s eyes welled with tears: “We could not save the students who were still on the road.”
For two days afterwards they heard nothing and feared he was dead. Then they received a phone call. “He called up from a hospital in Kathmandu; he had been rescued by the army,” said Ram Krishna Neupane. “He could not speak, he was crying so much and we were crying.”
It was, added his wife, “a miracle.”

Shanghai summit exposes cracks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
16:39:27 UTC
01:39:27 KST

The 25th anniversary summit of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) was held in Bishkek on Monday and Tuesday. Instead of reflecting a celebration, it was a mirror of the strategic fractures within Eurasia.
Twenty-five years ago, the Shanghai Five was a local arrangement aimed at stabilizing post-Soviet frontiers and dealing with the main anxiety around regional extremism. It has expanded into a weightier strategic institution, now gathering about 40 percent of the global population in its fold.
However, as leaders of its 10 members arrived in Kyrgyzstan’s capital to attend the summit and the opening of the Nomad Games, the SCO expressed a basic anxiety that lies at its core: Can such a body be an effective umbrella for rivalries among its members and yet be a stable balancer to the liberal, Westernized global order?
For China and Russia, the summit was an important event to manifest unity and to be seen as leading a multipolar alternative global system. Moscow used the SCO to show that Western sanctions and attempts to isolate it have not succeeded across the global south and Eurasia, as was also evident in the case of the Russia-ASEAN summit.
However, China uses economic capacity and its Belt and Road Initiative (BRI) to act as the unrivaled contributor to infrastructure development in Central Asia. Its commitments are coalescing around important trade corridors such as the China-Kyrgyzstan-Uzbekistan railway. Beijing continues to promote trade settlement in local currencies to circumvent the US dollar and make China the primary economic engine for the region.
China and Russia intend to institutionalize economic arrangements through an SCO development bank, with a parallel SCO development fund. Those institutions could make important differences in the region beyond what China has achieved through the BRI.
Those issues were discussed in Bishkek as important mechanisms to fund regional infrastructure and support members affected by Western sanctions, which is important for Russia and Iran in particular.
Progress remains slow because of internal differences. China seeks another version of the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank, from which there would be weighted capital allocations to the members. That would be in China’s interests, given the size of its economy. Russia and India, for instance, prefer a body in which voting rights are equally distributed, as is the governance, so that China does not become the dominant institutional force.
A political consensus around the necessity of a development financial institution has grown, but the idea is still under discussion and cannot be seen as a functional alternative to global lenders at present.
The summit emphasized the importance of the Regional Anti-Terrorist Structure (RATS), based in Tashkent, which has long provided the SCO with a strong instrument. RATS is supposed to deal with the SCO’s issues with terrorism, separatism and extremism. Given the low level of achievement of the SCO, RATS remains its most functional institution.
To its credit, intelligence sharing, growing unified watch lists and common exercise frameworks, which could deal with extremist networks across Central Asia, have been working to some extent.
However, the efficiency and impact of RATS are crippled by regional rivalries, and the inability to have common basic definitions and accept counterterrorism measures without pointing out national political repression by members. Those remain a challenge to its work.
Differences among member states have prevented seamless intelligence integration, which would make RATS more useful.
To blame India and Pakistan, who have only become members relatively recently, overlooks the fact that the problems persisted in the years before their membership and affected RATS’ efficacy as well.
National priorities and strategic rivalries were taken advantage of in India’s participation. India showed that it would not be simply co-opted into an anti-Western bias, meticulously maintaining its strategic autonomy.
In Bishkek, India asserted its national priorities on security. Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi criticized state-sponsored terrorism, double standards in dealing with cross-border violence and cautioned against such activity.
On connectivity, India supported regional infrastructure, but said it must respect national sovereignty and territorial integrity, referring to the BRI-funded China-Pakistan Economic Corridor running through Pakistan-occupied Jammu & Kashmir. Modi’s emphasis on digital public infrastructure, cultural diplomacy and trade stability showed that India intended to be a stabilizing, autonomous bridge rather than a passive participant in a China-led enterprise with Russian support.
The Central Asian republics, four of five of whom are members, as Turkmenistan is permanently neutral, dealt with the summit pragmatically, understanding the geopolitical atmosphere in which they operate.
Kyrgyzstan, as host, leveraged the summit to seek higher levels of investment, diversify trade and overcome the dominance of larger neighbors such as Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan. For those countries, the SCO is not a choice in a new Cold War, but a choice they make for their own autonomy and economic interests.
After 25 years, the SCO has shown that it is durable, but its focus remains unsettled. The Bishkek summit showed clearly that while it is a great convening platform for a shared Eurasian security and economic network, its fractures remain deep. Unless it transforms itself into a development institution, it will not really be able to build the Eurasian identity that it seeks.
China and Russia would prefer to have the SCO as a challenge to the liberal West, but India is not comfortable with ditching the West for Chinese suzerainty.
The SCO is a web of complex, competing visions rather than a monolithic power arrangement.
Gurjit Singh is a former Indian ambassador to Germany, Indonesia, ASEAN, Ethiopia and the African Union.

Russia’s and Iran’s war efforts are being materially supported by Chinese supplies of drone components and missile fuels. Indonesian fires impact Southeast Asia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
16:39:27 UTC
01:39:27 KST

Thick smog has blanketed parts of Indonesia as the vast archipelago for weeks battles to contain fires that have burned large swathes of Borneo and Sumatra.
The hazardous smoke has led to an increase in respiratory problems, forced schools to close and has been drifting to neighboring countries including Malaysia, Singapore and the Philippines.
Most of the fires are concentrated on Borneo island, home to vast tropical jungle that Indonesia shares with Brunei and Malaysia, as well as Sumatra.
Photo: AFP
So far this year, nearly 300,000 hectares of land have burned in Indonesia, the Nusantara Atlas estimated.
Indonesia saw an uptick in carbon emissions since late July, and by the end of last month, the levels were comparable to previous El Nino years of 2015 and 2019, Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service (CAMS) senior scientist Mark Parrington said.
Fires in the archipelago have released more than 23 million metric tonnes of carbon emissions between Friday last week and Thursday, CAMS’ Fire Emission Watch said.
It was higher than 20.7 million metric tonnes of emissions from fires over the same period in 2015, which was a strong El Nino year.
Analysts said the El Nino weather phenomenon has contributed to creating drier conditions in Indonesia and made it easier for fires to spread.
However, slash-and-burn land-clearing practices also contributed to the damage, Nusantara Atlas founder David Gaveau said.
“El Nino does not ignite fires. It creates the dry conditions that allow human-started fires to escape and become very large,” he said.
The fires are difficult to extinguish, because many occurred on peatlands, a wetland ecosystem with layers of partially decomposed organic materials that become flammable when dry.
Between January and last month, more than 210,000 hotspots were detected in peatland areas across the country, non-governmental organization Pantau Gambut said.
“Peat is a naturally wet ecosystem and stores large amounts of organic material. When peat is drained, this organic material is converted into fuel,” Pantau Gambut spokesman Wahyu Perdana said.
More than 5 million people across Borneo and Sumatra are directly exposed to the health risks from haze, Indonesian Deputy Minister of Health Dante Saksono Harbuwono said last month.
More than 1.4 million students were attending classes remotely, with many schools closed due to worsening air quality, an education ministry official said this week.
In Malaysia, soaring pollution levels prompted the government on Friday to declare an emergency in a region of the Sarawak state in Borneo, with nearly 650 schools closed next week.

Philippine Vice President Sara Duterte yesterday posted bail after an order was issued for her arrest the previous day on charges that she publicly threatened to arrange the assassination of Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr and two other people.
The vice president, who has denied the allegations, showed a court order lifting the arrest warrant and said her lawyers instructed her to keep a copy on hand. She urged journalists to surround her on the way to her car, because she did not feel safe.
“If possible please go with me, because I do not feel safe with all these police personnel who are harassing those at my home, harassing me since 2023,” Duterte said. “What does this administration really want to do with me?”
Photo: Reuter
Paul Lawrence Lim, one of her attorneys, said court staff took Duterte’s fingerprints and she posted 360,000 pesos (US$5,742) bail for three counts of grave threats.
Duterte would fight the charges, he said.
“She has no intention of evading the law and will continue to exercise all her legal remedies,” he added.
The case is seen as part of a high-stakes political showdown pitting Duterte against Marcos. A conviction may permanently disqualify her from holding public office and prohibit her from seeking the presidency in 2028, when Marcos’s six-year term ends.
The charges stem from an alleged threat Duterte made during a 2024 online news conference, during which she said she would have Marcos, his wife and then-Philippine House of Representatives speaker Martin Romualdez killed by an assassin if she was killed as their political disputes escalated.
The vice president warned during the event that her threat was not a joke.
Duterte later said she was expressing concern for her own safety and not threatening Marcos, as the remarks set off a criminal investigation and national security concerns.
The House of Representatives, which is dominated by Marcos’ allies, voted overwhelmingly in May to impeach Duterte over allegations of unexplained wealth, misuse of confidential state funds and the online news conference threats.
The Philippine Senate, acting as an impeachment court, opened her televised trial in July.
Marcos and Duterte were running mates in the 2022 elections in an alliance that combined two of the country’s most formidable political dynasties.
Marcos is the son of former Philippine president Ferdinand Marcos Sr, who held the office from the 1960s to the 1980s — a period of repression and martial law.
The vice president is the daughter of former Philippine president Rodrigo Duterte, who was arrested last year on orders of the International Criminal Court and detained in The Hague.
Rodrigo Duterte is scheduled to face a trial beginning in late November over alleged crimes against humanity connected to a brutal anti-drugs crackdowns that left thousands of mostly poor suspects dead.
He has denied authorizing extrajudicial killings, but repeatedly threatened suspects with death while in office.
Sara Duterte previously criticized the Marcos administration for surrendering her father to a foreign court, which currently has no jurisdiction over the Philippines.

MND ‘cyber hunt team’ plan revealed
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
16:39:21 UTC
01:39:21 KST

The Ministry of National Defense (MND) has proposed a NT$95.93 million (US$3.03 million) budget for next year to establish a new “military cyber hunt team” that would counter the Chinese Communist Party’s (CCP) increasing cyberinfiltration and “gray zone” threats.
The plan was revealed in the central government’s general budget proposal for the next fiscal year, under the ministry’s Information, Communications and Electronic Force Command.
The initiative marks a shift in the military’s cyberwarfare mindset — upgrading from a “defensive cybersecurity” strategy that relies on setting up firewalls to an “integrated offense and defense” strategy that seeks out and eliminates network blind spots.
Photo: AFP
The command’s training program involves active cyber threat hunting, the highest level of cybersecurity expertise, and has drawn high attention within military and cybersecurity communities.
Military cybersecurity had mostly relied on alerts and would scramble to patch vulnerabilities after a breach was detected, but the initiative’s training program would operate on the premise that “the system has been infiltrated.”
Foreign instructors would introduce live-combat adversarial training modeled after the US military’s Cyber Flag exercise. The goal is to teach Taiwan’s military personnel to act like detectives, sifting through billions of system logs and network traffic to hunt down and uncover enemy hackers who have bypassed defenses in military networks and critical infrastructure during peacetime.
A government official, speaking on condition of anonymity, said command head Lieutenant General Mao Chien-chiu (毛建秋) is establishing the team to counter the CCP’s cyber units, especially threats from their “long-term latency” and “continuous engagement” tactics.
State-sponsored hackers are skilled at advanced persistent threat attacks, often remaining dormant for months or even years after infiltrating Taiwan’s military systems, quietly stealing confidential data or waiting for the suitable time for destruction, they said.
Members of the “military cyber hunt team” would act as “scavengers” of the digital domain, completely eliminating these latent ghosts and backdoors before enemy attacks are launched, the official said.
The initiative also aligns with international standards, and would deepen joint defense between Taiwan and the US.
The US military has emphasized the importance of “persistent engagement” and “defend forward” cybersecurity strategies, saying that one cannot simply sit back and wait to be attacked, but must instead engage adversaries in the gray zone, the official said.
With the combat experience of elite foreign instructors, the command is expected to speed up its transformation into an “elite cyber tactical force,” which would maintain the resilience of key civilian infrastructure and military command systems in peacetime, and — with its shared technical protocols — swiftly engage in cross-border cybercodefense with like-minded allies during wartime, they said.
The initiative’s budget signals a profound strategic shift in the military’s digital warfare mindset.
In modern wars, cyberwarfare and electronic warfare would paralyze the command chain before the first wave of missiles hits. The establishment of the team aims to expose forces hidden in the shadows, and to reclaim dominance in the digital realm, ensuring that military command and communication systems can function reliably in case of a conflict and to safeguard overall national security.

Bangladesh measles child toll nears 1,000
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
16:39:19 UTC
01:39:19 KST

Bangladesh’s deadliest measles outbreak in decades is nearing the grim milestone of 1,000 child deaths, as a devastating epidemic sweeps through the country and crowded hospital wards fill with struggling babies.
Cries of sick children and the hiss of oxygen machines fill the air at Dhaka’s Shishu Hospital, where Rima Akter keeps a vigil beside her nine-month-old son.
“Just an hour ago, a child died, and they wheeled him out in front of us,” Akter said on Thursday. “We saw two children die today.”
Photo: AFP
Her son is one of scores filling the hospital’s measles wards.
At least 986 children have died since March, while suspected and confirmed cases have surged past 180,000, Bangladeshi Ministry of Health and Family Welfare figures showed.
Measles is highly contagious, spreading through coughs and sneezes, and has no specific treatment once caught.
Complications can include brain swelling and severe breathing problems. Although anyone can catch the disease, young children are particularly vulnerable.
More than 1,000 suspected cases are reported daily.
“I’ve been running to and from multiple hospitals since July to get my son the proper treatment,” Sanjana Islam Modina said, cradling her six-month-old son Ayan, who has an oxygen tube fixed to his nose.
He was first admitted to hospital with pneumonia in July, then contracted measles before finally securing a bed at the capital’s specialized children’s hospital last month.
The hospital has 101 children admitted with suspected or confirmed measles.
“His lungs were already very weak from the pneumonia, then with measles his breathing was affected more,” Modina said. “He’s been on oxygen constantly for the last five days.”
Most cases during the outbreak have been children aged between six months and five years.
Doctors said many of the children arriving at the hospital are already critically ill, with malnutrition further weakening their ability to fight the virus.
“The doctors gave my son a special milk specifically designed for malnourished children,” Modina said.
The outbreak has exposed gaps in Bangladesh’s efforts to protect its youngest.
SM Ziauddin Hyder, special assistant to Prime Minister Tarique Rahman for health, called the outbreak “devastating.”
Bangladesh had made major advances in vaccination against infectious diseases, but a measles drive planned for 2024 was delayed by the uprising that toppled former Bangladeshi prime minister Sheikh Hasina.
Workers’ strikes and political instability delayed a 2025 campaign.
The country has since rolled out a mass vaccination drive to combat the outbreak, but the number of cases continues to climb.

Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) Chairwoman Cheng Li-wun (鄭麗文) has had a tough week on the campaign trail in support of her party’s candidates for November’s local elections.
Trouble has been brewing in Changhua County for the past few months over the KMT’s nomination of Wei Ping-cheng (魏平政) for Changhua County commissioner. Incumbent Changhua County Commissioner Wang Hui-mei (王惠美) of the KMT is not eligible for re-election, as she has already served two terms, but she has conspicuously declined to attend campaign events with Wei.
On Friday, Wang posted a 2,000-character explanation of the situation on Facebook, writing that Cheng had sought her advice in December last year. Wang wrote that she had doubts, as she was unfamiliar with Wei’s background. She phoned Cheng on hearing that the nomination would go to Wei, but said that Cheng had not followed through on a promise to call back.
Wang added that her loyalties remain with the party and that her reluctance to endorse Wei was due to doubts that he was the best candidate. She expressed frustration over her suspicion that when Cheng had consulted her about the matter, the decision had already been made.
The situation in Hsinchu County’s Jhubei City (竹北市) has been equally contentious, with accusations that Cheng’s handling of the nomination process there has put the KMT’s alliance with the Taiwan People’s Party (TPP) at risk, as explained in a Taipei Times editorial (“Airing dirty laundry in public,” Aug. 30, page 8).
Joining Cheng onstage in Hsinchu County on Thursday campaigning for Hsu Hsin-ying (徐欣瑩), the KMT’s nomination for Hsinchu County commissioner, former Council of Agriculture chairman Fan Chen-tsung (范振宗) made a speech, but not before gesturing as though he was going to slap Cheng in the face.
The mock slap generated heated debate, with Chang Yu-tzu (張育慈), a New Power Party candidate for the Hsinchu County council, calling it a display of violence against women.
KMT Vice Chairman Lee Chien-lung (李乾龍) brushed the “slap” off as a jocular gesture between old friends.
The truth is probably somewhere between the two extremes: a clumsy gesture of an older man using the physical comedy of a previous generation that is at best condescending and at worst reflective of a culture in which violence toward women was regarded as allowable.
Leaving aside optics — which Cheng laughed off at the time, but should have taken more seriously — the debate diverts attention from what Fan said in the following minutes as he lambasted Cheng over her handling of the Jhubei City nomination process. Fan said that Cheng would bear responsibility if Hsu loses the county race, as she put the KMT-TPP alliance and the KMT’s internal unity at risk.
Fan, who served as a Democratic Progressive Party Hsinchu County commissioner from 1989 to 1997 before leaving the party in 2009, said that the results of the local elections would affect the KMT’s chances in the presidential election in 2028.
In Taichung, Deputy Legislative Speaker Johnny Chiang (江啟臣), a former KMT chairman himself, is the party’s mayoral candidate. Cheng had been accused of favoring Chiang’s rival for the nomination.
At an event in Taichung’s Shengang District (神岡) yesterday, a reporter asked Chiang about the political impasse in Changhua between Wang and Cheng. He gave a noncommittal response, providing more grist for the mill about doubts surrounding Cheng’s leadership, party morale and the question of internal unity.
On Sunday last week, in the heat of the Jhubei nominations controversy and internal concerns about the threat to the KMT-TPP alliance, Taichung Mayor Lu Shiow-yen (盧秀燕) stood on stage with Chiang and TPP Chairman Huang Kuo-chang (黃國昌). Lu extolled the benefits of unity in the alliance between the KMT and the TPP. Asked whether the show of unity with the TPP was her way of telling Cheng how to safeguard the alliance in other localities, she responded in political platitudes, as if avoiding exacerbating the threat to unity that she was referring to.
Lu spoke of the importance of unity in the context of the November and 2028 elections, but Cheng is putting both in jeopardy with her bull-in-a-China-shop approach to party leadership.

UN endorses using ‘Equal Earth’ map over Mercator
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
16:39:16 UTC
01:39:16 KST

The UN General Assembly on Friday endorsed a new world map that represents Africa’s larger size more accurately, a culmination of a campaign led by African countries and advocacy groups.
The resolution, which was sponsored by Togo and backed by members of the African Union, was passed with 164 member states voting in favor. Only the US voted against it while six other countries — Serbia, Estonia, Georgia, Lithuania, Moldova and Ukraine — abstained.
The vote encourages governments and institutions around the world to replace the traditional Mercator map, commonly used since the 16th century, with the Equal Earth projection that advocates and geographers said shows locations more accurately.
Photo: Equal Earth / AFP
The Mercator projection shows Greenland and Africa as appearing to be about the same size, whereas in the Equal Earth projection that shows continents in their true proportions. Africa is 14 times larger than Greenland.
The resolution does not ban the Mercator projection or impose a replacement, but only encourages the use of the Equal Earth projection, the UN said in its report.
“Maps shape our understanding of the world,” it quoted Togolese Minister of Foreign Affairs, Cooperation and African Integration Robert Dussey as saying before the vote. “They guide education, nourish the imagination, and influence collective perceptions.”
Africa No Filter, one of the lead campaigners for the adoption of the new map, hailed the resolution, saying: “We want to see accurate maps in schools, textbooks, newsrooms, businesses and on the digital platforms billions of people use every day.”
Several countries hailed the adoption and urged the adoption of the Equal Earth map.
“Changing the map obviously doesn’t change the world. But correcting a representation that distorts it is already an act of truth,” French Minister for Europe and Foreign Affairs Jean-Noel Barrot said on X after the vote.
The Mercator map was designed by Flemish cartographer Gerardus Mercator to help European navigators at sea, but advocates said it distorted landmasses by enlarging regions near the poles such as North America and Greenland while shrinking Africa and South America.
On the other hand, the 2018 Equal Earth projection follows the Earth’s curvature and shows continents in their true proportions.
Geographers say the traditional map is only useful for navigation.
“Outside of that very narrow navigation application, there is no point in using it,” Syracuse University geography professor Mark Monmonier said.

China’s paper-tiger alliance shows the US cannot isolate Iran
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
16:39:13 UTC
01:39:13 KST

The conflict between the US and Iran is beginning to flare again, and US President Donald Trump said he could not care less. He is confident his new plan for an “economic D-Day” that brings Iran to heel by collapsing its economy is a winner. Perhaps, but making it so would take a great deal of international cooperation. As US Secretary of the Treasury Scott Bessent put it: “You’re either with us or against us.”
Bessent was echoing then-US president George W. Bush, when he told US Congress after 9/11 that every country in the world would have to choose to either be with the US, or against it on the side of al-Qaeda, the Taliban and other terrorists. Sadly, for Bessent, his boss and a beleaguered Iranian people, this is not 2001. It is 2026, a time a world away in which the appeal is set up to fail.
That matters, because the difficulty with Trump’s economic strangulation is that the Iranian Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) is more comfortable with continuing a state of low-level war. Accepting a peace that leaves the regime without the major financial and geopolitical gains it would need to placate a still deeply hostile population is more dangerous to its survival. Trump needs a near-total financial blockade to swiftly force Tehran to capitulate, because the IRGC commanders, who now dominate decisionmaking, are unlikely to oblige otherwise.
Bush was able to command the rest of the world not just because there was genuine horror and sympathy at the carnage of 9/11, or because Osama bin Laden’s al-Qaeda was a non-state actor whose only ally was the Taliban. He could do so also because the US was still the world’s undisputed hegemon, with NATO allies so eager to help that they invoked the organization’s Article 5 collective defense clause on Washington’s behalf, so they could join the fight.
Back then, the only countries that did not accept US leadership were the so-called rogue states Bush listed in his January 2002 “axis of evil” speech: Iran, Iraq and North Korea (and even Iran at first cooperated against al-Qaeda). Moscow and Beijing had formed the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) just a few months before, with a major goal of managing competition between the two regional powers’ interests in central Asia. The BRICS alliance of emerging markets would not be conceived until five years later. The “global south” was not yet a thing.
So, Bush could be confident that the world would be “with us.” It was only two years earlier, after all, that Washington had led the NATO in a much more divisive cause. Its pilots bombed Serbia for 78 days straight, much as the US and Israel have been bombing Iran. Despite profoundly opposing this attack on a traditional ally, Russia decided it had no choice but to acquiesce; it even helped negotiate Serbia’s surrender.
None of this is imaginable today. The SCO, which held its 26th annual summit this week, now has a much more global focus and at least as much (or as little, depending on your point of view) substance as the G7 industrialized nations. It represents about 40 percent of the world’s people and one-quarter of nominal GDP. Much commentary focuses on the group’s limitations as a potential alliance, given that it includes NATO member Turkey, as well as India and that country’s bitter geopolitical rivals, China and Pakistan. However, that misses the point.
The SCO was not designed to be NATO-style military alliance. It can be a paper tiger and still serve its purpose, which at this point is to provide China and Russia with a forum and a toolkit for balancing US power and influence in Eurasia. In fact, judging by the comments of Western allies meeting in North Carolina for this week’s virtually simultaneous meeting of G20 finance ministers, the SCO is the more harmonious of the two blocs. In Asheville, North Carolina, Bessent boasted about US economic prowess, and defended measures — including a trade war with Canada and the sale of US reserves (using euros rather than dollars) to drive up the value of the yen — that damaged supposed allies. The SCO message was consensus driven by comparison: The common goal of that organization is to displace US hegemony, often now expressed in the form of sanctions, and India is on board for that, too.
So, the SCO is not “with” the US, it is with Iran. It is not with Western Europe or Ukraine, it is with Russia. Chinese President Xi Jinping (習近平) might have downplayed the protocol for his meeting with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, so as not to blow up his coming visit to Washington, but Russian President Vladimir Putin did the heavy lifting of supporting a fellow SCO member against US aggression for him. This is a world in which there are no longer “rogue” states, because there is a forum led by the world’s coming superpower that would embrace them.
The talk at the SCO summit in Bishkek on Monday and Tuesday was of how to invest more in and trade more with Iran. Tehran’s friends would still be cautious when it comes to delivery, because the US’ capacity to lash out and impose costs remains formidable. However, they would not be with the US. They would be against it, whenever and wherever they can.

Taiwan to leverage drone experience, ministry says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
16:39:12 UTC
01:39:12 KST

Taiwan is advancing its drone diplomacy by donating 145 uncrewed aerial vehicles (UAV) to diplomatic allies and establishing overseas branches of the “Global UAV Academy” (GUAVA), the Ministry of Foreign Affairs said.
“Drone diplomacy” is a spin on the concept of “chip diplomacy,” leveraging Taiwan’s strengths in key industries to enhance its diplomatic influence, the ministry said in its latest policy report to the Executive Yuan, with officials citing Minister of Foreign Affairs Lin Chia-lung’s (林佳龍) visit to Palau to attend events connected to the Pacific Islands Forum, where he presented drones to diplomatic allies at the Palau Taiwan Night event.
Drone diplomacy could serve as a pillar of the Diplomatic Allies Prosperity Project under its “integrated diplomacy” framework, the report said.
Photo courtesy of the Chiayi County Government
Drones can be integrated into areas such as smart agriculture, coast guard operations, disaster prevention, medical deliveries, digital governance and sovereign artificial intelligence, making them a key technology to help Taiwan’s diplomatic allies move from simply maintaining ties with Taiwan to achieving greater prosperity, it said.
Efforts to build drone resilience among Taiwan’s diplomatic allies should proceed gradually, with the first phase to focus on training drone pilots, the ministry said.
It has purchased about 145 drones in two categories — training and multifunctional models — which would be donated to diplomatic allies in stages, it said.
It would develop testing sites for use by allies, as well as help establish verification standards and develop regulations with the goal to build and expand overseas markets for Taiwan’s drone industry, it said.
The ministry established a Drone Diplomacy Task Force in October last year to bring together resources from the government, industry and academia, it said.
It helped establish the non-governmental organization GUAVA, which brings greater flexibility in assisting the government with international drone cooperation, it said.
GUAVA plans to set up its offices in Taipei and Chiayi this year, and would work with overseas organizations to establish branches abroad, the ministry added.
GUAVA’s core mission would be to promote international cooperation on uncrewed vehicles, it said.
Through education and training, it would cultivate international talent while connecting resources in areas such as technology research and development, industry alliances and certification mechanisms, it said.
GUAVA is intended to become a hub for Taiwan’s uncrewed vehicle expertise, certification, maintenance, regulatory compliance and institutional exports, serving as a key platform for the shift from “product exports” to “institutional exports” and strengthening its global influence in the uncrewed vehicle sector, it said.
In May, GUAVA — then operating as a preparatory office — signed a letter of intent with the US-based Association for Uncrewed Vehicle Systems International to promote Taiwan-US cooperation on drones.
In July, it signed a letter of intent with the Japan Drone Consortium to strengthen Taiwan-Japan cooperation.

MAC details the potential scope of Chinese artillery
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
16:39:11 UTC
01:39:11 KST

Potential improvements to munitions used by China’s long-range rocket-artillery units could extend their range to cover the entire Miyako Strait, which might give the Chinese People’s Liberation Army (PLA) the ability to secure the strategic waterway, the Mainland Affairs Council (MAC) said in a report.
The PLA’s long-range rocket-artillery units deployed along the Taiwan Strait are concentrated along the coast of Fujian Province, including Changle, Pingtan and Shishi, the quarterly report on China said.
The artillery brigades of the PLA’s 71st, 72nd and 73rd group armies have been deployed, with preparations for potential battlefield operations under way since August 2022, the report said.
Photo: Screen grab from a Mainland Affairs Council report
“Credible imagery” showed that the units have completed equipment upgrades and are fielding PCH191 modular long-range multiple rocket launchers, it said.
The system has a range of nearly 500km, while the Fire Dragon 480, a 750mm tactical ballistic missile, has a reported range of 480km, it said.
The PCH191 uses two modular launch pods, each of which can be loaded with five 300mm rockets, four 370mm rockets, one 750mm tactical missile, or one 380mm anti-ship cruise missile, the report said.
However, the standard munitions of the PCH191 cannot effectively reach the central waters of the Miyako Strait, which are about 600km from the launch positions in China’s Fujian and Zhejiang provinces, it said.
Technological improvements could extend the range of the Fire Dragon 480 to 600km or more, it said, adding that composite materials could reduce the weight of the missiles, while improved solid propellant could increase propulsion efficiency.
Such advances would allow the units along China’s southeastern coast to reach the western entrance to the Miyako Strait and potentially cover the entire strait, it said.
In March last year, Chinese state media showed the Feilong-60A being tested, describing it as China’s first loitering munition designed around a modular rocket-artillery platform.
The report said the Feilong-60A could be integrated with the PCH191 to scout the battlefield, identify targets and help direct precision strikes, giving the PLA a way to combine battlefield intelligence with long-range firepower, it said.
The longer ranges and ability to combine battlefield intelligence with firepower enabled by modular munitions could overcome the traditional geographic limitations of long-range strikes, giving the PLA the means to counter an island-chain blockade and secure strategic routes, it said.
The MAC cited a 2023 report by the China Maritime Studies Institute at the US Naval War College, which said that fielding the PCH191 and other munitions could make the Chinese army the most important contributor of firepower in a hypothetical joint landing campaign against Taiwan.

Two-time women’s doubles champions Venus Williams and Serena Williams rolled back the years on Arthur Ashe Stadium at the US Open on Friday, but the sisters were unable to get past Australia’s Maya Joint and Taiwan’s Chan Hao-ching, losing 6-3, 6-7(6), 7-6(10-7).
The Williams’ duo had showed flashes of their brilliant best after recovering from losing the first set to level the match after taking the second set on a tie-break.
Momentum and a raucous New York crowd appeared to be carrying them towards victory after they sprinted into a 5-0 lead in the third set tie-break. Chan and Joint fought back superbly to erase the deficit before clinching victory.
Photo: EPA
Meanwhile, defending champion Carlos Alcaraz continued to fly high while Aryna Sabalenka overcame a distraction from the smell of cannabis in the Flushing Meadows complex to reach the fourth round.
Alcaraz arrived in New York having been sidelined for more than four months with a wrist injury, but the Spaniard looked sharp again as he thumped China’s Wu Yibing 6-3, 6-4, 6-1 to stay on track for a third title.
“After four months without competing... when you play an official match with the nerves and everything, the day after or right after, your body can feel really tight,” Alcaraz said.
“It didn’t happen to me and I’m feeling better and better after every match. It feels like I’ve been competing the whole time. I’ve surprised myself with the way I’m recovering after every match.”
The seven-times Grand Slam champion next meets Tommy Paul after the American 20th seed beat Alexander Bublik 6-4, 3-6, 6-7(4), 6-1, 6-3.
Sabalenka’s pre-tournament form had raised plenty of concerns, but the top seed looked to have left her slump in the rear-view mirror as she did not face a single break point in her 6-3, 6-4 victory over Uzbekistan’s Kamilla Rakhimova.
Her only issue during the morning session match was the smell of cannabis drifting into Louis Armstrong Stadium and she stopped play to alert the chair umpire.
“Someone is smoking weed,” she said walking up to the chair umpire.
While smoking is not allowed inside the US Open grounds, recreational cannabis is legal in New York and smoke from the surrounding Flushing Meadows-Corona Park can drift into the tennis venue.
Sabalenka said that she did not object to anyone enjoying themselves and relaxing, but called for the smoking to be kept away from the courts.
“I was like, ‘guys, you can do whatever, you can smoke whatever, you can relax as much as you can, but please not around the tennis courts,’” she added.
“It’s a bit tricky to handle that smell while you’re trying to compete at your best,” she said.

Venezuelans skeptical of US oil deal reshaping their future
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
16:39:07 UTC
01:39:07 KST

Nothing has shaped what it means to be Venezuelan today more than oil.
For more than 100 years, in good times and bad, Venezuelans’ identity has been built on the belief that their country’s bountiful oil resources belong to the people, not a government or a company.
This belief, and a troubled nation’s pride, took a bruising last week when acting President Delcy Rodriguez agreed to give the US control of roughly one-fifth of Venezuela’s oil reserves — the largest in the world.
Photo: REUTERS
While the deal could eventually generate billions of dollars for an oil industry and economy wrecked by years of mismanagement, many Venezuelans see it as a surrender. Some say they are not surprised; they believe that gaining control of Venezuelan oil was the ultimate objective when US President Donald Trump ordered US forces to abduct then-Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro at the beginning of the year, leaving Rodriguez in charge.
“It’s not just worrying, it’s outrageous, because we, like a drop in the ocean, have no power to intervene,” said Lisandro Castro, an architect in the capital, Caracas, referring to fellow citizens. “There is genuine collective concern in Venezuela right now about what we are witnessing.”
INFLUENCES OF OIL
The 1920s discovery of oil in northwestern Venezuela sparked an industrial boom that transformed a poor, agrarian country into an urbanized regional power.
US energy company employees working in Venezuela went on to popularize baseball. The companies built ball fields in oil-producing areas, spreading the sport among working-class Venezuelans who then took it to the rest of the country.
Europeans facing post-World War II hardships headed to Venezuela looking for economic opportunities created by the oil riches. The Portuguese established bakeries that are still open. The Italians designed buildings that are still standing.
A democracy in its infancy, Venezuela got most of its revenues from oil exports rather than from taxing local citizens and businesses, and politicians tried to buy the will of citizens, said Ronal Rodriguez, a researcher at the Venezuela Observatory at Colombia’s Universidad del Rosario.
The country co-founded OPEC, and by the 1970s, when it boasted of the highest per-capita income in the region, the government nationalized the industry with the creation of the state-owned Petroleos de Venezuela SA.
PDVSA, as it is commonly known, only allowed foreign companies to operate as minority partners in joint ventures. Its revenues subsidized cheap gas for Venezuelans, scholarships to study abroad, free surgeries and many more benefits.
“Every Venezuelan sees oil as something they have the right to claim,” Rodriguez said.
BOOM AND BUST
Plummeting oil prices globally in the 1980s devastated Venezuela’s economy, requiring an IMF bailout. The state ended key subsidies, and social unrest followed. A military officer named Hugo Chavez attempted a failed coup.
Once elected president in 1998, Chavez expanded social services, including health, housing and education, thanks to resurgent oil prices that generated an estimated US$981 billion in revenues for PDVSA between 1999 and 2011. The government handed out homes, refrigerators and medicines, and many families benefited from well-paid jobs in the public and private sectors.
Emboldened by popular support, Chavez tightened his grip on the national oil company — to the detriment of US oil companies such as ExxonMobil and ConocoPhillips.
PDVSA’s fortunes eventually turned as oil prices fell once again. Corruption and mismanagement eroded profits and hurt production, first under Chavez, and then Maduro, his hand-picked successor.
By 2013, when Maduro became president following Chavez’s death, the country fell into a dire economic crisis. Sanctions imposed by the US over democratic and human rights concerns crippled the industry and the economy further.
Instead of attracting migrants, Venezuelans became migrants; the economic turmoil led to severe food shortages, among other deprivations, prompting millions to leave the country.
Even though markets and stores are well-stocked, people struggle to afford the basics because of soaring inflation.
Many of today’s public sector workers earn roughly US$160 per month, while the average private sector employee earned about US$237 per month last year.
“Something is better than nothing,” former oil worker Romel Abreu said, referring to the roughly 1 million barrels of oil per day that Venezuela currently produces. “If we didn’t have it, we would be fried.”
Abreu works as a security guard in Cabimas, the heart of the oil industry. Like many there, he hopes for another oil boom and the jobs it would bring.
SKEPTICISM
Some Venezuelans might have hoped that the capture of Maduro in January would end the ruling party’s 27-year hold on power. When that did not happen — Trump chose Rodriguez over Venezuela’s opposition — some people were still optimistic about economic improvement from the easing of crippling sanctions.
In February, a legal overhaul opened the path to private investment in the oil industry, which some saw as a prelude to bigger changes.
“Everything that happened on Jan. 3 was simply a strategy to get where we are today,” Castro said of Trump’s Venezuela policy. “That is, to fully immerse themselves in the country’s energy affairs for their own personal gain and benefit, not for a purpose that would truly benefit us Venezuelans.”
Under the deal, the US is entering a joint venture with Venezuela’s North American Blue Energy Partners, the second-largest private oil company operating in the country, behind Chevron.
Rodriguez is giving the joint venture 100-year rights over 17 oil fields with proven reserves of 65 billion barrels. The nation’s oil reserves have been estimated at roughly 300 billion.
Because Venezuela’s energy infrastructure has been severely degraded, it could take years before new investments lead to significantly higher oil production, experts say.
Speaking in Caracas on Wednesday, US Secretary of Energy Chris Wright said Trump’s mission in Venezuela “is to bring peace, freedom, opportunity and prosperity to the people.” In an address to the nation Saturday, Rodriguez defended the agreement — and said she wants her country to be an “energy powerhouse.”
Cabimas residents can only hope.
“Well, on the one hand, one feels and thinks that one of the largest oil reserves has been handed over,” Erwin Ayala, an oil company worker, said outside his home. “But if it’s for the good of the country and for future generations, then yes, we agree with that, because what good is having so much oil... if there’s no machinery, no technology, to extract it?”

Pharmacist accused of drugging his employee
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
16:39:06 UTC
01:39:06 KST

The Federation of Taiwan Pharmacists Associations yesterday said it could revoke the certification of a New Taipei City pharmacist who allegedly drugged a employee on Aug. 26.
The pharmacist, surnamed Chen (陳), runs a pharmacy in Tamsui District (淡水).
A college student working part-time at his pharmacy has accused him of drugging her water bottle.
Photo: Chiu Chih-jou, Taipei Times
The woman said she found the water bitter, cloudy and containing powder, and that she felt her heart was racing and experienced dizziness after drinking from her bottle.
She immediately went home and reported the case to the police on Aug. 28, the woman said.
The police found residue from her bottle that tested positive for benzodiazepines — a prescription central nervous system depressant — and raided the pharmacy on Aug. 29 to seize surveillance footage.
Chen was quoted by local media as saying that he was “testing the effectiveness of the expired medicines” and “playing a joke” on her.
The case was referred to the judiciary.
Pharmacist federation honorary president Huang Jin-shun (黃金舜) when reached for comment yesterday said the case is grave.
A pharmacist should not engage in such misconduct, which would damage the image of the profession, he said.
Huang said he has asked the New Taipei City Pharmacists Association to look into Chen’s case.
The federation would not cover up or condone such behavior if Chen is found to have acted wrongly, he said.
Federation deputy secretary-general Lee Yi-hsuan (李懿軒) said pharmacists are professionals expected to be highly accountable for the use of regulated medicines.
The federation would not tolerate anyone using pharmaceuticals on unsuspecting victims, he said, adding that the unlawful behavior of a pharmacist does not represent the entire profession.
The federation has no investigative authority and would wait for the judicial investigation’s findings and evidence, Lee said.
If there is evidence showing Chen contravined regulations, the local pharmacists association or local healthcare units can refer his case to the disciplinary authority for penalties in accordance with the Pharmacists Act (藥師法), he said.
Disciplinary actions include restricting the scope of practice, suspension from practice for a period ranging from a month to a year, or revocation of the pharmacist license, Lee said.
The maximum penalty is revocation of the pharmacist certificate — a career-ending penalty, he said.
Lee said benzodiazepines can be used to treat anxiety, insomnia, epilepsy, or to induce sedation.
They are strictly regulated, as they can affect people’s mental state and neurochemistry, he said.
Regulated medicines must be registered, and stored and handled properly if they are to be recalled and destroyed, Lee said.
The Ministry of Health and Welfare said separately yesterday that it is issuing notice to the New Taipei City Department of Health tomorrow, requesting an on-site inspection of the pharmacist’s practice and the management of the pharmacy.
If the investigation finds that Chen contravened the law or professional ethics, disciplinary proceedings would be initiated, with the most severe penalty being revocation of his license, it said.

Air force data indicate pilot issues
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
16:39:04 UTC
01:39:04 KST

A sharp rise in compensation to be paid by air force officers who leave before completing their required service could indicate an increase in pilots leaving the military early, an analyst said on Friday, warning that the trend could worsen a shortage of experienced personnel.
Chieh Chung (揭仲), a researcher at the Association for Strategic Foresight, issued the warning even though the number of volunteer military personnel is expected to increase next year.
The planned headcount for volunteer military personnel, covering officers, noncommissioned officers (NCO) and enlisted soldiers, is 158,223 for next year, up 4,258 from 153,965 this year, Chieh said.
Photo: Peter Lo, Taipei Times
The increase includes 2,044 volunteer soldiers in a planned headcount of 30,480 next year, he said.
It would mark the first increase in the number of volunteer service members since 2024, which Chieh attributed to increases in duty and combat allowances that took effect in April last year, as well as a reduction in nonessential duties.
However, air force staffing appears to be moving in the opposite direction, with headquarters revenue from compensation paid by officers who left before completing their required service more than doubling from last year, he said.
The air force’s expected compensation revenue for officers and NCOs leaving before completing required service is NT$50.59 million (US$1.6 million) next year, about 2.5 times the NT$20.26 million last year, he said.
Because air force pilots face substantially higher compensation obligations than other personnel when they leave before completing their required service, Chieh said the rise might indicate a rise in premature departures among pilots.
At the same time, incentive payments earmarked for pilots across the armed forces who remain in service beyond their minimum required period have declined for four consecutive years, falling from NT$838.28 million in 2023 to NT$755.78 million for next year, a decrease of about 10 percent.
The incentives are intended to retain majors, lieutenant colonels and colonels who have completed their minimum required service period, Chieh said, adding that the decline suggests that the departure of senior pilots in key leadership roles has not slowed.
Air force pilots who leave the military early might do so to become commercial airline pilots, Chieh added.
“That could lead to an imbalance in the ratio between senior and junior pilots,” Chieh said, adding that it could create a gap in the air force’s combat capabilities, even if the required number of pilots is eventually met.
The issue is particularly concerning given the air force’s plan to add 107 pilot officers to a newly established fighter wing that will operate the 66 F-16C/D Block 70 jets Taiwan has committed to purchasing from the US, he said.
The first two F-16 Block 70s purchased by Taiwan are expected to be delivered to the air force in the next few days.
Asked what could have contributed to the high turnover among air force pilots, Chieh said that the increased number of sorties and military drills resulting from China’s stepped-up “gray zone” activities around Taiwan was likely a major factor.

El Nino-driven drought slams Sri Lankan farms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
16:38:59 UTC
01:38:59 KST

For the first time in more than three decades, Sri Lankan farmer AM Pathmasena says, his well is running so dry that it barely provides enough water for his family and two cows. He has fallen victim to one of the country’s worst El Nino-driven droughts.
Sri Lanka is among the South Asian countries hardest hit by weather disruption this year, with some key farming districts recording rainfall deficits of 85 percent to 100 percent below long-term averages. The government has arranged for water to be delivered to tens of thousands of people.
“The drought has been intensifying. The amount of water seeping into the well is barely enough,” Pathmasena, 48, said while sitting in his hut in Galwela Yaya, a small village in one of the worst-hit districts, Ampara. “We dig a small hole and wait for the water to seep in to bathe.”
Photo: Reuters
El Nino is a weather pattern characterized by unusually warm sea-surface temperatures in the central and eastern equatorial Pacific Ocean, often bringing drier conditions to parts of Asia and severe storms elsewhere.
This year is likely to be marked by a “super” El Nino, which could become the strongest on record, weather forecasters have said.
Soaring temperatures have already left large swathes of Sri Lanka’s north, east and southern regions parched, with small tanks, rivers and lakes that usually feed crops and provide drinking water drying out.
The Sri Lankan government has said the impact this year could be the worst in decades and that water levels at hundreds of such tanks in the country have dropped to about 10 percent.
Many houses on the main roads and those that are easily accessible get drinking water trucked in every three to five days, while some in remote areas wait for as many as 23 days, according to government officials and interviews with residents.
INCOME IMPACT
In the affected districts, people often wait for water supplies at their gates with large blue plastic water barrels while others gather at tube wells to bathe and collect water to take home to wash dishes and clothes and to cook as well.
“We supplement the water deliveries by gathering the last bit of the water in our well for washing and bathing but even then we sometimes run out,” said Konara Mudiyanselage Sumanawathie, 49, who lives in one of the worst-affected areas, Monaragala, about 160km from Colombo.
Farmers’ incomes, as expected, are taking a big hit, making it difficult to repay loans and even manage proper meals daily.
Before the drought, Pathmasena said he earned about 20,000 Sri Lanka rupees (US$60) a month growing cowpeas, but the crisis means he has lost it all, forcing him to become a daily-wage laborer to survive.
His son shuttered his chicken farm weeks ago due to the heat and water shortages. On a recent evening, Pathmasena asked his wife to first give water in tin vessels to their cows, before they sat to consume their meal.
“On some days, when we have nothing, we skip meals,” he said.

China’s Zhang Ziyu had everyone looking up to her on the opening day of the Women’s Basketball World Cup on Friday.

Zhang is taller than basketball Hall of Famer Shaquille O’Neal and just an inch shorter than San Antonio Spurs big man Victor Wembanyama.
Photo: AP
The 1.91m Aliyah Boston looked small in comparison as she stubbornly held her ground to hold Zhang scoreless in the first quarter. Kiki Iriafen, also 1.91m, took her turn later as the US defense focused on limiting the damage Zhang could cause over the 18 minutes she played.
“There’s not much you can do to stop her when she gets it really close to the basket,” US coach Kara Lawson said. “She was really efficient from the free throw line as well.”
There was a buzz of excitement any time Zhang appeared on court and ultimately the teenager finished with 13 points on her worlds debut, nine of those from free throws.
“I would give her a pass,” China coach Gong Luming said in translated comments. “It’s excellent, pass or fail, so pass. As a young player to play against such great level of intensity and physicality, she’s doing OK,” he said.
Lawson was more forthcoming with her praise.
“We had a hard time and she got too close, and she makes you pay with that. So I think there’s a lot of upside to her,” the coach said. “She’s still a very young player, but I think to be this young and to be in a World Cup and to go against the top players is only going to help her continue to grow,” she added.
Zhang had support from 2.09m Han Xu, already familiar to the US team from her WNBA games with the New York Liberty.
If not for a passport mishap, Zhang and Han would have been joined by another center — 2.01m Li Yueru, who plays with the WNBA’s Dallas Wings. Li posted on social media on Wednesday that her passport was lost in the mail and she would not be able to compete.
Han finished with 11 points including one three-pointer.
Zhang did individual exercises with a personal trainer while the rest of the team warmed up on the court before Friday’s game.
Gong said the player needed a special training regime because of her physical attributes.
“She’s a very special and unique player with her size so she probably cannot have the same warmup routine with everybody else running the layup, passing, so the coaching team designed her own program for her to warm up and keep her fit and ready for the game,” the coach said.
Zhang missed China’s pre-tournament warmup against France on Tuesday and was not practicing during the brief time slots open to media on Wednesday and Thursday.
“She has [a] big body and tall girl, and she needs some time to rest a little bit,” Han said on Wednesday, alluding to her personalized training regime.
Zhang was not playing when the US beat China 83-61 in the 2022 World Cup final in Sydney for a fourth consecutive gold medal. She made her senior debut at the Women’s Asia Cup last year and helped China capture the bronze, averaging 14.8 points and 5.5 rebounds in the tournament.
Han praised her performance at that tournament and said she was ready to step onto the world stage.
As one of the oldest players in the Chinese roster at 26, Han takes on the responsibly of looking out for her younger teammates. She pointed out that Zhang is still “very young” and just starting her career.
“She’s a little girl, you know, like the heart is soft,” she said.
Few expect China to go further than it did in 2022, with France and Australia expected to be the most likely challengers to the US, but Zhang’s introduction gave the Chinese an extra weapon they did not have four years ago.
China next plays the Czech Republic today.

How the east became Germany’s far-right stronghold after World War II
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
16:38:55 UTC
01:38:55 KST

More than three decades after Germany’s 1990 reunification, lasting east-west divisions may be thrown into stark relief at Sunday’s election in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt.
The anti-immigration and Moscow-friendly Alternative for Germany (AfD) is expected to win big and even hopes to take power at the state level, which would be a first for a far-right party in German post-World War II history.
As much of the east has become an AfD stronghold, the government’s commissioner for eastern Germany, German lawmaker Elisabeth Kaiser, herself from Thuringia state in the east, discussed the historic and cultural factors shaping the region’s distinct politics.
Photo: AFP
When the Berlin Wall fell in 1989, spelling the end of the communist German Democratic Republic (GDR), many state-owned enterprises were shuttered, sparking large-scale unemployment and population flight, especially by young women.
“That was a difficult experience for many East Germans, one that has persisted across generations, becoming part of a collective east German memory,” Kaiser said. “It involved this sense of devaluation, this experience of loss and the realization that everything can change overnight.”
Decades on, wages and savings remain lower on average, most big business is still based in the west, and eastern Germans — one-fifth of the population — are under-represented in politics.
Billions spent on infrastructure and to stimulate the economy have born some fruit — with the region now home to many of the “industries of the future,” Kaiser said.
Nevertheless, there remain “big disparities in wealth” and, among many, a feeling of being “disadvantaged and not seen,” she said.
The AfD’s hostility to migration resonates in much of the east, even though it has fewer foreign-born residents than the west.
While West Germany’s post-WWII economic recovery was fueled by “guest workers,” the East invited contract workers from socialist “brother states” such as Vietnam and Mozambique.
They “were very much physically separated from East Germans” and on time-limited contracts, Kaiser said.
While state propaganda praised the GDR as internationalist, there was also “racism, xenophobia and right-wing extremism which unfortunately erupted in the 1990s,” she said.
Resentment has spread especially about Syrian and Afghan asylum-seekers, and the notion of “all the extra things they were getting for free,” she added.
The AfD advocates closer ties to Russia, and many in the east are keen on renewed diplomacy with Russia, Kaiser said.
Some in the west have suggested the richer part of Germany stop “subsidising” the east, which Kaiser said she finds “disastrous” and annoying as an east German.
Cutting transfer funds would “only strengthen the victim role that the AfD always likes to adopt,” she added.
In parts of the west, the AfD and their far-left competitors are also on the rise, she said, adding that Germany as a whole should view the east as a political “seismograph.”
