One teacher, ten students: India's foundational classrooms hit a new benchmark
Aadrita Halder / TIMESOFINDIA.COM / Sep 05, 2026, 16:40 IST
Comments
Share
AA
Text Size
Small
Medium
Large
UDISE+ 2025-26 numbers show a system that added capacity, tightened ratios, expanded infrastructure
Every year, a child who stays in school through Class 12 rather than dropping out at 14 usually has one adult to thank for it more than any policy document: a teacher who noticed, who followed up, who made the difference between a student staying enrolled and quietly disappearing from the rolls. The Unified District Information System for Education Plus (UDISE+) 2025-26 report, released this month by the Union Ministry of Education, is built around that basic unit of the school system. It tracks how many teachers India has, how they're distributed, and what that distribution means for millions of students. The numbers show a workforce that has grown steadily even as the system around it has become leaner and retained more students.More teachers, lower ratiosIndia's teacher count rose from 94,83,294 in 2022-23 to 98,07,600 in 2023-24, then to 1,01,22,420 in 2024-25 and 1,02,73,020 in 2025-26, an increase of 8.3% over four years, crossing the one-crore mark along the way. That growth is most evident in the Pupil-Teacher Ratio (PTR), which measures how many students each teacher is responsible for. At the Foundational level, the PTR now stands at 10 students per teacher, down from 11 in 2022-23.
Preparatory has moved to 12 from 14, Middle school to 17 from 18, and Secondary to 21 from 23. All four levels are now well within the 30:1 ratio recommended under the National Education Policy; a lower PTR generally means more attention per student and classrooms that are easier to manage. The improvement has been gradual rather than sudden: Preparatory PTR, for instance, moved from 14 to 13 to 13 before settling at 12, showing the kind of steady year-on-year correction that comes from sustained recruitment rather than a one-time push.
Dropout and retention figures follow the same broad trend, though not evenly across every level. Preparatory dropout fell from 8.7% in 2022-23 to 3.7%, then 2.3%, and now 1.8% in 2025-26, a decline of nearly 7 percentage points in four years. Secondary dropout came down from 13.8% to 7.0% over the same period, nearly halving. Middle school is the exception: after falling steadily from 8.1% to 5.2% to 3.5% across three years, its dropout rate ticked up slightly this year, from 3.5% to 3.6%, the only level where the four-year trend reversed rather than held.Retention tells a similar mixed story. Secondary retention jumped from 47.2% to 51.9%, helped by more schools now offering secondary education, and Middle retention rose from 82.8% to 83.7%, continuing a climb from 75.8% in 2022-23. Foundational retention eased this year, from 98.9% to 98.5%, after three straight years of gains from 92.1% in 2022-23. Preparatory retention also slipped, from 92.4% to 91.1% — but unlike Foundational, its four-year path wasn't a steady climb: it fell to 85.4% in 2023-24 before recovering to 92.4% the year after, and now sits only marginally above where it started in 2022-23, at 90.9%.
Retention tells a similar mixed story
Enrolment and transition numbers add to the picture. Secondary GER rose from 68.5% to 71.7% this year; across the four-year period it actually dipped to 66.5% in 2023-24 before climbing back and past its 2022-23 level of 67.6%. Middle GER has stayed roughly flat for four years, moving between 89.5% and 90.3% and settling at 89.6% now. Transition rates — the share of students who move on to the next stage rather than leaving school altogether — improved at every checkpoint: Foundational-to-Preparatory transition rose to 99.2% from 98.6%, Preparatory-to-Middle to 93.8% from 92.2%, and Middle-to-Secondary to 88.3% from 86.6%, each figure now at its highest point across the four years tracked.Fewer single-teacher schools, better-equipped classroomsThe growth in teacher numbers has also changed how schools are staffed. Single-teacher schools, where one person handles every grade and subject, fell by about 3% in 2025-26 to 1,00,843, continuing a decline from 1,18,190 in 2022-23 and 1,10,971 the year after. Zero-enrolment schools fell even faster — by around 29% in a single year, from 7,993 to 5,663, though the number had actually risen to 12,954 in 2023-24 before the sharp correction that followed. The report attributes both declines to how UDISE+ data itself is used, allowing planners to reallocate teachers to where enrolment actually needs them, rather than leaving schools overstaffed relative to the students they serve.
Growth in teacher numbers has also changed how schools are staffed
School infrastructure has improved along with the workforce. Computer access rose from 47.7% in 2022-23 to 69.9% in 2025-26, with the sharpest single-year jump, a 9.5 percentage point rise, coming in 2023-24. Internet access followed a close path, up from 49.7% to 67.4% over the same period. Basic facilities are now close to universal: 95.0% of schools have electricity, up from 91.7%; 99.5% have drinking water; 98.5% have girls' toilets and 97.2% have boys' toilets; and 96.9% have handwashing facilities, up from 94.1% four years ago. Library access has also grown steadily, from 88.3% to 90.5% of schools. Two areas lag behind the rest — playgrounds, present in 81.9% of schools, actually declined slightly from 83.0% the previous year, breaking an otherwise uninterrupted rise since 2022-23, and rainwater harvesting remains available in just 29.9% of schools despite steady incremental gains each year since a base of 28.0% in 2022-23. Ramps and handrails for students with disabilities have grown from 51.0% to 58.2% of schools, though more than four in ten schools still lack them.Women now make up most of the teaching workforceThe report also points to a shift in who is doing the teaching. Women now make up 54.9% of India's teachers, up from 52.3% four years ago and 53.3% the year after that — a steady climb of more than two-and-a-half percentage points across a workforce of over a crore people.
Girls' enrolment has moved more slowly but just as consistently, from 48.0% in 2022-23 to 48.1%, then 48.3%, and now 48.4% in 2025-26 — small annual shifts that add up to real change in a system enrolling tens of millions of students each year.
Report also points to a shift in who is doing the teaching
Read together, the UDISE+ 2025-26 numbers show a system that added capacity, tightened ratios and expanded infrastructure over four years, while still carrying a few gaps that didn't move like the rest of the data — a middle-school dropout rate that rose instead of fell, a Foundational and Preparatory retention dip after years of improvement, a zero-enrolment number that spiked before it fell, and a playground shortfall the other infrastructure numbers don't quite explain. None of these gaps undoes the larger trend, but they're the parts of the report worth watching in the years ahead, since they mark the points where the steady four-year climb didn't hold.

USA Seeking New Ground-Based Air Defense Artillery System to Protect Air Bases Abroad
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
11:10:38 UTC
20:10:38 KST

The U.S. Air Force is seeking a ground-based air defense artillery system to protect air bases in various countries around the world from drones and cruise missiles.
The U.S. Air Force published a Request for Information (RFI) on the government’s procurement portal.
The military is looking for companies that can offer a medium-caliber ground-based air defense gun system with relatively inexpensive ammunition. The primary targets are to be subsonic cruise missiles and drones.
Previously, ground-based air defense for U.S. military facilities was primarily the responsibility of the U.S. Army, and the Air Force did not have its own gun systems. That is why the U.S. Air Force is now seeking its own capabilities.
For now, this is only a market study, not a procurement of a specific system.
The request refers to a Ground-Based, Medium-Caliber Gun Weapon System—a ground-based, medium-caliber air defense gun system.
A specific caliber has not been specified. However, the U.S. Army classifies 20, 25, 30×113 mm, 30×173 mm, and 40 mm as medium calibers.
The U.S. Air Force seeks a system equipped with capabilities for target detection, tracking, and engagement. Fifteen key operational and technical parameters have been identified for evaluating the systems, including the probability of hitting a target with a single salvo, range and altitude of operation, ammunition characteristics, sensor capabilities, mobility, and cost of operation, among others.
One of the key performance indicators will be the salvo probability of kill (Pk)—the probability of destroying a target with several shots or a salvo.
The system must be lightweight, modular, and capable of being rapidly deployed to areas with limited infrastructure. C-130 Hercules, C-17 Globemaster III, and C-5 Galaxy military transport aircraft can be used to transport it.
The need to strengthen gun-based air defense became particularly apparent following the attacks by Iran. The massive strikes highlighted the problem of the high cost of intercepting large numbers of relatively inexpensive targets.
Similar systems are already in use by the U.S. Army and the Marine Corps. Specifically, the Centurion C-RAM is equipped with a 20 mm M61 Vulcan cannon, while the Sgt. Stout is equipped with a 30 mm XM914 cannon with programmable ammunition.
For example, a Shahed-136 is estimated to cost $35,000–$50,000, while a Patriot PAC-3 missile can cost around $5 million. Cannon systems can serve as a first line of defense and reduce the cost of countering such targets.
Interest in such weapons has also been influenced by Ukraine’s experience. The Ukrainian military is using German Gepard systems equipped with two 35 mm cannons against attack drones, demonstrating the effectiveness of cannon-based air defense against large numbers of aerial targets.
One potential option is the Skyranger 35 from Germany’s Rheinmetall. The system uses a 35 mm KDG 35/1000 cannon with a rate of fire of up to 1,000 rounds per minute and an effective range of up to 4,000 meters.
The system can use AHEAD programmable air-burst munitions and can be mounted on various wheeled and tracked armored platforms. Ukraine is already receiving such systems, and their combat use demonstrates the capabilities of modern cannon-based air defense against drones.
Another potential option is the new American Raid Hunter from Northrop Grumman. The company has unveiled a 50 mm ground-based air defense gun system that combines an automatic cannon, guided 50 mm ammunition, and a networked command-and-control system.

Chinese man, Nepali woman found alive 10 days after flood

Rescuers pulled out a 64-year-old Nepali woman alive on Saturday from her home, buried under thick mud and debris when the region was struck by massive flooding 10 days ago, killing over 1,300 people and leaving at least 5,500 missing.
Emergency personnel said earlier they had rescued a Chinese man, named only as Luhaitao, found alive inside a 225-metre tunnel of the Upper Trishuli-1 Hydropower Project in Nepal’s Rasuwa district.

“A police team found her as they were clearing the area. She has been airlifted to Kathmandu for treatment,” said police deputy superintendent Iqbal Hawari.
A video released by Nepal’s Armed Police Force showed only a part of her house visible, with the lower floors completely submerged by thick sludge.

New brain scan tool could help expose a devastating and incurable genetic condition
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
11:09:35 UTC
20:09:35 KST

About 8,000 people in the U.K. are living with Huntington’s disease, a devastating inherited condition that gradually affects movement, thinking and mood. Now, an advanced type of MRI scan could give researchers a way to estimate the cellular damage it causes in living people, which could eventually help show whether treatments are working.
New research from my colleagues and I found that the technique can detect abnormalities in the brains of people living with Huntington’s that match those previously identified by examining brain tissue after death.
Huntington’s disease is an inherited condition caused by a faulty gene. Its effects usually begin between the ages of 30 and 50. There is currently no cure, although new cell and gene therapies are being developed and tested.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
One of the main things that happens in Huntington’s is the loss of neuronal cells in the striatum, a part of the basal ganglia deep within the brain. These structures are important for controlling movement and other functions. As cells are lost, the brain tissue in these regions shrinks.
We can see this shrinkage using conventional MRI. But a standard brain scan tells us relatively little about what is happening inside the tissue at a cellular level. That’s where our approach comes in.
We used a technique called “soma and neurite density imaging”, or Sandi, to analyze diffusion MRI scans. Diffusion MRI detects how water moves through brain tissue. Because that movement is affected by the structures around the water, we can use it to make indirect estimates of properties such as the apparent size and density of cell bodies.
This means we can get indirect estimates of the structures within the tissue itself.
For our study, we analyzed scans from 56 people with Huntington’s disease and 57 healthy volunteers of a similar age and sex. The participants were scanned using a strong-gradient MRI scanner.
We focused on the basal ganglia, where we expected to see the effects of Huntington’s disease. We also looked at the thalamus, a nearby brain region that is relatively spared during the early stages of the disease, as a comparison. The results showed a clear difference.
In the basal ganglia of people with Huntington’s disease, we found lower estimates of apparent cell-body density, larger estimates of apparent cell-body size and more space between cells than in healthy volunteers. We didn’t see the same pattern in the thalamus.
These findings are particularly interesting because they resemble what has previously been seen in brain tissue after death. Postmortem studies have shown that Huntington’s causes a specific type of striatal neurons—the cells that send signals around the brain and nervous system—to be lost. At the same time, glial cells, which normally support and protect neurons, change in response to the damage. They become larger and more active, altering the environment around the remaining neuronal cells.
Our results suggest that Sandi may indirectly capture these biological changes in the living brain. The MRI measurements were also associated with the severity of Huntington’s disease and with poorer performance on finger-tapping tests, which are commonly used to assess motor control.
In some regions of the striatum, our estimates of apparent cell-body size and density, together with a person’s age, explained up to 63% of the observed brain shrinkage. This suggests that the measurements may be capturing some of the biological processes driving the loss of brain tissue, and could eventually be important for the development of treatments.
Future treatments
New cell and gene therapies for Huntington’s disease are being investigated, but researchers need ways of measuring what is happening inside the brain of a living person. If a treatment is designed to protect brain cells, we need to be able to measure whether that is actually happening.
Sandi could potentially provide such a measure. It might allow us to indirectly track cellular changes non-invasively and, in future clinical trials, help determine whether a treatment is altering the underlying disease process.
But we are not quite there yet. Our study was a snapshot, comparing people with Huntington’s disease and healthy volunteers at a single point in time. This does not tell us whether Sandi can track disease progression, or whether Sandi can reliably detect changes caused by a treatment.
We now need larger studies that follow people over a period of time to establish whether these measurements can track the progression of Huntington’s disease. The technique will also need to be adapted and validated for the MRI scanners routinely used in hospitals.
Sandi could give us something we currently lack: a way to look beyond brain shrinkage and gain an insight into the cellular changes taking place inside the living brain. And because the loss of brain cells is also a feature of more common conditions such as Parkinson’s and Alzheimer’s disease, the approach may have applications beyond Huntington’s.
This article was first published by The Conversation. Read the original article here.

Mathematicians discover the worst way to hang a painting
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
11:09:24 UTC
20:09:24 KST

You have two nails in the wall and a painting with a string on its back, which can easily be rested on the nails to hang the painting. If you remove one nail, the painting will still hang on the other. But mathematicians said, “We can make it worse.” In 1997 A. Spivak posed the following riddle: Is there a way to hang the painting so that removing either nail will cause the painting to fall? Since then, mathematicians have expanded this concept into an intriguing family of picture-hanging problems.
Retired computer scientist Tom Verhoeff first explored such problems in a workshop for a grade school math camp, where the campers investigated with actual string and carabiners but also translated the problem into symbols.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
In 2012 mathematicians posted a preprint proving that solutions exist for any k-out-of-n picture-hanging problem, where n is the number of nails and removing any k of the nails, but no fewer, will cause the painting to fall. Known solutions, however, can involve very elaborate string wrappings. At the workshop Verhoeff and the participants tackled the 2-out-of-4 problem, in which a painting will fall if any two of four nails are removed. They reduced the length of the shortest known solution from 80 to 58 wraps around the nails.
Later, Verhoeff worked it all the way down to 18—and, with the help of then Ph.D. student Jens Heuseveldt and a computer program to check all smaller hangings, down to the absolute minimum of 16. Initially Verhoeff showed Heuseveldt a computer program to solve the problem in about two hours. “I then told him my program could solve it in two seconds,” Heuseveldt says. “And now his program is even faster than mine.” Verhoeff posted the results along with the shortest known explicit solutions for large families of these problems to the preprint server arXiv.org.
Why are mathematicians so interested in hanging paintings in complex and terrible ways? Although the problem’s framing might sound silly, the underlying mechanics have deep connections to group theory, knot theory, graph theory, and other areas of mathematics. In the 1-out-of-n case, for example, solutions can be described as loops drawn on the edges of an n-dimensional cube that pass through every corner. Plus, it’s possible to find hangings for any “reasonable” set of rules for paintings to fall—for example, you can’t require that removing just nail A makes the painting fall but removing A and B leaves it hanging. These rules exactly correspond to the monotone Boolean functions—a function type crucial in fields such as cryptography and voting theory.
But asking whether the problem is useful is the wrong question, Verhoeff argues. “For humanity as a whole, we don’t know where our spaceship is going and what we will need to survive,” he says, “and play is one of the ways in which we learn.”

There was no immediate reaction from Moscow to Tokyo’s remarks.
Japan-Russia ties have been strained in recent months after Russian President Vladimir Putin visited a disputed island chain off Hokkaido last month, prompting a protest from Tokyo.

NABU details criminal organization headed by Prosecutor General's Office official
NABU announced this on Facebook, according to Ukrinform.
NABU and the Specialized Anti-Corruption Prosecutor's Office (SAPO) exposed a criminal organization whose members systematically received illicit payments from fraudulent call centers and laundered millions of hryvnias in proceeds.
The scheme was organized by one of the heads of a structural unit of the Prosecutor General's Office.
According to investigators, the PGO official established and headed the criminal organization in mid-2025. He involved both serving prosecutors and unofficial associates close to him in the illegal activities.
According to NABU, members of the criminal organization established a system for systematically collecting bribes in exchange for allowing so-called call centers to operate unhindered. These shadow structures carried out large-scale fraudulent activities targeting both Ukrainian citizens and foreigners.
The suspects laundered the proceeds through a number of schemes.
More than UAH 20 million was spent on purchasing real estate, jewelry and other valuable movable property.
Assets worth more than UAH 12 million at minimum market value were laundered by the organization's leader by transferring their ownership to third parties in order to conceal the actual beneficial owner. These assets included real estate in a popular apartment complex near the Carpathian Mountains.
The group members also placed more than UAH 10 million in bank accounts belonging to close associates, presenting the funds as legitimate income allegedly earned through business activities.
Five members of the criminal organization have so far been exposed.
The preliminary legal classification includes Article 255 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine – establishing or running a criminal community or criminal organization, as well as participation in one – and Article 209 – legalization (laundering) of property obtained through criminal means.
The investigation is ongoing. Authorities are identifying other possible members of the criminal organization.

Swiss canton Valais wants complete eradication of two wolf packs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
11:03:00 UTC
20:03:00 KST

Swiss canton Valais wants complete eradication of two wolf packs
The canton of Valais has applied to the Federal Office for the Environment (FOEN) for authorisation to cull two wolf packs in their entirety: those in Augstbord and the Nanz Valley. This measure follows the death of 219 farm animals this summer.
The request from Valais, submitted to the FOEN at the end of August, forms part of the fourth phase of wolf management in Switzerland. The packs in Augstbord and the Nanz Valley are to be completely eradicated, including their cubs, the Cantonal Service for Hunting, Fishing and Wildlife told news agency Keystone-SDA on Saturday, confirming a report in the Walliser Bote.
The canton justifies its request on the basis of the 219 livestock killed in 84 recorded attacks during the 2026 mountain pasture season. The Augstbord and Nanz/Ganter regions have been particularly hard hit, with 54 and 25 animals killed, respectively.
More
Preventive culling controls Swiss wolf population
The Augstbord pack, which was considered to have been wiped out last winter following the culling of 14 individuals, has reformed. At least three new cubs have been recorded there. The pack in the Nanz valley also has at least three young.
In addition to these two culls, the canton plans to cull two further packs. In Nendaz/Isérables (at least five cubs) and Les Toules, the plan is to cull two-thirds of this year’s cubs.
Other cantons, such as Graubünden, Ticino and St Gallen, have also issued new culling orders. The FOEN’s decision on the Valais application is expected by mid-September.

Brain damage reveals how a specific region generates mind-wandering
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
11:00:44 UTC
20:00:44 KST

Damage to a specific area of the brain limits a person’s ability to let their mind wander, according to a small study. Researchers found that this frontal brain region is necessary for generating the internal thoughts and memories that pull our attention away from the present moment. The findings were published in the journal Neuropsychologia.
The human mind frequently detaches from the immediate environment to focus on internal matters, such as planning for the future or recalling past events. Psychologists refer to this phenomenon as stimulus-independent and task-unrelated thought. In everyday language, it is more commonly known as mind-wandering.
Brain imaging studies have linked mind-wandering to the default mode network. This is a group of interconnected brain regions that activate when a person is resting or engaged in internal mental processes. One specific region in this network is the ventromedial prefrontal cortex, an area located in the lower front of the brain.
Past research indicated that damage to the ventromedial prefrontal cortex reduces mind-wandering, but the exact mechanism remained elusive. Scientists debated whether this brain region actually generates the wandering thoughts, or if it simply allows a person to become aware that their mind has wandered. A team of researchers based in Italy, led by Elisa Ciaramelli of the University of Bologna, designed an experiment to test these competing ideas.
If the ventromedial prefrontal cortex only controls a person’s awareness of their thoughts, damage to the region would cause individuals to underreport all types of distractions. However, if the region is responsible for generating internal thoughts, patients would specifically lack mind-wandering while still noticing external distractions. The researchers recruited 42 participants for a small study to investigate this distinction.
The study sample included nine patients with localized damage to the ventromedial prefrontal cortex. The researchers also included a control group of 14 patients with brain damage in other areas, along with a second control group of 19 healthy adults.
In the first phase of the experiment, known as the standard condition, participants completed a repetitive attention task on a computer. They watched a screen and pressed a button every time a pattern of vertical lines appeared among frequent patterns of horizontal lines.
Roughly every 40 trials, the program paused and asked the participants to rate their attention. If participants reported that their attention had drifted away from the task, they had to categorize the nature of the distraction.
Participants noted whether their distraction was an internal thought, a thought related to the repetitive nature of the task itself, or an external distraction like a noise in the room. If they reported an internal thought, they also specified whether the mental image was focused on the past, the present, or the future.
The patients with damage to the ventromedial prefrontal cortex reported drastically fewer internal thoughts compared to both the healthy adults and the other brain-damaged patients. They specifically lacked wandering thoughts focused on the past and the future.
These patients experienced the same amount of task-related thoughts and external distractions as the other groups. This suggests that their brains could still lose focus on the main activity, but they lacked the internal mental content needed to drift into true mind-wandering.
In a separate phase of the experiment, called the cued condition, the researchers altered the repetitive line task. Random cue words like the word seaside occasionally appeared on the screen beneath the center fixation point.
These words were designed to act as subtle triggers for autobiographical memories and wandering thoughts. When the thought probes appeared in this version of the task, participants could report if their mind-wandering had been sparked by one of the specific cue words.
When provided with these external cues, patients with damage to the ventromedial prefrontal cortex still struggled to generate wandering thoughts. They reported fewer internal thoughts triggered by the cue words than the healthy adults did.
As in the first experiment, this reduction was isolated to internal mind-wandering. The patients continued to report typical levels of external distractions and thoughts regarding the test itself.
The combined results indicate that the ventromedial prefrontal cortex is necessary for the spontaneous construction of internal events. The researchers propose that without this brain region initiating personal memories and future projections, a person’s attention is less likely to turn inward.
This finding aligns with the idea that the ventromedial prefrontal cortex helps build the mental scenes that fuel our daydreams. Because the patients retained the ability to notice external distractions, their lack of mind-wandering cannot be explained by a general failure to monitor their own thoughts.
The small number of participants in the study limits the sensitivity of the statistical analysis, meaning subtle differences between the patient groups might have gone undetected. The study format also required participants to be self-aware enough to categorize their own thoughts when prompted by the computer.
Future research will need to measure instances where people spontaneously catch themselves daydreaming, rather than relying on external computer prompts. This would help researchers confirm that the reported lack of mind-wandering holds true across different methods of measuring human attention.
Researchers might also investigate how this specific type of brain damage impacts daily functioning. A reduced capacity for mind-wandering could limit a person’s ability to plan for the future, reflect on past experiences, and engage in creative problem solving.
The study, “vmPFC damage reduces mind-wandering, but not other classes of off-task thought,” was authored by Elisa Ciaramelli, Virginia Pollarini, Andrea Crisafulli, Alessia Ferretti, and Manila Vannucci.

Kardashian curves: M&S launches £28 bodysuit with exaggerated hip padding
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
11:00:36 UTC
20:00:36 KST

For decades shapewear has been used to compress and cinch. But now there is a sub-genre emerging. Rather than shrinking a silhouette, it aims to add inches.
This week M&S launched a bodysuit that features exaggerated padding at the hip allowing the wearer to create an hourglass shape, or at least the illusion of one.
Similar to how bra inserts, AKA chicken fillets, are used to add extra volume to breasts, the £28 “hip boost” features pockets on each side of the suit that allow the wearer to add in enhancing pads.
Charlotte Davies, the director of lingerie at the retailer, says the idea stemmed from customer interest in “solutions that offer subtle enhancement alongside everyday comfort and confidence”, with the trend being driven by the catwalks and celebrities. The hip booster’s predecessors at M&S include padded bum shorts “to give the wearer a curvy, contoured look” and stick-on nipples for “a realistic raised profile beneath clothing”.
Kim Kardashian’s shapewear brand, Skims, launched shorts with hip padding last year. Many users online claim such type of strategic padding can help minimise “hip dips” – a phrase used to describe the natural inward curves between the hipbone and thigh bone.
The emergence of enhancing shapewear comes at a time when both the body and the idea of what a body can look like are increasingly scrutinised. From the widespread use of GLP-1 drugs to a rise in cosmetic surgery procedures, bodies have never been more malleable.
On the recent catwalks, designers have been playing with this idea of reconstruction too, coinciding with a return of ultra-thin models. At Schiaparelli, its creative director Daniel Roseberry used both visible and invisible padding to inflate hips and whittle waists. Meanwhile, Dior and Alaïa turned to panniers, rigid side hoop undergarments originally worn by women in the 17th and 18th century, to inspire modern-day dresses with hips similarly wide enough to force the wearer to turn sideways when passing through a door.
“Weight-loss medications have changed many bodies dramatically, but they don’t automatically deliver conventional, ideal beauty, which in the current era is quite hard to achieve,” says Victoria Pitts-Taylor, a professor at Wesleyan University and the author of Surgery Junkies: Wellness and Pathology in Cosmetic Culture. “To be very thin in some areas of the body and thick in others often requires building and sculpting, which can happen in a dressing room with fabric or an operating room with scalpels.”
This trompe d’oeil effect is also dominating the red carpet. Four years after Kim Kardashian wore a sauna suit to lose enough weight to squeeze into Marilyn Monroe’s dress, she and her hypercurves are back. At the body-themed Met Gala in May, she emphasised her shape with a fibreglass breast plate. Meanwhile, her sisters Kylie and Kendall Jenner opted for moulded corsets with fake nipples and amplified hips. Tulip-like silhouettes have also been embraced by the singers Rosalía and Teyana Taylor and more are expected at the Venice film festival that has just got under way.
Ali Bodley, a heritage specialist who curated the Shaping The Body exhibition at York Castle Museum, says everyone from the Tudors including Queen Elizabeth I to the Georgians and the Victorians played with their proportions. Long before Kardashian’s Skims empire, there were “bum shops” – stores specialising in padding.
Susie Orbach describes the trend as “grotesque”. The psychotherapist, psychoanalyst and social critic says it puts women in a “position where they are constantly having to create a body”.
Pitts-Taylor says the lives of celebrities in the 20th century were generally understood to be aspirational rather than attainable. However, “today consumer culture and social media put pressure on people in everyday walks of life to be image-minded”, she says. “The beauty ideal seems to promise belonging, being valued and successful, in a world in which actual, material equality is increasingly hard to achieve.”
Orbach says there is no such thing as “an ideal body shape” explaining the parameters are always shifting. “There is always some type of body shape being promoted. But as soon as you get there, it is wrong.” Rather than “living and being allowed to have safety in our bodies”, she adds, “we are now always in a process of transformation.”

First professional St Nick with Down’s syndrome inducted into International Santa Claus Hall of Fame
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
11:00:36 UTC
20:00:36 KST

After recently gaining recognition as the first professional Santa Claus with Down syndrome in the US, Bradley Carlisle has already gotten a lot more than the traditional serving of milk and cookies that is usually left out for Father Christmas each year.
That is because the 37-year-old community theater actor from suburban Atlanta landed an honorary induction into the International Santa Claus Hall of Fame upon completing one of the largest Christmas performer schools in the US in late August – a distinction meant to recognize the important representation his emergence on the holiday scene has brought, according to his supporters.
As his mother, Debbie Chadrix, told it, Carlisle’s path to his unique place among what she called the Claus family began at the 2023 holiday party of the Down Syndrome Association of Atlanta (DSAA). Chadrix said the organization’s executive director approached her during the gathering and remarked: “We need a Santa with Down syndrome who looks like the kids” who had been invited to the party as the guests of honor.
The group’s leader picked Carlisle because of his passion for acting on the local community theater circuit, Chadrix said. Yet Chadrix wasn’t completely sold.
She said her son feared Santa growing up because he evidently equated jolly old St Nick’s white gloves with those worn by healthcare providers who took care of him during difficult medical experiences. It was only after one Santa in particular slipped his gloves off for Bradley that he warmed up to the concept, she recounted.
Carlisle, however, gamely accepted the offer to transform into Santa for the next DSAA holiday party. He confidently wore the white beard and red suit, and interacted with more than 200 children.
Chadrix said she has never forgotten the looks on many of the children’s faces “when they realized Bradley looked like them – and talked like them, a little bit, too”. And then Bradley declared “he would be our Santa from now on”.
Local news media picked up Carlisle’s story by his second Christmas season as Santa, giving his profile a bump, Chadrix said. He also appeared on a podcast alongside Rick Rosenthal, who runs Atlanta’s Northern Lights Santa Academy and invited Carlisle to attend a four-day course beginning on 20 August.
At Rosenthal’s academy, which he described as the second-largest institution of its kind in the US, actors train to carry on in the spirit of figures such as Santa, Mrs Claus and the Christmas elves. Santas in particular receive an education on a wide range of topics, including how to properly dress for the part, adequately maintain their white beards and improvise answers to the heart-wrenching questions children can occasionally ask, especially if grappling with a terminal illness or grieving the loss of a loved one.
Carlisle excelled in that atmosphere, with Chadrix proudly noting that he underwent the same program as all of the other enrollees there. At a 23 August ceremony on the academy’s final day, Phil Wenz of the Santa Claus Oath Foundation called Carlisle up to a stage.
A video on a social media account for Carlisle showed Wenz complimenting him for the confident style he had displayed while personifying Santa Claus in the lobby outside the ceremony hall.
Wenz alluded to how some of Carlisle’s fellow Claus family members had banded together to cover a completely custom-made Santa suit for him. Carlisle’s photograph would also be shown in New York City’s Times Square as part of the US’s Down Syndrome Awareness Month beginning on 1 October, which is Bradley’s birthday, Wenz continued.
Then Wenz revealed the pièce de résistance: he said he had consulted with a number of Christmas community heavyweights to enshrine him as an honorary member of the International Santa Claus Hall of Fame.
Wenz punctuated the moment with handing Carlisle a badge. Carlisle triumphantly held it up and smiled widely as the audience applauded.
Rosenthal has belonged to the institution in the town of Santa Claus, Indiana, since late 2023; he considers it one of his greatest honors in his 58 years as a Santa. He said Carlisle merited enshrinement because of already showing “a magnified sensitivity” to people with Down syndrome who are among Santa’s faithful that others in the Claus family simply cannot.
Chadrix said she was notified in advance of the plan to welcome Carlisle to the International Santa Claus Hall of Fame. She said she made clear, essentially, that she did not want Bradley’s condition to be the only reason he was being enshrined.
She recalled Rosenthal assuring her: “Phil Wenz knows what he’s looking at. And as soon as he saw Bradley as Santa and talking to people and interacting, he knew he has something different and special – and that’s why he got to the hall of fame.”
Among the many to congratulate Carlisle was the DSAA, which shared a link to a television news segment about him published by the Atlanta station WXIA on Thursday.
“Saaaaantaaaaa we know him! So proud of our Santa Bradley,” the organization wrote, adding that those who attend Atlanta’s 3 October Buddy Walk – a DSAA fundraiser at the Kennesaw State University Marietta campus – “might see him incognito”.
Carlisle told WXIA that he enjoyed being Santa “because I like to help with the kids”.
The station also asked him what it feels like to slip into his Santa suit.
He replied: “It feels like love.”

Europe would not be able to sustain war of attrition with Russia, defence officials say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
11:00:35 UTC
20:00:35 KST

Defence planners working with Nato fear that if war broke out with Russia, Europe could not currently sustain a prolonged war of attrition owing to a public lack of war readiness, a conference on the future of European military coordination heard this week.
The pessimism reflects concern that Russia may be winning a so-called hybrid war with Europe, weakening the options available to Nato war planners in the event of military conflict.
The surge in support for the populist forces in Europe’s main military states is also endangering proposals for a group of five European countries, including the UK, to take on a new coordination role as the US prepares to reduce its commitments to the conventional defence of Europe.
Defence officials, speaking at a forum convened by the Munich Security Conference (MSC), the leading security foundation, said the European public may not have the appetite for a prolonged war, requiring Nato to focus its plans on a relatively quick conflict.
One recent British cabinet member admitted the west had been “crap” at educating its public about the scale of the hybrid conflict with Russia. Another UK diplomat claimed successive British prime ministers had done nothing to explain the scale of the threat.
They said this had left ministers locked in an unenviable task of persuading unprepared voters to cut welfare spending to fund defence. “The level of the debate has been at that of a kindergarten,” the UK diplomat admitted.
The private criticism has been fuelled by the UK government’s inability to adopt a call in its 2025 strategic defence review to launch a national conversation on the scale of the security threat facing Europe and to build national resilience.
A second diplomat said the collapse of the cold war dividing line with Russia had left Moscow free to exploit the anxieties of European publics on the left and the right. The remarks reveal a wider concern in senior European politicians that they may be losing the so-called hybrid war with Russia, and this may be reflected in rightwing populist surges next year in Poland, France and Italy.
Most populist parties, including Germany’s Alternative für Deutschland (AfD), are sympathetic to Russia and want an end to the Ukraine conflict.
The MSC discussion – held under rules forbidding identification of the speaker – was given added urgency by the German government this week blaming Russia for an attempted drone attack on Leipzig airport last month.
One of the suspected culprits in the attack on 4 August, where an armed drone exploded, has been identified as a Belarusian citizen with a Russian passport who appears to have entered Europe using an Italian tourist visa.
The MSC, an independent but influential foundation, has been promoting the idea of the five main European military powers working much more closely: one means of bringing the UK, outside the EU, to the centre of European defence planning.
Decisions in Washington on its troop deployments that could effectively leave Europe in charge of its own conventional defences are expected in the next few months. But the scale of hybrid war and the potential impact of next year’s elections, as well as the surge by the AfD in Germany, on plans for a stronger European defence coordination was described at the conference as “the elephant in the room”.
One proposal is for the EU to publish a collective statement on the Russian threat that the populist forces would be challenged to accept or decline.
The E5 group of European defence ministers already meet regularly, but they are at the early stages of agreeing of how to jointly procure capabilities such as integrated air and missile defence, deep precision strike and space-based early warning systems that are all currently provided mostly by the US.
“Europe is stagnating at a time when the external threats were assuming a dimension which is really very serious. These are really huge and existential challenges requiring greater integration in defence,” said Wolfgang Ischinger, the chair of the MSC.
He argued the E5 grouping offers a way of including all the European countries with substantial defence industrial capacity and may later be able to incorporate Ukraine in the context of a truce since Kyiv now has the largest and strongest army in Europe.
Advocates of the E5 insist it will neither duplicate nor underline Nato, but fears were expressed that the US would nevertheless block a stronger European pillar inside Nato. “The US are better at talking about burden shifting than power sharing,” said one diplomat.
Italy is one of the E5 states most concerned about the impact of Russia’s hybrid warfare on its domestic politics as Giorgia Meloni’s rightwing administration – which has governed more moderately than many expected, and cultivated a pro-Ukraine image abroad – becomes its longest-running since the second world war.
The Italian foreign minister, Antonio Tajani, warned Italy was suffering daily cyber-attacks, adding it was not immune from potential Russian interference in next year’s national elections, the first time an Italian politicians has warned the election may be manipulated.
“There are many ways to wage hybrid warfare, it is not done using bombs, planes or tanks,” the minister said.
Italy’s defence minister, Guido Crosetto, one of Meloni’s closest political allies, has said it was stupid not to recognise the level of Russian interference.
He warned this summer at the Nato summit in Ankara: “We don’t have the antibodies and we’re penetrable: analyse bots and you’ll see it. The increase occurred thanks to social media.”
His doubts have grown given Moscow’s ability to operate across so many domains, including social media, AI, cybersecurity, databases and critical infrastructure. On Tuesday, he said the Russian threat was growing all the time.
Crosetto also said he recognises Russia is exploiting real problems such as low wages, and so attributing government unpopularity to Russian disinformation risks misidentifying a malaise afflicting western societies, including a general weariness with the cost of the war in Ukraine,
In Italy, Roberto Vannacci, the leader of the far-right Futuro Nazionale who has challenged the stability of Meloni’s coalition, is widely seen as the most probable carrier of the Russian message in the coming election, that could come as early as April.
Speaking before the investigation into whether his party represents a revival of fascism, Vannacci gloried in the criticism. “Just discovered that I am a ‘Manchurian candidate’ sent by the Russian federation to complain about the unaffordable petrol prices in my country Italy,” he said. “Forgive me, but I still find it hard to accept the idea that dissent from Brussels’ orthodoxy is now, in practical terms, tantamount to disloyalty towards the west.”
In an attempt to shift perceptions so Ukraine is seen not as a financial burden but rather as teaching Europe modern warfare, Crosetto has recruited the former Ukraine defence minister Mykhailo Fedorov as his unpaid adviser for innovation. Ischinger praised the decision, describing Ukraine as possessing the best equipped and most modern army in Europe.
In Ukraine, 200,000 drones are being built each month, with the goal of producing more than 7m by 2026. To support this growth, 500 small and medium-sized companies have sprung up, assembling drones even in small workshops, using mostly Chinese components.

Reform continues to cast doubt on climate science. Do its supporters agree?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
11:00:34 UTC
20:00:34 KST

On the second day of the Reform UK conference, in the wake of an undercover investigation alleging party officials plotted to evade the law on foreign donations, the deputy leader, Richard Tice, addressed the audience. Within minutes, a banner appeared behind him reading: “Collect £5m, burn the planet.”
It was taken down promptly and Tice, who has repeatedly called on people to enjoy the summer’s five successive heatwaves and record drought, rolled on. As Reform members at the Birmingham venue applauded Tice, there was plenty of agreement with his views. “I enjoyed the heat this summer,” said Jeanette Bowden, of Bexley. “I don’t think people need telling to take care of themselves.” Her partner, James, added, without scientific backing: “Carbon dioxide was much higher in the past, it was 10 times higher than this during the ice ages. It’s not a human problem.”
Amid stalls offering simulated helicopter rides, gold as an investment, tattoos and discounts on rum, climate scepticism was common. “It’s overhyped,” said Yvonne, who did not wish to give a surname.
“I don’t believe the predictions,” said Jim Langford. “They told us Norwich would be underwater by now and it’s not Atlantis yet.” Ed Rennie, a former Labour councillor from north London, said the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change had reduced some of its higher predictions.
But many of the same people who, like Tice, cast doubt on climate science, also criticised the government for failing to protect people against the hot weather. Bowden pointed to new-build houses. “They have really small windows,” she said. “That might be good in winter, but in summer it must be too hot, you can hardly open them. The government should not force this on people.”
Yvonne added: “The government were all on their holidays in the summer, not doing their jobs [to help people during the heatwaves]. Government should ensure there is clean water and sewage, but they’re not even doing that.”
Nicholas, another delegate who did not wish to be named in full, said air conditioning should be installed in all hospitals, schools, libraries and public buildings, and made more easily available for homes.
Langford said the government was “absolutely not” doing enough to help people cope with the impacts of extreme weather. “They’re not preparing us at all, they’re just wasting resources.” Beryl Kingsbury said people should take responsibility for their own safety during hot weather, but farmers needed help. “They should have more support, but this government seems to hate farmers.”
For Mark Henderson, a facilities manager who works mostly outside looking after three large yards, the government’s role should be to apply common sense to health and safety. “I wear a helmet all the time, which was very hot [in the heatwaves], but I don’t need it all the time. You should be able to relax those rules in hot weather, to make them task-specific,” he said.
The confusion among Reform supporters, explained Michael Jacobs, an emeritus professor of political economy at the University of Sheffield, was to be expected given the party leadership’s peddling of “myths and lies” over the climate. Voters often say they want contradictory things, such as high standards of social care without tax rises to pay for them, Jacobs pointed out. But on the climate, they face an even more intense bombardment from contradictory viewpoints, as parties of the right try to turn the issue into a culture war.
“It’s really incoherent to be in favour of adaptation but not [cutting greenhouse gas emissions], but it’s not surprising people think that, given what they’ve been told,” Jacobs said. “Tice and Farage have claimed net zero would be economically ruinous, which is simply wrong. They try to say the UK is acting alone in cutting emissions, also untrue. These are pernicious myths. They have obscured the scientific fact that net zero is the description of where you need to get to, to stop the climate crisis getting any worse.”
Party activists of all stripes – the people who come to conferences – also tend to have stronger opinions than a party’s voters. Polls consistently show that Reform voters are much less likely to deny climate science than their leaders, and large majorities would like to see renewable energy sited near them, despite opposition to renewables from the party leadership. And although Reform has railed against “net stupid zero”, a significant minority, roughly a quarter by some polling, remain in favour of the target. In contrast to the leadership’s stance, which is to scrap the North Sea windfall tax, about 70% want higher taxes on fossil fuels, according to a poll taken last year.
Labour’s climate minister, Katie White, said Reform was out of step with voters. “After the summer we’ve just had, outright climate denial is a pretty lonely corner of British politics,” she said, noting that the government was investing in flood and coastal defences, and in strengthening the response to wildfires.
“My plea to Reform members, MPs and their leadership is a genuine one: please don’t turn climate change into another culture war. Britain has always been at its best when we lead, invent and build. I want our country developing the technologies the world will need, backing British businesses and innovators, and protecting the people and places we love.”
Dissenting voices were hard to find among delegates, but there were occasional flashes of doubt. One younger Reform member, a 25-year-old candidate to be a councillor in the north-west, was unusual in being less certain of the leadership’s stance. “I’m not sure what they should be doing on the climate,” he said. “But I know I and my generation will have to live with it.”

Both sides have engaged constructively with the IAEA for the sake of nuclear safety and security, it added.

The situation around the facility, Europe's largest nuclear power plant and one of the world's 10 largest, remains tense amid concerns over a possible nuclear disaster.
Moscow and Kyiv have frequently accused each other of attacks around the facility.
IAEA personnel have been present at the plant since Sept. 1, 2022. The facility has been under Russian control since March 2022.

Death toll hits 1,375 after devastating Nepal-China border floods
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
10:55:12 UTC
19:55:12 KST

The death toll from catastrophic flash floods and mudslides along the Nepal-China border rose to about 1,375 on Saturday, 10 days after an ice-rock avalanche triggered a massive debris flow through valleys on both sides of the border, according to official figures.
Nepal reported 1,344 deaths, while Chinese authorities said at least 31 people were killed in the southwestern Xizang Autonomous Region, also known as Tibet.
About 5,531 people remained missing, including roughly 850 foreigners, according to combined figures from the two countries.
Nepal's National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority said about 5,000 people were still missing in the country, including 589 foreigners.
Chinese authorities reported another 531 missing in Xizang.
The figures have shifted as rescue teams recover bodies and authorities reconcile reports from remote and heavily damaged areas.
The disaster began Aug. 26 when a large section of rock and ice on the northern flank of Mount Langtang Lirung fractured at an elevation of about 5,200 meters (17,060 feet).
The collapse unleashed a huge ice-rock avalanche that raced down the mountain before rapidly transforming into a debris flow carrying massive amounts of rock, mud, ice and water.
The torrent swept through the Lhende Khola valley along the Nepal-China border and reached the area around the Gyirong border crossing in Tibet, a key trade and transit route between the two countries.
The force of the avalanche and resulting debris flow temporarily blocked rivers, creating unstable natural dams and lakes that later overflowed or breached.
The resulting surge sent floodwaters and mud through downstream valleys and into Nepal's river systems.
In Nepal, the disaster devastated parts of Rasuwa, Nuwakot, Dhading and Kavre districts, as well as areas of the Kathmandu Valley and communities farther downstream.
Villages were buried or swept away, while roads, bridges, homes, schools and other critical infrastructure were destroyed or severely damaged.
Several hydropower projects along the Trishuli and Bhote Koshi river corridors were also hit.
Hundreds of workers were trapped in tunnels and facilities at some sites, prompting prolonged search-and-rescue operations. Some survivors were found and rescued more than a week after the disaster.
The scale of the flooding carried debris and bodies far downstream. Some remains were recovered as far as 240 kilometers away in neighboring India, further complicating identification efforts.
On the Chinese side of the border, the Gyirong crossing was largely buried beneath mud and debris, with buildings, vehicles and other infrastructure damaged or destroyed.
Access to the area remained difficult because of damaged roads, continuing landslide risks and unstable water bodies left behind by the disaster.
Tens of thousands of rescue workers from the Nepali Army, Nepal Police and Armed Police Force took part in the response, alongside Chinese teams and international assistance.
Helicopters and heavy machinery were deployed to reach isolated communities and clear roads blocked by mud, rock and debris.
More than 13,000 people had been rescued in Nepal, authorities said.
Rescue crews faced treacherous terrain, continuing rainfall, blocked transportation routes and the threat of additional flooding caused by unstable debris dams.
The condition of many recovered bodies also made identification difficult, leaving families waiting for confirmation of missing relatives.
Humanitarian agencies said the disaster affected more than 90,000 people, while widespread damage to transportation, power and other services disrupted the lives of many more.
Early assessments put property damage in Nepal at more than 387 billion Nepali rupees, or about $2.57 billion.
Scientists have warned that the disaster highlights the growing risks facing communities in the rapidly warming Himalayas.
Rising temperatures are contributing to glacier retreat and may increase instability in high-altitude slopes through changes in permafrost, precipitation and other environmental conditions.
Chinese officials and some analysts have linked the disaster to broader climate-related changes in the region, although scientists are still investigating the specific factors that caused the Langtang Lirung slope to fail.
The event illustrates how hazards in high-mountain regions can rapidly cascade. An ice and rock collapse can trigger a debris flow, block rivers and ultimately produce devastating floods far downstream. Similar chain-reaction disasters have occurred elsewhere in the Himalayas, including the deadly 2021 Chamoli disaster in northern India.
As of Saturday, authorities on both sides of the border continued searching for missing people, recovering and identifying remains and providing assistance to displaced survivors.
Rescue operations were increasingly being accompanied by efforts to restore roads and other critical infrastructure and address the longer-term humanitarian and economic damage.
The disaster ranks among the deadliest natural disasters in the recent history of the Nepal-Tibet border region.

Radiotherapy remains a cornerstone of cancer treatment
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
10:53:14 UTC
19:53:14 KST

Radiotherapy remains a cornerstone of childhood cancer treatment
TEHRAN - World Radiotherapy Awareness Day is marked on September 7 to raise awareness of radiotherapy as a vital cancer treatment. Radiotherapy helps cure cancer, relieve symptoms, and improve quality of life for millions of people around the world. "One voice for radiotherapy" is this year's theme of World Radiotherapy Awareness Day.
Radiotherapy is one of the oldest established methods of cancer treatment and remains a cornerstone of modern oncology, alongside surgery and chemotherapy. Its clinical history dates back to the late 19th century, following the discovery of X-rays and the early development of radiation-based treatments.
Despite its long-standing role in cancer care, access to radiotherapy remains highly unequal around the world. Low- and middle-income countries are home to the vast majority of the world's population, yet they have a disproportionately small share of global radiotherapy resources. Historically, countries in the developing world have accounted for around 85% of the global population but only about 35% of radiotherapy facilities, highlighting the significant global gap in access to essential cancer care, according to Mitra Ghalibafian, head of the radio-oncology department at Mahak Hospital.
Overall, approximately half of all cancer patients are estimated to require radiotherapy at some point during the course of their treatment, with some estimates placing the figure at 50–60% depending on cancer type, stage and treatment strategy.
Radiotherapy also plays an important role in the diagnosis, staging and treatment planning of childhood cancers. Advanced medical imaging is often essential for identifying the location and extent of a tumor, assessing its relationship with surrounding organs and tissues, and monitoring the response to treatment. Radiotherapy itself is then used, when clinically indicated, to destroy cancer cells and control or eliminate tumors.
In children, however, radiation treatment requires special consideration because growing and developing tissues can be more sensitive to radiation and survivors may live for many decades after treatment. For this reason, pediatric radiation oncology increasingly focuses on highly precise treatment techniques that deliver the necessary dose to the tumor while minimizing exposure to healthy organs.

Unnamed customer receives XTEND’s newest ground robot
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
10:51:53 UTC
19:51:53 KST

- XTEND deployed its first XOS-powered AtlasROVER ground robot to an Asia-Pacific customer, the company's first such deployment since acquiring Atlas.
- XTEND is merging with JFB Construction Holdings in a $1.5 billion deal and says it has deployed more than 12,500 systems across over 30 countries.
XTEND has deployed its first XOS-powered AtlasROVER ground robot to a customer in the Asia-Pacific region, the company’s public parent, JFB Construction Holdings. It’s the first such deployment since XTEND completed its acquisition of Latvia-based robotics company Atlas earlier this year.
The deployment extends XTEND’s software platform, called XOS, beyond the aerial drones it was originally built for and into ground robotics. XOS is designed to run across different types of robots using the same underlying software, letting operators use similar controls and mission tools regardless of whether they’re flying a drone or driving a ground vehicle. Bringing AtlasROVER into that system means the ground platform now runs on the same software architecture as XTEND’s existing drone lineup.
“This is an important step in demonstrating the strategy behind XOS,” said Aviv Shapira, CEO and co-founder of XTEND. “Our goal is not to build isolated robotic products, but to create a common software layer that can extend across air, ground and ultimately maritime systems. Bringing AtlasROVER into the XOS ecosystem moves us closer to a future where different robotic platforms can work together, while humans remain in control of the decisions that matter.”
AtlasROVER is built to operate in difficult environments and carry a range of mission-specific payloads, according to XTEND. The company did not disclose which country or organization received the system, how many units were delivered, or what mission the customer intends to use it for.
XTEND, an Israeli defense technology and robotics company, was founded in Tel Aviv in 2018 by brothers Aviv and Matteo Shapira, Rubi Liani, and Adir Tubi. The company acquired Atlas earlier in 2026 and completed the integration of its operations on July 27, adding more than 4,200 previously deployed robotic systems to its portfolio along with four intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance platforms and a tactical communications system called AtlasRADIO. The acquisition also gave XTEND a manufacturing and engineering hub in Latvia, expanding its commercial reach to roughly 40 European countries.
XTEND is in the process of going public through a $1.5 billion all-stock merger with JFB Construction Holdings, a deal announced in February. Once completed, the combined company is expected to be renamed XTEND AI Robotics and trade on Nasdaq under the ticker XTND. The company, now headquartered in Tampa, Florida, says it has deployed more than 12,500 systems across more than 30 countries, including use in five active combat zones. XTEND employs close to 300 people, more than half of them in Israel, with additional manufacturing sites in the United Kingdom, Singapore and Latvia alongside its Tampa production facility.
The AtlasROVER deployment follows a string of contract announcements from XTEND this year, including a $9 million defense order in June and a separate $3 million follow-on order two days later, which the company said pushed its cumulative defense orders past $12 million. XTEND has not disclosed pricing or delivery timelines for the AtlasROVER program specifically, or whether additional Asia-Pacific customers are currently evaluating the platform.

States reach agreement at autonomous weapons talks in Geneva

States reach agreement at autonomous weapons talks in Geneva
GENEVA – The 128 states party to a framework that regulates or bans weapons considered as indiscriminate, or causing too many injuries, agreed on a document on Sept 5 that could pave the way to international rules on autonomous weapons.
Agreement to the non-binding text marks a significant step after more than a decade of talks on how to regulate weapons systems that can identify and engage targets with varying degrees of autonomy, sometimes called “killer robots”.
However, one rights group said the text definition of an autonomous weapon and the measures to reduce their possible harmful effects on civilians appeared to have been watered down.
“It’s a real shame that all the work done by states on the text over the past three years has been substantially diluted in the last hours,” Nicole van Rooijen, executive director at Stop Killer Robots, told Reuters.
The member states of the Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons had been meeting this week in the Swiss city of Geneva and reached consensus overnight.
The agreement comes as alarm grows over the use of lethal autonomous weapons systems in conflicts, including those in Ukraine, Sudan and the Middle East.
The document, reached by consensus, is non-binding but could open the door to formal treaty negotiations.
Talks went late into the night to overcome differences over language amid opposition from states such as the United States and Russia.
The US and Russia favour national guidelines over international legally binding rules.
Washington sought flexibility in the non-binding text, including in areas related to exercising human judgment. REUTERS
