Commentary: Trump's vanity arch is coming and it's no triumph for taxpayers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

Trump’s vanity arch is coming and it’s no triumph for taxpayers
-    Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
- Construction is set to begin on Trump’s 250-foot Great Triumphal Arch between the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington National Cemetery, a monument critics say would dominate key views of the capital.
- Estimated to cost up to $250 million from taxpayers and private donors, the arch would dwarf the Lincoln Memorial and even outsize Paris’ Arc de Triomphe.
- Veterans, local officials and preservationists are suing and sounding alarms over rushed approvals, missing safety reviews and what they see as a gaudy vanity project imposed on hallowed ground.
The president has called it an “arc.” Others, such as the rest of the English-speaking world, refer to it as an “arch.”
Whatever you choose to call Donald Trump’s latest vanity project, construction crews will soon break ground on the bigliest and most beautiful monument ever in the history of America, the Great Triumphal Arch.
Interior Secretary Doug Burgum made the announcement Thursday on social media:
“After a very long wait (over 125 years!), we are preparing to start, over the next two-week period, the excavation work necessary for Great Triumphal Arch and Military Observation Deck,” he wrote. “This will be one of the Great Pieces of American Architecture, honoring the history and significance of Arlington Cemetery and befitting the most powerful Capital in the World.”
Occupying the sacred space between Lincoln Memorial and Arlington National Cemetery, the Great Triumphal Arch will stand 250 feet tall, two and half times taller than Lincoln’s memorial and big enough to obscure views of the cemetery.
And because size matters, it will be nearly 90 feet taller than Paris’ Arc de Triomphe, which was built by order of Napoleon Bonaparte and dedicated to the soldiers who fought and won victories alongside him.
Trump has not fought in a war that involves actual combat, though he (and Israel) did start one. After six months, it’s still not clear why we’re there or who’s winning, so it’s unlikely that D.C.’s arch-to-be will be dedicated to our glorious victory over Iran.
When CBS News asked who the arch is for, Trump said, “Me.” He’s also said the reason he’s pushed to build the monument is because “something’s supposed to be here.” “They have 57 cities throughout the world that have them,” Trump said. “We’re the only ones that don’t.” He added that Washington has waited 200 years for the structure, adding 75 years to Burgum’s estimate.
Two hundred years is a long time to go without a gargantuan, costly arch in D.C.’s Memorial Circle. Americans are tough and have endured the hardship, and now, we’ll finally get our just deserts. The payoff is a vanity project like no other, except maybe Saddam Hussein’s commissioned Victory Arch of swords in Baghdad, or Kim Il Sung’s North Korean Mansu Hill Grand Monument.
The Great Triumphal Arch is estimated to cost at least $100 million, with some estimates reaching up to $250 million. A mix of taxpayer funds and private donations is expected to pay for the project, according to administration officials. The aim is to complete construction before the end of the presidential term, making it more difficult for incoming President Gavin Newsom or Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez to justify knocking it down.
The arch joins a list of Trump “beatification” projects. Most notable is the White House State Ballroom, which is currently being erected where the historic East Wing of the White House used to stand. Initially the administration said the ballroom would cost $200 million, none of which would come from taxpayers’ money. The Washington Post reported in June that the project would cost $600 million, with more than half coming from taxpayers.
If all of us pull together and work 60 hours a week, our taxed wages could help make Trump’s ballroom dream a reality before he terms out. And the Triumphant Arch won’t pay for itself, or Trump’s vision of topping it with a golden, winged Lady Liberty statue, flanked by two golden eagles. Don’t worry. There’s still time to look for a second job if you’re not making enough at your main gig to prop up The Arch.
Not everyone is happy with the fast-tracked building of a gargantuan monument to an unpopular president.
A group of Vietnam War veterans has sued to stop construction, citing the lack of congressional approval for the project and arguing that the arch would obstruct the view between the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington National Cemetery.
The Trump administration has said that it does not need congressional approval, pointing to a 1925 plan authorized by Congress to build columns close to the proposed arch site as proof that they don’t need further legislative oversight.
It’s also been reported that an FAA review of The Arch’s potential impact on flights has not been completed.
Representative Donald S. Beyer Jr., a Virginia Democrat whose district includes the nearby Arlington National Cemetery, said in a statement Thursday that Trump and Burgum were “disregarding the risks and rushing this towering monument to Trump’s vanity because they believe Republicans will get crushed in November.”
Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. famously said, “The arc of the moral universe is long, but it bends toward justice.” The arch is not long, but it’s expensive and intrusive, and it bends toward Trump’s vanity.

Everyman Economics: Why Growth Requires Measuring More than GDP
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

In its 250th year, America finds itself confronting an age-old question with new urgency: what, exactly, counts as progress? 1776 was a hinge year for the modern world. Adam Smith published The Wealth of Nations, America adopted the Declaration of Independence, and Matthew Boulton and James Watt commercialized the steam engine—three developments that unleashed an age of capitalism, bringing unprecedented growth and unprecedented inequality.
And while growth and inequality are often treated as separate stories, fetishized respectively by the right and the left, corporate America and labor unions, and Wall Street and Main Street, this November’s midterm elections will put them on a collision course. But they have always gone hand in hand, their fates inextricably intertwined.
America’s triumphs are real. The United States is still the world’s largest economy. It remains a global engine of innovation. Its stock market is booming thanks to artificial intelligence, while its capital markets remain the deepest and most powerful in the world. And despite tariffs, a labor market slowed by restrictive immigration and repeated energy price shocks, its growth—as attested to by its $32.3 trillion GDP, larger than China, India, and Germany combined—appears to defy the odds and remains resilient.
Yet this dynamism is only half the story. Affordability has become the defining issue of the moment, and many signs indicate that the midterms in November will be decided on that basis. The Pew Research Center has found that the voters place the economy front and center by a wide margin, even as only 24% of Americans describe it as “good” or “excellent.” Gallup, meanwhile, reports that voters identify the cost of living as their foremost concern in the election.
GDP, the single statistic that now determines a country’s economic might, traces its roots to the scholarship of the American economist Simon Kuznets during the Great Depression, particularly his landmark 1934 report, National Income, 1929-1932. But as the Cambridge economist Diane Coyle points out, Kuznets was, himself, aware of the many flaws and pitfalls of the metric he had developed and warned against confusing economic output with human welfare.
What even fewer people know is that the “godfather” of GDP was also a pioneer in the study of inequality. The Kuznets curve—his famous prediction that inequality would eventually decline as economies grew richer—is not one history has obliged, but it points to the Janus-headed quality of modern capitalism.
Indeed, it’s been exactly 15 years since the Occupy Wall Street protests radiated out of Zuccotti Park in New York’s Financial District. Born in the aftermath of the Great Recession of 2008, the movement became the most visible public outcry against economic inequality in recent American history and gave the country an enduring rallying cry: “We are the 99%.”
While the movement dissipated, the issues it raised have not. If anything, the concerns it foregrounded have migrated from the political margins to the mainstream in American politics, championed by progressive figures like Bernie Sanders, Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, and Zohran Mamdani.
The World Inequality Report 2026 finds that the top 0.001% of the globe’s population own “three times more wealth” than the entire bottom half of humanity combined, and within “almost every region, the top 1% alone” hold more wealth than the bottom 90% combined. Inequality in America is no longer only a question of who has more; increasingly, it is a question of who has enough to make ends meet. According to the Brookings Institution, 45.5% of American households do not earn enough to cover even basic necessities, with housing, health care, and childcare among the most acute pressures.
The problem is that a single statistic can conceal as much as it reveals. GDP can tell us how the economy is performing without telling us how Americans are faring. It can tell us how much an economy produces, but not who receives the rewards, whether those gains improve people’s lives, or what is destroyed and what is sacrificed in producing them.
Some of the things on which society most depends—unpaid caregiving, clean air, cohesive communities—barely register in its accounts. Economists classify many of these costs as “externalities”: consequences borne by people and places that fall outside the transaction being measured.
Climate change provides perhaps the starkest example of GDP’s glaring blind spots. A natural disaster can destroy homes, lives, and ecosystems without being registered as an equivalent loss in GDP; the money spent to rebuild afterward, meanwhile, counts as additional economic activity. The meter can rise even as human welfare falls.
But the two metrics—GDP, our shorthand for growth, and the Gini coefficient, our shorthand for inequality—are not rival ways of describing the economy so much as incomplete halves of the same story; the two key consequences of capitalism, joined at the hip. One shows us how large the pie has grown; the other, something about how it has been sliced.
On growth and inequality
When it comes to growing the pie, the relentless efficiency of global capitalism in allocating resources is hard to match. It has allowed, in the aggregate, societies to eke out more from finite resources than ever before. Its advocates point out that most people live longer and better lives: they are better fed, more securely housed, and better protected against diseases that once routinely killed them.
Capitalism’s champions can reasonably claim that it has helped lift much of humanity above bare subsistence while proving more compatible with individual freedom than its major rivals. It holds out the promise of a game that everyone has an equal chance to play—and win. Its defenders often invoke the specter of repression and unfreedom associated with state-led communism or socialism as a cautionary tale.
Capitalism’s unique two-plus-two-equals-five quality—its capacity to produce more than the sum of its parts—may also have helped pave the way for the material foundations of modernity. The shift from sustenance to surplus created, in many ways, the foundations for our moral revolutions, from liberalism and feminism to cosmopolitanism.
Yet, beyond some vague gestures toward “trickle-down economics,” the discipline’s approach has largely been to focus on growing the pie and argue about slicing it later. Economics has tried to separate the two: markets create wealth; politics distributes it. Friedrich von Hayek, the Nobel Prize-winning economist, who was an early and influential proponent of free-market economics, warned against the “fatal conceit” that governments could know enough to design an economic order from above.
The Kaldor–Hicks principle, a dominant idea in modern economics, offered a technical basis for avoiding the reckoning with distributive questions. An outcome counts as an improvement if the winners gain enough that they could compensate the losers—even if they never do. That “even if” is a significant caveat.
Kenneth Arrow’s Impossibility Theorem, another foundational result in economics, exposes the deeper difficulty: there is no perfect mathematical procedure for turning individual preferences into a coherent collective choice. At some point, as even mainstream economists recognize, economic calculation must give way to political judgment. It follows that morality should trump mathematics.
But what if inequality is baked into the pie itself? Thomas Piketty coined the famous formulation for the notion that the odds may be stacked against the ordinary person: r > g, the proposition that the return on capital tends to exceed the rate of economic growth. History suggests that the playing field was never level.
In Empire of Cotton and, now, Capitalism, Sven Beckert excavates the blood-soaked origins of modern capitalism through slavery, colonialism, and state power; Ha-Joon Chang shows how rich countries used tariffs and industrial policy before prescribing freer markets to poorer ones. Such empirical evidence reinforces a broader idea: markets do not simply materialize, as the spectral metaphor of the “invisible hand” suggests. Markets are made—by human hands.
If the economy is a game, then the question is not merely who wins and who loses. The question instead is: Who designed the board, who wrote the rules, and whether the game was rigged from the start? Today, capitalism treats Monopoly money as real while human beings are reduced to pieces on a chessboard.
Perhaps the most important omission from the current economic paradigm concerns the psychology of the sport. Research on “inequality aversion,” the idea that who gets what matters as much as how much there is, suggests that people care deeply about how the pie is sliced, even when a fairer division means settling for a slightly smaller one.
The economics of the everyman
Can growth, given enough time, deliver widely shared prosperity, as capitalism’s champions still insist? Or does the way the game is designed predetermine who benefits from growth? Far from disappearing, could excessive inequality gnaw away at the very foundations of economic growth?
GDP’s shortcomings have inspired repeated attempts to devise a better answer. In Mismeasuring Our Lives, Joseph Stiglitz, Amartya Sen, and Jean-Paul Fitoussi argued for moving beyond economic production and measuring well-being, distribution, and sustainability. Sen’s capabilities approach asks a still more fundamental question: not merely what resources people possess, but what those resources actually enable them to be and to do.
The late Pakistani economist Mahbub ul Haq’s Human Development Index, inspired in part by Sen’s work, was an attempt to translate that insight into numbers, treating health, education, and income as measures of human progress.
The point is not to dispense with GDP. Growth matters enormously. It has financed scientific discovery, lengthened lives, reduced material deprivation, and expanded the range of human possibility. But human progress may be better represented by a dashboard of indicators rather than by a single number. More fundamentally, what should be a means to an end has too often become an end in itself. A metric intended to crudely measure the output of the market economy has gradually acquired the authority to tell us whether society itself is succeeding.
America’s 250th anniversary offers an unusually apt moment to question that bargain. The Declaration of Independence did not promise Americans the pursuit of economic growth. It promised something considerably more ambitious: the pursuit of happiness. Two and a half centuries later, perhaps the most important economic question America can ask is also the simplest: Who is the economy for?
Fittingly, this fall, American voters will have an opportunity to offer their answer. If the elections of the past decade were won in part by rejecting an outdated economic playbook, 2026 may present a more constructive opportunity: not merely to discard the economic playbook, but to redesign and rewrite it with Everyman, the ordinary American, as its protagonist.
Adapted with permission from Everyman: The Untold Story of Economics by Antara Haldar.

Sweetening the new year: How Jewish food becomes family tradition - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
09:58:48 UTC
18:58:48 KST

What makes Jewish food Jewish?
“Not food Jews eat,” said the late Gil Marks in an interview about his monumental Encyclopedia of Jewish Food in 2010.
After all, he pointed out, contemporary Ashkenazi Jews probably eat more salsa and sushi than schmaltz. Jewish food, he said, is food that “almost becomes sanctified by its use in Jewish life.”
Marks, a rabbi, historian, and extraordinary repository of culinary knowledge, was born in West Virginia and died, far too young, in Jerusalem in 2014.
His words came back to me as I began going through my food lists and recipes, stained from years of cooking in preparation for Rosh Hashanah.
What are the foods that have become sanctified in our family?
Tradition, with room for change
The main courses have remained fairly constant over the years. We have also adopted many of the Rosh Hashanah simanim, symbolic foods long associated with Sephardi and Mizrahi holiday tables. Their Hebrew and Aramaic names become puns for our hopes for the coming year. We eat beets, selek, while expressing the hope that our enemies will be removed, and leeks, karti, with a prayer that those who hate us will be cut off.
Those ancient puns require little explanation at an Israeli Rosh Hashanah table.
But what about dessert?
Where I grew up in Colchester, Connecticut, my aunt made teiglach, those little knots of dough boiled in honey. In my early married years, I made them, too. Mine came out more like fossils. So teiglach disappeared from our family menu.
Honey cake, ubiquitous in Israel and with a history that goes back nearly a thousand years in Jewish sources, seemed the obvious replacement. There was only one problem. I didn’t like honey cake.
For a while, I moved on to a complicated honey cake recipe that a dear friend had published in The Boston Globe. It had chopped apples and nuts and a glaze and required considerable time and attention.
Eventually I passed the recipe on to the next generation, asking our children and grandchildren to make it. Their verdict was that it wasn’t worth the effort. None of us really liked honey cake that much.
This brought me back to another cake of my Connecticut childhood: babka. Babka has become fashionable in recent years, but it was a holiday staple in Colchester, a small Connecticut town of about 5,000 residents.
We had something unusual for such a small town: the famous Colchester Bakery, owned by Walter and Mary Gadle, of Lithuanian heritage. They weren’t Jewish, but the bakery stood next to our synagogue and had rabbinical supervision. Its baked goods became part of Jewish communal life, the default choice for every kiddush.
A green loaf of Colchester rye was presented to the governor of Connecticut for St. Patrick’s Day. Adm. Hyman G. Rickover, father of America’s nuclear navy, was reportedly such a fan that he once made a 3 a.m. request for bread from the bakery to be brought to him at the submarine base in Groton.
The Gadles shaped my lifelong taste in pastry. And among their pastries was babka, cinnamon babka with raisins.
Making room for a new babka
MARKS TRACED Jewish babka to Eastern Europe in the early 19th century. Housewives used extra challah dough, rolled it out, and filled it with ingredients such as cinnamon, jam, or honey.
Jewish bakers used oil rather than butter, keeping the cake parve so that it could be eaten after a meat meal. The dough was less rich than that of some non-Jewish versions, making the swirls of filling and the crumb topping particularly important.
Chocolate came later, largely an American Jewish contribution. I remember very clearly when chocolate babka entered my life.
I was 17 and had just returned from a Young Judaea summer in Israel. I stayed overnight with a fellow Young Judaean who lived in New Jersey. Her father was a baker, and in honor of his daughter’s return he had prepared an enormous chocolate babka.
I had never tasted anything like it. It was a revelation. My favorite cake ever.
Decades later, babka would acquire another kind of fame when Jerry Seinfeld and Elaine Benes went to a bakery to buy a chocolate babka for a dinner party, only to discover that another couple had taken the last one. Forced to settle for cinnamon, Elaine protested that it was the “lesser babka.” Seinfeld insisted that cinnamon “takes a back seat to no babka.”
I am unwilling to take sides.
This year, as Rosh Hashanah approached, I found myself talking babka with Robin and Yussie Chait, the owners of Emmer & Cane, an artisan bakery they run in Ramat Beit Shemesh.
When I first saw the name Emmer & Cane, I thought it sounded rather like an elegant English company with a royal warrant. The explanation is simpler. Emmer is an ancient form of wheat. Cane is sugar.
Montreal-born Robin and American-born Yussie both came from business backgrounds. During the pandemic, Robin began perfecting sourdough baking at home. Eventually the couple, parents of six, decided to create a bakery specializing in baked goods that North American immigrants long for.
There are English muffins. And, importantly for me, there is babka.
“The dough shouldn’t be sweet, but the creamy inside is plentiful, and the crumble tops it off,” Robin says. “A perfect comfort food.”
Babka is a diminutive of baba, grandmother or old woman in Slavic languages, a cousin of the Yiddish bubbe. The older, tall, fluted Eastern European cakes bearing the name were said to resemble the pleated skirts worn by grandmothers.
As a grandmother myself, I like that. But I also think grandmothers are allowed to edit tradition.
We’re going to skip the foods no one actually likes. We can borrow customs from Jews whose ancestors lived in different countries from ours. Our children and grandchildren can add something new.
So this year, I’ve ordered three babkas: cinnamon, chocolate, and Emmer & Cane’s Cookie Dough Babka.
The first two have history. The third? I haven’t tasted it yet. Maybe that’s the one for the grandchildren.
Shana Tova. May it be a sweet one.■
The writer is the Israel director of public relations at Hadassah, the Women’s Zionist Organization of America. Her latest book is A Daughter of Many Mothers, co-written with Holocaust survivor and premier English-language witness Rena Quint.

Former NSC chief Eiland warns Israel’s diplomatic approach is harming vital interests
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
09:58:43 UTC
18:58:43 KST

Former National Security Council chief Maj.-Gen. (res.) Giora Eiland warned that Israel is facing a difficult diplomatic situation, saying world leaders lack trust in the government and that its conduct is pushing countries away and could harm vital interests, during a Thursday interview with 103FM's Roni Bar-On and Aryeh Eldad.
Eiland, a former head of the IDF Operations Directorate and former head of the Planning Directorate, said Israel’s diplomatic challenges stem partly from a lack of trust among world leaders toward the government.
He argued that statements made by government officials, combined with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s silence on them, have shaped international perceptions of Israel’s policies.
"I agree that our diplomatic situation is problematic in almost every arena, including with the US," Eiland said. "A process of trying to align positions is needed here. One of Israel’s problems is that most world leaders simply do not believe the Israeli government on the one hand. On the other hand, they listen very clearly and loudly to what people like Smotrich and Ben-Gvir say. They assume Netanyahu’s silence reflects the true policy of the Israeli government, and there is a lot of criticism over this."
Eiland also criticized what he described as Israel’s confrontational approach toward the international community, warning that the country’s conduct is pushing allies and other countries away.
"I think this entire conduct is stupid, childish and dangerous," Eiland said, arguing that Israel should focus on dialogue and presenting its arguments rather than trying to prove it is right and others are wrong. "But when the approach is confrontational, condescending and forceful on every issue, the world moves away from us, and that is dangerous." He added that he agrees with former prime minister Naftali Bennett that Israel needs to "listen and conduct different dialogues."
Eiland urges Israel to distinguish between core interests, compromises
Eiland also addressed the need for Israel to prioritize its interests, arguing that the government should distinguish between issues that are vital and those where compromise is possible.
"Clearly there are interests, but even when it comes to interests, you have to prioritize your own," Eiland said. He pointed to Gaza and the West Bank as examples, saying Israel must remain firm on core security issues in Gaza, while addressing issues in Judea and Samaria that he said harm Israel’s international standing.
Regarding the West Bank, Eiland criticized illegal activity by Jewish extremist settlers against Palestinians, which he said is documented by foreign reporters and perceived as the Israeli government "implicitly turning a blind eye," leading to international criticism.
"Instead of being in a position where you correct things in places that do not contradict your interests, you act in the opposite way, and as a result you erode vital interests that are the exact opposite of that," he explained.
Israel can still influence global opinion through dialogue
Eiland said Israel can still influence international opinion on disputed issues if it presents its arguments clearly and approaches discussions with a willingness to engage.
"You can convince many people, even on issues that seem far from the approach or interests of the other side, provided that you come with clean intentions and with genuinely security-based arguments," he said, adding that such efforts cannot be achieved "through slogans or wild attacks in the media."
Eiland concluded that the international community expects Israel to communicate openly and acknowledge mistakes when necessary. "The main thing the world expects is that we speak honestly, that we do not lie, that we present the real arguments and that we sometimes admit mistakes and change things," he said.

The second year: Anticipating the Jewish High Holidays after experiencing grief and loss
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
09:58:20 UTC
18:58:20 KST

While this is not a column about the life of a two-year-old, but rather about my second year of widowhood and the upcoming holidays, there are, indeed, many similarities. As many readers may remember, my husband passed away suddenly last August. At times, the loss feels very recent; at other times, it feels like it was forever ago. I barely remember last year’s holidays. This year will be different.
I tell myself that while my husband is no longer physically present, and I now run the show solo on the ground, he is very much with me in my thoughts and actions. In a strange way, this gives me comfort. After being together for 47 years, how can I not hear his voice and know almost word for word what he might say at any given time?
Some days are easier than others, and thankfully, while occurring infrequently, there are times when I feel angry, sad, mad, frustrated, and a host of other less positive feelings. I know that, too, is okay.
I don’t ask “why,” because that would not be helpful at all. Typically, I ask “what.” What takes me forward and away from “stuckness” or a “poor me” moment? It’s often the small things that can feel big. Life is different now, and if I want to be okay, my job is to adapt.
Initially, after a loss, we may be somewhat naive and feel numb as we stumble our way through the many “firsts.” The focus is often on survival and getting through the day. That may be more difficult than we ever could have imagined. The second year is different, and if in no other way, it’s no longer a year of firsts and therefore fewer things are new. That said, as the shock wears off, reality moves in.
Now, as we toddle into the second year, with both curiosity and apprehension, we want to believe that this year will be easier. We may be surprised to discover that in many ways it is, but in some ways it is not. Often, we don’t know when it will be difficult until we feel teary and the wave of sadness washes over us unexpectedly. After all, our new reality – with its knowledge of “forever” and “finality” – is not an easy part of the adjustment process.
When my colleague Gina Junger and I recently participated in a book launch for our new book (The Jewish Journey through Loss: From Death to Healing), the rabbi interviewing us commented that he was impressed it went beyond the first year, which was an unusual bonus. In fact, many people think that grieving should last about six weeks; you move on, and all is okay.
We pointed out that while the “official” mourning period (avelut) in Judaism ends at a year, one may grieve in their own way forever. Judaism, in its wisdom, acknowledges this as well, offering an opportunity to recite the Yizkor prayer for the deceased several times a year and to mark the yahrzeit (anniversary of a death) annually.
This, too, is very much in sync with the psychological stages of loss, since one’s grief changes over time, but often remains in the background or foreground for a very long time. Not including a discussion about the healing process and how to cope beyond the first year does a huge disservice to anyone who grieves for someone they love.
Imagine someone who had major open-heart surgery. Even if he has made an excellent recovery, a scar will remain. Likewise, we heal after a loss, but our emotional scar remains. When we lose someone we love deeply, they remain forever in our heart. We heal and grow around our grief, and we take our departed loved ones with us as we go on.
Handling the holidays: Memories of the past
Now, with the holidays upon us again, as we have described in our book (pp. 187-190), those who have lost a loved one may feel the loss even greater.
The holidays always bring up memories of past celebrations, as we see the empty seat around the family table, or feel our loved one’s absence in the synagogue. Now they will forever be missed.
You may experience an upsurge in grief at this time, even years later. They may last for a short period, but in anticipation of these events, more likely several days. This may not feel good, but it is normal.
During the first year of mourning, you may have felt distanced or in shock; now, too, during the second year and beyond, you may find yourself absorbing the words of prayer differently. You may feel that you are backsliding if these waves of grief wash over you, but in reality, you are just more aware of the loss of your loved one.
While those who have been through this know that it will get better again, you will breathe a sigh of relief when these events are over, and life seems to settle down once again.
Considering that the Jewish calendar has so many holidays, it may seem as if a death often falls around or between them. The holidays are a stark reminder of your loved ones’ absence and pose many challenges. Remember that regarding holiday preparations, which are often overwhelming and anxiety-producing, you can choose what you would and would not like to do.
You may want to delegate some of the planning or cooking, or it might be very important to you that you be involved in every small detail. While holidays can be exciting, they are also exhausting and probably will be more so this year than in the past.
Your goal may be to simply get past them. You may worry about how you will cope, and each decision may feel weighty, but you must do what’s right for you. Often, the dread and anticipation are worse than the actual event.
Change, in itself, may feel scary, but it can make things easier, too. You may not know just how you will feel about anything; the things that you think may concern you won’t, and those things that you least expect may affect you more than you might have imagined.
As the holidays approach, just as in your daily life, you may feel as if you are simply going through the motions, so it is not surprising that you feel quite unsettled. This is all part of the grief process. There is no right or wrong way. It just is, and that, in itself, may feel difficult.
You may face the challenge of separating the “how you are feeling” from the “what you are doing” with respect to holiday observance. Give yourself permission to take things one step at a time.
In a strange way, during the height of the Second Intifada, my husband unknowingly helped prepare me for his permanent absence. Having recently made aliyah, and fearful that he might lose his job here, and with Canada literally continuing to beg him to create and develop the medical genetics department in the major teaching hospital he had left, my husband began commuting back and forth to Canada.
Although we spoke at least once or twice a day, more than most couples do, I learned to live between trips without his physical presence. When we were together, we were inseparable. Little did we fully appreciate then just how short life can be.
Before and after: Appreciating the gifts in life 'afterward'
Along with the sense of sadness – that now I am unlikely to travel in the same way, and do many of the things my husband and I did together; finding it hard to imagine we have two new grandchildren he never got to meet; and armed with so many things on my imaginary very long list that I would love to be able to share – I recognize that life is different now. There was life before his death, and now there is life afterward.
That said, I’m trying more than ever to appreciate the many gifts I am blessed with on a daily basis, the people who have been so incredibly supportive, and simply the life around me. I take nothing for granted. Life is short, and now, more than ever, as the holidays approach, it is important to let your loved ones know just how important they are to you.
Wishing you a Shana Tova. May we all be inscribed for a year filled with good health, compassion, and strength.■
The writer is a licensed clinical psychologist in private practice in Ra’anana and co-author of the book The Jewish Journey through Loss: From Death to Healing (Koren Publishers). She has written about psychology in The Jerusalem Post since 2000 and specializes in trauma and bereavement. batyaludman@gmail.com, drbatyaludman.com

In the kitchen with Henny: Sweetness in every course
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
09:58:09 UTC
18:58:09 KST

Rosh Hashanah marks a new beginning for all of us, but for me, it also marks the start of my career as a kitchen coach.
Back in 2020, after months of quarantine, my daughter finally started first grade. That first day she went back to school, I sat down at my computer to plan our Rosh Hashanah menus and thought, maybe I can share these ideas and recipes with others.
The name “In the Kitchen with Henny” popped into my head; I put together a simple PDF for friends and family, and a new chapter began.
Ever since then, Rosh Hashanah has felt even more special to me. It reminds me how something small can turn into something you never expected, which somehow feels very fitting for the start of a new year.
I love that we can incorporate the simanim into the meal itself, using these traditional symbolic foods throughout. So I worked them into simple, festive dishes, using honey, silan, pomegranate, apples, and other familiar Rosh Hashanah flavors. Nothing complicated, just food that feels special and lets you enjoy the sweetness of the simanim from the first bite to the last spoonful.
Honey-orange salmon bites
By the time we fill our plates with sweet challah, apples, and honey, dates, pomegranate, and all the other simanim, there is already a lot going on. I love the idea of adding fish in a way that doesn’t turn it into a whole extra course.
These bite-sized salmon pieces make it easy for everyone to have a taste, while the honey-orange glaze keeps them festive and right at home on the Rosh Hashanah table.
Yields 6-8 servings, as a starter or siman
600 gr. skinless salmon fillet, cut into 5-6 cm. cubes
2 Tbsp. honey
3 Tbsp. fresh orange juice
1 Tbsp. grated orange zest
2 Tbsp. olive oil
2 garlic cloves, crushed
½ tsp. salt
¼ tsp. black pepper
Pomegranate seeds, fresh parsley, and orange slices for garnish 
In a bowl, whisk together the honey, orange juice, olive oil, garlic, salt, pepper, and orange zest. Add the salmon cubes and gently toss until well coated. Let marinate in the refrigerator for 20-30 minutes.
Arrange the salmon in a single layer on a baking-paper-lined pan and pour any remaining marinade over the top. Bake at 200°C / 400°F for 10-12 minutes, or until the salmon is just cooked through and lightly glazed. Transfer to a serving platter and garnish with pomegranate seeds, chopped parsley, and a few orange slices. Chill until serving.
Silan-roasted carrots & squash
By now, you’ve probably noticed how much I love cooking with – and eating – zucchini. So when I came across a version of this dish made with just carrots and butternut squash, which honestly is delicious enough on its own, I had to try adding zucchini.
I love the extra flavor, and especially the pop of green it brings to the platter. Best of all, the oven and silan do all the work, caramelizing the vegetables beautifully without you having to stand over a pan to sauté them. Serve them as is, or spoon them over warm brown rice for a more substantial side.
Yields 6 servings
4 large carrots, peeled and cut into thick diagonal slices
1 small butternut squash, peeled and cut into 3-4 cm. cubes
2 medium zucchini, cut into thick half-moons
8-10 garlic cloves, peeled
3 Tbsp. olive oil
2 Tbsp. silan
1 Tbsp. lemon juice
½ tsp. salt
¼ tsp. black pepper
2 Tbsp. chopped fresh parsley, for garnish
6 Medjool dates, pitted and chopped, for garnish 
Preheat the oven to 200°C / 400°F. In a small bowl, whisk together the olive oil, silan, lemon juice, salt, and pepper. Place the carrots, butternut squash, and garlic in a large baking pan. Pour about two-thirds of the marinade over the vegetables and toss well to coat. Roast for 25 minutes.
Meanwhile, toss the zucchini with the remaining marinade. Add the zucchini to the pan and gently mix with the other vegetables. Return to the oven and roast for another 15 minutes, or until the vegetables are tender and caramelized. Transfer to a serving platter and scatter the chopped dates and parsley over the top. Serve warm or at room temperature.
Sweet & shallot chicken
I like to have two different mains available when we’re hosting a large crowd, which is usually the case for the first night of Rosh Hashanah. So I was on the lookout for a chicken dish that looked and tasted a little different.
I love the idea of roasting lots of whole shallots alongside the chicken. They become soft and caramelized, and add a rich flavor that balances the sweet and tart glaze.
Although this recipe is written for chicken, the marinade would also work beautifully with brisket or short ribs, just allowing for a longer, slower cooking time.
Yields 6-8 servings
8-10 bone-in chicken thighs or a mix of thighs and drumsticks
10-12 small shallots, peeled and left whole
3 Tbsp. pomegranate molasses
2 Tbsp. honey
3 Tbsp. olive oil
3 garlic cloves, crushed
1 tsp. salt
½ tsp. black pepper
½ tsp. paprika
Pomegranate seeds and chopped parsley, for garnish 
Preheat the oven to 160°C / 325°F. Line a baking pan with baking paper. Arrange the chicken in the pan, pour the marinade over the top, and tuck the whole shallots around the chicken. Place a sheet of wet baking paper directly over the chicken, then cover the pan tightly with foil to seal. Bake for 1½ hours.
Raise the oven to 175°C / 350°F, remove the foil and baking paper, and bake uncovered for another 30 minutes, until the chicken is browned and the sauce is glossy and caramelized. Transfer to a serving platter and garnish with pomegranate seeds and parsley.
Apple-honey upside-down layer cake
A few years back, I shared my Bubby’s delicious honey cake recipe. It’s a no-fail, perfectly delicious honey cake, and one I come back to every year.
When I saw the idea of an upside-down apple-honey cake, I knew her recipe would be perfect for it. Since the apples add more volume to the pan than usual, I scaled the recipe down to about two-thirds so it bakes nicely in a 9-inch round springform pan.
And while Rosh Hashanah is not usually the holiday when we like to turn things upside down, maybe there is something fitting about it as we start a new year. We all have things in our lives we would love to see turn around for the better, and there is something especially sweet about watching that apple-honey layer on the bottom become the beautiful top of the cake.
Yields 1 - 9” round springform pan
3 medium apples, peeled, cored, and thinly sliced
3 Tbsp. honey
2 Tbsp. brown sugar
½ tsp. cinnamon
Cake batter:
3 eggs
½ cup sugar
²⁄³ cup oil
1 cup honey
2 cups flour
2 tsp. baking powder
½ tsp. baking soda
²⁄³  cup cold strong coffee
½ tsp. cinnamon
¼ tsp. nutmeg
Preheat the oven to 190°C / 375°F. Line the bottom of a deep 9-inch round springform pan with baking paper, then grease the baking paper and the sides of the pan well. Drizzle the honey over the bottom of the pan, then sprinkle with the brown sugar and cinnamon. Arrange the apple slices on top in a circular pattern, slightly overlapping. Bake for 8–10 minutes, until the apples begin to soften and caramelize.
In a mixing bowl, beat the eggs and sugar until combined. Add the remaining ingredients, alternating between the dry and wet ingredients, and mix until smooth. Gently pour the batter over the apples.
While the apples are baking, prepare the cake batter. In a mixing bowl, beat the eggs and sugar until combined. Add the remaining ingredients, alternating between the dry and wet ingredients, and mix until smooth.
Remove the caramelized apple layer from the oven and carefully pour the cake batter over the apples. Return the pan to the oven and bake at 190°C / 375°F for 35–45 minutes, or until a toothpick inserted in the center comes out clean.
Let the cake cool in the pan for 15–20 minutes. Run a knife around the sides, release the springform, then carefully invert the cake onto a serving plate and remove the baking paper.
Enjoying simanim throughout the meal
FROM THE first bite to the last spoonful, these recipes let us enjoy the simanim throughout the meal, not just at the beginning. And maybe that is something we can carry beyond the table, too.
As we begin a new year, may all the sweetness we eat inspire us to bring a little more sweetness into our homes, our families, and our communities. May we be kinder to one another, more united, and more aware of how much we need each other.
And especially here in Israel, may this be a year of peace, healing, and good news, with our soldiers safely home with their families, and a year in which we have so much more to celebrate together.
Shana tova u’metuka! ■
The writer is a kitchen coach who teaches women how to meal plan and cook, so they get dinner on the table and prepare for Shabbat and chag on time. Learn more about one-on-one coaching and food workshops: www.inthekitchenwithhenny.com

Why is Trump threatening to strike Iran’s Pickaxe Mountain again, now?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
09:56:53 UTC
18:56:53 KST

Why is Trump threatening to strike Iran’s Pickaxe Mountain again, now?
As oil tanker struck off Kharg island, Trump threatens one of the remaining parts of Iran’s nuclear complex.
United States President Donald Trump says Washington may strike Iran’s Pickaxe Mountain “very soon”, in just the latest in a series of threats he has made against the heavily fortified underground site located next to the bombed-out Natanz enrichment complex.
Just hours after he made that threat, an Iranian oil tanker off Kharg Island was struck by four US missiles, according to Iranian news outlet Khabar Fouri. Kharg Island is the main hub for Iran’s oil exports, handling about 90 percent.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Iran war: Why US midterms could be a pivotal moment
- list 2 of 4South Korea mulls ‘contributions’ in Strait of Hormuz
- list 3 of 4Diesel price hits all-time high in US amid Iran war woes
- list 4 of 4US imposes sanctions on Turkish bank, prompting legal threat
Trump made the threat against Pickaxe Mountain as he was speaking to reporters in the Oval Office on Friday, saying the US knows “everybody that’s moving at Pickaxe” and across Iran.
His remarks echoed a similar threat he made back in mid-July, when he stated on the Hugh Hewitt Show: “We’re going to take out Pickaxe Mountain. Tell the Iranians to be ready … We’ll probably give Pickaxe a shot relatively soon.”
The latest threat comes more than six months into the war that the US and Israel launched on Iran on February 28, amid mixed messages about the war from the Trump administration.
On Friday, Trump sought to downplay the war in Iran, calling it “small potatoes”, while a day earlier, at a White House news briefing, Vice President JD Vance appeared to suggest the conflict had cooled and to shrug off an alleged US strike on a wedding in southern Iran with “sometimes things happen“.
At a White House briefing this week, Vance said of the conflict with Iran that he “wouldn’t call it a war” and claimed there was “no active shooting right now”.
But the US and Iran have exchanged attacks this week, including a US hit close to Iran’s oil infrastructure on Kharg Island.
Meanwhile, talks related to Iran’s nuclear programme have remained in limbo since a 60-day negotiating window expired in mid-August without a deal.
Iran says it is not undertaking any work at the Natanz nuclear site.
Its Khatam al-Anbiya central military headquarters has warned that bombing the nearby mountain would amount to a renewal of war across the region, at a time when the Trump administration would prefer to keep the war contained before pivotal mid-term elections.
So why has Pickaxe Mountain become the latest focus of Trump’s threats – again?
What is Pickaxe Mountain?
Known in Iran as Kuh-e Kolang Gaz La, the site sits roughly 220km (140 miles) south of the capital Tehran, in Isfahan province, and just 2km (1.2 miles) from the Natanz enrichment plant.
US intelligence reports indicate that the facility has been excavated deep inside the mountain, beneath hundreds of metres of solid granite rock, to protect it from powerful bombs designed to penetrate bunkers.
The main chambers are thought to lie at least 100 metres (330ft) underground.
Some Western analysts have speculated that the mountain was intended to house an undeclared enrichment plant, a hedge against attacks on Iran’s known facilities.
The Institute for Science and International Security, which tracks the site by satellite, has assessed that it is still under construction and not yet operational.
However, Iran has always maintained that it is developing a nuclear power programme only, and does not have plans to build a nuclear weapon.
Why does Pickaxe Mountain matter?
Because it is intact.
Pickaxe Mountain was left alone during the US’s June 2025 strikes on Fordow, Natanz and Isfahan at the end of the 12-day Israel war on Iran, and has escaped the current war almost entirely; the Institute for Science and International Security has recorded only the destruction of a vehicle on a nearby spoil pile.
With Iran’s centrifuge manufacturing base and enrichment halls at other sites damaged in the war, analysts see the tunnels as the most obvious place for Tehran to rebuild: For component production, assembly or enrichment of uranium.
The Wall Street Journal reported in July that Israel had passed Washington intelligence suggesting thousands of centrifuges had been moved inside the facility late last year, a claim the US has not confirmed.
Trump has been less alarmist than Israel.
Centrifuges only matter if there is uranium to put through them; the machines concentrate uranium gas, and without a supply of it they cannot produce anything.
How much damage has been done to Iran’s nuclear sites?
According to most estimates, a considerable amount.
The European Council on Foreign Relations estimates that the 2025 strikes likely destroyed many of the roughly 18,000 centrifuges then operating at Iran’s Natanz and Fordow facilities, along with several centrifuge production sites and Ardakan, Iran’s only yellowcake milling plant. Yellowcake is powdered uranium concentrate obtained from milled uranium ore.
Nearly 4,000 additional centrifuges were installed but idle at the time; however, they may have survived the strikes.
The International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) confirmed further damage to the entrance buildings of Natanz’s underground enrichment plant in March 2026, although it detected no additional impact on the plant itself.
The Institute for Science and International Security reported in June that tunnel entrances at all three main sites remain sealed, that there is no evidence of any enrichment taking place, and that the centrifuge programme still appears to have been destroyed.
Didn’t Trump say Iran’s nuclear sites had already been destroyed?
Yes. After the June 2025 attacks, Trump said the three sites had been “completely and totally obliterated”.
However, just days later, a leaked preliminary US Defence Intelligence Agency assessment concluded that the sites had been significantly damaged but not destroyed, estimating that the strikes had set Iran’s nuclear programme back by less than six months.
The situation today remains unclear.
“No one really knows what the state of Iran’s nuclear programme is at this moment; there’s a lot of uncertainty and ambiguity about how much damage Iran has suffered as a result of these last two wars,” Nader Hashemi, a professor of Middle East politics at Georgetown University, told Al Jazeera.
Iran is currently believed to be holding about 440kg (970lb) of uranium enriched to 60 percent.
But having the material is only part of the equation, Hashemi said.
In order for Iran to produce a nuclear weapon, it would have to enrich that uranium up to 90 percent.
That would require access to its centrifuges, “of which we don’t know to what extent they may have been damaged”, he said.
No inspector has entered the bombed sites, and Trump’s framing has shifted from “obliteration” to a promise to hit any site where Iran is “even thinking about nuclear”.
What do we know about Iran’s nuclear programme?
Less than at any point in two decades.
Just before the US-Israel attacks on Iran in June 2025, the IAEA verified about 10 tonnes of enriched uranium in total, including the 440kg stockpile enriched to 60 percent.
In theory, this amount of enriched uranium – should it be enriched to 90 percent – is enough to produce more than 10 nuclear warheads, IAEA chief Rafael Grossi told Al Jazeera in early March. It is unclear where this stock may be, however.
Iran suspended cooperation with the agency after the strikes, and the IAEA now says it has no way to report on the size, location or composition of that stockpile, though it believes much of the 60-percent material is bottled up in tunnels at Isfahan.
On Friday, Trump claimed again that the US had prevented Iran from developing a nuclear weapon, arguing that Washington’s intervention had protected Israel and the wider Middle East.
Tehran insists the programme is peaceful, and has dismissed Washington’s focus on Pickaxe Mountain as a manufactured pretext for attacking it.

Breaking: US envoys Witkoff, Kushner arrive in Ukraine for the first time to discuss peace talks, sources say
Editor's note: This is a developing story and is being updated.
U.S. President Donald Trump's envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner arrived in Ukraine on Sept. 6 as part of Washington's diplomatic effort to end the Russia-Ukraine war, people familiar with the matter told the Kyiv Independent.
The arrival came only a day after the two envoys held more than three hours of talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow, a discussion both sides described as "substantive."
"We are interested in bringing the end of the war closer," President Volodymyr Zelensky said on X after meeting top Ukrainian officials ahead of the envoys' visit.
"Peace is needed. Security guarantees are needed. A dignified character of the postwar peace is needed. Our proposals are ready."
Zelensky is expected to meet the envoys later in the day. Two people familiar with the matter told the Kyiv Independent that national security advisors from Germany, France, and the U.K. are also expected to attend the discussions.
Witkoff and Kushner are making their first, repeatedly postponed visit to Ukraine's capital amid the fresh U.S.-led push to broker a conclusion to the full-scale Russian invasion, which has been ongoing for more than four and a half years.
The negotiations have been effectively in deadlock since earlier this year as Moscow continues to reject a ceasefire along the current front lines and demands that Kyiv cede Donbas — a partially occupied and strategically vital region in Ukraine's east — and give up on its NATO membership aspirations.
Zelensky's Chief of Staff Kyrylo Budanov told the New York Times that the U.S.-mediated peace talks could resume in late September, shortly after the Russian State Duma elections and weeks before the U.S. midterm elections.
Nevertheless, the Kremlin has not signaled an intent to concede on its territorial demands, and Kyiv warned that Russian forces are preparing to escalate strikes against Ukrainian cities and the energy grid in winter.
The talks in Moscow did not seem to yield a breakthrough, as Putin said he expects Russia to meet its "goals" and that Moscow wants the root causes of its war to be resolved.
A White House official told journalists that the two parties "discussed substantive plans for next steps, which will be announced in the coming weeks," without disclosing further details.
Russia and Ukraine agreed to refrain from aerial strikes against each other's capitals to ensure the safety of the U.S. negotiators. Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said on Sept. 5 that Putin had ordered Russian forces not to strike Kyiv for three days beginning "at midnight," according to Russian state media.
Ukraine had proposed a broader three-day ceasefire that would go beyond attacks on the two capitals and include fighting along the front line. Putin said during his meeting with the U.S. envoys that Russia had not agreed to the broader proposal.
Russian forces nevertheless launched multiple attacks across Ukraine overnight on Sept. 5, including strikes on Kyiv, according to Zelensky.
A further wave of attacks followed overnight on Sept. 6, including against Kyiv Oblast, though no hits in the city of Kyiv were reported.

Fatah Central Committee secretary-general reveals Hamas talks in Turkey, doubts elections - report

2026-09-06
10:01:38 UTC
19:01:38 KST

Jibril Rajoub met with Hamas leaders Khalil al-Hayya and Zaher Jabarin in Turkey two weeks ago, the secretary-general of the Fatah Central Committee confirmed to the Hamas-affiliated Quds News Network on Friday.
According to a source who spoke with the Palestinian Press Network, Rajoub also met with mukhtars, or clan leaders, from the Gaza Strip in an effort to potentially create his own alliance ahead of the election.
Rajoub told Quds that he doubted the Palestinian Legislative Council elections scheduled for November would go ahead, though he called for a meeting of all Palestinian factions to develop a roadmap for national dialogue and reform with Egyptian support.
Rajoub said such a meeting would renew legitimacy for the Palestinian political system, arguing that Palestinians are currently facing an impasse that has evolved into an existential threat. Renewed Palestinian unity, he said, would be an essential step toward establishing a Palestinian state.
Hamas meets with multiple Fatah officials
Yoni Ben Menachem, a senior researcher at the Jerusalem Center for Security and Foreign Affairs, told The Jerusalem Post that Hamas has met with several Fatah officials in recent weeks and has found a foothold among those disappointed by Palestinian Authority President Mahmoud Abbas’s attempts to position his son as his successor.
The officials, who reject Yasser Abbas as a potential new president, are considering new alliances with Hamas and Palestinian Islamic Jihad as a way to signal their disappointment with Abbas and pressure him to prioritize Palestinian interests over his personal aspirations, Menachem continued.
Menachem also agreed with Rajoub’s assessment that Abbas would again postpone the long-delayed elections, saying he had been warned that doing so would be a “dangerous gamble” for Fatah, given that Hamas won a majority of the seats in the last PLC election in 2006, securing 74 seats. Hamas has since mounted a new campaign to win over Abbas’s critics, Menachem said.
Beyond unity, Rajoub said the Palestinian political focus should be on addressing the refugee crisis, unifying the Palestinian approach toward Israel and defining a pluralistic and democratic national identity.
That unified approach toward Israel, he argued, should center on confrontation rather than normalization, with “popular resistance” representing the most effective way to handle the conflict with Israel.
However, opposing factions that have engaged with Hamas recently told The Post that it was becoming more widely understood that violent campaigns against Israel had not been successful and that it was more effective to focus on combating “the occupation” through diplomacy.
Rajoub also advocated for political, judicial, security, administrative and financial reforms, as well as changes to the Palestinian curriculum. He said it was also necessary to address the “issue” of payments to Palestinian prisoners and their families, who receive financial assistance from the Palestinian Authority under a system that critics have long said ties payments to the length of a prisoner’s sentence in an Israeli prison.
The PA has struggled to maintain the payments in recent months amid US pressure and Israel’s withholding of tax revenues. Palestinian Media Watch has reported that Palestinians who carried out attacks against Israeli and American citizens and now live outside the territories have continued to receive payments, while recipients inside the territories have reported delays.
Rajoub advocates for PLO strength
Rajoub also said that the Palestinian Liberation Organization must remain the sole legitimate representative of the Palestinian people. He argued that the biggest mistake made by the Palestinian political system was allowing the PA to become dominant over the PLO.
His comments come as the FDR faction appears to be gaining influence within Fatah. Rajoub rejected the possibility of former Fatah leader and current FDR leader Mohammed Dahlan returning to the Palestinian political sphere, though Dahlan also met with Hamas’s leadership only weeks ago and has been pushing for renewed Palestinian unity across the factions.
Menachem explained that Hamas was building support with as many high-profile players as possible, seeing the PLC elections as an opportunity to “rehabilitate themselves” from the military failure in Gaza through a democratic success.

The way to Jerusalem: A modern-day pilgrimage in the land’s ‘diverse embrace’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-06
10:01:28 UTC
19:01:28 KST

Four Christians, three Jews, four languages, six days, and 111 kilometers from Jaffa Port to Jaffa Gate.
That’s how Michigan resident Jody Bernat, 67, summed up the parameters of the modern-day pilgrimage she and her husband, John Belsher, took last spring under the leadership of The Way to Jerusalem (W2J).
“We were two Taiwanese women, a gentleman from Catalonia, a man from West Virginia, an Israeli woman, and John and me. With a variety of language barriers and fitness levels, we needed to find a group pace and a way to communicate,” she recalls.
“Sometimes it was gestures, glances, knowing looks. Sometimes we walked in silence. Often, we sang, and many times we exchanged views on life,” Bernat says.
Led by an English-speaking guide, the pilgrims bonded through their shared exploration of the places, people, and cultures they encountered along the route.
“Our stays in Christian monasteries, Arab villages, and Jewish quarters were all part of the landscape that outsiders rarely see or understand in the diverse embrace of this powerfully beautiful land,” Bernat says.
“The Ethiopian restaurateur, the man selling flowers on the street, the market bustling as Shabbat approached – all the people living day to day in this region who want to live simply, peacefully, and in harmony,” she continues, describing her impressions.
If ancient pilgrimages were about holy sites, religious ritual, forgiveness, and redemption, modern pilgrimages are about personal growth and connection with people and places, say W2J co-founders Yael Tarasiuk-Nevo and Golan Rice, both secular Jewish Israelis who formerly worked in El Al security.
“It can be an inner spiritual experience or even a culinary or social experience. It’s different for each type of person. We give a platform for Jews, Christians, Muslims, or non-believers to experience what they want on their pilgrimage to Jerusalem,” Rice says.
Tarasiuk-Nevo adds that meeting residents and hearing their stories is key. “Pilgrimage has always been a community journey, even in biblical times. People would journey with you, and others would host you. You’ll have good food, a warm shower, and a comfortable bed at the end of each day of your journey.”
‘We went on faith’
Bernat recalls that the military escalation with Iran earlier in April made getting to Israel complex and expensive. Yet the stress of those difficulties dissolved when they arrived at Jaffa Port.
“It was quite profound to see where the [ancient] ships came in with pilgrims like us, making their way to Jerusalem. For a moment, we were voyageurs from centuries past, with the same desires and the same uncertainty of what we would encounter as we embarked on this journey,” Bernat says.
“We walked in a calm week – a surprise to all who begged us not to go to a war zone,” she notes. “We went on faith.”
Faith was the primary pull for W2J pilgrim Suju Ellen Chen, 55, of Taitung, Taiwan.
“I am an Evangelical Christian. Over the past seven years, I have traveled to Israel three times. Twice, I came with church groups during the Feast of Tabernacles (Sukkot),” Chen says.
“In 2023, I came for Shavuot and joined a gathering of intercessors from around the world who had gathered at the Southern Wall to pray for Israel,” she adds.
After October 7, Chen yearned to gain a deeper understanding of the region’s modern history and reality but waited until the Gaza conflict simmered down.
“Toward the end of 2025, I came across a post by a Taiwanese YouTuber called Israel Mega about W2J’s first international pilgrimage group. I signed up almost without hesitation.”
For Chen, the first highlight of the itinerary was Rishon Lezion, where she learned about the influence of the Rothschild family, the origins of Israel’s flag and national anthem, and the stories of the early settlers scrambling for water and other essential resources.
“Even before the establishment of the State of Israel, there were people who clearly knew who they were and understood that they were building a home in the Promised Land. This continuity of identity and its connection to the land deeply moved me,” she says.
“Every place we visited along the way allowed me to experience Israel personally and to discover a country that is vibrant, resilient, remarkably diverse, and open-hearted,” Chen notes. “We often pray for Israel, but we do not necessarily truly know the people we call ‘our family in Israel.’”
According to her, “This pilgrimage allowed me, for the first time, to hear their voices, share their spaces, and begin to see Israel not simply as a place we pray for, but as a people and a land we are called to know.”
The shared multifaith encounters of the diverse pilgrims drew them close, Chen continues. “We were so different from one another, yet somehow, we were able to walk this road together without offending or excluding one another.”
The power of modern pilgrimage
This effect is exactly what W2J’s founders hoped to achieve.
“In building W2J, we had our own pilgrimage journey,” Tarasiuk-Nevo reflects.
In October 2021, Rice completed his first of three pilgrimages along the Camino de Santiago, a European network of walking and cycling routes frequented annually by half a million people for fitness, history, or personal growth. He started writing a book about his experiences.
In July 2022, after his final Camino de Santiago trek, he met with his former El Al coworker at a café. Tarasiuk-Nevo, then managing social projects for the Bat Yam Municipality, agreed to help with his book.
Their discussion turned to the power of modern pilgrimages.
“Why did Golan [Rice], a nonreligious Jew, start to cry along the Camino de Santiago? We tried to understand what this was about,” Tarasiuk-Nevo recalls. “We realized it was the human encounters.”
“We are not businesspeople or tourism executives, but we felt a mutual call to start a pilgrimage route to Jerusalem. We just came with a dream that W2J can make a real change,” she says.
Funding the project out of pocket, they conducted research and started a closed Facebook group for Israelis to explain their idea and recruit trial participants.
“At the beginning, we were aiming for Spanish-speaking people from Europe because they know the Camino de Santiago. But we knew that the local community had to be engaged in this,” explains Tarasiuk-Nevo.
“In January 2023, we made the first pilot journey with Israelis,” says Rice. “We started with six people at Jaffa Port and ended with more than 50 at Jaffa Gate because each day more people joined us.”
In September, they registered W2J to Jerusalem as a nonprofit association. “The only way this dream will last is if it’s not beholden to any agenda,” Tarasiuk-Nevo notes. “Israel has always been a place of conflict, and that’s our reality. This pilgrimage is above conflict and politics; it gives another point of view.”
The first organized group, Pioneer Pilgrimage, took place in May 2025 and was led in Hebrew by a certified tour guide trained by W2J. The second one followed in October 2025. Itzik Albachari, an Israeli participant in the first Pioneer Pilgrimage, coordinates the Hebrew-language treks.
Global Pioneers
Bernat inspired the inaugural English-speaking Global Pioneers pilgrimage in April.
She had completed the 500-mile Camino de Santiago across Spain for her 65th birthday and found it empowering, she says.
“But in each town we were encouraged to go to Mass in the local churches. As a Conservative, fairly observant American Jew, I had wished there was something that had more of my Jewish history. I thought maybe there might be a Camino de Santiago in Israel. So I searched and came across The Way to Jerusalem. I wrote to [Tarasiuk-Nevo] and asked if it was possible to go on this journey.”
With Bernat’s welcome persistence, the founders made it happen despite the linguistic, religious, and cultural differences among their international clientele.
“Each pilgrim speaks a different language and eats different food,” Rice says. “Without W2J, they probably wouldn’t meet. Suddenly they’re walking together for seven days to the same places. Yet each translates that place individually. They are very excited by the stories in each place.”
“We ask local people along the way to tell their stories. We don’t edit those stories,” Tarasiuk-Nevo adds. “If someone in Rishon Lezion wants to tell the story of Zionism and the first synagogue, if the shawarma vendor in the Ramla Market wishes to tell the story about his family there, we enable them to do so. We work hard to ensure that every encounter will be a good encounter.”
When the Global Pioneer group arrived at Jaffa Gate, Rice says, “They were crying because the adventure culminated in one place called Jerusalem. This is a powerful way to bring people together and give them an opportunity to express their journey in any way they want.”
Bernat comments that although she lived on a kibbutz for a summer, visited Israel several times with her family, and has children living in Tel Aviv, “I was not expecting to feel the immense heart-and-soul response that overcame me as we marched into Jerusalem with our awesome guide, Alon.”
Chen adds, “As I have been reflecting on this journey, I have increasingly realized something very simple: I now have friends in Israel. Real relationships are beginning to grow between us.”
Pilgrimage of light on Hanukkah
Most of the W2J pilgrimages, which are not kosher or Sabbath-observant, are conducted in Hebrew and geared to locals.
The next Global Pioneer trek in English is planned for December 5-12, paralleling the eight days of Hanukkah, the festival of lights.
Dubbed the First Pilgrimage of Light, this journey from Jaffa Port will culminate in Jerusalem with a nighttime tour of hanukkiot illuminating the windows of the Old City.
“A lot of Jews and non-Jews from abroad are excited about this, wanting to share and experience this together, the reality of this holiday in Israel,” Rice says.
Details are available on W2J’s website, thewaytojerusalem.org/general-5, or write to mail@thewaytojerusalem.org
W2J Global Pioneer: A travelogue
Below are excerpts from Jody Bernat’s travelogue from her Global Pioneer pilgrimage this past year, April 30-May 5.
Day 1
Our pilgrimage began early this morning in Jaffa. The seven pilgrims and our guide, Alon, walked to Jaffa Port, where original pilgrims once arrived in the Holy Land by sea.
Our journey took us through the busy streets of Tel Aviv and briefly through a sandy route to Rishon Lezion. We got our pilgrim credential stamped in several locations. Along the way, we saw a powerfully moving memorial tree garden for the victims of October 7.
We visited the Museum of the History of Rishon Lezion, where the Israeli flag was first created, the national anthem was written, and the first all-Hebrew school was launched. We checked into the Raphael House Hotel and made our way to an authentic Ethiopian restaurant where we met up with the creators of the Way to Jerusalem, Yael and Golan.
Day 2
We walked to a synagogue where a cantor sang a prayer for us. It was so beautiful. His great-grandfather was the rabbi there. The lay leader was surprising: Yael’s husband, Gad. We walked on to Be’er Ya’acov and then into Ramle, where we visited an ancient water source, and we all paddled in the water.
We came upon a man selling flowers. He offered us cold water and then allowed our guide to put a sticker on his store for the W2J. We walked through a local market that was bustling with people shopping for Shabbat.
Day 3
We left Ramle and made our way into the countryside. The path was rugged and the scenery beautiful. Golan and Yael organized a wonderful rest stop with drinks and snacks just before we climbed up to the Tel Gezer lookout. This site is where, thousands of years ago, civilizations built upon one another, including King Solomon’s.
We are walking history. From here we headed to the Monastery of Our Lady of the Seven Sorrows (the Trappist Abbey) in Latrun, where we were greeted by one of the monk-padres, attended Mass (chanted in French), and ate dinner in the courtyard. They made us a special dish that was created for the pope. The women slept in a spacious house next to the church bell – no sleep for me!
Day 4
We left the Trappist Monastery early and climbed up to an old cemetery with a nearby dome that had incredible acoustics. We sang a few songs there. We kept climbing hills for hours and stopped for a picnic hosted by Yael and Golan in the forest.
The rest of the day was spent climbing up and up and up into Abu Ghosh, where we visited the Saxum Visitor Center, which depicts religious history.
We climbed up some more to the Benedictine monastery. The monks cooked us a fabulous dinner – they are French and have the cuisine touch! Father Olivier came and talked with us about life, love, and being a monk.
Day 5
We attended early morning prayer at the 12th-century Benedictine monastery church. After a quick breakfast, we set off along beautiful pathways, climbing toward Jerusalem. We stopped for a picnic snack with W2J guide Miri and climbed up to an old ruin near Nataf. It’s believed to be perhaps an olive oil production ruin.
We continued climbing up to Sataf – panoramic views of the Judean Hills. We had lunch at the amazing café before making our way down the steep ancient stone steps on the Israel National Trail, then began to ascend again to Ein Kerem.
At the Franciscan monastery, Yael and Golan greeted us with a gift of limoncello liqueur made by the Benedictine monks. Dinner tonight was by the Italian Franciscan monks. Tomorrow we make our way into Jerusalem.
Day 6
The majority of the morning we walked up and up and then more up on a path toward Jerusalem. Construction blocked the path just before entering the city, causing us to maneuver over big rocks to a memorial for a Righteous among the Nations who saved many Jews when the Nazis marched in.
[When] we arrived at the Jaffa Gate, Yael and Golan and a Tourism Ministry representative greeted us. They stamped our credentials, gave us our certificates, and then escorted us to a private tour in the Tower of David.
We gathered for an emotional farewell, collected our belongings, and made our way through the market to the Western Wall. A powerful and amazing week of wonder. It was not an easy walk, but one that was worth the long miles and hours on the trail.
The experience is profound. One hundred and eleven kilometers from Jaffa Port to Jaffa Gate. We did it!!!

An Egyptian television presenter and social media influencer was sentenced to death by hanging after being convicted of belonging to an organized crime gang that imported chemical substances used to manufacture and traffic illegal drugs.
Sara Khalifa, 39, was convicted along with 11 other members of the criminal organization after authorities uncovered drug laboratories hidden in two apartments in Egypt’s capital. Khalifa, who has 2.5 million followers on Instagram, is best known to the Egyptian public for hosting the popular crime program “Mission Impossible.”
Khalifa’s role in the trafficking network was uncovered after armed police forces seized more than 750 kilograms of synthetic drugs, along with raw chemicals, weapons, and ammunition, during raids last year on two apartments in Cairo.
According to reports in Egypt’s state-owned newspapers Al-Ahram and Akhbar Al-Youm, the gang was convicted of establishing a criminal organization specializing in obtaining materials used to produce drugs for the purpose of trafficking them, as well as possessing firearms and ammunition without a license.
The gang was also accused of manufacturing synthetic drugs after importing raw materials from outside the country.
Prosecutors told the court that Khalifa, who also owns a plastic surgery clinic and an event production company, effectively financed the cartel and traveled abroad to communicate directly with international crime bosses.
The prosecution presented 20 testimonies, alongside a range of digital evidence, including recorded conversations and incriminating video footage.
Khalifa disputes allegations, verdict subject to appeal
Khalifa strongly denies the allegations against her, and the verdict is currently subject to appeal. When questioned by the judge in September of last year about her alleged involvement in the case, she claimed that she had never seen drugs until she was filmed next to them at the offices of the local anti-narcotics authority.
The death sentences of the network’s members were approved and officially announced on Saturday, after the case was referred for the nonbinding opinion of Egypt’s Grand Mufti, a step required by law in death penalty cases in the country.
Of the 28 defendants who stood trial, 12 were sentenced to death by hanging, nine were sentenced to life imprisonment, and seven others were acquitted.
In addition to the death sentence, Khalifa and several other defendants were sentenced to five years in prison in a separate case involving the kidnapping and physical assault of a young man.
All 12 individuals sentenced to death have the legal right to appeal their sentences before Egypt’s Court of Cassation.
